_readme: Per-animal, per-jurisdiction legal status, for the legal hub and its US map.
STATUS VALUES, which are the map colour buckets:
banned      cannot be kept as a pet, no permit route exists
permit      legal, but a permit or licence is required first
conditional legal without a permit only if a stated condition is met
restricted  on a restricted list, permit regime applies but pet keeping is not clearly ruled out
legal       expressly allowed by name in the jurisdiction own rules
unclear     the rule is genuinely ambiguous for this animal. Render grey,
never as legal. Used where a definition arguably reaches an
animal but does not name it, e.g. Texas ends its list with
"or any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision" and
the Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal is not itself listed.
(absent)    not researched, OR researched and no rule found. Which one is
decided by coverage.researched, never by the absence itself.
PER-ENTRY FIELDS beyond status:
sourceId      required, keys into `sources`
cite          the section number
quote         the operative wording, verbatim, where short enough
note          anything a reader needs that the quote does not carry
grandfathered { before, detail } if existing owners are exempt. "Banned"
and "banned unless you already had one" are different answers
to the question being asked.
localOverride true where the state says in terms that cities or counties
may prohibit what the state allows. Without this the map
tells someone in a city with its own ordinance the wrong thing.
permitFor     "personal" or "commercial-exhibition-research". New Jersey
issues a hobbyist permit; California only research, exhibition
and pre-1992 animal care. Both read as "permit" and mean
opposite things.
verifiedOn    ISO date the source was actually read. Exotic pet law moves.
Primary sources only: the regulation, the statute, or the enforcing agency
own page. Never a secondary summary.
NYC is separate from NY because its Health Code is stricter than state law
and covers eight million people. The same applies to any city rule worth mapping.

coverage.note: All 50 states and DC have been researched, 51 jurisdictions in all, plus New York City, but not every animal was checked against every one of them: a jurisdiction was read for the animals on the list at the time. 13 of the 52 jurisdictions have now been read for all 52 animals and 34 for at least 43 of them, while the least-read are down at 15. So an entry means that jurisdiction was read for that animal and this is what it says, including a status of "legal" which means read and nothing found. No entry means it has NOT been read for that animal and the answer is unknown. Never render a missing entry as unrestricted. coverage.perAnimal below records how far each species actually got, and it now spans a wide range because eight encyclopedia animals were added to the matrix later than the rest and start with only the jurisdictions that decide their answer.

HI.name: Hawaii
HI.scope: HAR chapter 4-71: the prohibited list at § 4-71-6, the conditionally approved list, and the restricted list at § 4-71-6.5. Hawaii runs an inverted rule, so an animal on none of the three is barred by default rather than unregulated.

PA.name: Pennsylvania
PA.scope: Both Pennsylvania agencies, because they split the animal kingdom between them. The Game Commission holds wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 limits to wild birds and wild mammals, and enforces it through the prohibited list at 58 Pa. Code § 137.1 and the exotic wildlife permit at 34 Pa.C.S. § 2961 and 2963 as the Commission applies it. The Fish and Boat Commission holds reptiles and amphibians under 58 Pa. Code Ch. 79, which regulates native species only. Terrestrial invertebrates fall to neither.

AZ.name: Arizona
AZ.scope: R12-4-406, restricted live wildlife, which lists by order and family rather than by species and so catches whole groups at once. All of Carnivora is restricted; the pet reptile trade almost entirely is not, the exceptions being crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the state's own gopher tortoises. Two carve-outs are written in by name, the pet hedgehogs in Atelerix and the domestic rabbits in Oryctolagus, which the rule says are not wildlife at all. Subsection D exempts domestic animals, defined as species that do not exist in the wild, and subsection E pulls hybrids back in whenever one parent species is listed. Terrestrial invertebrates sit outside all of it, because A.R.S. § 17-101 defines wildlife as mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans and fish. Taking a native species alive from the wild is a separate regime under R12-4-404, R12-4-405 and Commission Order 43, and needs a hunting licence.

MI.name: Michigan
MI.scope: Four regimes, none of which is a general exotic pet law. The Large Carnivore Act at MCL 287.1101 covers seven named cats and bears. The Wolf-dog Cross Act covers wolf hybrids. The DNR's permit to hold game in captivity under NREPA Part 427 covers a closed list of native game species and captive-bred animals only. Fisheries Order 224.21 covers reptiles and amphibians, but only a state species taken from the wild. Anything outside all four meets Michigan law only at the border, through the MDARD certificate of veterinary inspection under MCL 287.731. Local override is set across this jurisdiction because Michigan preserves municipal authority in terms, a large carnivore permit being valid only in a local unit that has not prohibited possession by ordinance, and cities and townships regulate exotic keeping widely under home rule.

NV.name: Nevada
NV.scope: Two lists over a statutory default. NAC 503.110 prohibits a named set of species outright, with permits only for zoos, universities, scientific institutions, aquaculture and nonprofit educational exhibitors. NAC 503.140 clears forty-five categories that need no permit at all, and three of its lines carry most of the pet trade: all felines except mountain lions and bobcats, all nonvenomous nonindigenous reptiles, and all nonindigenous amphibians except bullfrogs. Anything on neither list falls to NRS 503.597, which requires the Department's written consent to bring wildlife into the state. Insects and arachnids sit outside all of it, because NRS 501.097 defines wildlife as mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks and crustaceans. Local override is set across this jurisdiction because NAC 503.140(4) preserves county and city ordinances in terms, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter.

VA.name: Virginia
VA.scope: 4VAC15-30-40, the Department of Wildlife Resources rule on importing, possessing and selling nonnative exotic animals. Its subsection A table is the operative list; anything absent from it needs no permit under this section.

NM.name: New Mexico
NM.scope: 19.35.7 NMAC and the Director's Species Importation List it points at, now readable in full. Four groups: I is semi-domesticated and needs no importation permit, II needs a permit, III needs a permit with specific provisions attached, and IV is prohibited to the general public and allowed only for scientific study, restoration, zoological display, temporary events, service animals or qualified experts. An animal on none of the roughly 1,300 rows defaults to group IV. Note the rule's own scope, persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs importation rather than possession of an animal already here. The list carries no terrestrial invertebrates at all, which is why the pet invertebrates on this map are recorded unclear rather than barred by default.

VT.name: Vermont
VT.scope: An inverted three-list scheme, now readable in full. 10 V.S.A. App. § 18 and Regulation 881 make it unlawful to bring in or possess any live wild animal without a permit unless the species is on the Domestic, Unrestricted, or Domestic Pet list, and the Unrestricted list closes by saying a species on none of the lists is considered Restricted. The Restricted list is the appendix the Unrestricted list keeps pointing at, clawing families back species by species. What makes the scheme bite is Regulation 881's limit on the permit itself: the Commissioner shall not issue one for keeping a wild animal in captivity except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes, so restricted means no pet, not extra paperwork. The 2010 Domestic Species List is the one piece still unread, because its text is embedded as glyph outlines and cannot be extracted here; it is what the remaining parrot and rabbit cells depend on.

DE.name: Delaware
DE.scope: Two regimes with a clean seam. Del. Code tit. 3 c. 72 and 3 Del. Admin. Code 903, run by the State Veterinarian, cover exotics, meaning live wild mammals, hybrids of wild mammals and reptiles not native to Delaware. Regulation 6.1 exempts a named list of pets outright, 6.2 requires a $25 Individual permit for everything else, and 4.7 names the only three animals that may not be permitted at all: gila monsters, beaded lizards and komodo dragons. Non-native venomous snakes are banned by statute. Anything native to Delaware is not exotic and belongs to DNREC instead, which does not make native wildlife available as pets except for a captive-bred native snake in an aberrant colour morph held under permit. Birds, fish, amphibians and invertebrates are outside the exotic chapter entirely, because § 7201 names only mammals, their hybrids and reptiles.

NC.name: North Carolina
NC.scope: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 14-417, the only statewide statute regulating exotic animal possession, and § 153A-131, which delegates the rest to counties. There is no statewide exotic pet permit scheme to read.

NH.name: New Hampshire
NH.scope: Fis 800, the Fish and Game Department rules on importation and possession of wildlife, which is the whole framework: non-controlled, prohibited and controlled lists for both importation and possession.

MO.name: Missouri
MO.scope: RSMo § 578.023, the dangerous wild animal registration statute, and 3 CSR 10-9, the Wildlife Code chapter on confined wildlife. Between them these are the two places Missouri restricts keeping an animal.

KS.name: Kansas
KS.scope: K.S.A. 32-1301 and following, the Dangerous Regulated Animals Act, which is the state's only exotic pet statute. Native wildlife possession is handled separately under KAR 115-20 and was not read for this entry.

SC.name: South Carolina
SC.scope: S.C. Code Title 47 Chapter 2, the large wild cat, non-native bear and great ape ban, and Title 50 Chapter 16, the wildlife importation permit chapter. Native game and furbearer harvest rules elsewhere in Title 50 were not read.

MT.name: Montana
MT.scope: MCA Title 87 chapter 5 part 7 and ARM subchapter 12.6.22, the exotic wildlife scheme. Native Montana species such as the prairie dog and tiger salamander are governed by the separate native wildlife rules, which were not read for this entry.

WV.name: West Virginia
WV.scope: W. Va. Code Chapter 19 Article 34, the Dangerous Wild Animals Act. Native wildlife held in captivity is governed separately under Chapter 20 and was not read for this entry.

AK.name: Alaska
AK.scope: 5 AAC 92.029, the live game possession rule, which is Alaska's whole answer for mammals, birds and reptiles. Invertebrates fall outside the definition of game in AS 16.05.940 and were not researched.

SD.name: South Dakota
SD.scope: ARSD chapter 12:68:18, the Animal Industry Board's nondomestic animal control rules, whose permit list covers mammals. Reptiles, amphibians and native wildlife fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules in ARSD title 41, which were not read for this entry.

AL.name: Alabama
AL.scope: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26, the Game and Fish Division rule on possession, sale, importation and release of certain animals. Native Alabama species are separately protected under the same title and were not researched for this entry.

IN.name: Indiana
IN.scope: 312 IAC 9-11, the wild animal possession permit rule. Its own applicability clause limits it to animals referenced in the rule plus state endangered and threatened species, so an animal on none of the three class lists needs no permit.

ND.name: North Dakota
ND.scope: NDCC chapter 36-01, the Board of Animal Health statute, and NDAC title 48.1, its current rules. NDCC title 20.1 chapter 02 was also read: its permit requirement is for transplanting or introducing animals into the state, meaning release, not pet keeping.

WY.name: Wyoming
WY.scope: Wyoming Game and Fish Commission Regulation Chapter 10, live warm-blooded wildlife, and Chapter 69, live cold-blooded wildlife. Together these are the state's importation and possession framework.

MS.name: Mississippi
MS.scope: 40 Miss. Admin. Code Part 2, Rule 8.3, the inherently dangerous wild animal rule, revised April 2025. Native Mississippi wildlife held in captivity is covered by other rules in the same chapter, which were not read for this entry.

LA.name: Louisiana
LA.scope: LAC Title 76 Part V § 115, potentially dangerous wild quadrupeds, big exotic cats and non-human primates, and LAC Title 76 Part XV § 101, the reptile and amphibian rule as amended January 2025.

OK.name: Oklahoma
OK.scope: OAC 800:25-25, the subchapter classifying wildlife as domesticated and exempting it from licensing. Anything outside the exemption needs an import or export permit and a commercial or noncommercial wildlife breeder's licence rather than being banned.

NE.name: Nebraska
NE.scope: 166 NAC 8, Keeping Wildlife in Captivity, which covers wild birds and wild mammals. Reptiles and amphibians are handled by 166 NAC 10 and the fisheries regulations in 164 NAC and were not read for this entry.

ca-671.title: California Code of Regulations Title 14 § 671, via CDFW Restricted Species Laws and Regulations Manual
ca-671.note: § 671(b) defines (D) detrimental and (W) welfare. § 671.1(a) lists permit types; none covers pet keeping. The only possession permit, Animal Care, requires lawful possession in California before January 1992.

ga-391-4-8-05.title: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. Subject 391-4-8, Wild Animals, and O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4
ga-391-4-8-05.note: Georgia sorts wild animals into three tiers and none of them is a pet tier. Rule .03 prohibits outright, and its only pet-relevant entry is the monk parakeet. Rule .04 is inherently dangerous animals needing a licence AND liability insurance: all Felidae, four canid genera, bears, hyenas, kangaroos, great apes, crocodilians, the venomous snake families and a short list of fish and scorpions. Rule .05 requires a licence, and it works by taxonomic order rather than by species, which is why it is so wide: all Carnivora, all hedgehogs, all lagomorphs, all marsupials, all primates, and all rodents except six named genera. The thing to read before any of it is O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4(b)(1), because it says who a licence is issued to: the wild animal trade and public exhibitors, plus no-cost permits for science, education, a capuchin monkey for a person with a permanent disability, and grass carp for a pond owner. No pet. So an animal on .04 or .05 is not a permit animal for a keeper, it is a no, and the rule proves it by writing express "may be held as a pet without a license" exceptions for exactly two animals, the European ferret and the sugar glider.

hi-4-71-6.title: Hawaii Administrative Rules § 4-71-6, List of Prohibited Animals
hi-4-71-6.note: Also carries the default rule: introduction is 'prohibited except for those animals on the lists' incorporated in § 4-71-6.5.

hi-4-71-6-5.title: Hawaii Administrative Rules § 4-71-6.5, List of Restricted Animals, Part A (research and exhibition)
hi-4-71-6-5.note: Part A animals may be brought in by a university or a licensed exhibitor under permit and may not be kept as pets. Part B, published separately as AR-71RB, is the private and commercial use list and was checked as well: it runs to hoofed stock, giraffes, otters, seals, macropods and three named parrots, and contains none of the animals in this dataset.

dc-8-1808.title: D.C. Code § 8-1808(j), Prohibited conduct
dc-8-1808.note: Closed list. Seven permitted categories; everything else is barred as a household pet.

nyc-161-01.title: New York City Health Code § 161.01, Wild and other animals prohibited
nyc-161-01.note: A city rule that is stricter than any state on this map, and it works in three layers. It opens with a standard rather than a list, deeming a wild animal to be "any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings". It then adds, at (b)(ii), any wildlife protected or endangered under federal, STATE or local law, which imports New York State's protected wildlife scheme into the city wholesale. And it closes with 24 numbered clauses that work mostly by family: all cats other than Felis catus and their hybrids, all dogs other than Canis familiaris, all Mustelidae including the ferret by name, all squirrels, all marsupials, all large rodents, all Boidae, all Pythonidae, all Varanidae, all Iguanidae, all teiidae, all Chelydridae, all venomous spiders including the tarantula by name, and all turtles under four inches. § 161.01(c) is the short answer to what is left: gerbil, hamster, guinea pig, domesticated rabbit, and small birds such as parakeet, parrot, canary and finch.

nj-7-25-4-4.title: N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4 Exempted Species and 7:25-4.5 Additional Species
nj-7-25-4-4.note: The Division's handout of the 4.4 exempt list, which is closed, and of 4.5, which is the catch-all. Anything not named in 4.4 needs a permit, so the exempt list is the only route to a plain 'legal' in New Jersey.

me-unrestricted.title: Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Unrestricted Species List
me-unrestricted.note: The list 12 M.R.S. § 12152(1-A) requires the department to maintain and 09-137 CMR ch. 7 § 7.06(1) describes: species needing no importation, exhibition, propagation, research or possession permit, which pet shops may also trade. Dated 11 August 2017 on every page, and this is the version IFW still serves. Three headings do most of the work: Reptilia, Serpentes and Testudines each carry "Captive Bred Origin Only", and an asterisk on an entry removes anything on the USFWS injurious or threatened and endangered lists, in CITES Appendix I, or on the IUCN Red List as Endangered, Critically Endangered or Extinct in the Wild.

wi-169.title: Wisconsin Statutes Chapter 169, Captive Wildlife
wi-169.note: § 169.01(37) defines wild animal; § 169.11(1)(a) designates harmful wild animals as cougars, ursidae, wild and feral swine. § 169.04(4)(b) exempts most non-native species from licensing.

fl-prohibited.title: 68-5.004, 68-5.006 and 68-5.007, F.A.C., Conditional and Prohibited Non-Native Species
fl-prohibited.note: Florida's nonnative species chapter, and the rule that answers the animals Florida is famous for. 68-5.006 is the prohibited list, and its reptile section is what the 2021 rulemaking rewrote: the yellow, Beni, DeSchauensee's and green anacondas, the brown tree snake, the Burmese, reticulated, Northern African, Southern African, amethystine and scrub pythons, the Nile monitor, the green iguana and the tegus of genera Salvator and Tupinambis. Its mammal section is short and has nothing a pet keeper would want, and its bird section names four. 68-5.007 governs what a prohibited species owner can do, and the answer is close to nothing: personal possession permits are issued only to people who already held the animal before listing, for that animal's life, PIT-tagged, with no new specimens ever. 68-5.004 is the separate conditional list, which for this map means one animal, the red-eared slider.

ny-11-0103.title: N.Y. Environmental Conservation Law §§ 11-0103, 11-0107, 11-0511, 11-0512 and 11-0515
ny-11-0103.note: New York answers exotic and native animals through two entirely separate mechanisms, and the famous one is the smaller. § 11-0103(6)(e) is a closed "wild animal" list, six clauses long, that § 11-0512 then bars keeping as a pet: primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of large constrictors and monitors plus all venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. It carries two express carve-outs that decide cells on this map, for registered Felis catus hybrids five generations clear of wild parentage and for captive bred fennec foxes. The other mechanism is the one that catches natives, and it is a definition rather than a list: § 11-0103(2)(c) makes native frogs, salamanders, turtles, lizards and snakes SMALL GAME, therefore game, therefore protected wildlife under § 11-0103(6)(c), and § 11-0107(2) bars possessing protected wildlife "whether taken within the state or coming from without the state". The only licence, § 11-0515, is for propagation, banding, scientific or exhibition purposes, so there is no pet route behind it.

ct-26-40a.title: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 26-40a, Possession of potentially dangerous animal
ct-26-40a.note: Potentially dangerous animals are 'the felidae... the canidae... the ursidae... and the hominidae', or any hybrid. Narrow: no rodents, marsupials, mustelids or insectivores. Civil penalty up to $2,000 per offence and a class A misdemeanour for a wilful violation.

ma-321-9-01.title: 321 CMR 9.00, Exotic Wildlife: 9.01 Exemption List and 9.02 List of Domestic Animals
ma-321-9-01.note: Massachusetts runs a closed white list and says so in terms: a species not on it, or listed as requiring a permit, is not exempt from M.G.L. c. 131, § 23. Two structural points decide most of this state. First, 9.01(2) defines "species" as a "distinct non-domestic VERTEBRATE animal population", and § 23 itself reaches only fish, birds, mammals, reptiles and amphibians, so terrestrial invertebrates are outside the scheme entirely. Second, 9.01(3) is a categorical override that most readings of this rule miss: no species may be exempted if it is listed under the federal Endangered Species Act, appears in the IUCN Red Book(s), or is on the Massachusetts endangered, threatened and special concern list at 321 CMR 10.90. Nearly every group listing in 9.01 repeats the cross-reference, so it operates as a live carve-out rather than as drafting furniture, and it is what pulls the Burmese python out of Boidae, the crested gecko out of Gekkonidae and the box turtle out of the turtle allowance.

ma-131-77.title: M.G.L. c. 131, § 77, ferrets; possession and use
ma-131-77.note: Massachusetts legalised the pet ferret by statute in 1996 and attached the conditions to the purchase rather than to a permit: neutered or spayed at the time of purchase, inoculated against distemper and rabies, and evidence of both kept available for inspection. 321 CMR 9.02(2)(b) points here rather than treating the ferret as an ordinary domestic animal, which is why the ferret is the one conditional entry on an otherwise binary domestic list. Breeding is a separate licence at not less than $1,000 a year under § 77(2). The section also makes merely having a ferret where birds or mammals may be found evidence of hunting with it, which is a real trap for anyone who takes one outdoors.

co-w11.title: Colorado 2 CCR 406-11, Chapter W-11, Wildlife Parks and Unregulated Wildlife
co-w11.note: Secretary of State's official text of the current version, effective 1 May 2026. Carries the #1103(A) domestic animal list and the #1103(B) unregulated wildlife list. The 2026 version moved every reptile and amphibian provision out of #1103(B) and into Chapter W-7, so a pre-2026 copy of this chapter still shows a reptile list that is no longer here.

az-r12-4-406.title: Ariz. Admin. Code R12-4-406, Restricted Live Wildlife
az-r12-4-406.note: The operative rule. Restricted live wildlife needs a special licence, and the lists run by order and family rather than by species, so the whole of Carnivora is caught while most of the pet reptile trade is not. Two exceptions are written in by name: the genus Atelerix, the pet hedgehogs, and the genus Oryctolagus, which the rule says are not wildlife at all. Two subsections do quiet work: (D) exempts domestic animals, defined at R12-4-401 as a species that does not exist in the wild, and (E) pulls hybrids back in whenever one parent species is on the list. Note that the AZGFD commission rules PDF circulating as Supp. 13-2 is a 2013 edition and predates the Atelerix and Oryctolagus exceptions; read the current text, not that one.

or-609-305.title: Or. Rev. Stat. § 609.305, 'Exotic animal' defined, with §§ 609.341 and 609.351
or-609-305.note: A five-line closed definition run by the Department of Agriculture: non-indigenous Felidae except Felis catus, non-human primates, non-wolf non-indigenous Canidae except the domestic dog, bears other than the black bear, and Crocodylia. § 609.341 bars keeping one without a permit and § 609.351 shut the application window, which was 90 days after 1 January 2010, or one year for an animal already held then. There is no hybrid clause anywhere in it. This statute answers cats, canids and crocodilians only; every other animal on this map is decided by the ODFW rules in OAR 635-056.

wa-rcw-16-30.title: Wash. Rev. Code ch. 16.30, Dangerous Wild Animals, § 16.30.010(2) and § 16.30.030
wa-rcw-16-30.note: An enumerated definition. Felidae is limited to lions, tigers, captive-bred cougars, jaguars, cheetahs, leopards, snow leopards and clouded leopards; Canidae to wolves excluding wolf-hybrids. § 16.30.030: 'A person shall not own, possess, keep, harbor, bring into the state, or have custody or control of a potentially dangerous wild animal', grandfathering lawful possession before 22 July 2007.

oh-935-01.title: Ohio Rev. Code § 935.01, Dangerous Wild Animals and Restricted Snakes definitions
oh-935-01.note: Two enumerated lists. Dangerous wild animals need an Ohio Department of Agriculture wildlife shelter permit; anything on neither list needs no state permit. Restricted snakes are constrictors of 12 feet or more plus venomous families.

tx-822-101.title: Tex. Health & Safety Code §§ 822.101-822.116, Dangerous Wild Animals
tx-822-101.note: The statute everyone cites for Texas, and the one that answers the fewest questions on this map. § 822.101(4) is a closed list of twenty clauses, nineteen named mammals plus "any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision". It contains no reptile, no bird, no rodent and no invertebrate. Where it does bite it bites hard: § 822.103(a) requires a certificate of registration issued by the local animal control office, or the county sheriff where there is none, rather than by a state agency; § 822.107 requires liability insurance of at least $100,000 per occurrence; and § 822.116(b) expressly preserves the power of any municipality or county to prohibit the animal outright.

mi-large-carnivore.title: Mich. Comp. Laws ch. 287, Large Carnivore Act and Wolf-dog Cross Act
mi-large-carnivore.note: Michigan splits this across three bodies of law: the Large Carnivore Act, the Wolf-dog Cross Act, and Part 413 of the Natural Resources and Environmental Protection Act. Penalties run to misdemeanour charges, fines up to $2,000 per animal and forfeiture.

il-720-48-10.title: 720 ILCS 5/48-10, Dangerous animals
il-720-48-10.note: A closed list of 15 named mammals plus a blanket bar on primates, and nothing else. It replaced the Dangerous Animals Act at 720 ILCS 585, which P.A. 98-752 repealed effective 1 January 2015; the old citation is still what most secondary sources give. The section says in terms that it does not reach reptiles or amphibians. Exemptions: primates lawfully held before 1 January 2011 and registered by 1 April 2011, and one service capuchin for a person with a severe mobility impairment.

mn-346-155.title: Minn. Stat. § 346.155, Possessing regulated animals
mn-346-155.note: Revisor of Statutes text. 'Regulated animal' is the whole family Felidae, bears, and all non-human primates, plus any hybrid with a domestic animal and all subsequent generations. Possession has been unlawful since 1 January 2005 except for animals already held then and brought into federal Animal Welfare Act compliance. Note the carve-out inside the Felidae clause, which excludes not only domestic cats but cats registered and shown as a domestic breed by a multibreed registry; it and the hybrid sentence pull in opposite directions.

nv-nac-503.title: Nev. Admin. Code § 503.110 (prohibited species) and § 503.140 (species needing no permit)
nv-nac-503.note: Two lists: 503.110 prohibits, 503.140 names species that may be possessed, transported, imported and exported without a permit. Nevada counties and cities are frequently stricter than the state, notably Clark County, Henderson and Las Vegas.

va-4vac15-30-40.title: 4 Va. Admin. Code § 15-30-40, Importation requirements, possession, and sale of nonnative (exotic) animals
va-4vac15-30-40.note: Virginia permits by table. Subsection A requires a special permit from the department for every animal listed in it, on the ground that the board has declared the species predatory or undesirable because releasing it would harm Virginia's native fish and wildlife. Subsection B grandfathers asterisked animals held before 1 July 1992 if they were declared in writing by 1 January 1993, renewable every five years and not transferable. Subsection C then carves the monk parakeet back out.

md-10-621.title: Md. Code, Criminal Law § 10-621, Importing, selling or possessing certain animals
md-10-621.note: Maryland's dangerous animal list, on the General Assembly's own site. Eight clauses and nothing else: fox, skunk, raccoon or bear; caiman, alligator or crocodile; any cat other than the domestic cat; a cat hybrid over 30 pounds; any dog other than the domestic dog and any dog hybrid; non-human primates; and venomous snakes of four named families. A misdemeanour, and subsection (e) says in terms that counties and municipalities may go further. Note COMAR 15.11.16.01, titled List of Prohibited Animals, is an agriculture rule about feral swine and is not this provision.

nm-19-35-7.title: N.M. Admin. Code 19.35.7, Importation of Live Non-domesticated Animals, Birds and Fish
nm-19-35-7.note: Four groups. Group I is semi-domesticated and needs no importation permit; Group IV is 'dangerous, invasive, undesirable, state or federal listed threatened, endangered, a furbearer or any other species of concern' and is barred to the general public, allowed only for scientific study, restoration, zoological display, temporary events, service animals or qualified experts. The operative default: 'Any species of live non-domesticated animal not currently on the species importation list will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.' The group assignments themselves live in a separate Director's Species Importation List, roughly 27 pages, which I could not obtain.

vt-reg-881.title: Vermont Regulation 881 (12-021 Code Vt. R.), Governing the Importation and Possession of Wild Animals, with 10 V.S.A. § 4709
vt-reg-881.note: Closed list. § 4709 bars bringing in, transporting or possessing any live wild bird or animal without authorisation. Reg 881: 'the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for the keeping or possession of any wild animal in captivity, except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes' unless the species is designated domestic, a domestic pet, or unrestricted. The Unrestricted Wild Animals List is maintained separately on the department website and was not obtainable.

vt-20-3541.title: Vt. Stat. Ann. tit. 20, § 3541(3), definition of ferret
vt-20-3541.note: Ferrets were legalised in 1989 and are defined as a domestic pet alongside dogs and cats, limited to 'the European ferret Mustela putorious furo'.

de-3900.title: 7 Del. Admin. Code 3900, Wildlife, exotic animal provisions
de-3900.note: An exotic animal is 'ecologically foreign to Delaware, but allowed for possession, sale, and exhibition if a permit has been issued by the Department', covering live wild mammals, hybrids of wild mammals, and live reptiles not native to the state. A prohibited sublist sits on top, barred to everyone outside parks, zoos, aquariums, museums and research facilities. Administered by the State Veterinarian.

tn-70-4-403.title: Tenn. Code Ann. § 70-4-403, Classifications of wildlife, with §§ 70-4-401, 70-4-402 and 70-4-404
tn-70-4-403.note: Five classes. Class I is a specific list of inherently dangerous animals, possessable only by zoos, circuses and commercial propagators. Class II is "native species, except those listed in other classes". Class III "requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes", followed by seventeen illustrative subdivisions. Class IV is black bear, white-tailed deer and wild turkey; Class V is whatever the commission designates as injurious. The catch-all sitting at Class III rather than Class II is what makes Tennessee permissive, and the exception clause in Class II is what keeps native reptiles out of it. Tennessee's official code is behind LexisNexis and publications.tnsosfiles.com refuses this container, so the wording here was taken from two independent reproductions that agree: animallaw.info, which carries the current post-2024 text, and lawserver.com, whose copy is marked effective until 1 July 2024 and differs only in the snake clause, which the 2024 amendment changed from "poisonous" to "venomous".

ar-unrestricted.title: Arkansas Game and Fish Commission Code Book, Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
ar-unrestricted.note: Species exempt from Codes 09.02 (possession of non-native wildlife restricted), 09.07 (breeder/dealer permit) and 09.10 (importation permit), named individually with binomials. Read it out of the codebook rather than the compiled PDF AGFC posted at agfc.com in 2022, which is the version that circulates as "the Arkansas list" and is two revisions behind: it lacks the rosy boa and the whole Anoline Lizards entry with its Arkansas-native exception. The compiled PDF says so itself, that the codebook lists "take precedence".

id-020427.title: IDAPA 02.04.27, Idaho Department of Agriculture, Rules Governing Deleterious Exotic Animals
id-020427.note: Section 100.01 bars possession of a deleterious exotic animal without a possession permit from the Administrator. Sections 401 to 412 are the list itself, by taxon.

id-130110.title: IDAPA 13.01.10, Idaho Department of Fish and Game, Rules Governing Importation, Possession, Release, Sale, or Salvage of Wildlife
id-130110.note: Section 010.06 defines conventional pets, which sit outside the wildlife permit regime. Unusually explicit: it names ferrets, hedgehogs and sugar gliders in the rule text.

ia-717F.title: Iowa Code Chapter 717F, Dangerous Wild Animals
ia-717F.note: § 717F.3 bars owning, possessing, breeding or importing a dangerous wild animal. § 717F.1(5) defines the class by family and order rather than by species name, so the boundaries are read off the taxonomy. § 717F.4 grandfathers animals already owned on 1 July 2007.

ia-481A.title: Iowa Code Chapter 481A, Wildlife Conservation
ia-481A.note: The native wildlife side. § 481A.67 governs taking turtles.

ky-301-2-082.title: 301 KAR 2:082, Transportation and holding of live exotic wildlife
ky-301-2-082.note: Three lists. Section 4(1) is prohibited species, injurious to native ecosystems. Section 4(2) is inherently dangerous exotic wildlife. Section 7 is the permit-exempt list. Anything on none of the three may be possessed, but a transportation permit is needed to bring it into the state. KRS 65.877, cited in the regulation itself, lets local governments prohibit inherently dangerous wildlife outright.

ri-250-40-05-3.title: 250-RICR-40-05-3, Rules and Regulations Governing the Importation and Possession of Wild Animals
ri-250-40-05-3.note: One of the most species-specific schemes in the country. § 3.6 defines domestic animals, § 3.7 sets general prohibitions, § 3.9 governs permits, and § 3.17 is the long exempt list of animals that need no exotic animal possession permit. Anything not domestic, not native and not on the § 3.17 list needs a permit.

nh-fis800.title: New Hampshire Code of Administrative Rules, Fis 800, Importation and Possession of Wildlife
nh-fis800.note: Readopted in full by Document #14558, effective 21 April 2026. Four buckets and a closing rule. Fis 804.02 is the non-controlled possession list, Fis 804.03 the prohibited list, Fis 804.05 with Table 800.2 the controlled table, and Fis 804.04(b) then says "All species not specifically listed under the categories of non-controlled, prohibited, or controlled shall be designated as prohibited." Fis 803 runs the same three-way split for importation against Table 800.1. The number beside a species in either table is the permittee category from Fis 802.01: 1 is an individual, 5 an exhibitor, so a species marked 5 alone cannot be held privately. Fis 802.05 is the waiver for unlisted species and subsection (c) closes it to categories 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7, which leaves only exhibitors.

mo-578-023.title: Missouri Revised Statutes § 578.023, Keeping a dangerous wild animal
mo-578-023.note: Missouri does not ban these animals. It requires that they be registered with the local law enforcement agency in the county where they are kept. Failure to register is the offence.

mo-3csr10-9.title: 3 CSR 10-9, Missouri Wildlife Code: Confined Wildlife
mo-3csr10-9.note: Class I is native Missouri mammals, reptiles and amphibians plus birds native to the continental United States. Class II is the venomous natives, mountain lion, wolf and black bear. Class III is cervids. An animal that is none of these is outside the Wildlife Code entirely.

ks-32-1301.title: K.S.A. 32-1301, Dangerous regulated animals; definitions
ks-32-1301.note: Kansas restricts three things and nothing else. The definition is short enough to read in full, which is what makes it useful: everything outside it is untouched by the Act.

sc-47-2.title: S.C. Code Title 47, Chapter 2, Large Wild Cats, Non-Native Bears and Great Apes
sc-47-2.note: The 2018 Act. It is narrow on purpose: genus Panthera, non-native bears, great apes, and hybrids of those. Anyone in lawful possession before 1 January 2018 could register with the local animal control authority and keep the animal for its life.

sc-50-16.title: S.C. Code Title 50, Chapter 16, Importation and Possession of Wildlife
sc-50-16.note: § 50-16-20 requires a permit to bring in certain groups of live wildlife, chiefly furbearers, cervids, pigs, bovids, coyote, bear and turkey. § 50-16-60 then exempts a named list of pet trade animals from even that.

mt-87-5-7.title: Montana Code Annotated Title 87, Chapter 5, Part 7, Importation, Introduction, and Transplantation of Wildlife
mt-87-5-7.note: Montana runs a white list, which is unusual. § 87-5-705(1) says a person may not import, possess or sell any exotic wildlife unless it is allowed by law or commission rule, so an animal that appears on none of the three lists is not permitted rather than unregulated. § 87-5-706 is the statutory noncontrolled list and § 87-5-702 puts rodents, cats, dogs and Eurasian ferrets outside the scheme as domestic animals.

mt-arm-12-6-22.title: Administrative Rules of Montana, Subchapter 12.6.22, Exotic Wildlife
mt-arm-12-6-22.note: 12.6.2205 is the noncontrolled list, 12.6.2208 the controlled list, 12.6.2215 the prohibited list. The noncontrolled definition at 12.6.2201(8) expressly preserves county and city ordinances.

wv-19-34.title: W. Va. Code § 19-34, Dangerous Wild Animals Act
wv-19-34.note: Unusual structure, and the reason most entries here are unclear. § 19-34-4 bans possession of a dangerous wild animal, but § 19-34-2 defines the term by character rather than by species and § 19-34-5 directs a three member board to create the actual list by legislative rule. The statute itself names no animal. Until that list is confirmed in force, the ban has no species attached to it.

ak-5aac92-029.title: 5 AAC 92.029, Permit for possessing live game
ak-5aac92-029.note: The strictest structure in the country and the clearest. Subsection (a) bars possessing live game without a permit, (b) is a short clean list of species needing no permit, and (c) then removes the escape hatch: the department may not issue a permit for any game animal for use as a pet. So an animal missing from the clean list cannot be kept, permit or not.

sd-12-68-18.title: ARSD 12:68:18, Nondomestic Animal Control
sd-12-68-18.note: Two separate requirements sit in the same chapter and are easy to conflate. An entry permit, free and obtainable by telephone, is required to import any nondomestic animal. A possession permit, ten dollars per animal, is required only for the mammal families listed in 12:68:18:03. The only outright prohibition is the raccoon dog.

al-220-2-26.title: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26, Restrictions On Possession, Sale, Importation And/Or Release Of Certain Animals And Fish
al-220-2-26.note: Alabama's prohibited list, not a permitted one, so absence from it means an animal is unrestricted. The official code site is a React app that serves nothing to a fetcher, but /api/rule/<number> returns the current rule as a PDF; use it, because Cornell LII's copy is the 2020 version and the current one differs. Two clauses do most of the work: everything the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service lists as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act is banned by reference, and a block of mammals is banned when it comes from outside Alabama.

in-312-9-11.title: 312 IAC 9-11, Wild Animal Possession Permits
in-312-9-11.note: Three classes by risk. Class I is rabbits and squirrels, Class II is a long and specific list of small wild cats plus Indiana's furbearers, Class III is wolves, bears, all other wild cats, venomous reptiles and large crocodilians. Both the Class II and Class III lists end with the same sentence exempting hybrids with a domestic dog or cat, which is the clearest hybrid answer any state gives.

nd-36-01.title: North Dakota Century Code Chapter 36-01, Board of Animal Health
nd-36-01.note: The chapter names only three restrictions relevant to pets: skunks and raccoons may not be kept at all, mountain lions and wolves need a tattooed identification number, and the board is to make rules on primates. § 36-01-08.1 says the board may require a licence for nontraditional livestock, meaning any wildlife held in confinement, but the wording is permissive.

nd-48-1.title: North Dakota Administrative Code Title 48.1, State Board of Animal Health
nd-48-1.note: The old title 48, which carried the nontraditional livestock category system, is repealed. What replaced it is a set of importation health chapters. Chapter 48.1-13-02 covers everything else and asks only for a certificate of veterinary inspection and an importation permit number from the state veterinarian.

wy-ch10.title: Wyoming Game and Fish Commission Regulation Chapter 10, Importation and Possession of Live Warm-Blooded Wildlife
wy-ch10.note: Two closed lists do the work. Domestic animals and domesticated animals are both defined by enumeration, with the phrase for the purpose of this regulation, only the following animals are considered domestic. Anything on neither list is wildlife, and Section 13(d) leaves it to a permit that may be authorised upon approval.

wy-ch69.title: Wyoming Game and Fish Commission Regulation Chapter 69, Importation and Possession of Live Cold-Blooded Wildlife
wy-ch69.note: Section 10(a)(i) is the sentence that matters for reptile keepers: amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 need no permit at all.

ms-40-2-8-3.title: 40 Miss. Admin. Code Part 2, Rule 8.3, Regulations For Animals Inherently Dangerous To Humans
ms-40-2-8-3.note: A short list drawn by genus and family, covering apes and some monkeys, wolves and three wild dogs, bears, the wolverine, hyenas, the big cats, elephants, rhinos, hippos and African buffalo. Nothing smaller appears. The rule also notes that since the federal Big Cat Public Safety Act took effect in December 2022 no new big cat permits are issued at all.

la-76-v-115.title: LAC 76:V.115, Possession of Potentially Dangerous Wild Quadrupeds, Big Exotic Cats, and Non-Human Primates
la-76-v-115.note: A short mammal ban: three bears, two wolves, wolf dog hybrids, all non-human primates, and six big cats with their subspecies and hybrids. Existing permit holders were grandfathered but may not acquire more.

la-76-xv-101.title: LAC 76:XV.101, Reptiles and Amphibians, Recreational and Commercial Harvests; Prohibitions
la-76-xv-101.note: Rewritten in January 2025 and now one of the strictest reptile rules in the country. Three tiers: prohibited nonnative species, restricted nonnative species needing a permit, and a general rule that any constrictor over eight feet needs a restricted snake permit.

ok-800-25-25-3.title: OAC 800:25-25-3, Exemptions
ok-800-25-25-3.note: One of the most permissive exemption lists in the country, naming the fennec fox, the sugar glider, the coatimundi, the wallaby and primates individually. Note what the exemptions are from: import and export permits and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder licences, not a ban. Subsection (c) exempts non-indigenous reptiles and amphibians as a class, with a two-limb carve-out for species that could establish here and are injurious under federal rules. Oklahoma's own rules site, rules.ok.gov, returns 403 to this container, so this is read from Cornell LII and cited to the official section.

ne-166-nac-8.title: 166 Neb. Admin. Code ch. 8, Keeping Wildlife in Captivity, and ch. 10, Nongame Species In Need Of Conservation
ne-166-nac-8.note: Nebraska renumbered its Game and Parks regulations: what used to be 163 NAC ch. 4 is now Title 166, and captive wildlife has its own chapter 8 rather than a subsection. Anything on this map citing "163 NAC ch. 4, § 008" is pointing at a title that is now called ADMINISTRATION. Chapter 8 has three operative parts. § 001.01B bars retaining any WILD BIRD or WILD MAMMAL in captivity except a listed set of Nebraska natives under a Captive Wildlife Permit. § 001.07A prohibits six species outright, none of them a pet: the Asian raccoon dog, white-tailed and mule deer, red deer, wild pigs and bighorn or thinhorn sheep. And § 001.08A is a closed importation list, which is what actually answers most exotic mammals here, because they are not wild mammals and so the permit scheme never reaches them. Chapter 10 does the same job for reptiles and amphibians and is limited to species native to Nebraska.

hi-conditional.title: Hawaii Administrative Rules, List of Conditionally Approved Animals (Hawaii Department of Agriculture official PDF)
hi-conditional.note: The list that matters most for pet keepers and the one almost never quoted. Conditional approval means importation and possession are allowed subject to the conditions the Board of Agriculture sets, unlike the restricted list, which is research and exhibition only.

nc-153a-131.title: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 153A-131, Possession or harboring of dangerous animals
nc-153a-131.note: The reason North Carolina looks unregulated from the state house and is anything but on the ground. A county may by ordinance regulate, restrict or prohibit possession of animals dangerous to persons or property, and many have. Your county code is the operative law here, not the General Statutes.

nc-14-417.title: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 14-417, Regulation of ownership or use of venomous reptiles
nc-14-417.note: North Carolina's entire statewide exotic animal statute, and it reaches venomous reptiles only. It does not ban them either: it requires an escape-proof, bite-proof, lockable enclosure, a label reading Venomous Reptile Inside naming the species and the right antivenin, a written bite protocol kept in sight, and immediate notice to law enforcement on an escape. Nothing else in the General Statutes restricts keeping an exotic animal.

pa-2961.title: 34 Pa.C.S. § 2961, Game and Wildlife Code, exotic wildlife definition
pa-2961.note: The definition names bears, coyotes, lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs, cougars, wolves and their crossbreeds, and none of the animals in this dataset. The entire prohibition rests on four words earlier in the sentence, includes, but is not limited to, which the Game Commission reads as reaching small exotic mammals. That is an agency interpretation of a definition rather than anything a legislature wrote about these species, which is why bills to reverse it keep being introduced.

hi-hrs150A-6-2.title: Hawaii Revised Statutes § 150A-6.2, Animal import
hi-hrs150A-6-2.note: The statute behind the lists. Subsection (c) is the default rule: anything not on the conditionally approved, restricted or prohibited list is prohibited until the board reviews it.

mt-87-5-116.title: Montana Code Annotated § 87-5-116, Limited taking of certain nongame wildlife for commercial purposes
mt-87-5-116.note: Restricts commercial taking of native Montana amphibians and reptiles. It does not reach personal possession, which is why native species sit outside the exotic wildlife permit regime.

ak-as16-05-940.title: Alaska Statutes § 16.05.940(19), definition of game
ak-as16-05-940.note: Game means any species of bird, reptile and mammal. Amphibians and invertebrates are outside the definition, so the live game permit rule at 5 AAC 92.029 does not reach them at all.

wa-wac-220-640-200.title: WAC 220-640-200, Deleterious exotic wildlife
wa-wac-220-640-200.note: Washington's second exotic animal rule. Checked and found to cover only ungulates, mongooses, wild boar, peccary and the mute swan, so it does not reach any common exotic pet.

ga-dnr-legal-pets.title: Georgia DNR Law Enforcement Division, Guide to Legal Pets
ga-dnr-legal-pets.note: The agency page that answers the native half of Georgia, which the wild animal rule does not reach. It states the operative rule in one line, "By Georgia Law, most native species of wildlife cannot be held without permits or licenses. These licenses are not issued for the purpose of holding native wildlife as pets", and adds the sentence that closes the captive-bred argument: "These restrictions apply to the various species of animal, regardless of the origin or morphology." It then lists native species that may not be held as a pet, among them the corn snake, milksnake, garter snake, green anole, both hognose snakes, all four box turtles and the flying squirrel. Two limits are worth carrying: the list says of itself that it "does not include all native wildlife that is prohibited", and a separate paragraph names the natives Georgia does allow to be taken, "rats, mice, armadillos, coyotes, groundhogs, beaver, freshwater turtles, venomous snakes, frogs, spring lizards, fiddler crabs, freshwater crayfish, freshwater mussels, and nutria".

il-herps-act.title: Illinois Administrative Code, Title 17, Part 885, Herptile Code
il-herps-act.note: Official Joint Committee on Administrative Rules text, amended effective 31 July 2025. § 885.40 is the list of Illinois native herptile taxa, which decides whether the possession cap applies to a species at all; § 885.20 sets the seasons and limits; § 885.80 sets the $50 Herpetoculture Permit; and § 885.105(j), new in 2025, sweeps named corn snake morph lines into the endangered species regime.

mn-97a-401.title: Minn. Stat. § 97A.401, Special permits
mn-97a-401.note: Subd. 8, added in 2021, is the pet reptile rule: the commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue breeder permits, and a snake, lizard or salamander is possessable as a pet if it came from a permitted breeder or was held before 1 August 2021. Subd. 3 is the older, broader route, allowing special permits without a fee to possess wild animals as pets.

pa-exotic-wildlife-permit.title: 58 Pa. Code Chapter 147, Subchapter N — Exotic Wildlife Possession
pa-exotic-wildlife-permit.note: Official Pennsylvania Code text of the Game Commission's exotic-wildlife permit framework; no dedicated descriptive PGC web page could be confirmed, and the Commission has issued no new permits under this framework since January 1, 2014.

sc-act177.title: S.C. Code of Regulations, Chapter 123, Article 5 (§§ 123-150 through 123-153.4)
sc-act177.note: Official codified text implementing 2021 Act 177; §123-151.3 carves out captive-bred corn snakes under 20 inches and eastern milksnakes under 10 inches from the general native-reptile sale/possession ban.

pa-58-79-3.title: 58 Pa. Code § 79.3 — Season and Daily Possession Limits (Chapter 79, Reptiles and Amphibians)
pa-58-79-3.note: Official Pennsylvania Code text; the catch-all 'native species not listed' line sets a 1-per-day/1-in-possession limit, and companion §79.4 requires a permit for continued possession regardless of the animal's origin.

ut-r657-53-tables.title: Species Tables for Utah's Reptiles and Amphibians
ut-r657-53-tables.note: The division's classification tables under R657-53. Every table on the page is about animals taken from the wild in Utah: six prohibited natives, six naturalized non-natives at unlimited, four native lizards at Expanded, and the Standard and Limited controlled lists. The page says outright that 'the DWR does not maintain a full list of non-native species', so it answers a pet species only when that species also lives wild in Utah.

wi-nr-16-12.title: Wisconsin Admin. Code NR 16.12 — Amphibian and Reptile Regulations
wi-nr-16-12.note: Official Wisconsin State Legislature code text; caps take/possession of native, non-listed amphibians, lizards and snakes at 5 individuals per species, with NR 16.13 layering on the purchase restriction for native species.

az-co43-reptile-regs.title: Arizona Reptile and Amphibian Regulations 2026–2030 (Commission Order 43)
az-co43-reptile-regs.note: Official AZGFD regulations booklet effective Jan. 1, 2026; lists rosy boa (Lichanura roseofusca/trivirgata) with a take limit of 2 per year and 4 in possession under a valid hunting license.

al-native-nongame.title: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.92, Protected Nongame Species
al-native-nongame.note: The native side of Alabama, and the rule that catches what 220-2-.26 does not. Protection means no possession without a scientific collection permit or a written permit from the Commissioner. The reptile list is species by species, the amphibian list is not: it protects all native salamander species by genus. Cornell LII still shows the older per-species salamander list, so read the official PDF.

az-license-take.title: Ariz. Admin. Code R12-4-406, R12-4-407
az-license-take.note: Arizona Game and Fish Commission's live wildlife rules, hosted by AZGFD, R12-4-406 sets the restricted wildlife special license requirement and R12-4-407 lists exemptions from it.

ca-5-60.title: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 14, § 5.60
ca-5-60.note: CDFW's current Freshwater Sport Fishing Regulations booklet, which reprints Title 14 section 5.60 in full, including species bag limits and county closures.

ct-26-55-6.title: Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 26-55-6, Importation, possession or liberation of wild birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates
ct-26-55-6.note: Connecticut's official eRegulations text, served as a PDF. This is the operative rule for every animal on this map, and it sorts wild animals into four categories. Category One (four mammal families) and Category Two (a long specific list) may be possessed only by institutions; Category Three, which is Connecticut's own native species, bars import and export but not possession; Category Four, the state endangered, threatened and special concern species, needs a permit. An animal in none of the four is not restricted by this section. The definitions in subsection (a) do more work than the lists: 'wild animal' reaches invertebrates, and 'domestic animal' is defined in a way that takes the pet rabbit and the ferret out of the scheme entirely.

de-native-wildlife.title: Del. Code tit. 7, c. 7
de-native-wildlife.note: Delaware Code Online's game and fish possession chapter administered by DNREC, paired with a separate exotic species permit chapter at Del. Code tit. 3, c. 72.

md-native-herp.title: COMAR 08.03.11, Reptile and Amphibian Possession and Permits
md-native-herp.note: Maryland's native reptile and amphibian chapter, adopted 1993 and amended through 2016, renumbered from 08.03.09. It works off three lists in Regulation .03: .03A species may be kept four per species without a permit, .03B species one only, and .03C species not at all outside a scientific collection or endangered species permit. A species on none of the three lists is not native to Maryland and the chapter does not reach it. Regulation .03D provides that where both names are given, the scientific name controls.

nj-7-25-4-8.title: N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.8(a) Potentially dangerous species, restricted and endangered species notice
nj-7-25-4-8.note: The Division's restricted species notice. It reproduces the 4.8(a) table and then adds things that are nowhere in the rule text: that it treats an IUCN Red List entry as an endangered listing, that only nine named corn snake morphs may be kept, and that axolotls and larval salamanders may not be kept at all.

nv-unprotected-reptiles.title: NAC 503.090
nv-unprotected-reptiles.note: Nevada Legislature's administrative code chapter defining unprotected reptiles as any species not classified protected, sensitive, threatened, or endangered.

or-635-056-0060.title: OAR 635-056-0060, Noncontrolled Species
or-635-056-0060.note: The allow-list. Wildlife on it may be imported, possessed, sold, purchased, exchanged or transported without an ODFW permit. It is long and written to genus or family with named exceptions, and it uses the taxonomy current when each entry was added rather than the current one.

pa-58-79.title: 58 Pa. Code Ch. 79
pa-58-79.note: Official Pennsylvania Code and Bulletin chapter, Fish and Boat Commission rules that apply only to species native to Pennsylvania and only to wild take, which requires a fishing license.

ut-r657-53.title: Utah Admin. Code R657-53, Amphibian and Reptile Collection, Importation, Transportation and Possession
ut-r657-53.note: The whole of Utah's herp rule, self-hosted by the Division of Wildlife Resources because the Office of Administrative Rules site is a React app that serves nothing to a fetcher. Written for collection from the wild: 53-4(1) bars possession outright and 53-5 then gives it back, 53-12 is the only certificate of registration that attaches to possession and it covers native venomous reptiles only, and 53-8(1) lifts captive-bred and out-of-state animals out of the possession limits.

vt-10-app-18.title: 10 V.S.A. App. § 18
vt-10-app-18.note: Vermont Legislature's official text requiring an Importation and Possession Permit for any wild animal not on the Commissioner's Unrestricted Wild Animals List.

wi-nr16-12.title: Wis. Admin. Code NR 16.12-16.15
wi-nr16-12.note: Wisconsin Legislature's codified DNR chapter on captive wildlife, sections 16.12 through 16.15 set possession and take limits for native reptiles and amphibians.

wi-import-permit.title: Wis. Stat. § 169.04
wi-import-permit.note: Wisconsin Legislature's captive wildlife statute requiring lawful acquisition, animals sourced from out of state also need a DATCP import permit.

tx-71-001.title: Tex. Parks & Wild. Code § 71.001 and 31 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 65.371-65.375, fur-bearing animals
tx-71-001.note: The definition at § 71.001(1) reads "wild beaver, otter, mink, ring-tailed cat, badger, skunk, raccoon, muskrat, opossum, fox, or nutria", and the bare word "fox" is what makes people read Texas as a fox ban state. It is not one. Chapter 71 and the proclamation at 31 TAC §§ 65.371-65.375 govern taking, trapping, pelts and fur dealing; § 65.375(a)(2) says there are no bag or possession limits for fur-bearing animals; and nothing in either bars keeping one. The series is also headed by "wild", which a captive-bred animal is not.

fl-class3.title: 68A-6.002, 68A-6.003 and 68A-6.004, F.A.C., Captive Wildlife
fl-class3.note: Florida sorts all wildlife into three classes and then exempts a list from the scheme entirely, and the exemption list is what most pet questions turn on. 68A-6.002 puts 24 taxa in Class I, which 68A-6.003(6) says may not be possessed for personal use at all, and 38 in Class II, which needs a $140 annual permit plus documented experience and caging. Class III is everything else, and 68A-6.003(8) requires a no-cost personal use permit for it. Then 68A-6.003(14) lists 22 categories needing no permit at all, and that list is the answer for most of this map: nonvenomous unprotected reptiles and amphibians, gerbils, hedgehogs, sugar gliders, rabbits, squirrels, ferrets, guinea pigs, hamsters, prairie dogs, chinchillas and parrots among them. Read the class lists without 68A-6.003(14) and Florida looks like a permit state for a bearded dragon. Read (14) without the class lists and it looks like a free-for-all for a capybara.

nc-113-272-5.title: North Carolina General Statutes § 113-272.5
nc-113-272-5.note: North Carolina's captivity-license statute, which bars issuing a license for a wild animal acquired merely as a pet.

wi-nr-10-02.title: Wisconsin Administrative Code NR 10.02
wi-nr-10-02.note: Lists Wisconsin's protected wild animals, which may not be taken, transported or possessed without DNR authorization.

il-520-5.title: Illinois Wildlife Code, 520 ILCS 5
il-520-5.note: § 2.2 says the Act applies only to wild birds and wild mammals, then lists the protected species by name and family. Parrots are not among them; the flying squirrel is. § 3.23 (DocName 052000050K3.23) carries the Class A noncommercial breeder permit that lets a private keeper hold a protected species, plus the two named-species clauses that decide the rabbit and the monk parakeet.

oh-1531.title: Ohio Revised Code Chapter 1531
oh-1531.note: Ohio's Division of Wildlife chapter, which defines game quadrupeds (including the flying squirrel) and requires a permit to possess native wildlife.

hi-4-71-6-prohibited.title: Hawaii Administrative Rules § 4-71-6, List of Prohibited Animals
hi-4-71-6-prohibited.note: HDOA's prohibited species list, which bans the entire squirrel family Sciuridae except two zoo-exhibition species and university-research marmots.

ny-dangerous-animal.title: 6 NYCRR § 180.1, Animals Dangerous to Health or Welfare
ny-dangerous-animal.note: The department regulation behind ECL § 11-0511, and it reaches further than the statutory wild animal list. It adds the raccoon dog, the wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses, and it extends the constrictor list to the DeSchauensee's and Beni anacondas and the Southern African python while naming the Burmese by its current binomial, Python bivittatus. Its exemptions at subdivision (d) are ten kinds of licensee and institution and none of them is a pet keeper, so an animal on this list has no personal route at all. It repeats the two carve-outs from the statute word for word, for captive bred fennec foxes and for five-generation registered cat hybrids.

wi-datcp-birds.title: Wisconsin Statutes § 169.01(25m)
wi-datcp-birds.note: Defines pet bird as a non-native, non-endangered, non-migratory psittacine or soft-bill bird, the category Wisconsin's captive wildlife law leaves unregulated.

ut-r657-3b.title: Utah Admin. Code R657-3b, Collection, Importation, Possession and Propagation of Birds and Mammals
ut-r657-3b.note: Birds and mammals only. 3b-1(3) points at Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 for the domestic animals the rule does not govern at all, which is the section that answers most pet mammals in Utah.

de-nonnative-reptile-permit.title: Delaware Code, Title 3, Chapter 72 — Possession of Mammals or Reptiles Exotic to Delaware
de-nonnative-reptile-permit.note: §7201 requires a permit before bringing in, possessing, selling, or exhibiting any live wild mammal or reptile not native to Delaware; the California kingsnake, a Pacific coast species, falls under this permit requirement.

al-exotic-birds.title: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26, Restrictions On Possession, Sale, Importation And/Or Release Of Certain Animals And Fish
al-exotic-birds.note: Same rule already sourced for other species' prohibited list; its bans reach only federally-listed Lacey Act injurious wildlife and named out-of-state mammal/fish species, with no bird species named, so a captive-bred parrot or cockatoo falls outside it.

az-exotic-birds.title: Arizona Revised Statutes § 17-306, Importation, Transportation, Release or Possession of Live Wildlife
az-exotic-birds.note: General prohibition on unauthorized live wildlife; enforced in practice through the companion restricted-species rule (R12-4-406), which is aimed at native and dangerous wildlife and does not name common psittacine pets.

de-birds-exempt.title: Delaware Code, Title 3, Chapter 72 — Possession of Mammals or Reptiles Exotic to Delaware
de-birds-exempt.note: The permit requirement in §7201 names only wild mammals and non-native reptiles; birds are absent from the chapter's operative text despite appearing in its older title reference, so a pet cockatoo needs no permit under this chapter.

nv-unprotected-birds.title: Nevada Administrative Code § 503.110, Restrictions on Importation, Transportation and Possession of Certain Species
nv-unprotected-birds.note: The prohibited-species list under this section names only three birds (Pink Starling/Rosy Pastor, Red-billed Dioch, Red-whiskered Bulbul); cockatoos and other companion parrots are absent.

ny-6nycrr-3-3.title: 6 NYCRR § 3.3, Native Snakes, and DEC reptile and amphibian seasons
ny-6nycrr-3-3.note: Two sentences and a list. Subdivision (a) defines native snakes as sixteen named species including the common garter snake, the eastern milk snake, the eastern hognose snake and the black rat snake, and subdivision (b) reads in its entirety "Open season. None." That is what turns the small game classification into a prohibition. DEC states the result plainly in its own season summary: for turtles, "The only turtle species for which there is an open hunting season is the snapping turtle. You may not harvest, take, or possess any other turtle species at any time", and for the rest, "You may not harvest, take, or possess any native snakes, lizards, or salamanders at any time." New York publishes the NYCRR only through Westlaw, which serves document pages to a browser User-Agent but not the Part 175 possession chapter, so the seasons and this section are the readable half of the regulation.

wi-nr40.title: Wis. Admin. Code ch. NR 40, Invasive Species Identification, Classification and Control
wi-nr40.note: DNR's regulated invasive species list. Among animals kept as pets the only terrestrial vertebrate named is the monk or Quaker parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus), Prohibited. The other terrestrial vertebrates are nutria and wild/feral swine. No pet reptile, amphibian or small mammal appears.

wi-29-604.title: Wis. Stat. § 29.604 and Wis. Admin. Code ch. NR 27, Endangered and Threatened Species
wi-29-604.note: Listed species may not be taken, transported, possessed, processed or sold without an endangered/threatened species permit, and DNR issues those only for education, research and conservation, not pet keeping. The ornate box turtle (Terrapene ornata), Wisconsin's only native box turtle, is state Endangered.

ut-table-3b-1.title: Utah DWR Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (May 1, 2023), under Utah Admin. Code R657-3b
ut-table-3b-1.note: Five sections: domestic mammals and birds not covered by the rule, noncontrolled mammals and birds, controlled mammals, and prohibited mammals. The header sets an inverted default: 'Except as otherwise listed, all species are presumed prohibited. All species not listed will require an assessment before collection, importation, or possession will be authorized.' The prohibited section adds that 'personal possession will not be authorized'.

pa-34-102.title: 34 Pa.C.S. § 102, Game and Wildlife Code definitions of wildlife, wild animals and wild birds
pa-34-102.note: The definitional chain that decides what the Game Commission can reach at all. Wildlife is wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates fall outside the Game Code entirely and sit with the Fish and Boat Commission or with nobody. Wild birds is a closed set: federally listed migratory birds, game birds, and any other birds the Commission designates by name. Wild animals is the opposite, all mammals except the five livestock groups in 1 Pa.C.S. § 1991, so the mammal side sweeps far wider than the Commission enforces. The Pennsylvania General Assembly site blocks automated access, so this wording was read from two independent reproductions of the section that agree verbatim, FindLaw and the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies law research library.

pa-58-137-1.title: 58 Pa. Code Ch. 137, Game Commission wildlife regulations, § 137.1 importation, possession, sale and release of certain wildlife and § 137.31 possession of live wildlife
pa-58-137-1.note: The Game Commission's actual prohibited list, and the document most Pennsylvania exotic pet questions turn on rather than the § 2961 definition. Eleven categories, of which three matter most here: all Felidae except house cats, the monk parakeet by name, and a catch-all barring possession of any wildlife held in captivity or captive bred in another state or nation.

pa-pfbc-native-species.title: Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission, Pennsylvania Native Reptile and Amphibian Species
pa-pfbc-native-species.note: The enforcing agency's own native species list, which is what 58 Pa. Code § 79.1 points to when it says the Commission will publish the species it has determined are native. Membership on this list is the switch that decides whether Chapter 79 reaches an animal at all.

mi-fo-224.title: Michigan Fisheries Order 224.21, amphibians and reptiles, as published in the Michigan Fishing Guide
mi-fo-224.note: The order that actually governs herps in Michigan, and the one most summaries miss because it sits in the fishing rules rather than the wildlife rules. Its reach is the phrase "any state reptile or amphibian from the wild", so it binds native species taken here and leaves captive-bred non-native pets alone. Michigan.gov blocks automated access, so this was read from the official guide as published by the state's regulations publisher.

mi-captive-game.title: Michigan DNR Permit to Hold Game in Captivity, under NREPA Part 427, MCL 324.42701 et seq.
mi-captive-game.note: Michigan's route for keeping a native mammal or game bird, and it is a closed list of species rather than a general exotic pet permit. It authorizes captive-bred animals only, so a wild-caught animal cannot be brought under it. Non-native species are outside it entirely, which is why a native red fox needs this permit and a fennec fox does not.

mi-287-731.title: Mich. Comp. Laws § 287.731, Animal Industry Act, importation of animals, with the MDARD import requirements issued under it
mi-287-731.note: The import side, which is where most lawful Michigan exotics actually meet a rule. The director may require an entry permit for wild or exotic animals, and MDARD's published requirements call for a certificate of veterinary inspection to import exotic animals, native wild animals, nonnative rodents, nonnative reptiles and amphibians, and non-poultry birds. MDARD does not issue entry permits for exotic, circus and zoo animals, so in practice the certificate is the requirement. Large carnivores and wolf-dog crosses are barred here except as their own acts allow.

hi-4-71-rule.title: Hawaii Administrative Rules Chapter 4-71, Non-Domestic Animal Import Rules, § 4-71-2 definitions and § 4-71-6.5 permitted introductions
hi-4-71-rule.note: The rule text the three species lists hang off, and the part that explains why Hawaii answers differently from everywhere else. Two things matter. § 4-71-6.5 allows introduction only for animals on the conditionally approved or restricted lists, which is what makes an unlisted animal barred by default rather than unregulated. And § 4-71-2 defines a set of domestic animals, the European rabbit among them, then says that as used in the chapter the word animal means non-domestic animal, so the lists never reach those species at all.

vt-unrestricted-list.title: Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department, Unrestricted Wild Animal List, July 2025
vt-unrestricted-list.note: The list the whole Vermont answer turns on, and the one earlier research could not obtain. Anything on it may be kept with no permit. Its closing line is the important part: species not found on the Restricted, Unrestricted or Domestic species lists are considered Restricted, which makes Vermont an inverted-list state like Hawaii. Several entries are marked Captive Bred Only, which is a real condition rather than a note. The site refuses automated requests without a User-Agent header.

vt-restricted-list.title: Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department, Restricted Wild Animal List, July 2025
vt-restricted-list.note: The appendix the Unrestricted list keeps pointing at. Headed: species below are exceptions to Unrestricted Wild Animal List status and require an importation and possession permit. It matters because several families are unrestricted as a whole and then clawed back species by species here, which is how Vermont ends up allowing a ball python and not a Burmese, a California kingsnake and not an eastern milk snake.

nm-importation-list.title: New Mexico Department of Game and Fish, Director's Species Importation List, updated January 2023
nm-importation-list.note: The roughly 1,300 row table that 19.35.7 NMAC points at and that earlier research could not obtain. Every row gives a family, a scientific name, a common name and a roman numeral group. Group I is semi-domesticated and needs no importation permit. Group II is not known to be invasive or dangerous and needs a permit. Group III presents minimal or manageable concerns and needs a permit with specific provisions attached. Group IV is prohibited to the general public. The list is reached from the download page rather than a direct file URL, and the site needs a User-Agent header.

nv-nac-503-140.title: Nev. Admin. Code § 503.140, species for which certain permits and licenses are not required
nv-nac-503-140.note: Nevada's clearance list, and the section that decides most pet questions here. Forty-five entries that may be possessed, transported, imported and exported without any Department permit. Three of them do enormous work: all felines except mountain lions and bobcats, all nonvenomous nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies, and all nonindigenous amphibians except bullfrogs. Subsection 4 preserves county and city ordinances, which matters because Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state.

nv-nrs-503-597.title: Nev. Rev. Stat. § 503.597, importation of wildlife, with the definition of wildlife at NRS 501.097
nv-nrs-503-597.note: The default nobody had pinned down. NRS 503.597 makes it unlawful without the written consent and approval of the Department for any person to receive, bring or have brought or shipped into the state any aquatic life or wildlife, so an animal that is neither prohibited by NAC 503.110 nor cleared by NAC 503.140 needs Department approval rather than being unregulated. NRS 501.097 defines wildlife as any wild mammal, wild bird, fish, reptile, amphibian, mollusk or crustacean found naturally in a wild state, which leaves insects and arachnids outside the Department's authority entirely.

az-ars-17-101.title: Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 17-101, definitions, including wildlife
az-ars-17-101.note: Sets the outer edge of what the Game and Fish Commission can reach. Wildlife means all wild mammals, wild birds and the nests or eggs thereof, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans and fish, including their eggs or spawn. Insects and arachnids are absent, so a terrestrial invertebrate is outside Title 17 altogether.

de-903.title: 3 Del. Admin. Code 903, Exotic Animal Regulations, with Del. Code tit. 3 § 7201
de-903.note: The regulation that actually decides Delaware, and it is much narrower than the list circulating in secondary sources. § 7201 requires a permit before anyone brings in, possesses, sells or exhibits a live wild mammal, a hybrid of a wild mammal, or a live reptile not native to Delaware, and bans non-native venomous snakes outright with no permit available. Regulation 6.1 then exempts a named list of pets from the permit entirely, and 6.2 says everything else needs one. The only species the State Veterinarian may not permit at all are at 4.7: gila monsters, beaded lizards and komodo dragons. Pythons, anacondas and boas appear only at 7.5.2.10, a restriction on what Sales Permit holders may breed, not a possession ban. The Delaware regulations site is a single-page app that serves no text to a fetcher, so this was read from a full reproduction and cross-checked against the Department of Agriculture's own exotic animals page.

co-w7.title: Colorado 2 CCR 406-7, Chapter W-7, Herpetofauna
co-w7.note: Secretary of State's official text of the new herpetofauna chapter, effective 1 May 2026. A closed-list scheme: #701 makes possession of any live reptile or amphibian unlawful unless the chapter allows it, Appendix A is free possession, Appendix B is free possession with documentation, Appendix C is wild collection under a resident licence, and anything on none of them is regulated wildlife.

co-w0-008.title: Colorado 2 CCR 406-0, Chapter W-0, § 008(B), Possession of Terrestrial Wildlife
co-w0-008.note: The Commission's prohibited species list. Nineteen entries, and the grandfather clause in the opening paragraph reaches only subsections 1 through 8, so the later additions, monk parakeet and prairie dogs among them, have no route for existing owners.

co-crs-33-1-102.title: C.R.S. § 33-1-102(51), definition of wildlife
co-crs-33-1-102.note: Sets the outer boundary of what Colorado Parks and Wildlife may regulate at all. Wild vertebrates, mollusks and crustaceans, which leaves every terrestrial arthropod outside Title 33.

co-cpw-species-list.title: Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Wildlife and Animal Possession in Colorado, species determination lists
co-cpw-species-list.note: CPW's own page, with four downloadable lists, herpetofauna, mammals, birds, and fish and marine animals, each row giving a species and the regulation that decides it: Domestic, Unregulated, Appendix A or B, Appendix C, Regulated or Prohibited. Updated 1 May 2026. Not exhaustive, and CPW takes questions on unlisted species by email. This is the agency applying its own rule, which matters most where Appendix A turns on whether a species is native only to the tropics.

il-510-68.title: Illinois Herptiles-Herps Act, 510 ILCS 68
il-510-68.note: The statute behind 17 Ill. Adm. Code 885, and the only Illinois law that reaches pet reptiles and amphibians. § 5-5 sets the possession limits, § 15-5 clears the family Boidae from the permit system outright, § 25-5 defines 'monitor lizards' as only the crocodile monitor and Komodo dragon, and § 85-5 bars possession of a special use herptile. Sections are served individually from this endpoint by DocName, 051000680K<section>.

il-520-10.title: Illinois Endangered Species Protection Act, 520 ILCS 10/3
il-520-10.note: Makes it unlawful to possess any animal on the Illinois List unless otherwise authorized by law. There is no captive-bred carve-out in the statute, so a species on the list stays on it however the animal was produced.
