il-1010.title: Illinois Administrative Code, Title 17, Part 1010, Illinois List of Endangered and Threatened Fauna
il-1010.note: Amended effective 30 October 2025. Three entries here reach animals sold in the pet trade: the Great Plains ratsnake is endangered, and the plains hog-nosed snake and the ornate box turtle are threatened.

il-805.title: Illinois Administrative Code, Title 17, Part 805, Injurious Species
il-805.note: Adopts the federal injurious wildlife list at 50 CFR 16.11-15 and adds to it, then bars possession of anything on it without a permit issued only to institutions. § 805.10 excludes herptiles expressly, sending them to the Herptiles-Herps Act, so this Part never decides a reptile or amphibian question in Illinois.

mn-97a-015.title: Minn. Stat. § 97A.015, Definitions
mn-97a-015.note: Two subdivisions decide most Minnesota questions. Subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures 'wild by nature' and includes reptiles and amphibians, with no geographic limit, so a ball python is a wild animal here. Subd. 39 makes snakes, salamanders, lizards, turtles and frogs protected wild animals as categories rather than as native species lists. Invertebrates other than crustaceans and mollusks are outside the definition entirely.

mn-97a-501.title: Minn. Stat. § 97A.501, Wild animals; general restrictions
mn-97a-501.note: The operative prohibition: a person may not possess a protected wild animal unless allowed by the game and fish laws, and ownership of all wild animals is in the state until lawfully acquired. It reaches protected wild animals only, which is why an unprotected native mammal sits differently from a native reptile here.

mn-97c-605.title: Minn. Stat. § 97C.605, Turtles
mn-97c-605.note: Turtles are handled apart from the 2021 snake, lizard and salamander rule and were not included in it. Subd. 1 requires an angling licence plus a recreational turtle licence to take, possess or transport turtles; subd. 2c exempts, among others, buying a turtle at a retail outlet, which is what leaves a pet-shop turtle or tortoise unlicensed.

mn-84d-05.title: Minn. Stat. § 84D.05 and Minn. R. 6216.0250, prohibited invasive species
mn-84d-05.note: Section 84D.05 bars possessing, importing, purchasing, selling, propagating or transporting a prohibited invasive species except under a permit, and Minn. R. 6216.0250 subp. 5 is the mammal list: Asian raccoon dog, Eurasian swine, European rabbit and nutria. No reptile or amphibian is on the prohibited list, and no bird at all.

mn-dnr-pet-trade.title: Minnesota DNR, Pet-trade sales of amphibians and reptiles in Minnesota
mn-dnr-pet-trade.note: The agency's own page. It gives the native turtle list, the endangered and threatened herptiles, the frog importation list, and the DNR's summary of the 2017 change, which it describes as reaching wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards and salamanders. It does not mention the 2021 breeder-permit rule at all, which is the gap the reptile entries here flag.

or-635-056-0020.title: OAR 635-056-0020, Animals Exempt from These Rules
or-635-056-0020.note: ORS 496.004(19) leaves it to the commission to say which mammals are wild, and this rule is that list: 32 species declared not wild and outside the wildlife rules entirely. It carries the guinea pig, gerbil, chinchilla, ferret, European rabbit, domestic cat breeds and all Psittaciformes. Read the binomials rather than the common names; the hamster entry is the one that does not say what it looks like it says.

or-635-056-0050.title: OAR 635-056-0050, Prohibited Species
or-635-056-0050.note: The ban list, and the one to check before assuming a common pet is fine in Oregon. It reaches the prairie dog, the capybara, the southern flying squirrel, the tiger salamander, the snapping turtle and the whole of Trachemys, all of which are ordinary pet-trade animals elsewhere on this map.

or-635-056-0130.title: OAR 635-056-0130, Classification Requests
or-635-056-0130.note: Subsection (1) is what makes Oregon a closed-list state: for species not listed in the rules, no person may possess, import, purchase, sell or exchange the species. An animal that is simply absent from all three lists is barred, not unregulated, and the only routes are a petition to the commission or a request to the director to classify it as Noncontrolled.

or-496-004.title: Or. Rev. Stat. § 496.004(19), definition of wildlife
or-496-004.note: Fish, shellfish, amphibians and reptiles, feral swine, wild birds as defined by commission rule and other wild mammals as defined by commission rule. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife by statute with no rule needed, which is why every reptile question in Oregon runs through OAR 635-056. Terrestrial invertebrates are outside it.

or-603-052-1320.title: OAR 603-052-1320, Approved Species (Non-Regulated)
or-603-052-1320.note: Oregon's second closed list, run by the Department of Agriculture and covering terrestrial invertebrates, which the Fish and Wildlife rules never reach. Subsection (3) bars possessing any live invertebrate not on the list without a Department permit, and subsection (1) limits the clearance to stock collected within the continental United States. The list is long and written to species with the intended use in brackets, and most pet-trade arachnids, myriapods and roaches are on it. It does not apply to marine or aquatic invertebrates.

ct-deep-fact-sheets.title: Connecticut DEEP wildlife fact sheets, listing status
ct-deep-fact-sheets.note: DEEP's own species pages carry the state listing status in their header, which is what decides whether an animal is a Category Four Wild Animal under § 26-55-6. The eastern box turtle and the eastern hog-nosed snake are both State Species of Special Concern; the common snapping turtle is not listed. Fact sheet URLs follow the common name with hyphens, but not predictably: eastern-hog-nosed-snake works and eastern-hognose-snake does not.

md-10-902.title: Md. Code, Natural Resources § 10-902, Permit required for native wildlife
md-10-902.note: The captive wildlife permit requirement, and the reason a native Maryland mammal is not a free pet here: anyone wishing to possess any wildlife native to Maryland must first obtain a permit or licence from the Department. Subsection (b)(2) lets the Secretary exempt species by regulation, which is what COMAR 08.03.11 does for reptiles and amphibians. Section 10-903 gives a separate power to restrict NON-native wildlife by regulation, which Maryland has used for aquatic organisms and not for pet mammals, birds or reptiles. Section 10-101(dd) defines wildlife broadly enough to reach an invertebrate, but the permit only ever attaches to natives.

md-snapping-turtle.title: COMAR 08.02.06, Snapping Turtles
md-snapping-turtle.note: Maryland handles the snapping turtle through the Fisheries Service rather than the wildlife rules, which is why it appears on none of the three native herptile lists in COMAR 08.03.11. This chapter governs taking one from the wild: prohibited gear, a season, a measuring method and a harvest permit card.

tn-70-1-101.title: Tenn. Code Ann. § 70-1-101(40), definition of wildlife
tn-70-1-101.note: Wild vertebrates, mollusks, crustaceans and fish. The classification scheme in § 70-4-403 applies to "live wildlife", so this definition sets its outer limit and leaves every terrestrial arthropod outside it. Same reproduction caveat as the classification statute.

tn-twra-permits.title: Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency, Wildlife Permits Available
tn-twra-permits.note: The agency page that administers the classification statute, useful for two things. It restates the § 70-4-404(c)(1) position in one line, "Personal possession of any Class 1 species is not allowed", and adds that Class I animals may be held only by permitted exhibitors and commercial propagators, which is how the agency reads a fee schedule that still lists a $150 personal possession permit for grandfathered animals. And it names the rule chapter carrying the commission's own additions to the classes, 1660-01-18, Rules and Regulations of Live Wildlife, which sits on publications.tnsosfiles.com and cannot be read from this container.

tx-nongame.title: 31 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 65.325-65.331, Commercial Nongame Permits, with Tex. Parks & Wild. Code § 67.001
tx-nongame.note: The rule that decides a Texas pet question whenever the animal is native, and the one the dangerous wild animal statute distracts from. § 65.327(a) starts from a prohibition, "no person may collect, acquire, possess, import, export, cause the import or export of, or engage in a commercial activity involving nongame wildlife", and § 65.327(b)(3) then gives an unlicensed keeper two numbers: 25 of a species on the § 65.331(d) list, six of anything else. Three definitions carry the weight. § 65.325(a) says nongame wildlife "includes captive-bred nongame wildlife", so buying from a breeder does not lift the cap. The same sentence limits the subchapter to VERTEBRATE wildlife, which is narrower than the statute it implements, since Parks & Wild. Code § 67.001 says "vertebrate and invertebrate", and that gap is what leaves every terrestrial invertebrate outside the scheme entirely. And § 65.326(2) defines commercial activity as "the sale, offer for sale, exchange, or barter", so buying is not itself commercial activity, and § 65.327(b)(1)(B) lets a permitted dealer "sell lawfully obtained nongame wildlife to anyone". The two species lists are attached figures rather than statutory text: the (d) list names about 100 species, and the (e) list is longer and expressly "not limited to" what it names, so a native species on neither list falls to the six cap.

tx-64-002.title: Tex. Parks & Wild. Code § 64.002, Protection of Nongame Birds
tx-64-002.note: A very wide prohibition and a one-sentence carve-out for the whole pet trade. Subsection (a) makes it unlawful to "catch, kill, injure, pursue, or possess, dead or alive, or purchase, sell, expose for sale, transport, ship, or receive or deliver for transportation, a bird that is not a game bird", which read alone would reach every pet bird in the state. Subsection (d) answers it: "Canaries, parrots, and other exotic nongame birds may be sold, purchased, and kept as domestic pets." A summary that quotes only (a) makes Texas look like a bird ban state.

tx-exotic-snakes.title: Tex. Parks & Wild. Code § 43.851 and 31 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 55.651-55.653, Controlled Exotic Snakes
tx-exotic-snakes.note: Texas regulates six constrictors by name and every nonvenomous snake beyond them not at all. The list is in the statute at § 43.851(a)(2) and repeated in the rule at 31 TAC § 55.651(2): African rock python, Asiatic rock python, Burmese python, green anaconda, reticulated python, southern African python, plus any hybrid, plus all venomous snakes not indigenous to Texas. H.B. 2326 in 2021 added Python bivittatus by name, after the Burmese was split off from Python molurus and the older wording left it arguable. A recreational permit is available to private keepers under 31 TAC § 55.652(a)(1), which is what separates this from a ban, and § 55.653(c) makes the sales receipt a temporary permit for 21 days from purchase.

ma-131-23.title: M.G.L. c. 131, § 23, propagation, dealing in, and possession of fish, birds, mammals, reptiles or amphibians
ma-131-23.note: The licensing statute behind the exemption list, and the origin of the categorical bar. It directs the director to draw up the special exemption list against four criteria and then forbids listing anything protected: "No animal listed in any category of the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources' Red Data Books shall be listed; no animal protected by either federal endangered species law or by section 4 of chapter 131A shall be listed." It also provides for individual licences: "For the granting of an individual license for an animal that is not on the special exemption list, the applicant shall satisfy the director that he can maintain in good health, properly confine and protect the animal." And it grandfathers a keeper whose animal is later removed from the list, for that animal's lifetime, on evidence of when it was acquired.

ma-131-77a.title: M.G.L. c. 131, § 77A, wild canid and felid hybrids
ma-131-77a.note: A flat prohibition with one exit. "No person shall possess, sell, trade, breed, import, export or release a wild canid hybrid or wild felid hybrid, except as otherwise provided by rules and regulations of the division." The exit is the last paragraph: the section does not apply to "a domesticated show or pet cat registered with a nationally or internationally recognized breeding association or registry which certifies the pedigree and registration of such cat to be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of three generations." So Massachusetts writes a generation rule without using filial numbers, and 321 CMR 9.02(2)(e) points to this section by treating wild felid hybrids as the one hybrid class that is not automatically domestic.

ma-321-10-90.title: 321 CMR 10.90, Massachusetts list of endangered, threatened and special concern species
ma-321-10-90.note: The third leg of the categorical bar in 321 CMR 9.01(3)(c), and the one that catches ordinary pet-trade animals. Three entries matter for this map: the Eastern Box Turtle (Terrapene carolina), special concern; the Eastern Hog-nosed Snake (Heterodon platirhinos), special concern; and the Eastern Ratsnake (Pantherophis alleghaniensis), endangered, which the exemption list already carves out of Pantherophis by name. The tiger salamander is NOT on it, so the general amphibian clearance reaches it.

ma-masswildlife-pets.title: MassWildlife, Wildlife as pets
ma-masswildlife-pets.note: The agency's own restatement of 321 CMR 9.00, cached because it answers two things the regulation leaves open. It reads the categorical bar the same way this map does, saying that any animal "listed in any rarity category of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature Red List of Threatened Species, any category of federal endangered species law, or listed on the Massachusetts List of Endangered, Threatened, and Special Concern species may not be possessed without a permit", and it paraphrases the reptile groups as "except rare species". And it states what a licence application actually gets you: permits "are issued only for certain scientific, educational, commercial, or other specific reasons" and "You will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet." It carries its own disclaimer that the lists "may not be all-inclusive", and it is inconsistent with itself on turtles, where it omits the rarity clause it applies to snakes and geckos, so the regulation governs where the two differ.

ne-37-477.title: Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 37-245, 37-246, 37-247, 37-477 and 37-479
ne-37-477.note: The statute does two things the regulation does not. § 37-477(2) is a flat ban with no permit behind it: "no person shall keep in captivity in this state any wolf, any skunk, or any member of the families Felidae and Ursidae", excepting only Felis domesticus, accredited zoos and public facilities, and lynx or bobcat fur producers. And §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define wild birds and wild mammals by geography rather than by wildness, as species "native to, migrating to or through, or having established free-ranging populations in the State of Nebraska". That definition is the hinge of the whole state: a Nebraska native is caught by the captive wildlife scheme and an exotic is not, which sends the exotic question to the importation list instead. § 37-247 defines wildlife far more broadly, reaching every arthropod and invertebrate, and that breadth sits awkwardly with an importation list containing only mammals and birds.

fl-turtles.title: 68A-25.002, F.A.C., General Provisions for Taking, Possession and Sale of Reptiles
fl-turtles.note: The rule that reaches Florida's native turtles, and it is separate from both the captive wildlife chapter and the nonnative one, which is why it is easy to miss. Subsection (6) caps take at one turtle per day, bars taking snapping turtles, cooters and two other groups from the wild entirely, caps possession at two for the Florida native box turtles and two other species, and bars buying or selling any turtle taken from the wild. None of it turns on a permit for an ordinary keeper; it is a set of numbers and a sale ban.

fl-arthropods.title: 5B-57.004, F.A.C., Introduction, Possession or Movement of Arthropods, Plant Pests and Biological Control Agents
fl-arthropods.note: The rule that catches invertebrates in Florida, and it belongs to the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services rather than to FWC, which is why reading only the wildlife chapters gets this wrong. It makes it unlawful to possess "any arthropod ... regulated by the Department or the USDA" without a state permit, unless a federal PPQ 526 has issued with the Department's concurrence. The test is therefore federal as much as state: an arthropod USDA treats as a plant pest is caught, and one it does not is not. That splits the four invertebrates on this map, since the giant African millipede and the Madagascar hissing cockroach are both moved under PPQ 526 and a tarantula and a scorpion are not plant pests at all. Permits turn on containment: the Department must find the animal can be contained to prevent escape.

ny-part-575.title: 6 NYCRR Part 575, Prohibited and Regulated Invasive Species
ny-part-575.note: A two-tier invasive species scheme that is much milder than the name suggests for two animals on this map. Prohibited species may not be possessed with intent to sell, or sold, imported, purchased, transported, introduced or propagated. REGULATED species "shall be legal to possess, sell, buy, propagate and transport" and may only not be knowingly introduced into a free-living state. The monk parakeet and the red-eared slider are both on the regulated list, not the prohibited one, alongside goldfish and koi. The duty the listing creates falls on the seller: a business selling a regulated species must label it as such.

ny-endangered-list.title: NYSDEC list of endangered, threatened and special concern species (6 NYCRR Part 182)
ny-endangered-list.note: The list that decides which native New York herptiles are protected twice over. Three entries matter here: the eastern tiger salamander, Ambystoma tigrinum, is ENDANGERED; the woodland box turtle, Terrapene carolina carolina, is threatened or special concern; and the eastern hognose snake, Heterodon platyrhinos, is special concern. Species of special concern are named directly in the definition of protected wildlife at ECL § 11-0103(6)(c), so a listing here is a second and independent route to the same prohibition the small game definition already produces. No flying squirrel appears anywhere on the list.

nj-njac-7-25.title: N.J.A.C. 7:25 Subchapter 4, Endangered, Nongame and Exotic Wildlife
nj-njac-7-25.note: NJDEP's own courtesy copy of the whole of N.J.A.C. 7:25. Subchapter 4 starts at 7:25-4.1 and carries the definitions, the permit requirement at 4.2, the three species lists at 4.3, 4.4 and 4.8, the pet bar at 4.9(a)3 and 4.15(b), and the state endangered list at 4.13. The three list PDFs the Division hands out are extracts of this.

nj-7-25-4-3.title: N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.3 Exotic Species and Nongame species requiring a permit for possession
nj-7-25-4-3.note: The Division's handout of the 4.3 permit list. It is open-ended, 'include, but are not limited to', and works by family as often as by species, so Pythonidae, Boidae, Lampropeltis, Varanus, Scincidae and Gekkonidae each answer several pet species at once.

nj-njsa-23-4-63-3.title: N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3, Possession, release of certain animals, prohibited; terms defined
nj-njsa-23-4-63-3.note: The statutory possession bar that sits above subchapter 4. New Jersey publishes its statutes through a Folio viewer that does not serve a plain document URL, so the section was read from this reproduction and is cited to the official section. Its definition of 'exotic animal' is narrower than the rule's: it reaches mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, molluscs and crustaceans only, and it carves out domesticated companion animals.

ut-r657-3a.title: Utah Admin. Code R657-3a, Collection, Importation, Transportation and Possession of Animals
ut-r657-3a.note: The umbrella rule that replaced R657-3, which no longer exists. R657-3a carries the definitions and the collection, importation, possession and propagation sections; the species classifications live in R657-3b for birds and mammals, R657-3c for aquatic animals, and R657-53 for herps. 3a-2(2)(b) expressly puts Amphibia and Reptilia outside it. Its 3a-2(20)(b) is the inverted default: a species that has not gone through the division's classification process is a prohibited species.

ut-23a-1-101.title: Utah Code § 23A-1-101, Wildlife Resources Code definitions
ut-23a-1-101.note: The statutory definition that decides Utah's invertebrates. Subsection (65) limits wildlife to crustaceans, molluscs and vertebrate animals living in nature, so an arachnid, an insect or a myriapod is outside the Division of Wildlife Resources' authority entirely. Note that le.utah.gov serves the section text only from the versioned URL, /xcode/Title23A/Chapter1/C23A-1-S101_<version>.html; the plain section page is a shell.

al-220-2-98.title: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.98, Invertebrate Species Regulation
al-220-2-98.note: Alabama does have an invertebrate rule, which most states do not, and it is a closed list of protected natives: cave crayfish, mussels, snails, one beetle. It protects rather than restricts, so a pet arthropod is outside it.

al-220-2-142.title: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.142, Turtle Dealer/Farmer Regulation
al-220-2-142.note: Commercial turtle rule. Its one provision that reaches an ordinary keeper is 2(b), which allows taking up to two turtles a day from the wild for personal use and caps it there.

in-312-9-5.title: 312 IAC 9-5, Reptiles and Amphibians
in-312-9-5.note: The rule 312 IAC 9-11 does not reach. 9-5-1(b) makes every reptile and amphibian native to Indiana a protected wild animal, 9-5-6(f) caps possession at four per species, and 9-5-7 bars selling a native species "regardless of place of origin" against a list of 99 taxa given by binomial. 9-5-7(f) then exempts captive-bred albinistic, leucistic and xanthic morphs. Indiana's own rules site, iar.iga.in.gov, serves its React shell for every path including its own script bundles, so this is read from Cornell LII and cited to the official section.

in-312-9-9.title: 312 IAC 9-9, Invertebrates
in-312-9-9.note: Five short sections covering crayfish, mussels, endangered invertebrates, and then 9-9-5, which says any invertebrate the rule does not identify is an exempted wild animal. 312 IAC 9-1-6 defines that term as a wild animal "which is unprotected and may be taken or possessed at any time". It is the most explicit invertebrate answer any state on this map gives.

ok-800-25-7.title: OAC 800:25-7-7 to 800:25-7-9, Reptiles and Amphibians
ok-800-25-7.note: The part that reaches Oklahoma's own herps, and the one that 800:25-25-3 does not answer. 7-7(2) requires a hunting or fishing licence of anyone taking or possessing a reptile or amphibian, 7-8 gives every reptile a year-round season at six per species per day and in possession with a twelve-species closed list, and 7-9 does the same for amphibians at four. 7-7(1) separately bars commercial activity involving wild-collected indigenous species.

ok-800-15-9-3.title: OAC 800:15-9-3, Commercial turtle harvest; general operating provisions
ok-800-15-9-3.note: Sits in the commercial aquatic species chapter, and its subsection (3) is the sentence everyone quotes about Oklahoma box turtles: possession, buying and selling of box turtles is prohibited. The Department's own noncommercial turtle page reads it more narrowly, as a sale bar sitting alongside a six-per-species possession limit.

ok-29-7-502.title: 29 O.S. § 7-502, General Prohibition on Possession of Wildlife; Exceptions
ok-29-7-502.note: The statutory possession bar, and much narrower than its title suggests. It reaches wildlife during a closed season, endangered or threatened species, and native bears and native cats that will reach fifty pounds. Subsection (B)(4) then exempts anyone possessing legally obtained wildlife from a source other than the wild as a pet, which is the provision that decides most captive-bred animals in Oklahoma and which nothing else in the code says as plainly.

ok-odwc-turtle.title: Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation, Turtle & Bullfrog Regulations
ok-odwc-turtle.note: The Department's summary of the noncommercial turtle rules, which is where it states its own reading of the box turtle clause: six of each species in possession, and terrestrial turtles may not be sold. The page says outright that it is an interpretive summary and not a legal document.

vt-domestic-list.title: Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department, Domestic Species List, August 2010
vt-domestic-list.note: The third of Vermont's three lists and the one earlier sittings could not read; it extracts cleanly with pypdf from this URL, fetched with a browser User-Agent. It is what makes the domestic cat, the dog, the ferret and the domestic rabbit lawful in a state where anything unlisted is Restricted. Its bird section is a closed list of about thirty psittacines, every one marked Captive Bred Only, and it decides the parrot cells: budgerigar, cockatiel, lovebirds, rosellas and Psittacula are on it, and Cacatua, Psittacus and Myiopsitta are not.

wi-169-04.title: Wis. Stat. § 169.04, Possession of live wild animals, with § 169.01 definitions
wi-169-04.note: The section that answers almost every pet in Wisconsin, and it answers by exempting rather than by listing. 169.04(4)(b) exempts nonnative wild animals from any licence unless they are endangered, certain hunting-preserve game birds, nonnative migratory waterfowl, or harmful wild animals. 169.04(4)(a) then exempts seventeen native groups, arthropods first among them. 169.01(37) defines a wild animal as one "of a wild nature that is normally found in the wild and that is not a domestic animal", which is what keeps domestic pets out of the chapter altogether.

nc-113-129.title: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 113-129(15), definition of wild animals
nc-113-129.note: The definition that decides North Carolina and is easy to miss, because the answer is not in the captivity licence section but in what that section can reach. Wild animals are game animals, fur-bearers, feral swine and other wild mammals, and then reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates only where they are on the federal endangered or threatened list. Everything else in those three groups is outside the Wildlife Resources Commission's jurisdiction, which is why North Carolina has no state reptile law worth the name.

sc-123-151.title: S.C. Code Regs. 123-151.3 and 123-151.4, native reptiles and amphibians (Act 177)
sc-123-151.note: The 2021 native reptile rules. 123-151.3(A) bars selling, purchasing, trading, exchanging, bartering, exporting, shipping, transferring or re-homing any native reptile or amphibian, with twelve exceptions that are mostly named snakes under a size limit. 123-151.4 adds possession caps for turtles, two for the eastern box turtle with shell notching and registration. 123-151.4(I) is the clause that matters most: the pet-trade exemption at S.C. Code § 50-16-60 does not privilege a native reptile.

oh-1531-01.title: Ohio Rev. Code § 1531.01(X), definition of wild animals
oh-1531-01.note: Ohio defines wild animals as "mollusks, crustaceans, aquatic insects, fish, reptiles, amphibians, wild birds, wild quadrupeds, and all other wild mammals". The word aquatic in front of insects is the whole answer for a terrestrial invertebrate: a land insect or an arachnid is not a wild animal in Ohio and the Division of Wildlife has nothing to say about it.

ar-code-0900.title: Arkansas Game and Fish Commission Code Book, Chapter 09.00 (Captive Wildlife) and Chapter 01.00 definitions
ar-code-0900.note: Code 09.01 makes it unlawful to hold any live wildlife captive unless otherwise specified, and its exceptions include terrestrial invertebrates. Code 09.02 conditions non-native wildlife on sourcing and veterinary certification. Code 09.14 caps native wildlife pets at six per household. Chapter 01.00 supplies the two definitions that decide the rest: WILDLIFE reaches "all other wild animals, regardless of classification", and WILD means "living in a state of nature and not domesticated". Addendum R1.02 closes with "Species not listed in Addenda R1.01, R1.02, or R1.03 are prohibited until evaluated", so absence is a bar rather than a silence.

me-09-137-c7.title: 09-137 CMR ch. 7, Rules for Importation, Possession, Propagation, Rehabilitation, and Exhibition of Wildlife
me-09-137-c7.note: Maine is a closed-list state and § 7.06(4) is the sentence that makes it one: "A person may not possess any species that has not been categorized", and an uncategorised species "will not be eligible for a permit under this chapter". The four categories are the Unrestricted List, the Prohibited list at § 7.18(1), and Restricted Categories 1 and 2. Category 1 permits go only to exhibitors, rehabilitators, USDA-registered laboratories and accredited research facilities, so it is not a pet tier; Category 2 is open to "an individual with demonstrated experience". § 7.05 and § 7.06(5) are the route for getting an unlisted species classified.

me-12-12152.title: 12 M.R.S. § 12152, Permit to possess wildlife in captivity
me-12-12152.note: Subsection 1-A is the bar: "a person may not import wildlife into or possess wildlife in the State or receive or possess wildlife imported into the State", with the unrestricted list as the exception. Subsection 1-B is the only wild-take allowance and it reaches reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates native to Maine and nothing else: five amphibians per species, two reptiles per species, invertebrates with no limit, with importation, sale, exhibition, propagation and export all still barred without a permit. It does not reach native mammals.

mo-3csr10-4.title: 3 CSR 10-4, Missouri Wildlife Code: General Provisions
mo-3csr10-4.note: The general prohibition at 3 CSR 10-4.110(1) bars possessing any form of wildlife except as the Code permits, and then ends with the clause that answers every invertebrate question in the state: "however, this Code shall not apply to other invertebrates except as specifically provided". 3 CSR 10-4.117 is the separate prohibited species rule, which is fish, crayfish and aquatic plants.

mo-252-020.title: Missouri Revised Statutes § 252.020, definitions
mo-252-020.note: Defines wildlife as "all wild birds, mammals, fish and other aquatic and amphibious forms, and all other wild animals, regardless of classification". The open catch-all is broad enough to reach an insect, which is why the disclaimer in 3 CSR 10-4.110(1) rather than the definition is what puts invertebrates outside the Code.

mo-mdc-field-guides.title: Missouri Department of Conservation, A Guide to Missouri's Snakes and A Guide to Missouri's Lizards
mo-mdc-field-guides.note: The agency's own species accounts, which is what "native to Missouri" in 3 CSR 10-9.110(2) turns on. The snake guide gives the state five Pantherophis (emoryi, obsoletus, spiloides, ramspotti, vulpinus) and no P. guttatus, and gives the eastern milksnake, Lampropeltis triangulum, a statewide distribution. The lizard guide (https://mdc.mo.gov/sites/default/files/2023-04/E00213%20A%20Guide%20to%20Missouri%27s%20Lizards.pdf) runs to eleven natives plus one introduced wall lizard and contains no anole.

id-36-201-202.title: Idaho Code §§ 36-201 and 36-202, classifications and definitions
id-36-201-202.note: § 36-202(g) defines wildlife as "any form of animal life, native or exotic, generally living in a state of nature", excluding only domestic cervidae. § 36-201 then lists the eight classes the commission may sort wildlife into, all of them vertebrate groups, with predatory wildlife fixed by statute at seven named animals. IDAPA 13.01.06.250 sweeps up the remainder: "Unprotected Wildlife includes all wildlife not classified in the preceding categories."

id-130106.title: IDAPA 13.01.06, Rules Governing Classification and Protection of Wildlife
id-130106.note: Section 200 is the Protected Nongame list: fourteen named mammals, all native birds except game birds, all native amphibians, all native reptiles and seven fish. Section 250 makes everything unclassified Unprotected Wildlife. Worth reading alongside 13.01.10 for two reasons: the northern flying squirrel is Protected Nongame at 200.01(j), and no invertebrate is classified anywhere in the chapter.

nh-rsa-207-1.title: N.H. Rev. Stat. § 207:1, definitions
nh-rsa-207-1.note: Paragraph XXXV is what Fis 800 means by wildlife, and it names invertebrates in terms: "all species of mammals, birds, fish, mollusks, crustaceans, amphibians, invertebrates, reptiles or their progeny or eggs which, whether raised in captivity or not, are normally found in a wild state". That is the provision that pulls a terrestrial arthropod into the Fis 804 scheme, where it is on none of the three lists.

wy-23-1-101.title: Wyo. Stat. § 23-1-101(a)(xiii), definition of wildlife
wy-23-1-101.note: A closed list of taxa: "all wild mammals, birds, fish, amphibians, reptiles, crustaceans and mollusks, and wild bison designated by the Wyoming game and fish commission and the Wyoming livestock board within Wyoming". No insect or arachnid is in it, which is what puts a terrestrial arthropod outside both Commission regulations. Chapter 69 repeats the same closed list at Section 2(c) for cold-blooded wildlife.

ky-301-2-081.title: 301 KAR 2:081, Transportation and holding of live native wildlife
ky-301-2-081.note: The companion to 2:082 and the rule that reaches any Kentucky native. § 1(3) defines native wildlife as species that have historically existed, currently exist or have naturally expanded their range into Kentucky, "regardless of ... origin or location of an individual animal" and of "being captive-bred or taken from the wild", so captive breeding is no exit. § 2(3) then requires a captive wildlife permit before acquiring one, with a five-per-species free allowance for native reptiles and amphibians at § 2(5) and nothing comparable for mammals. § 3(2) is the noncommercial permit, § 4 the transportation permit, § 6 the prohibited natives.

ky-krs-150-010.title: KRS 150.010, definitions for chapter
ky-krs-150-010.note: Defines wildlife as "any normally undomesticated animal, alive or dead, including without limitations any wild mammal, bird, fish, reptile, amphibian, or other terrestrial or aquatic life, whether or not possessed in controlled environment, bred, hatched, or born in captivity". The open catch-all reaches an insect, and the head term, "normally undomesticated animal", is what puts a domestic rabbit outside before the exemption list is even reached.

la-rs-56-8.title: La. R.S. 56:8, definitions
la-rs-56-8.note: Two definitions decide most of Louisiana. Subsection (152): "Wildlife means all species of wild vertebrates", a closed definition that leaves every terrestrial invertebrate outside the Department of Wildlife and Fisheries. Subsection (151)(a)(i): game quadrupeds are "wild deer, bears, squirrels, and wild rabbits", which is what pulls a flying squirrel into the game breeder scheme and leaves a domestic rabbit out of it.

la-76-v-107.title: LAC 76:V.107, Game Breeder's License
la-76-v-107.note: The rule that reaches a native Louisiana mammal kept as a pet. § 107(C)(2)(a): "A game breeder's license must be issued before any game quadrupeds (deer, rabbits, squirrels, etc.) are obtained", and § 107(C)(1)(a) bars taking them from the wild at all. § 107(B)(6) writes pen specifications for "Squirrels (gray, fox, red, flying and others endemic to North America)" by name, so the flying squirrel is expressly inside the scheme rather than caught by inference.

wa-rcw-77-08-010.title: Wash. Rev. Code § 77.08.010, definitions, and WAC 220-640-200
wa-rcw-77-08-010.note: The sentence that decides most of Washington is subsection (74): "Wildlife means all species of the animal kingdom whose members exist in Washington in a wild state." The list that follows is inclusive down to invertebrates, so the taxonomic reach is total, and the qualifier is geographic: a species that does not live wild in Washington is not Washington wildlife at all. Subsection (72) does the same for "wild animals", class Mammalia, and expressly drops feral domestic mammals and old world rats and mice. The other half of the scheme is subsection (13), deleterious exotic wildlife, which is a designated list rather than a category: WAC 220-640-200 designates the mute swan, mongooses, wild boar, javelina, six bovid genera and a run of cervids, and nothing else.

va-4vac15-20-50.title: 4 Va. Admin. Code § 15-20-50, definitions of wild, native, naturalized, nonnative (exotic) and domestic animal
va-4vac15-20-50.note: The definitions that decide which of Virginia's two schemes reaches an animal, and the one place a species can be written out of both. "Wild animal" is "any member of the animal kingdom, except domestic animals", and the list that follows names arthropods expressly. "Nonnative (exotic) animal" excludes domestic AND naturalized species, so a naturalized animal is not an exotic and goes to the native rules instead. The domestic animal list is closed and unusually specific: it clears "Domesticated breeds of European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) recognized by the American Rabbit Breeders Association, Inc." and "Domesticated morphs of red cornsnake (Pantherophis guttatus) visibly distinguishable from native red cornsnakes". Native and naturalized status is fixed by the department's List of Native and Naturalized Fauna of Virginia, incorporated by reference: https://dwr.virginia.gov/wp-content/uploads/media/virginia-native-naturalized-species.pdf

va-4vac15-360-10.title: 4 Va. Admin. Code § 15-360-10, taking aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, and nongame fish for private use
va-4vac15-360-10.note: The rule the exotic permit table does not reach, and the one that answers a Virginia native or naturalized herp: one individual of any native or naturalized species of amphibian or reptile per physical address, live, for private use and not for sale or export. It covers aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles and nongame fish, and no mammal.

CA.quote: Order Insectivora-Shrews, Moles, Hedgehogs, etc. All species (D)

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's licence rule works by taxonomic order rather than by species, which is what catches the hedgehog. The entry is "Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species", spelling and all, so there is no room to argue about which hedgehog. DNR puts insectivores among the exotics that "may not be held as pets in Georgia". The reason a licence does not help is in the statute rather than the rule. O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4(b)(1) says wild animal licences "will be issued only to persons engaged in the wholesale or retail wild animal business or persons exhibiting wild animals to the public", and permits only for scientific or educational purposes, for a capuchin monkey held by a person with a permanent disability, or to a pond owner for grass carp. There is no pet category anywhere in it, which is why the rule has to write an express pet exception where it wants one, as it does for the European ferret and the sugar glider.

HI.quote: The introduction into Hawaii of live animals or live non-domestic animals ... is prohibited except for those animals on the lists
HI.note: Not named. Barred by the default rule. The only hedgehog Hawaii names is Hemiechinus auritis, not the pet species.

PA.quote: all bears, coyotes, lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs, cougars, wolves and any crossbreed of these animals which have similar characteristics in appearance or features
PA.note: No hedgehog appears in the definition, or anything resembling one. The ban is the Game Commission's reading of includes, but is not limited to. House co-sponsorship memo 44994, filed by Rep. David Zimmerman in January 2025 to legalise hedgehogs and sugar gliders, describes it the same way: they are banned through the Commission's regulations and their interpretation of Title 34. Versions of that bill have been introduced every session since 2017 without passing.

DC.note: Closed list permits 'domesticated rodents and rabbits'. Hedgehogs are Eulipotyphla, not rodents, so no category fits.

NYC.quote: No person shall sell or give to another person, possess, harbor, keep, or yard wild or other animals identified in this section ... other than in: (i) a zoological park or aquarium ...; or (ii) a laboratory ...; or (iii) a veterinary hospital ...; or (iv) a temporary exhibit, performance or display that has been issued a permit by the Commissioner. ... For the purposes of this Code, a wild animal is deemed to be any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings and all such animals are hereby prohibited ... Such animals shall also include: (i) any animals specified by the Commissioner in regulations ...; (ii) any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule; and (iii) any of the following animals:
NYC.note: Clause (23) covers "Insectivorous mammals (Insectivora)" and lists "hedge hog" as its last example, spelled as two words. The order name is obsolete, since hedgehogs are now placed in Eulipotyphla, but the animal is named, so the taxonomy does not help. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: Mammals: ... iv. European hedgehog - Erinaceus europeaus;
NJ.note: The 4.3 permit list names one hedgehog, the European hedgehog, Erinaceus europaeus. The hedgehog kept as a pet is the African pygmy, Atelerix albiventris, which is not that animal and is not named anywhere in the subchapter. It reaches the same answer by the other road: 4.4 does not exempt it, so 4.5 requires a permit for it as an "other" exotic mammal. Worth saying plainly because the species mismatch invites the wrong conclusion in both directions, that the listing does not apply so the animal is free, or that the listing applies so the pet species is covered by it.

ME.quote: Atelerix albiventris  Four-toed Hedgehog, African Pygmy Hedgehog
ME.note: Commonly misreported as a permit state.

WI.note: Not a designated harmful wild animal; Ch. 169 licensing does not reach it. Commonly misreported as a permit state.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Named at (14)(b) alongside the gerbil. Florida exempts it from the permit scheme entirely rather than putting it in Class III, so there is nothing to apply for and no renewal.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the African pygmy hedgehog is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. Erinaceidae appears in none of them, so the African pygmy hedgehog is unrestricted.

MA.quote: List of Mammals. (a) The following mammals may be kept without a permit: 1. Four-toed (African pygmy) hedgehog (Erinaceus albiventris) (= Atelerix pruneri) 2. Chinchilla (Chinchilla spp.) derived from captive stock. 3. Deer Mouse and White-footed Mouse 4. Degu (Octodon degus) 5. Egyptian Spiny Mouse 6. House Mouse 7. Jerboas 8. Norway Rat 9. Paca 10. Southern Flying Squirrel (Glaucomys volans) 11. Striped hamster ... 12. Sugar Glider (Petaurus breviceps) 13. American Bison
MA.note: Named at 9.01(12)(a)(1), using the older binomial Erinaceus albiventris with Atelerix pruneri given as a synonym. The mammal list is thirteen entries long and being on it is the only way a wild mammal is keepable here, so the naming is the whole answer.

CO.quote: African pygmy hedgehog (Atelerix albiventris, Erinaceus albiventris)
CO.note: Named on the unregulated wildlife list, so no CPW licence. The species matters here more than in most states: § 008(B)(9) of the prohibited list bars Erinaceus generally, along with the whole of Hemiechinus and Paraechinus, and exempts only Erinaceus albiventris and Atelerix albiventris by name. So the pet African pygmy hedgehog is cleared and the European, long-eared, desert, Brandt's, Indian and bare-bellied hedgehogs are prohibited, a split CPW's mammal list sets out row by row. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Erinaceomorpha. Common names include: European hedgehogs, gymnures, and moonrats. Except members of the genus Atelerix, which are not restricted.
AZ.note: Arizona restricts hedgehogs as an order and then exempts the pet genus by name, so the African pygmy is legal and the European is not.

OR.quote: Four-toed hedgehog -- Erinaceidae -- Atelerix albiventris.
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. The African pygmy hedgehog is named to the species. Which species matters here more than in most states: the three Eurasian hedgehogs, Erinaceus europaeus, E. concolor and E. amurensis, are on the prohibited list. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

WA.note: Not within the enumerated definition.

OH.note: On neither list, so no state permit.

TX.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means: (A) a lion; (B) a tiger; (C) an ocelot; (D) a cougar; (E) a leopard; (F) a cheetah; (G) a jaguar; (H) a bobcat; (I) a lynx; (J) a serval; (K) a caracal; (L) a hyena; (M) a bear; (N) a coyote; (O) a jackal; (P) a baboon; (Q) a chimpanzee; (R) an orangutan; (S) a gorilla; or (T) any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision.
TX.note: Texas has no exotic pet permit scheme, so an animal is legal here unless a specific list names it. The dangerous wild animal list is closed and contains no insectivore. The nongame possession caps in 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O reach only wildlife indigenous to Texas, which Atelerix albiventris is not, and Texas has no importation permit for exotic mammals.

MI.note: Outside all three bodies of law; kept as an ordinary pet.

IL.quote: "Dangerous animal" means a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, bear, hyena, wolf or coyote. Dangerous animal does not mean any herptiles included in the Herptiles-Herps Act.
IL.note: Illinois runs a closed list of 15 named mammals plus a blanket bar on primates, and it has no catch-all clause, no size test and no dangerousness test. An animal that is not on the list and is not native Illinois wildlife is simply outside the statute. No insectivore appears on it, and no hedgehog is on the Part 805 injurious species list, which is the other place Illinois bars an exotic mammal. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: all members of the Felidae family including, but not limited to, lions, tigers, cougars, leopards, cheetahs, ocelots, and servals, but not including domestic cats or cats recognized as a domestic breed, registered as a domestic breed, and shown as a domestic breed by a national or international multibreed cat registry association; (2) bears; and (3) all nonhuman primates
MN.note: Minnesota's regulated animal definition is three groups and nothing else: the cat family, bears, and non-human primates. No insectivore is in it, and no hedgehog appears on the prohibited invasive species list.

NV.quote: African pygmy hedgehogs (Atelerix albiventris)
NV.note: Named on the no-permit list. Several secondary sources claim hedgehogs are illegal in Nevada; the regulation says otherwise.

VA.note: The permit table works family by family and Erinaceidae appears nowhere in it, so no special permit applies.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. No insectivore appears in the eight clauses, and the African pygmy hedgehog is not native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

NM.quote: Mammal | Hedgehog | Erinaceidae | Atelerix ssp | Hedgehog (Common) | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Resolved from a previous unclear entry now that the list is in hand. The whole genus is covered, so the African pygmy hedgehog of the pet trade is included.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

VT.quote: Erinaceomorpha | Erinaceidae | Atelerix | albiventris | African pygmy hedgehog (U.S. Captive Bred Only)
VT.note: Resolved. The previous entry was left unclear because the Unrestricted list could not be obtained; it is now in hand and the African pygmy hedgehog is on it by name. The condition is the U.S. Captive Bred Only marker, which requires a statement of origin or a certificate of veterinary inspection identifying the business of origin. A wild-caught or foreign-bred hedgehog does not qualify.

UT.cite: Utah Admin. Code R657-3b-1(3); Table 3b-1, domestic mammals and controlled mammals
UT.quote: Domestic mammals and mammalian livestock not covered under this rule ... Hedgehog, "white-bellied", "African pygmy", etc. Atelerix species includes hybrids ... Controlled mammals ... Hedgehogs family Erinaceidae except "while-bellied" (see domestic animals)
UT.note: Utah is unusually careful about the hedgehog and gets the taxonomy right where several states get it wrong. Table 3b-1 lists Atelerix species, described as "white-bellied" or "African pygmy" and expressly including hybrids, among the domestic mammals the rule does not govern. It then lists the rest of family Erinaceidae as controlled, with the parenthetical "except while-bellied (see domestic animals)", typo and all. So the pet hedgehog is free and a European hedgehog would need a certificate of registration. Compare Nebraska, whose importation list says "Eurasian Hedgehogs, Erinaceus spp." and leaves the pet species unanswered. This entry previously cited R657-3, a rule that no longer exists.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Corrected. Hedgehogs appear by name on the exempt mammal list at regulation 6.1.1, so no permit is required. The previous entry treated this animal as a non-exempt wild mammal needing an exotic animal permit, which was the right framework read against the wrong list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q).
TN.note: Tennessee's catch-all sits in the no-permit class rather than the permit class, which is the single fact that decides most questions here: an animal that appears nowhere in Classes I, II, IV or V is Class III and needs no wildlife permit. The African pygmy hedgehog is not on the Class I list, is not native to Tennessee, and is not among the three Class IV species. No insectivore appears anywhere in the classification.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: Previously recorded as unclear on the strength of a secondary source, which was wrong on both counts. North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, so it does not reach a hedgehog, and § 153A-131 leaves everything else to county ordinance. Legal at state level, worth checking your county.

AR.quote: Four-toed or African Pygmy Hedgehog (Atelerix albiventris)

ID.quote: Conventional Pets. Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders.
ID.note: The deleterious exotic animal list reaches only the European hedgehog, Erinaceus europaeus, not the African pygmy hedgehog kept as a pet.

KY.note: On neither the prohibited nor the inherently dangerous list. Not on the Section 7 permit-exempt list either, so a transportation permit is required to bring one in from out of state, but possession itself is unrestricted.

RI.quote: Four-toed (African pygmy) Hedgehog (Erinaceus albiventris) (Atelerix pruneri),

NH.quote: African pigmy hedgehog;

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds... native to the continental United States, and those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri.
MO.note: Not native to Missouri, so not Class I, and not on the § 578.023 list either. Missouri regulates confined wildlife, and an African pygmy hedgehog is neither.

KS.note: Outside the definition of a dangerous regulated animal, which is the only state level restriction on keeping an exotic pet in Kansas.

SC.note: Not a furbearer, cervid, pig, peccary, bovid, coyote, bear or turkey, so no import permit is needed, and Chapter 47-2 reaches only big cats, bears and great apes.

MT.quote: African pygmy hedgehog - Atelerix albiventris and Atelerix algirus;

WV.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means a mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian or aquatic animal, including a hybrid, that is dangerous to humans, other animals or the environment due to its inherent nature and capability to do significant harm.
WV.note: The categories the board is pointed at are bears, big cats, canids, primates, large constrictors, venomous snakes and crocodilians. Nothing in the Act reaches a hedgehog.

AK.quote: Hedgehog, African Pygmy   Erinaceus albiventris

SD.quote: A permit from the board is required to import nondomestic animals.
SD.note: No possession permit: the list runs to carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates, and an insectivore is none of those. Bringing one in from out of state still needs a free entry permit from the Animal Industry Board.

AL.note: Not a rodent, not on the prohibited list, and not federally injurious.

IN.quote: a person must have a permit issued by the department under this rule to possess a wild animal if the wild animal is either of the following: (1) Referenced in this rule. (2) Listed in this article as an endangered species or a threatened species.
IN.note: Referenced nowhere in the rule, so no permit applies.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: That sentence, plus tattooing for mountain lions and wolves, is the whole of the state's prohibition list. No rule currently licenses small exotic pets.

WY.quote: domesticated hedgehog (Erinaceus spp.),
WY.note: Listed as a domesticated animal, and Section 16 lets domestic and domesticated animals be imported or possessed without a permit.

MS.note: The list runs to primates, carnivores, elephants, rhinos, hippos and African buffalo. No insectivore appears.

LA.note: The regulation lists three bears, two wolves, wolf dog hybrids, all non-human primates and six big cats. Nothing smaller appears.

OK.quote: The following wildlife species are exempt from import and export permits, commercial wildlife breeders licenses, noncommercial wildlife breeders licenses and commercial hunting area license requirements... (15) Hedgehogs.

NE.quote: 001.08A Importation: the following wildlife may be imported: Alpaca ... Chinchilla, Chinchilla spp. ... Coatimundi ... Degu, Octodon spp. ... Fox, Vulpes spp. ... Genet ... Gerbil, Gerbillus spp. ... Guinea pig, Cavia porcellus ... Eurasian Hedgehogs, Erinaceus spp. ... Jerboa, greater ... Sugar Glider(s), Petaurus spp. ... Wallabies ... All Ratites, All Waterfowl, All Peafowl, All Game Birds, All Cage and Aviary Birds
NE.note: The importation list reads "Eurasian Hedgehogs, Erinaceus spp." and the pet is the African pygmy hedgehog, Atelerix albiventris, which is neither Eurasian nor an Erinaceus under current taxonomy. Read strictly, the pet hedgehog cannot be imported into Nebraska. There is a real argument the other way, and it is a drafting-vintage argument rather than a wishful one: this species was classified as Erinaceus albiventris for decades, and Massachusetts still writes it that way in its own exemption list, as "Four-toed (African pygmy) hedgehog (Erinaceus albiventris) (= Atelerix pruneri)". So a list written when Nebraska's was may well have meant the pet. Recorded unclear because the common name in the entry, "Eurasian", cuts against the reading that would save it, and nothing published by the Commission resolves it.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: Not a canid, hyaenid, felid, ursid, rhino, elephant, primate or swine, which is the whole of the mammal half of the definition.

CA.quote: Family Mustelidae-All species (D)
CA.note: Exceptions are otters only.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: One of only two animals in the whole Georgia scheme with an express pet exception written into the rule. The European ferret "may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit", on two documented conditions: sexual neutering before seven months of age, and rabies vaccination with a USDA-approved ferret vaccine, with valid documentation of both in the owner's possession. Without the paperwork the animal falls back to Order Carnivora, where no pet licence exists.

DC.quote: Ferrets

NYC.quote: No person shall sell or give to another person, possess, harbor, keep, or yard wild or other animals identified in this section ... other than in: (i) a zoological park or aquarium ...; or (ii) a laboratory ...; or (iii) a veterinary hospital ...; or (iv) a temporary exhibit, performance or display that has been issued a permit by the Commissioner. ... For the purposes of this Code, a wild animal is deemed to be any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings and all such animals are hereby prohibited ... Such animals shall also include: (i) any animals specified by the Commissioner in regulations ...; (ii) any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule; and (iii) any of the following animals:
NYC.note: Named at the end of a clause covering "All fur bearing mammals of the family Mustelidae", and the naming is what matters, because a ferret is not obviously an animal "naturally inclined to do harm" under the standard the section opens with. New York City is the most-litigated ferret ban in the country and the text is unambiguous. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: Mammals: i. Ferrets - Mustela pertorius furo;
NJ.note: The domestic ferret is answered by name on the 4.3 permit list rather than by the catch-all. It is the first mammal on the list, spelled "Mustela pertorius furo" for Mustela putorius furo. The list is written by family as often as by species, and 4.3 is open-ended, "include, but are not limited to", so being on it settles the permit question but not being on it settles nothing. The permit is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, subject to the general possession criteria at 4.7. New Jersey is one of the states where the ferret is a permit animal rather than a banned one or a free one, so the answer is neither of the two extremes people expect from the ferret map.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the domestic ferret is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. Worth separating from New York City, which is a distinct jurisdiction on this map and bans ferrets outright under its Health Code.

CT.quote: "Domestic animal" means any animal that humans have selectively bred in captivity to produce genetic changes affecting the temperament, color, conformation, or other attributes of the species to an extent that makes such animal unique and distinguishable from wild individuals of the species, and that has been raised in a life intimately associated with and advantageous to humans. "Domestic animal" does not include any wild animal raised in captivity, even over many generations, that has become accustomed to human interaction but that is still wild by nature.
CT.note: The domestic ferret is a domestic animal on this definition and so is not a wild animal at all, which is the cleanest of the several routes to the same answer. It matters here more than it looks: Mustelidae is a Category Three Wild Animal, listed with the weasels, mink, fisher, otter and marten, so a wild mustelid is restricted on import and export while the pet ferret sits outside the regulation. This entry previously rested on § 26-40a, which reaches four mammal families and no mustelid; true, but the regulation is the rule that would otherwise catch it.

MA.quote: A person may possess a ferret (mustela furo or mustela putorium furo) for the following purposes:— (1) As a household pet; provided, however, that such pet has been at the time of purchase neutered or spayed and has received inoculation against distemper and rabies or other inoculations that the director may require; and provided, further, that evidence of neutering, spaying and inoculation is kept available for inspection by the director.
MA.note: Legal as a household pet on three conditions that all attach at purchase: neutered or spayed, inoculated against distemper and rabies, and documentary evidence of both kept available for inspection. Breeding is a separate licence at not less than $1,000 a year under § 77(2). The section closes with a hunting prohibition that has teeth in an unexpected way: merely having a ferret in a place where birds or mammals may be found makes the keeper liable to its penalties.

CO.quote: Domesticated races of European ferret (Mustela putorius)
CO.note: On the domestic animal list rather than the unregulated wildlife list, which is the stronger of the two positions: a domestic animal is exempted from Parks and Wildlife Commission regulations outright. Colorado names the domesticated race of Mustela putorius, so the carve-out is for the pet ferret and not for the wild European polecat. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

AZ.note: No Mustelidae entry in the restricted mammal list.

OR.quote: Pursuant to the definition of "wildlife," the following species are not subject to these rules because they are not "wild" ... (10) Ferret (European polecat) — Mustela putorius.
OR.note: This is the strongest position an animal can hold in Oregon. ORS 496.004(19) leaves it to the commission to define which mammals count as wild, and this rule is that definition: the 32 species on it are declared not wild and fall outside the wildlife rules altogether, rather than being permitted by them. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

WA.quote: A person shall not own, possess, keep, harbor, bring into the state, or have custody or control of a potentially dangerous wild animal
WA.note: The definition is enumerated rather than general. Felidae is limited to eight big cats and Canidae to wolves excluding wolf hybrids, and no mustelid appears at all.

OH.quote: Servals, excluding hybrids with domestic cats commonly known as savannah cats
OH.note: Ohio runs two enumerated lists, dangerous wild animals and restricted snakes, and an animal on neither needs no state permit. The dangerous list names specific carnivores such as the serval; the domestic ferret is not among them.

TX.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means: (A) a lion; (B) a tiger; (C) an ocelot; (D) a cougar; (E) a leopard; (F) a cheetah; (G) a jaguar; (H) a bobcat; (I) a lynx; (J) a serval; (K) a caracal; (L) a hyena; (M) a bear; (N) a coyote; (O) a jackal; (P) a baboon; (Q) a chimpanzee; (R) an orangutan; (S) a gorilla; or (T) any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision.
TX.note: Not on the closed list, and not indigenous to Texas, so neither of the two rules that restrict mammals here applies. Texas is one of the states where the ferret question is simply never asked, which is worth contrasting with California and Hawaii, where it is asked and answered no.

MI.note: Keeping one is unrestricted, but breeding needs a permit, with an exemption for hobby breeders holding up to four ferrets aged six months or more, or a litter under five months kept temporarily for recreational purposes.

IL.quote: No person shall breed, raise, sell or offer to sell ferrets without first obtaining from the Department either a Class A noncommercial game breeder permit or a Class B commercial game breeder permit; such permit shall not, however, authorize the use or sale of ferrets for taking any of the wild birds or wild mammals protected by this Act.
IL.note: Keeping a pet ferret needs nothing: the ferret is not on the closed dangerous animal list at 720 ILCS 5/48-10 and not on the Wildlife Code's protected species list. Breeding or selling one is a different question, and this is the clause that answers it. Illinois requires a game breeder permit to breed, raise or sell ferrets, free of charge for the Class A noncommercial version, and the same sentence bars using a ferret to hunt protected wildlife, which is the practice the rule was written about. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: all members of the Felidae family including, but not limited to, lions, tigers, cougars, leopards, cheetahs, ocelots, and servals, but not including domestic cats or cats recognized as a domestic breed, registered as a domestic breed, and shown as a domestic breed by a national or international multibreed cat registry association; (2) bears; and (3) all nonhuman primates
MN.note: Minnesota's regulated animal definition is three groups and nothing else: the cat family, bears, and non-human primates. No mustelid is in it. Minnesota's own least weasel is a species of special concern under Minn. R. 6134, but that reaches the wild native animal, not the domesticated European ferret.

NV.quote: European ferret (Mustela putorius)

VA.quote: Mustelidae   All Species   (except Mustela putorius furo)   Weasels, Badgers, Skunks and Otters   Ferret
VA.note: Virginia restricts the entire weasel family and then writes the domestic ferret straight back out of it by binomial. One of the clearest ferret carve-outs in any state table.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. No mustelid appears in the eight clauses; the small carnivores named are the skunk and the raccoon, and both are named as rabies vector species rather than as mustelids. The domestic ferret is not native Maryland wildlife either. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

NM.quote: Mammal | Ferret | Mustelidae | Mustela putorius furo | Ferret, Common | I | all species except as restricted in another group
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Resolved from unclear.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

VT.quote: 'Ferret' meaning only the European ferret Mustela putorious furo
VT.note: Classed as a domestic pet, so outside the wild animal permit regime entirely.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Corrected. Ferrets appear by name on the exempt mammal list at regulation 6.1.1, so no permit is required. The previous entry treated this animal as a non-exempt wild mammal needing an exotic animal permit, which was the right framework read against the wrong list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Ferrets and chinchillas
TN.note: Named alongside the chinchilla in its own subdivision of the no-permit class. Worth noting for a state that is otherwise strict about carnivores: the ferret is not treated as one here.

NC.quote: A county may by ordinance regulate, restrict, or prohibit the possession or harboring of animals which are dangerous to persons or property.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches the ferret. North Carolina's only exotic animal statute, § 14-417, is limited to venomous reptiles, and everything else is left to county ordinance. Check your county before assuming yes.

AR.quote: European Domestic Ferret (Mustela putorius)

ID.quote: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders

KY.note: On neither restricted list. The regulation reaches exotic wildlife, defined as species that have never naturally existed in the wild in Kentucky.

RI.quote: Ferret (Mustela putorius). Note: Possession of a ferret does not require obtaining an exotic animal possession permit. Possession of a ferret does require a ferret possession permit issued through the Division of Fish & Wildlife.
