RI.note: Rhode Island is the state that most people miss on ferrets: they are not banned, but they carry their own dedicated permit.

NH.quote: Ferrets, domesticated (Mustela putorius furo);

MO.note: Not Missouri wildlife and not on the dangerous wild animal list.

KS.note: Outside the definition of a dangerous regulated animal.

SC.quote: Furbearer includes, but is not limited to, red and gray fox, raccoon, opossum, muskrat, mink, skunk, otter, bobcat, weasel, and beaver;
SC.note: The domestic ferret is not named, but the list is expressly not exhaustive and it does name mink and weasel, the ferret's closest relatives. Ferrets are also absent from the § 50-16-60 pet trade exemption list, which names hamsters, guinea pigs and gerbils. Worth a call to DNR before importing one.

MT.quote: The term includes livestock, as defined in 81-2-702, dogs, cats, rodents, Eurasian ferrets, and poultry.

WV.quote: "Wildlife"... "livestock"... and "domestic animals", as defined in this section, are excluded.
WV.note: The definition of domestic animal at § 19-34-2(3) expressly reaches an animal bred as a companion animal.

AK.quote: European ferret   Mustela putorius furo

SD.quote: (1) Of the order Carnivora, all nondomestic members of the following families: ...(d) Mustelidae;
SD.note: The permit reaches nondomestic mustelids. Mustela putorius furo is the domesticated one, which is why it falls outside a clause that otherwise covers weasels, mink and badgers.

AL.note: Mustelids are absent from a list that does name raccoons, skunks and foxes, the other rabies vector species.

IN.quote: (10) Weasel (Mustela frenata, Mustela nivalis, and Mustela rixosa).
IN.note: The mustelids on the Class II list are named by binomial and the domestic ferret, Mustela putorius furo, is not among them.

ND.quote: Any dog, cat, or ferret imported into the state for a period of over thirty days must be accompanied by a certificate of veterinary inspection.
ND.note: The ferret gets its own chapter alongside dogs and cats, which settles it: it is treated as a companion animal, subject to a rabies vaccination certificate on import.

WY.quote: domestic ferret (Mustela furo),
WY.note: On the domestic animal list alongside the dog and the cat, not merely the domesticated list.

MS.note: The only mustelid on the list is the wolverine.

LA.note: Not among the listed animals.

OK.quote: (10) Ferrets (except black-footed, Mustela nigripes).

NE.quote: Wildlife means any member of any nondomesticated species of the animal kingdom, whether reared in captivity or not, including any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate and includes any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof or the dead body or parts thereof.
NE.note: Nebraska's native mustelid of that name is the black-footed ferret, Mustela nigripes, which appears on the state endangered list at 166 NAC 4 and cannot be held at all. The domestic ferret is a different species and a domesticated one, so neither § 37-246 nor § 37-247 reaches it. The pairing is worth knowing because the two names are close enough that secondary summaries sometimes report Nebraska as a ferret ban state.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The domestic ferret is not in the definition. The word appears in Iowa Code only in the hunting chapter, which bars using a ferret to drive game, not keeping one.

HI.note: Named on Part A, which is headed FOR RESEARCH AND EXHIBITION. A university or licensed exhibitor can hold one by permit; a pet keeper cannot, and no pet permit exists. This is the origin of Hawaii's well known ferret ban.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Ferret, European - Mustela putorius furo - domestic
UT.note: Listed under 'Domestic mammals and mammalian livestock not covered under this rule', so R657-3b does not reach it and no certificate of registration arises.

PA.quote: In the family Mustelidae. All species of the skunks.
PA.note: The Game Commission's prohibited list reaches Mustelidae only through its skunk line, and the domestic ferret is not a skunk. No other category in § 137.1(a) names it, and Pennsylvania is not one of the states that treats ferrets as wildlife. Read literally, § 137.1(a)(11) bars possessing any wildlife captive bred in another state, and 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines wild animals as every mammal except horses, cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, so the text reaches far wider than the Game Commission applies it. The Commission draws its line at undomesticated species, which is why hedgehogs and sugar gliders are pursued and long domesticated pets are not.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Named at (14)(h) as "Ferrets (domestic; European)", which is the pet in both of its usual names. No permit, no neutering condition of the kind Massachusetts attaches, and no import rule.

CA.quote: Order Marsupialia-Marsupials or Pouched Animals: All species (W)

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: The other express pet exception. Marsupials are licensed as two whole orders, and Petaurus breviceps "may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit if the owner thereof possesses valid documentation that the animal originated from a source inspected and regulated by the United States Department of Agriculture". The condition is provenance rather than paperwork about the animal: a glider from an unlicensed backyard breeder does not qualify however healthy it is.

PA.quote: all bears, coyotes, lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs, cougars, wolves and any crossbreed of these animals which have similar characteristics in appearance or features
PA.note: Same agency interpretation as the hedgehog, and the same pending bill covers both. A marsupial has nothing in common with any animal the definition names.

DC.note: A marsupial, so the 'domesticated rodents and rabbits' category does not reach it.

NYC.quote: No person shall sell or give to another person, possess, harbor, keep, or yard wild or other animals identified in this section ... other than in: (i) a zoological park or aquarium ...; or (ii) a laboratory ...; or (iii) a veterinary hospital ...; or (iv) a temporary exhibit, performance or display that has been issued a permit by the Commissioner. ... For the purposes of this Code, a wild animal is deemed to be any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings and all such animals are hereby prohibited ... Such animals shall also include: (i) any animals specified by the Commissioner in regulations ...; (ii) any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule; and (iii) any of the following animals:
NYC.note: Caught twice in one clause. It covers "All marsupials" and then lists examples ending "pigmy, sugar and greater glider", so the sugar glider is both inside the class and named. New York State exempts it entirely; the city bans it. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: New Jersey is a closed-list state in the strict sense. 7:25-4.2(a) bars possession of any exotic or nongame species without a permit, 4.4 then names the handful that may be kept without one, and 4.5 sweeps everything else back in. The sugar glider appears on none of the Division's three lists, so it is not exempt under 4.4, not one of the families singled out in 4.3, and not potentially dangerous under 4.8. That leaves 4.5, and the permit it points to is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, which 4.7 conditions on diet, caging that prevents escape, lawful acquisition, veterinary care and freedom from disease. The Division's own handout tells readers to phone the permits office for anything the lists do not name, which is a fair signal that the catch-all is where these end up rather than an oversight.

ME.note: Maine publishes a list of species needing no importation, exhibition or possession permit, and the sugar glider is on it by binomial. An express clearance rather than an inference.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Named at (14)(c) as "Honey possums, sugar gliders". Being on this list rather than in Class III is the whole difference: a Class III marsupial like the wallaby needs the free personal use permit and the sugar glider needs nothing.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the sugar glider is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. Category Two names eleven marsupial genera and subgenera, and every one of them is a macropod: tree kangaroos, forest wallabies, hare-wallabies, red and grey kangaroos, nail-tailed and rock wallabies, the quokka, pademelons and the swamp wallaby. Petaurus is not among them, so the sugar glider is unrestricted while most of the kangaroo family is barred.

MA.quote: List of Mammals. (a) The following mammals may be kept without a permit: 1. Four-toed (African pygmy) hedgehog (Erinaceus albiventris) (= Atelerix pruneri) 2. Chinchilla (Chinchilla spp.) derived from captive stock. 3. Deer Mouse and White-footed Mouse 4. Degu (Octodon degus) 5. Egyptian Spiny Mouse 6. House Mouse 7. Jerboas 8. Norway Rat 9. Paca 10. Southern Flying Squirrel (Glaucomys volans) 11. Striped hamster ... 12. Sugar Glider (Petaurus breviceps) 13. American Bison
MA.note: Named at 9.01(12)(a)(12). Worth contrasting with the states that answer the sugar glider by silence: in a closed-list state silence is a no, so this animal is legal in Massachusetts only because someone put it on the list.

CO.quote: Sugar Gliders (Petaurus breviceps)
CO.note: Named to the species on the unregulated wildlife list, so no CPW licence is required. Unregulated is not unmonitored: § 1103(B) remains subject to the importation, prohibited-species and release rules in Chapter W-0, and intentionally releasing unregulated wildlife is separately unlawful. Colorado's marsupial entries are unusually generous, running to five wallabies and kangaroos alongside the short-tailed possum. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

AZ.note: The only marsupial entry is 'All species of the genus Didelphis. Common name: American opossums.'

OR.quote: Sugar glider -- Petauridae -- Petaurus breviceps;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Named to the species, alongside the feathertail glider, the kangaroos and wallabies at family level, the striped possums and the cuscuses. Oregon prohibits two other marsupials by name, the common brushtail and the common ringtail possum. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

WA.quote: A person shall not own, possess, keep, harbor, bring into the state, or have custody or control of a potentially dangerous wild animal
WA.note: The enumerated definition covers big cats, wolves, bears, primates, elephants, rhinos, hippos, crocodilians and venomous snakes. No marsupial is named.

OH.note: On neither the dangerous wild animal list nor the restricted snake list, so no Ohio Department of Agriculture permit applies. Marsupials appear nowhere in either.

TX.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means: (A) a lion; (B) a tiger; (C) an ocelot; (D) a cougar; (E) a leopard; (F) a cheetah; (G) a jaguar; (H) a bobcat; (I) a lynx; (J) a serval; (K) a caracal; (L) a hyena; (M) a bear; (N) a coyote; (O) a jackal; (P) a baboon; (Q) a chimpanzee; (R) an orangutan; (S) a gorilla; or (T) any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision.
TX.note: Nineteen named mammals and no marsupial among them. Petaurus breviceps is not indigenous to Texas, so the nongame caps do not reach it, and no Texas rule regulates exotic marsupials as a group.

MI.note: Michigan splits this across the Large Carnivore Act, the Wolf-dog Cross Act and Part 413 of the Natural Resources and Environmental Protection Act. A large carnivore means a big cat or a bear, so a marsupial is outside all three.

IL.quote: "Dangerous animal" means a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, bear, hyena, wolf or coyote. Dangerous animal does not mean any herptiles included in the Herptiles-Herps Act.
IL.note: No marsupial appears on the list. Illinois does bar one marsupial elsewhere, the brushtail possum, as an injurious species under 17 Ill. Adm. Code 805.20(a), and the sugar glider is not on that list either. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: all members of the Felidae family including, but not limited to, lions, tigers, cougars, leopards, cheetahs, ocelots, and servals, but not including domestic cats or cats recognized as a domestic breed, registered as a domestic breed, and shown as a domestic breed by a national or international multibreed cat registry association; (2) bears; and (3) all nonhuman primates
MN.note: Minnesota's regulated animal definition is three groups and nothing else: the cat family, bears, and non-human primates. No marsupial is in it.

NV.quote: Marsupial

VA.note: Petaurus is absent from the permit table. The marsupial entries there are other genera.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. No marsupial appears in the eight clauses, and the sugar glider is not native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

NM.quote: Mammal | Marsupial | Petauridae | Petaurus breviceps | Sugar Glider | II
NM.note: Group II on the Director's list: not known to be invasive or dangerous, but an importation permit is still required before the animal may be brought into New Mexico. Resolved from unclear.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

VT.quote: Diprotodontia | Phalangeriformes | Petauridae | Petaurus | breviceps | Sugar glider
VT.note: Resolved. Named to the species on the Unrestricted list with no captive bred condition attached, so no permit is needed. Secondary sources disagreed on this and the list settles it.

UT.cite: Utah Admin. Code R657-3b-1(3); Table 3b-1, domestic mammals
UT.quote: Domestic mammals and mammalian livestock not covered under this rule ... Sugar glider Petaurus breviceps
UT.note: Petaurus breviceps is named in Table 3b-1's domestic mammals section, so R657-3b does not govern it at all. Worth reading against the same table's other marsupials, because Utah does not treat the group as one: the gray short-tailed opossum is noncontrolled, kangaroos and wallabies are controlled, and the Virginia opossum is prohibited outright. Four marsupials, four different answers, and the sugar glider gets the most permissive of them. This entry previously cited R657-3, a rule that no longer exists.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Corrected. Sugar gliders appear by name on the exempt mammal list at regulation 6.1.1, so no permit is required. The previous entry treated this animal as a non-exempt wild mammal needing an exotic animal permit, which was the right framework read against the wrong list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Marsupials
TN.note: The whole group is named as Class III, so no marsupial question arises in Tennessee.

NC.quote: A county may by ordinance regulate, restrict, or prohibit the possession or harboring of animals which are dangerous to persons or property.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches the sugar glider. The state statute covers venomous reptiles only, so the question is entirely a county one.

AR.quote: Sugar Glider (Petaurus)
AR.cite: Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.note: Arkansas names permitted species individually with binomials rather than listing what is banned, so this is an express clearance rather than an inference from silence. No permit is needed to hold one.

ID.quote: non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders
ID.note: The marsupial entry on the deleterious exotic animal list is the brush tailed possum only.

KY.note: On neither restricted list. A transportation permit covers bringing one into the state.

RI.quote: Sugar Glider (Petaurus breviceps),

NH.quote: Sugar glider (Petaurus breviceps);

MO.note: Not Missouri wildlife and not on the dangerous wild animal list.

KS.note: Outside the definition of a dangerous regulated animal.

SC.note: Outside every group named in the import permit provision.

MT.quote: Sugar gliders - Petaurus breviceps;

WV.quote: that is dangerous to humans, other animals or the environment due to its inherent nature and capability to do significant harm

AK.quote: The department may not issue a permit for the capture, possession, import, or export of any game animal, including a hybrid of a game animal and a species listed in (b) of this section, for use as a pet
AK.note: Absent from the clean list, and subsection (c) closes the permit route for anything kept as a pet. This is the trap in Alaska: it is not a list of banned animals, it is a list of allowed ones.

SD.quote: A permit from the board is required to import nondomestic animals.
SD.note: Marsupials are absent from the possession permit list. The free entry permit still applies to importing one.

AL.note: Marsupials appear nowhere in the rule.

IN.quote: a person must have a permit... to possess a wild animal if the wild animal is either of the following: (1) Referenced in this rule. (2) Listed in this article as an endangered species or a threatened species.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.

WY.quote: domesticated sugar gliders (Petaurus breviceps),

MS.note: No marsupial appears on the list.

LA.note: Not among the listed animals.

OK.quote: (31) Sugar gliders

NE.quote: 001.08A Importation: the following wildlife may be imported: Alpaca ... Chinchilla, Chinchilla spp. ... Coatimundi ... Degu, Octodon spp. ... Fox, Vulpes spp. ... Genet ... Gerbil, Gerbillus spp. ... Guinea pig, Cavia porcellus ... Eurasian Hedgehogs, Erinaceus spp. ... Jerboa, greater ... Sugar Glider(s), Petaurus spp. ... Wallabies ... All Ratites, All Waterfowl, All Peafowl, All Game Birds, All Cage and Aviary Birds
NE.note: Listed as "Sugar Glider(s), Petaurus spp.", one of the few marsupial entries on the list alongside the wallabies. Not a wild mammal under § 37-246, so nothing else in the chapter reaches it.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: Not a canid, hyaenid, felid, ursid, rhino, elephant, primate or swine, which is the whole of the mammal half of the definition.

HI.quote: Any animal that is not on the lists of conditionally approved, restricted, or prohibited animals shall be prohibited until the board's review and determination for placement on one of these lists
HI.note: Petaurus appears on none of the four lists, so the default rule bars it rather than any decision about sugar gliders. The special permits the subsection goes on to describe are for medical or ecological emergencies and for filming, not for pets.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

CA.quote: Domesticated races of golden hamsters of the species Mesocricetus auratus and domesticated races of dwarf hamsters of the Genus Phodopus are not restricted

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia licenses whole taxonomic orders and then writes short exception lists inside them, so being named in one of those lists is the whole answer here. The hamster is excepted by genus, Mesocricetus, from a rule that otherwise reaches all of Rodentia. Six genera are excepted and the degu, capybara and prairie dog are outside them, which is a good measure of how much work the naming does.

HI.note: Part A is research and exhibition only, so no pet keeping.

DC.quote: Domesticated rodents and rabbits

NYC.quote: In addition to domesticated dogs and cats, an animal may be kept, possessed, harbored or sold in the City of New York provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law, including federal, state and local laws regulating domestic animals and livestock or protecting wildlife and endangered species. Such animals include, but are not limited to, gerbil, hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and fowl or small birds such as parakeet, parrot, canary and finch.
NYC.note: Named in § 161.01(c) with a binomial, "hamster (Mesocricetus auratus)", which is the only scientific name in the permitted list and excludes the dwarf hamsters of other genera on a strict reading. § 161.01(c) is the article's short affirmative list, and it is written as examples rather than as a closed set: "an animal may be kept ... provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law", followed by gerbil, hamster, guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and small birds. So the question in New York City is always whether something else in § 161.01(b) reaches the animal.

NJ.quote: Mammals: i. Hamster - Mesocricetus auratus;
NJ.note: The golden hamster is on the closed exempt list at 4.4, which is the only route to keeping an animal in New Jersey with no permit at all. It is named by species, Mesocricetus auratus, so the exemption covers the pet hamster and not the dwarf species sold alongside it, which are Phodopus and reach 4.5 instead. 4.4(b) attaches the one condition that survives exemption, that the animal "must be housed or caged in such a manner as to prevent liberation".

MI.note: None of Michigan's three relevant acts reaches a domesticated rodent. The Large Carnivore Act is about big cats and bears.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Rodents--Gerbils, hamsters, guinea pigs, rats, mice, squirrels and chipmunks
TN.note: Class III wildlife needs no wildlife permit at all, only whatever the Department of Agriculture requires. Named in the rodent subdivision, so no inference from a class definition is needed. The documentary evidence requirement in § 70-4-401(b), a supplier name, address and acquisition date, applies to Class I and Class II wildlife and not to this class.

ID.quote: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: A rodent, and not among the rodents named on the deleterious exotic animal list.

KY.quote: Hamster (Mesocricetus spp.);

RI.quote: Domestic Hamster derived from (Mesocricetus auratus) and (Phodopus sp.),
RI.note: Listed as a domestic animal, and separately as an exempt exotic at § 3.17(A)(6)(a)(9) for captive bred pet trade species.

NH.quote: Hamsters, domesticated (Cricetus cricetus);

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...13. hamsters

MT.quote: The term includes livestock, as defined in 81-2-702, dogs, cats, rodents, Eurasian ferrets, and poultry.

WV.quote: that is dangerous to humans, other animals or the environment due to its inherent nature and capability to do significant harm

AK.quote: Hamster (golden)   Mesocricetus auratus
AK.note: The list gives one species. Dwarf hamsters of the genus Phodopus, which are common in the pet trade, are not named.

SD.note: No rodent appears on the possession permit list.

AL.note: A domesticated rodent, so outside the wild rodent clause, and named nowhere else in the rule.

IN.note: Not referenced in the rule.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.

WY.quote: domesticated hamster (Mesocricetus auratus),

MS.note: No rodent appears on the list.

LA.note: Not among the listed animals.

OK.quote: (14) Hamsters.

NE.quote: Wildlife means any member of any nondomesticated species of the animal kingdom, whether reared in captivity or not, including any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate and includes any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof or the dead body or parts thereof.
NE.note: Two definitions clear it and the importation list is not one of them, which is worth spelling out because the list carries the guinea pig and the chinchilla and no hamster. § 37-246 makes wild mammals a matter of Nebraska geography, and Mesocricetus auratus is neither native nor established here. § 37-247 defines wildlife as "any member of any nondomesticated species", and the golden hamster is a domesticated animal descended from a single 1930 capture. On both routes it falls outside the chapter rather than off the end of a list.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: Not one of the six named cats or a bear, so outside the only exotic pet statute Kansas has.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches it. § 153A-131 hands the question to counties, several of which have used it.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: Absent from the permit table, so no special permit applies.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: Not a canid, hyaenid, felid, ursid, rhino, elephant, primate or swine, which is the whole of the mammal half of the definition.

MO.quote: those species of mammals... native to Missouri
MO.note: Not Missouri wildlife and not on the § 578.023 dangerous animal list.

ME.note: All the pet hamsters are named: the golden, the Chinese and striped dwarf, and all three Phodopus, the Campbell's, Roborovski's and Dzhungarian. Maine's rodent list is species by species rather than by family.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Hamster (Mesocricetus auratus, Phodopus campbelli, P. sungorus, P. roborovskii, Cricetulus griseus)
AR.note: All five pet hamster species are named, so no permit and no importation permit is needed.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: No rodent appears on the dangerous wild animal list, which runs to large carnivores, elephants, crocodilians and primates.

WA.quote: (a) Class mammalia (i) Order carnivora ... (ii) Order perissodactyla, only rhinoceroses; (iii) Order primates, all nonhuman primate species; (iv) Order proboscidae, all elephants
WA.note: The mammal side of the statute is four orders: carnivores, rhinoceroses, primates and elephants. Rodentia is not among them.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Hamster, golden - Mesocricetus auratus
UT.note: Listed under 'Domestic mammals and mammalian livestock not covered under this rule', so R657-3b does not reach it and no certificate of registration arises.

PA.quote: Unless otherwise provided in this section or the act, it is unlawful for a person to import, possess, sell, offer for sale or release within this Commonwealth the following wild animals or wild birds or the eggs of the birds or a crossbreed or hybrid of the wild animals or wild birds, which are similar in appearance
PA.note: The golden hamster appears in none of the eleven categories the Game Commission prohibits, which run to cats, canids, bears, raccoons, nutria, skunks, primates, listed species, the monk parakeet, and wildlife taken from the wild or captive bred out of state. Read literally, § 137.1(a)(11) bars possessing any wildlife captive bred in another state, and 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines wild animals as every mammal except horses, cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, so the text reaches far wider than the Game Commission applies it. The Commission draws its line at undomesticated species, which is why hedgehogs and sugar gliders are pursued and long domesticated pets are not.

VT.quote: Rodentia | Myomorpha | Cricetidae | Mesocricetus | all species | Hamsters
VT.note: Named at genus level, and the list separately covers Cricetus and the dwarf hamsters in Phodopus, so every hamster in the pet trade is unrestricted and needs no permit.

NM.quote: Mammal | Rodent | Muridae | Mesocricetus auratus | Hamster | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (i) Hamsters;
NV.note: The hamster is named outright on the no-permit list, so it may be possessed, transported, imported and exported with no Department permit. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: Order Erinaceomorpha, all species, except members of the genus Atelerix, which are not restricted. Common name: longeared and pygmy hedgehogs; Order Lagomorpha, all species, except members of the genus Oryctolagus containing domestic rabbits, which are not wildlife and are not restricted; Order Rodentia, the families Capromyidae, Castoridae, Dipodidae, Echimyidae, Erethizontidae, Geomyidae, Sciuridae
AZ.note: Arizona restricts rodents by family rather than as an order, and the seven families named are Capromyidae, Castoridae, Dipodidae, Echimyidae, Erethizontidae, Geomyidae and Sciuridae. The golden hamster is Cricetidae, which is not among them, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Hamsters appear by name on the exempt mammal list, so no permit is required.

CO.quote: Domesticated races of hamsters (Mesocricetus spp.)
CO.note: Colorado's domestic animal list is the shortest route through this chapter: an animal on it is exempted from Parks and Wildlife Commission regulations outright, with no licence, no possession limit and no importation approval to obtain. The Syrian hamster is named at genus level. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: "Dangerous animal" means a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, bear, hyena, wolf or coyote. Dangerous animal does not mean any herptiles included in the Herptiles-Herps Act.
IL.note: Illinois runs a closed list of 15 named mammals plus a blanket bar on primates, and it has no catch-all clause, no size test and no dangerousness test. An animal that is not on the list and is not native Illinois wildlife is simply outside the statute. No rodent appears on it, and the hamster is not a native Illinois wild mammal, so neither the Wildlife Code nor this section reaches one. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: all members of the Felidae family including, but not limited to, lions, tigers, cougars, leopards, cheetahs, ocelots, and servals, but not including domestic cats or cats recognized as a domestic breed, registered as a domestic breed, and shown as a domestic breed by a national or international multibreed cat registry association; (2) bears; and (3) all nonhuman primates
MN.note: Minnesota's regulated animal definition is three groups and nothing else: the cat family, bears, and non-human primates. No rodent is in it. The other place to check for a mammal here is the prohibited invasive species list at Minn. R. 6216.0250, which runs to four species, the Asian raccoon dog, Eurasian swine, European rabbit and nutria, and the hamster is not among them.

OR.quote: For species that are not listed in these rules, no person may possess, import, purchase, sell, exchange, or offer to purchase, sell or exchange the species in Oregon.
OR.note: Oregon appears to have exempted the wrong hamster. The not-wild list at OAR 635-056-0020(14) reads "Common Hamster — Cricetus cricetus", which is the European common hamster, a large wild burrowing rodent nobody keeps as a pet. The pet-shop animal is the Syrian or golden hamster, Mesocricetus auratus, and that binomial appears nowhere in the division: not on the not-wild list, not on the noncontrolled list, which clears the dwarf hamsters of the genus Phodopus, and not on the prohibited list, which names Calomyscus and Cricetulus. An unlisted mammal is not unregulated in Oregon; OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing it. Read literally, the commonest small pet in the country cannot be kept here. Recorded unclear rather than banned because the exemption plainly means to reach the pet hamster and attaches the wrong name to it, and because pet hamsters are sold openly in Oregon. It is the clearest drafting slip found on this map, and the fix is one binomial. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: A member within the order Rodentia, except for guinea pig (Cavia porcellus), gerbil (Meriones unguiculatus), chinchilla (Chinchilla lanigera), rat (Rattus norvegicus), mouse (Mus musculus), hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), dwarf hamster (genera Phodopus and Cricetulus), Patagonia mara (Dolichotis patagonum) and American beaver (Castor canadensis)
CT.note: Connecticut puts the whole order Rodentia in Category Two, which bars private possession, and then excepts nine species. The Syrian or golden hamster, Mesocricetus auratus is one of them, so it is named in the regulation rather than merely absent from it. Connecticut names the binomial correctly and separately excepts the dwarf hamsters of the genera Phodopus and Cricetulus, so both pet hamster groups are covered. Oregon writes the same exception with the wrong binomial and leaves the pet hamster unlisted; this is what the clause is supposed to look like.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. No rodent appears in the eight clauses, and the hamster is not native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TX.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means: (A) a lion; (B) a tiger; (C) an ocelot; (D) a cougar; (E) a leopard; (F) a cheetah; (G) a jaguar; (H) a bobcat; (I) a lynx; (J) a serval; (K) a caracal; (L) a hyena; (M) a bear; (N) a coyote; (O) a jackal; (P) a baboon; (Q) a chimpanzee; (R) an orangutan; (S) a gorilla; or (T) any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision.
TX.note: A domesticated rodent, and Texas restricts rodents in exactly one place: the § 65.331(d) nongame list, which names eight native squirrels, prairie dogs, kangaroo rats and jackrabbits. Mesocricetus auratus is not indigenous to Texas and is nowhere on it. The dangerous wild animal list has no rodent at all.

MA.quote: Domestic animals as listed in 321 CMR 9.02(3) shall be exempt from the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131, § 23, and may be possessed, propagated, maintained, imported, bought, sold, or otherwise disposed of ... Any vertebrate taxa not listed in 321 CMR 9.02 shall be presumed to be wild and shall be subject to the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131.
MA.note: Answered twice over, which is unusual. The golden hamster, Mesocricetus auratus, is on the domestic animal list at 9.02(3), and the exemption list adds the Chinese or Siberian dwarf hamster, Cricetulus barabensis, at 9.01(12)(a)(11) with a note pointing back to the domestic list for the golden. Both routes end in no permit.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Named at (14)(j) for possession and at 68A-6.003(12) for sale. Florida is one of the states where the hamster is answered explicitly rather than by falling outside a definition.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the golden hamster is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species.

CA.note: Order Rodentia is restricted (D) and gerbils are not among the five exceptions, though the order's own heading names them.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia licenses whole taxonomic orders and then writes short exception lists inside them, so being named in one of those lists is the whole answer here. Two gerbil genera are excepted, Gerbillus and Meriones, and the pet Mongolian gerbil is a Meriones. Georgia is one of the few states whose exception list names the right genus for this animal rather than the wrong one.

NJ.quote: Mammals: ... ii. Gerbil - Meriones mongolinensis;
NJ.note: The Mongolian gerbil is on the closed exempt list at 4.4, which is the only route to keeping an animal in New Jersey with no permit at all. The list spells it "Meriones mongolinensis", an old name for Meriones unguiculatus, which is the animal sold as a pet gerbil. 4.4(b) attaches the one condition that survives exemption, that the animal "must be housed or caged in such a manner as to prevent liberation".

MI.note: None of Michigan's three relevant acts reaches a domesticated rodent.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Rodents--Gerbils, hamsters, guinea pigs, rats, mice, squirrels and chipmunks
TN.note: Class III wildlife needs no wildlife permit at all, only whatever the Department of Agriculture requires. Named in the rodent subdivision. The documentary evidence requirement in § 70-4-401(b), a supplier name, address and acquisition date, applies to Class I and Class II wildlife and not to this class.

ID.quote: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians

AK.note: Worth knowing: the gerbil sold in pet shops is the Mongolian gerbil, Meriones unguiculatus, and the list names Gerbillus and Pachyuromys instead. On the literal wording the common pet gerbil is not the one cleared.

SD.note: No rodent appears on the possession permit list.

AL.note: A domesticated rodent, so outside the wild rodent clause.

IN.note: Not referenced in the rule.

All Ratites, All Waterfowl, All Peafowl, All Game Birds, All Cage and Aviary Birds

Read as a common-name entry the listing plainly means the pet gerbil, and read as a scientific listing it names a genus almost nobody keeps. The common name governs here in a way it does not for the hedgehog entry two lines down, because "Gerbil" includes the pet species while "Eurasian Hedgehogs" actively excludes the African one.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: Not one of the six named cats or a bear, so outside the only exotic pet statute Kansas has.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.

AR.quote: Gerbils (Subfamily Gerbillinae)
AR.note: Cleared at subfamily level rather than by species, which is broader than Maine's single Meriones unguiculatus entry and covers the fat-tailed gerbil as well as the Mongolian.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Not a dangerous wild animal and not a restricted snake, so Chapter 935 does not apply.

WA.quote: (a) Class mammalia (i) Order carnivora ... (iii) Order primates ... (iv) Order proboscidae
WA.note: No rodent order is listed, so gerbils are unrestricted. Worth contrasting with California, which bans them outright.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Gerbil = Mongolian jird - Meriones unguiculatus
UT.note: Listed under 'Domestic mammals and mammalian livestock not covered under this rule', so R657-3b does not reach it and no certificate of registration arises.

PA.quote: Unless otherwise provided in this section or the act, it is unlawful for a person to import, possess, sell, offer for sale or release within this Commonwealth the following wild animals or wild birds or the eggs of the birds or a crossbreed or hybrid of the wild animals or wild birds, which are similar in appearance
PA.note: The Mongolian gerbil appears in none of the eleven categories the Game Commission prohibits, which run to cats, canids, bears, raccoons, nutria, skunks, primates, listed species, the monk parakeet, and wildlife taken from the wild or captive bred out of state. Read literally, § 137.1(a)(11) bars possessing any wildlife captive bred in another state, and 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines wild animals as every mammal except horses, cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, so the text reaches far wider than the Game Commission applies it. The Commission draws its line at undomesticated species, which is why hedgehogs and sugar gliders are pursued and long domesticated pets are not.

VT.quote: Rodentia | Myomorpha | Muridae | Meriones | unguiculatus | Gerbils
VT.note: Named to the species, which matters because the list also carries Gerbillus and Gerbillurus under the same common name and the pet gerbil is neither of those. Meriones unguiculatus is the one on the shelf.

NM.quote: Mammal | Rodent | Muridae | Meriones unguiculatus | Gerbil | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (k) Gerbils;
NV.note: The gerbil is named outright on the no-permit list, so it may be possessed, transported, imported and exported with no Department permit. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: Order Erinaceomorpha, all species, except members of the genus Atelerix, which are not restricted. Common name: longeared and pygmy hedgehogs; Order Lagomorpha, all species, except members of the genus Oryctolagus containing domestic rabbits, which are not wildlife and are not restricted; Order Rodentia, the families Capromyidae, Castoridae, Dipodidae, Echimyidae, Erethizontidae, Geomyidae, Sciuridae
AZ.note: Arizona restricts rodents by family rather than as an order, and the seven families named are Capromyidae, Castoridae, Dipodidae, Echimyidae, Erethizontidae, Geomyidae and Sciuridae. The Mongolian gerbil is Muridae, which is not among them, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Gerbils appear by name on the exempt mammal list, so no permit is required.

CO.quote: Domesticated races of gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus)
CO.note: Named to the species on the domestic animal list, so the wildlife chapters do not reach it. Colorado draws its line at the domesticated race rather than the genus, which is worth noting for anyone importing a wild-type Meriones. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: "Dangerous animal" means a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, bear, hyena, wolf or coyote. Dangerous animal does not mean any herptiles included in the Herptiles-Herps Act.
IL.note: Illinois runs a closed list of 15 named mammals plus a blanket bar on primates, and it has no catch-all clause, no size test and no dangerousness test. An animal that is not on the list and is not native Illinois wildlife is simply outside the statute. No rodent appears on it. The Wildlife Code reaches only wild birds and wild mammals native to or brought into Illinois and named in its § 2.2 list, and the gerbil is on neither. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: all members of the Felidae family including, but not limited to, lions, tigers, cougars, leopards, cheetahs, ocelots, and servals, but not including domestic cats or cats recognized as a domestic breed, registered as a domestic breed, and shown as a domestic breed by a national or international multibreed cat registry association; (2) bears; and (3) all nonhuman primates
MN.note: Minnesota's regulated animal definition is three groups and nothing else: the cat family, bears, and non-human primates. No rodent is in it, and the gerbil is not on the prohibited invasive species list either.

OR.quote: Pursuant to the definition of "wildlife," the following species are not subject to these rules because they are not "wild" ... (11) Gerbil (Mongolian Jird) — Meriones unguiculatus.
OR.note: This is the strongest position an animal can hold in Oregon. ORS 496.004(19) leaves it to the commission to define which mammals count as wild, and this rule is that definition: the 32 species on it are declared not wild and fall outside the wildlife rules altogether, rather than being permitted by them. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: A member within the order Rodentia, except for guinea pig (Cavia porcellus), gerbil (Meriones unguiculatus), chinchilla (Chinchilla lanigera), rat (Rattus norvegicus), mouse (Mus musculus), hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), dwarf hamster (genera Phodopus and Cricetulus), Patagonia mara (Dolichotis patagonum) and American beaver (Castor canadensis)
CT.note: Connecticut puts the whole order Rodentia in Category Two, which bars private possession, and then excepts nine species. The gerbil, Meriones unguiculatus is one of them, so it is named in the regulation rather than merely absent from it. Named to the species. Everything in Rodentia that is not one of the nine, the prairie dog and the degu included, is Category Two and barred to private keepers.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. No rodent appears in the eight clauses, and the gerbil is not native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TX.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means: (A) a lion; (B) a tiger; (C) an ocelot; (D) a cougar; (E) a leopard; (F) a cheetah; (G) a jaguar; (H) a bobcat; (I) a lynx; (J) a serval; (K) a caracal; (L) a hyena; (M) a bear; (N) a coyote; (O) a jackal; (P) a baboon; (Q) a chimpanzee; (R) an orangutan; (S) a gorilla; or (T) any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision.
TX.note: Meriones unguiculatus is Mongolian, so the nongame rules, which reach only species indigenous to Texas, do not apply, and no rodent appears on the dangerous wild animal list. Nothing at state level touches a pet gerbil.

MA.quote: Domestic animals as listed in 321 CMR 9.02(3) shall be exempt from the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131, § 23, and may be possessed, propagated, maintained, imported, bought, sold, or otherwise disposed of ... Any vertebrate taxa not listed in 321 CMR 9.02 shall be presumed to be wild and shall be subject to the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131.
MA.note: The Mongolian gerbil, Meriones unguiculatus, is on the domestic animal list by name. That list matters more than it looks: 9.02(2)(c) provides that any vertebrate taxon not on it is PRESUMED WILD and subject to c. 131, so in Massachusetts being domestic is itself a listed status rather than a description.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Named at (14)(b) with the hedgehog, and named again at 68A-6.003(12), which says no permit is required for the SALE of poultry, hamsters, guinea pigs, domestic rats and mice, gerbils, or chameleons. Florida answers this animal twice, once for keeping and once for selling.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the Mongolian gerbil is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species.

NYC.quote: In addition to domesticated dogs and cats, an animal may be kept, possessed, harbored or sold in the City of New York provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law, including federal, state and local laws regulating domestic animals and livestock or protecting wildlife and endangered species. Such animals include, but are not limited to, gerbil, hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and fowl or small birds such as parakeet, parrot, canary and finch.
NYC.note: Named in § 161.01(c) by common name. § 161.01(c) is the article's short affirmative list, and it is written as examples rather than as a closed set: "an animal may be kept ... provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law", followed by gerbil, hamster, guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and small birds. So the question in New York City is always whether something else in § 161.01(b) reaches the animal.

CA.quote: Family Psittacidae-Parrots, Parakeets: Myiopsitta monachus (Monk or Quaker parakeet) (D)

GA.quote: The following wild animals are considered a significant threat to wildlife or other natural resources and live individuals are prohibited. ... (b) Birds: ... 2. Order Psittaciformes: Family Psittacidae - Myiopsitta monachus (monk parakeet or Quaker parrot) except those individuals possessing monk parakeets or Quaker parrots under a wild animal license that is current on the effective date of this rule may continue to possess these animals according to their license conditions;
GA.note: This entry previously read as unrestricted and it is the opposite: the monk parakeet is one of only nine entries on Georgia's prohibited list, the tier above the licence tiers, where live individuals may not be held at all. The grandfathering is narrower than most on this map, since it runs only to someone who held a current wild animal licence on the effective date, not to any prior owner. Georgia's Department of Agriculture reaches the same bird from the other direction, having determined it prohibited from entry into the state as a species capable of breeding in the wild and threatening agriculture.

grandfathered.before: the effective date of the rule
grandfathered.detail: Only a person possessing monk parakeets under a wild animal licence current on the effective date may continue, on that licence's conditions.

NYC.quote: In addition to domesticated dogs and cats, an animal may be kept, possessed, harbored or sold in the City of New York provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law, including federal, state and local laws regulating domestic animals and livestock or protecting wildlife and endangered species. Such animals include, but are not limited to, gerbil, hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and fowl or small birds such as parakeet, parrot, canary and finch.
NYC.note: The bird clause at (b)(11) prohibits "All predatory or large birds" and named poultry, and a monk parakeet is neither. § 161.01(c) then names "parakeet" among the permitted small birds. New York State treats this species as a regulated invasive that is legal to possess, so both layers agree. § 161.01(c) is the article's short affirmative list, and it is written as examples rather than as a closed set: "an animal may be kept ... provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law", followed by gerbil, hamster, guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and small birds. So the question in New York City is always whether something else in § 161.01(b) reaches the animal.

NJ.quote: Psittaciformes Psittaculis spp.--Ring-necked parakeets / Myiopsitta spp.--Monk parakeets / Cyanoliseus patagonus--Patagonian Conures ... The potentially dangerous species shall not be kept as a pet, for hobby purposes or in situations, which, in the judgment of the Department, could adversely affect the health of the animal or which could constitute a hazard to the public.
NJ.note: The quaker is Myiopsitta monachus and 4.8(a) puts Myiopsitta spp. in the potentially dangerous table, alongside the ring-necked parakeets and the Patagonian conure, on the agricultural pest limb of the definition rather than the dangerous animal limb. A permit exists for potentially dangerous species under 4.8(b), which is why this entry read "permit" before, but 4.9(a)3 says in terms that such a species "shall not be kept as a pet, for hobby purposes". The permit is real and it is simply not a pet permit, so for a keeper the practical answer is a ban. The Division states it flatly in its own notice: potentially dangerous species "may not be kept as pets or for hobby purposes for any reason".

ME.note: Expressly carved out of the unrestricted list: 'Except for: Myiopsitta monachus'.

MA.quote: List of Birds. (a) The following groups of birds are prohibited without a permit: 1. Species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3). 2. Migratory birds listed in the Code of Federal Regulations, 50 CFR 10.13. 3. Any other bird native to the United States and Canada. (b) Except for species listed in 321 CMR 9.01(11)(a), the birds or groups of birds may be kept without a permit: ... 6. Psittacidae (parrots and their allies)
MA.note: Psittacidae is exempt as a family, and the monk parakeet clears the three prohibitions in 9.01(11)(a) as well: it is IUCN least concern, it is not on 50 CFR 10.13, and it is not native to the United States or Canada. Massachusetts is worth flagging on this species because it is one of the states most often listed as banning it, and the regulation does not.

CO.quote: Monk parakeet.
CO.note: Two Colorado rules point in opposite directions here and the prohibited list wins. Chapter W-11 § 1103(B) clears "All Psitticine birds" on the unregulated wildlife list, but § 1103(B) is expressly subject to § 008 regarding prohibited terrestrial wildlife, and § 008(B)(11) names the monk parakeet. CPW resolves it the same way in public, restating the unregulated line as "All Psitticine birds (except Monk Parakeet/Quaker Parrot)" and saying the species is not allowed in Colorado. The grandfather clause in § 008(B) reaches only subsections 1 through 8, so it does not help an existing owner of a bird listed at 11. Reading the parrot line on its own is how this species gets recorded legal in Colorado, and it is not.

VA.quote: Exception for certain monk parakeets. No permit is required for monk parakeets (quakers) that have been captive bred and are closed-banded with a seamless band.
VA.note: Virginia lists Myiopsitta monachus in the subsection A permit table and then writes an exception for the birds people actually buy. A captive bred quaker wearing a seamless closed band needs no permit. A wild caught bird, or one with an open band that could have been fitted later, does. The band is the whole test, so keep the paperwork that came with the bird.

grandfathered.detail: An asterisked animal held before 1 July 1992 could be kept if declared to the department in writing by 1 January 1993. That declaration works as a possession-only permit, renews every five years and cannot be transferred.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders
ID.note: The only bird on the deleterious exotic animal list is the mute swan.

KY.quote: Monk or Quaker parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus);
KY.note: The permit-exempt list confirms the exclusion: it clears parrots, lovebirds, budgerigars, macaws and parakeets except the monk parakeet.

RI.quote: Psittacidae (Parrots and their allies) except for Myiopsitta monachus (Monk Parakeet), which requires a permit,

NH.quote: Parrots (Psittaciformes);
NH.note: Listed by order rather than species, and no monk parakeet exception appears anywhere in Fis 800.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds (including ring-necked pheasants and gray partridge) native to the continental United States
MO.note: Myiopsitta monachus is South American. Naturalised colonies exist in the United States but the species is not native to it.

SC.quote: 6. shell parakeets 7. love birds 8. cockatiels 9. parrots
SC.note: The only bird needing a permit under § 50-16-20 is turkey of the genus Meleagris. South Carolina makes no monk parakeet exception, unlike most states that name the species.

MT.quote: Psittacidae (parrots)
MT.note: Montana clears the whole parrot family on its statutory noncontrolled list and makes no monk parakeet exception, which most states do.

WV.quote: The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: No bird category appears in the guidance at all.

AK.quote: Parrot, parakeet, cockatiel, macaw, and other members of the Family Psittacidae not prohibited by federal or international law
AK.note: The family is cleared as a whole with no monk parakeet exception, which is unusual.

AL.note: The only bird restrictions in the rule are wild turkey strains and anything federally listed as injurious. The monk parakeet is neither.

IN.note: No bird appears on any of the three class lists.

ND.note: No bird restriction appears in the chapter. The only bird provision is a seven dollar annual licence fee for bird species that the board requires to be licensed.

WY.quote: a permit shall not be issued for importation or possession of the following live warm-blooded wildlife in Wyoming... (iii) Monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus);
WY.note: Not merely unpermitted. The regulation says a permit shall not be issued, which closes the route entirely.

MS.note: No bird appears on the list.

LA.note: The regulation reaches wild quadrupeds, big exotic cats and non-human primates. No bird is listed.

OK.quote: The following list of birds shall be exempt from import and export requirements... (2) Psittacine birds (parrots, parakeets and budgerigars).
OK.note: Cleared by group with no monk parakeet exception.

NE.quote: Cage and Aviary Birds - Means those captive-reared birds, not native to Nebraska, such as parrots, exotic finches, and canaries, which are adapted to live and breed in a cage. For purposes of this regulation, the monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus) is not a cage and aviary bird.
NE.note: Nebraska bans this bird by writing it out of a definition, which is the only instance of that technique on this map. The importation list ends with "All Cage and Aviary Birds", and the chapter defines that term as captive-reared birds not native to Nebraska, such as parrots, exotic finches and canaries, and then adds one sentence: "For purposes of this regulation, the monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus) is not a cage and aviary bird." So every other pet parrot is importable and this one is not. The reason is agricultural rather than about the pet trade, since the monk parakeet is the species that builds communal stick nests on power infrastructure, and Nebraska also keeps a separate Nuisance Birds chapter at 166 NAC 7.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No bird is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. Your county code is the operative layer.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles. No bird appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: Nondomestic birds are handled by ARSD 12:68:13 rather than the mammal permit list here.

DC.quote: Captive-bred species of common cage birds, including chickens
DC.note: A monk parakeet is a common cage bird and captive bred, so it clears the bird category. DC is one of the few places that does not single the species out.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: The bird list runs to dozens of parrots by name and the monk parakeet is not among them, so it stays inside Code 09.02 rather than being exempted. This is the usual pattern: the monk parakeet is the one parrot states single out, because established colonies damage electrical infrastructure.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: No bird of any kind is on the dangerous wild animal list, and Ohio has no separate monk parakeet provision, so the species is unrestricted here while most states single it out.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: No bird is a potentially dangerous wild animal, and the only bird on the deleterious exotic wildlife rule is the mute swan. Washington is one of the states where the monk parakeet is simply unregulated.

WI.quote: Monk or Quaker parakeet or parrot (Myiopsitta monachus) - Prohibited
WI.note: The one psittacine Wisconsin prohibits. NR 40 Prohibited status bars possession, transport and transfer without a permit, so this is the rare case where the parrot order's general clearance as an unregulated pet bird does not apply.

UT.quote: Parrots - Family Psittacidae - All species not native to North America
UT.note: Utah clears the whole parrot family by one line, provided the species is not native to North America. Unlike Wisconsin and a number of other states, Utah draws no monk parakeet carve-out, so the Quaker sits in the same noncontrolled column as the African grey and the cockatoo.

PA.quote: The Monk Parakeet, Myiopsitts monachus , sometimes referred to as the Quaker Parakeet or Gray-headed Parakeet.
PA.note: Named outright, which makes this one of the few Pennsylvania exotic pet answers that needs no interpretation at all: import, possession, sale, offering for sale and release are each unlawful.
