The scientific name is misspelled in the official text, which prints Myiopsitts for Myiopsitta. This is the only parrot Pennsylvania designates, and the designation is what brings the species inside the Game Code, since 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 otherwise limits wild birds to federally listed migratory birds and game birds.

MI.quote: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection is required for the import of exotic, circus and zoo animals, native wild animals, domestic rabbits, nonnative rodents, nonnative reptiles and amphibians, and non-poultry birds
MI.note: The monk or quaker parakeet is named in no Michigan statute or order. The Large Carnivore Act covers cats and bears, the captive game permit covers native game, and the herp order covers reptiles and amphibians, so nothing reaches a pet parrot. The only requirement is the certificate of veterinary inspection for a non-poultry bird moved into the state. Worth checking against your own state, because Michigan does not follow Pennsylvania, which bans this species by name.

NM.quote: Bird | Parakeet | Psittacidae | Myiopsitta monachus | Parakeet, Quaker Monk | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Worth flagging against other states, because this is the species Pennsylvania bans by name. New Mexico treats it as semi-domesticated.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (e) Parakeets; ... (h) Parrots;
NV.note: Parakeets and parrots are both cleared by name, and Nevada's prohibited bird list is only three species, the pink starling, the red-billed dioch and the red-whiskered bulbul. The monk parakeet is on none of them. Worth flagging against Pennsylvania, which bans this species by name. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: The following species within the family Phasianidae ... All species listed under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act listed under 50 CFR 10.13
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted bird list is a handful of quail, grouse and turkeys plus everything covered by the federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act. No psittacine appears, and the only parrot the state names anywhere is the thick-billed parrot, a native species. The monk or quaker parakeet is neither, so no licence is required. Worth flagging against Pennsylvania, which bans this species by name.

DE.quote: No person shall bring into this State, possess, sell or exhibit any live wild mammal or hybrid of a wild mammal or live reptile not native to or generally found in Delaware without first securing a permit under this chapter.
DE.note: The permit requirement names live wild mammals, hybrids of wild mammals and non-native reptiles, and stops there. Birds are absent from the operative text despite the chapter's title mentioning them, and the Department of Agriculture's own guidance states that all birds and fish are exempt from the permitting process. The monk or quaker parakeet therefore needs nothing.

IL.quote: No person shall release, or propagate for the release any Nutria (Myocastor coypus), and monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus), in this State at any time.
IL.note: Illinois names the monk parakeet in statute and then stops short of the thing most states do with it. The clause bars releasing one and bars propagating one for release, and says nothing about keeping or selling. Two sentences earlier in the same section Illinois shows what a possession ban looks like when it wants one, barring anyone from holding or possessing San Juan rabbits or raccoon dogs with no permit available; the monk parakeet clause is deliberately narrower. Nor is the species on the Part 805 injurious list or the § 2.2 protected list. Illinois has a naturalized monk parakeet population on the south side of Chicago that has been there since the 1970s, which makes the restraint here more pointed, not less. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: "Protected wild animals" means big game, small game, game fish, native rough fish, minnows, leeches, chubs, frogs, turtles, clams, mussels, wolf, mourning doves, bats, snakes, salamanders, lizards, any animal species listed as endangered, threatened, or of special concern in Minnesota Rules, chapter 6134, and wild animals that are protected by a restriction in the time or manner of taking, other than a restriction in the use of artificial lights, poison, or motor vehicles.
MN.note: The protected list is worth reading in full for Minnesota, because it names five herptile categories and then almost nothing among birds beyond game birds and mourning doves. The monk parakeet falls outside it, so § 97A.501's possession bar does not apply. Minnesota is one of the states that never picked this species up. It is on neither the prohibited nor the regulated invasive species list, and there is no counterpart to the release bans other states wrote for it. The reason is probably climate rather than policy: the naturalised colonies that prompted those rules are in warmer states.

OR.quote: Pursuant to the definition of "wildlife," the following species are not subject to these rules because they are not "wild" ... (28) Parrots, Parakeets, Lories, and Cockatoos — Psittaciforme (All species).
OR.note: Oregon is unusual in that its parrot exemption is written at order level with no carve-out at all, so the monk parakeet sits in it alongside every other psittacine. The species is named nowhere in the division: not on the prohibited bird list, not among the controlled birds, which are the mute swan, the raptors, the game birds and three named passerines. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: Monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus)
CT.note: Connecticut names the monk parakeet by species in Category Two, and it is the only psittacine anywhere in the regulation. Every other parrot falls outside all four categories and is unrestricted, so this is a single-species rule sitting in the middle of an otherwise untouched order. Subsection (b)(3) allows possession of a Category Two animal only by a vet treating it, a municipal park, zoo, marine mammal park, aquarium, nature centre, museum, exhibitor, laboratory or research facility. There is no private permit.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. The statute reaches no bird at all, and the monk parakeet is named nowhere in Maryland law. That is worth stating plainly, because this is the species most states single out if they single out any parrot: California, Connecticut, New Jersey and Virginia all name it, and Colorado prohibits it outright. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Avian species not otherwise listed, excluding North American game birds, ostriches and cassowary
TN.note: The statute does not reach the monk parakeet. It is named nowhere in the five classes, and the avian catch-all at (3)(F) puts it in the no-permit class. What keeps this unresolved is Class V, which is not a list at all but whatever the commission designates by rule as injurious to the environment, and an agricultural pest bird is exactly what a Class V designation is for. Those designations live in Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 1660-01-18, Rules and Regulations of Live Wildlife, which could not be read here: publications.tnsosfiles.com, sos.tn.gov and tnsos.org all sit behind a filter that returns 403 to this container, and Tennessee's official code is behind LexisNexis. Tennessee appears on most circulated lists of states banning the monk parakeet, and if that is right the rule chapter is where it comes from. Recorded unclear rather than legal because the statute alone cannot settle a question the commission was given the power to answer elsewhere.

TX.quote: (a) Except as provided by this code, no person may: (1) catch, kill, injure, pursue, or possess, dead or alive, or purchase, sell, expose for sale, transport, ship, or receive or deliver for transportation, a bird that is not a game bird ... (d) Canaries, parrots, and other exotic nongame birds may be sold, purchased, and kept as domestic pets.
TX.note: Subsection (a) would reach a monk parakeet on its face, since it covers possessing, purchasing or selling "a bird that is not a game bird" and says nothing about where the bird came from. Subsection (d) is the answer, and it is written for exactly this: parrots and other exotic nongame birds may be kept as pets. Texas is worth flagging because it has large established monk parakeet colonies and the state has chosen to deal with them through the depredation provisions in § 64.002(c) rather than through a possession ban. No Texas rule bars keeping one.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the entry at (14)(q), which is the single word "Parrots", sitting in a list that separately names shell parakeets, canaries, lovebirds, cockatiels, finches, myna birds and toucans. The monk parakeet is a parrot and is not carved back out anywhere. That is worth stating plainly, because Florida has large established monk parakeet colonies and is often assumed to restrict the species for that reason. It does not: the prohibited list at 68-5.006(5) names four birds, the dioch, the Java sparrow, the pink starling and the red-whiskered bulbul, and this is none of them.

NY.quote: Prohibited invasive species cannot be knowingly possessed with the intent to sell, import, purchase, transport or introduce. In addition, no person shall sell, import, purchase, transport, introduce or propagate prohibited invasive species. Regulated invasive species, on the other hand, are species which cannot be knowingly introduced into a free-living state, or introduced by a means that one should have known would lead to such an introduction, although such species shall be legal to possess, sell, buy, propagate and transport.
NY.note: The monk parakeet is on New York's invasive species list, and the tier matters more than the listing. Regulated species "shall be legal to possess, sell, buy, propagate and transport" and may only not be knowingly introduced into a free-living state; it is the prohibited tier that bars possession. The duty the listing creates falls on the seller rather than the keeper: a pet shop selling a regulated species must label it as one. Goldfish and koi are on the same list, which is a useful measure of how much it restricts. New York has long-established monk parakeet colonies in Brooklyn and Queens, and the state's answer to them is a labelling rule and a release prohibition rather than a possession ban, which is a real contrast with the states that ban the bird outright.

VT.cite: Vermont Domestic Species List, August 2010; Regulation 881; 10 V.S.A. § 4709
VT.quote: Birds Psittaciformes Psittacidae Melopsittacus undulatus Budgerigar Captive Bred Only ... Nymphicus hollandicus Cockatiel Captive Bred Only ... Psittacula krameri manillensis Indian ringneck parakeet Captive Bred Only
VT.note: Vermont is an inverted-list state and the quaker parakeet falls through all three of its lists. 10 V.S.A. § 4709 bars bringing in, transporting or possessing any live wild bird or animal without authorisation, and the Unrestricted Wild Animal List closes the loop by saying a species found on none of the Restricted, Unrestricted or Domestic lists is considered Restricted. the quaker parakeet is on none of them: the Unrestricted list's birds are the rock dove, the European buzzard, a run of estrildid finches and the canary, with no psittacine at all, and the Domestic Species List's psittacine section is a closed list of about thirty species that names the budgerigar, the cockatiel, the lovebirds, the rosellas, the conures and Psittacula, and stops. What makes Restricted a ban rather than paperwork is Regulation 881: "the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for the keeping or possession of any wild animal in captivity, except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes". There is no pet category to apply under. Worth noting how differently Vermont arrives here from the states that ban this bird. California, Connecticut, Georgia and Kentucky name Myiopsitta because it is an agricultural pest that builds nests on power infrastructure. Vermont names nothing: the quaker is banned for the same reason a Nile monitor is, which is that nobody put it on a list.

CA.quote: Domestic cats and hybrids of domestic cats are not restricted

DC.quote: Domestic cats, excluding hybrids with ocelots or margays
DC.note: The Bengal derives from the Asian leopard cat, which is neither.

NYC.quote: No person shall sell or give to another person, possess, harbor, keep, or yard wild or other animals identified in this section ... other than in: (i) a zoological park or aquarium ...; or (ii) a laboratory ...; or (iii) a veterinary hospital ...; or (iv) a temporary exhibit, performance or display that has been issued a permit by the Commissioner. ... For the purposes of this Code, a wild animal is deemed to be any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings and all such animals are hereby prohibited ... Such animals shall also include: (i) any animals specified by the Commissioner in regulations ...; (ii) any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule; and (iii) any of the following animals:
NYC.note: The fifteenth Bengal answer on this map and the only one with no exit at all. The cat clause ends "and any hybrid or cross-breed offspring of a wild cat and domesticated or other cat", with no filial number, no weight test and no registry exception. New York State allows a registered hybrid five generations clear of wild parentage; inside the five boroughs that carve-out does not exist, so the same cat is lawful in Buffalo and not in Brooklyn. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: The thirteenth Bengal answer on this map and the strictest generation rule on it. Felidae "and all hybrids thereof" is a wild animal, with one exit: hybrids of Felis catus "that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations". So F5 and later, and only with ACFA or TICA registration. Two conditions rather than one, exactly as in Massachusetts, but at five generations rather than three. 6 NYCRR § 180.1(b)(8) repeats the sentence word for word, which is unusual and useful: the regulation cannot be read as narrowing the statute here.

MN.quote: all members of the Felidae family including, but not limited to, lions, tigers, cougars, leopards, cheetahs, ocelots, and servals, but not including domestic cats or cats recognized as a domestic breed, registered as a domestic breed, and shown as a domestic breed by a national or international multibreed cat registry association; (2) bears; and (3) all nonhuman primates
MN.note: Two sentences of the same definition point opposite ways for this animal, and Minnesota has never said which wins. The Felidae clause excludes "domestic cats or cats recognized as a domestic breed, registered as a domestic breed, and shown as a domestic breed by a national or international multibreed cat registry association", and the Bengal is registered and shown as a domestic breed by TICA. But the definition closes with a sentence providing that a regulated animal "includes any hybrid or cross between an animal listed in clause (1), (2), or (3) and a domestic animal and offspring from all subsequent generations of those crosses or hybrids", and the Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal is a clause (1) animal. Read the hybrid sentence alone and every Bengal is banned at every generation. Read the carve-out as doing real work and the Bengal is exempt, since the registered domestic breeds it could describe are almost all wild hybrids and the carve-out would otherwise add nothing to "domestic cats". This entry previously read as banned on the hybrid sentence alone, without the carve-out. Recorded unclear rather than either, because the conflict is on the face of the statute and enforcement sits with local animal control rather than one agency that could settle it.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland is the one state on this map that answers the hybrid cat question by weight. The prohibition reaches a cat hybrid only "if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds", with no generation test, no registry requirement and no reference to filial number at all. Most Bengals are well under that, so most Bengals are lawful, and the same clause would catch a large Savannah. The line is drawn on the individual animal rather than on its ancestry, which means the answer can in principle change as a cat grows. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

grandfathered.detail: Lawful possession on or before 31 May 2006 may continue, but only if the keeper gave written notification to the local animal control authority by 1 August 2006, with the number and type of animals and a photograph or a description of a tattoo or microchip. That window is long closed.

ID.quote: Geoffroy's Cat (Felis geoffroyi). Margay (Felis wiedii). Ocelot (Felis pardalis). Serval (Felis serval).
ID.note: The small felidae list is these four. The Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal, Prionailurus bengalensis, is not on it, and cats are conventional pets under IDAPA 13.01.10.

IA.quote: The bengal must be the fourth or later filial generation of offspring with the first filial generation being the offspring of a domestic cat and an Asian leopard cat, and each subsequent generation being the offspring of a domestic cat.
IA.note: F4 and later are carved out of the definition. F1 to F3 are dangerous wild animals and are banned.

KY.quote: Lions, jaguars, leopards, or tigers (Genus Panthera); Lynx (Genus Lynx);
KY.note: Prionailurus bengalensis appears on neither list, and the hybrid clause in Section 4(2)(v) reaches only hybrids of species in that subsection.

RI.quote: Domestic Cat (Felis catus) excluding hybrids with wild felines,
RI.note: An F1 cross is plainly excluded from the domestic animal list and then caught by the § 3.9(B) bar on permits for Carnivora hybrids. A late generation Bengal is the offspring of two domestic cats, so on the § 3.6(A)(13) definition of hybrid it arguably is not one. The regulation sets no filial generation cut off the way Iowa and New York do. Ask the Division of Agriculture before buying.

NH.quote: 5   Tiger; Golden Tabby, Siberian, White Siberian, Bengal   Panthera tigeris
NH.note: The only Bengal in the controlled table is the tiger colour morph. Neither Prionailurus bengalensis nor domestic cat hybrids appear, and domestic cats are not wildlife under these rules.

MO.quote: any lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, Canada lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi
MO.note: The statute names species and says nothing about hybrids or filial generations.

KS.quote: Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof;
KS.note: The hybrid clause attaches to those six species. Leopard here means Panthera pardus, not the Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal.

SC.quote: Family Felidae, Genus panthera—all lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cougars, cheetahs, snow leopards, and clouded leopards;
SC.note: The hybrid clause in § 47-2-10(2) attaches to those animals. The Asian leopard cat is Prionailurus, not Panthera.

MT.quote: The term includes livestock, as defined in 81-2-702, dogs, cats, rodents, Eurasian ferrets, and poultry.
MT.note: Cats are domestic animals under the definition, and nothing in the exotic wildlife lists mentions the Asian leopard cat or its hybrids.

WV.quote: "Domestic animal" means an animal which, through extremely long association with humans, has been bred to a degree which has resulted in genetic changes affecting the temperament, color, conformation or other attributes of the species to an extent that makes it unique and distinguishable from a wild individual of its species, and includes an animal that has been bred as a companion animal.
WV.note: Domestic animals are excluded from the definition of a dangerous wild animal. A registered Bengal is bred as a companion animal.

AK.quote: The following species, not including a hybrid of a game animal and a species listed in this subsection, may be possessed, imported, exported, bought, sold, or traded without a permit
AK.note: Cat, Felis catus, is on the clean list but hybrids of a listed species and a game animal are carved straight back out, and subsection (c) then bars any pet permit for such a hybrid by name. The rule sets no filial generation cut off, so it gives no comfort to a late generation Bengal the way Iowa and New York do.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The words or any of its hybrids sit in the operative sentence rather than in a separate clause, so a Bengal is caught by the Felidae entry. No filial generation cut off is given.

AL.quote: black bear (Ursus americanus), mountain lion (Felis concolor), bobcat (Felis rufus)
AL.note: No hybrid clause appears anywhere in the rule.

IN.quote: (12) Leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis)... A hybrid of any of these species with a domestic dog or domestic cat is exempt from permitting under this section.
IN.note: Indiana answers the Bengal question outright. The leopard cat itself needs a Class II permit, and its hybrid with a domestic cat is exempt by name, with no filial generation condition attached.

ND.quote: "Domestic animal" means dog, cat, horse, bovine animal, sheep, goat, bison, farmed elk, llama, alpaca, or swine.
ND.note: Cats are domestic animals under the statute and no hybrid clause appears anywhere in the chapter.

WY.quote: "Domestic Animals" means those populations of animals, their viable gametes (eggs and sperm), fertilized eggs, or any hybrid or transgenic product thereof, which through long association with humans have been bred to a degree which has resulted in genetic changes of the species to an extent that makes them unique and distinguishable from wild individuals of their species. For the purpose of this regulation, only the following animals are considered domestic: ...cat (Felis catus),
WY.note: The definition folds hybrids into the domestic category rather than carving them out, which is the opposite of how Rhode Island and Alaska handle the same question.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: Prionailurus is not named, and the only hybrid clause in the rule is the one for wolf crosses under Canidae.

LA.quote: vii. all subspecies of the above listed exotic cats; viii. hybrids resulting from cross breeding of the above listed exotic cats.
LA.note: The Asian leopard cat is not one of the six listed cats, so a Bengal is outside the hybrid clause.

OK.quote: (4) Cats (except native cats and bears).

NE.quote: (1) No person shall keep in captivity in this state any wild birds, any wild mammals, any nongame wildlife in need of conservation as determined by the commission under section 37-805, or any wildlife determined to be an endangered or threatened species ... without first having obtained a permit. (2) Except as provided in subsection (3) of this section, no person shall keep in captivity in this state any wolf, any skunk, or any member of the families Felidae and Ursidae. This subsection shall not apply to (a) the species Felis domesticus, (b) any zoo, park, refuge, wildlife area, or nature center owned or operated by a city, village, state, or federal agency or any zoo accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums or the Zoological Association of America, or (c) any person who holds a captive wildlife permit ... and who raises Canada Lynx (Lynx canadensis) or bobcats (Lynx rufus) solely for the purpose of producing furs.
NE.note: The eleventh Bengal answer on this map, and it turns on two words with no generation rule attached. Nebraska bans every member of Felidae and then excepts "the species Felis domesticus". A late-generation Bengal registered and sold as a domestic cat is Felis catus and clears it. An early-generation animal is a hybrid rather than a member of that species, and nothing in the statute or in 166 NAC 8 says where the line falls: the chapter defines a hybrid as "an animal produced by crossing species or subspecies" and then never uses the definition to answer this. So the condition is real and its threshold is not written down anywhere, which is a different problem from the states that pick a filial number and stick to it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches it. § 153A-131 hands the question to counties, several of which have used it.

VA.quote: Felidae   All Species   Cats*
VA.note: The table restricts the cat family without exception and without a hybrid clause, which is the problem. A Bengal is registered as Felis catus but carries leopard cat ancestry, and the rule offers no filial generation line to settle which side it falls. Ask the Department of Wildlife Resources before buying.

HI.quote: Felis catus crossed with lynx, ocelot, margay, puma, jaguarandi, bobcat, leopard cat, wild cat, etc. ... cat, hybrid; (all hybrid-crosses where one or both parents are prohibited or restricted)
HI.note: Hawaii is one of the few states to write the hybrid question into the rule instead of leaving it open. The prohibited list names the leopard cat cross specifically, and § 150A-6.2(b) sets up an expert committee to settle disputed lineage. There is no filial generation cutoff, so a late generation Bengal is in the same position as an F1.

ME.quote: Carnivora (Carnivores)   Mustela putorius furo   Domestic Ferret
ME.note: A Bengal is registered as Felis catus, and a domestic cat is not wildlife, so the unrestricted list is arguably the wrong document to consult. But the list clears exactly one carnivore, and Maine regulates hybrids of wild species elsewhere in its wildlife rules. Nothing here settles which side a Bengal falls on. Ask Inland Fisheries and Wildlife before buying.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: The unrestricted list names one hybrid, the wolf and dog cross, and no cat of any kind. A Bengal is registered as a domestic cat, so whether Code 09.02 reaches it at all is the question, and this document does not answer it. Ask the Game and Fish Commission.

OH.quote: All of the following, including hybrids with domestic cats unless otherwise specified: (a) Cheetahs; (b) Lynxes ... (c) Cougars ... (d) Caracals; (e) Servals, excluding hybrids with domestic cats commonly known as savannah cats.
OH.note: Ohio is unusually clear about cat hybrids, and the Asian leopard cat is not on the dangerous wild animal list in any form. The five cats whose hybrids are caught are named, and Prionailurus is not among them, so a Bengal is an ordinary domestic cat here. Ohio even carves the savannah cat out expressly, which shows the drafters had hybrids in mind.

WA.quote: Family felidae, only lions, tigers, captive-bred cougars, jaguars, cheetahs, leopards, snow leopards, and clouded leopards
WA.note: The word only is doing the work. Washington names eight big cats and reaches their hybrids, but Prionailurus bengalensis is not among them, so a Bengal falls outside the statute no matter what filial generation it is.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Cat - Felis catus - including breeds that are recognized by The International Cat Association as Preliminary New, Advanced New, Non-championship, and Championship Breeds
UT.note: Utah resolves cat hybrids by TICA recognition rather than by generation, and the Bengal is a TICA Championship breed, so it lands in the domestic column outside the rule. That is an unusually clean answer next to the generation tests used by New York and Iowa.

PA.quote: In the family Felidae . Species and subspecies, except species which are commonly called house cats which may be possessed but not released into the wild.
PA.note: Genuinely unresolved, and the ambiguity is structural. The Bengal is a cross between the domestic cat and the Asian leopard cat, so it sits on both sides of this line at once: the opening sentence of § 137.1(a) prohibits a crossbreed or hybrid of the listed animals which are similar in appearance, while the Felidae line exempts species commonly called house cats. Nothing in the regulation names a filial generation, a percentage of wild ancestry, or the Bengal itself, so an early generation animal and a late generation one get the same silent text. Rendered grey rather than guessed.

MI.quote: any of the following cats of the Felidae family, whether wild or captive bred, including a hybrid cross with such a cat: a lion, a leopard (including a snow leopard or clouded leopard), a jaguar, a tiger, a cougar, a panther, or a cheetah
MI.note: The Large Carnivore Act runs on a closed list, and the drafters showed how they expand it: they wrote leopard and then spelled out that snow leopards and clouded leopards count. The Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal is Prionailurus bengalensis, a small Asian cat that is not a leopard and is not one of the animals they chose to name. The hybrid clause reaches a cross with such a cat, meaning one of the listed seven, so it does not catch this cross either. Nothing else in Michigan names domestic cat hybrids.

VT.quote: Carnivora | Feliformia | Felidae | All wild-domestic hybrid cats of F4 generation or greater
VT.note: Vermont draws the line by generation, which is unusually precise. An F4 or later Bengal is unrestricted. An earlier generation animal is on no list and therefore restricted, and the permit that would cover it is not issued for pet keeping. Ask the breeder for the filial generation before you buy, because it is the whole answer here.

NM.quote: Mammal | Cat | Felidae | Felis catus | Common house cat & hybrids | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. An unusually clean answer for a Bengal, because New Mexico writes hybrids into the domestic cat row rather than leaving them to be argued about. The wild parent species, Prionailurus bengalensis, sits separately in Group IV as a federally endangered animal, but the hybrid does not inherit that.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (q) All felines, except mountain lions and bobcats;
NV.note: Nevada disposes of the whole hybrid cat question in seven words by clearing the entire family and naming only two exceptions, neither of which is a small cat. A Bengal is a feline, so no filial generation argument arises and no permit is needed. This is the most permissive answer of any state on this map. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: Hybrid wildlife, as defined in R12-4-401, that result from the interbreeding of at least one parent species of wildlife that is listed under this Section are regulated by this Section.
AZ.note: Arizona is one of the few states with an express rule on hybrids, and it points the wrong way for the Bengal. The whole order Carnivora is restricted, which takes in the Asian leopard cat behind the breed, and subsection E then says hybrids resulting from the interbreeding of at least one listed parent species are regulated by the same section. No filial generation cutoff appears, so on the text a late-generation Bengal is caught alongside an F1. The counterweight is subsection D, which exempts domestic animals, defined as a species that does not exist in the wild, and a Bengal is a cross rather than a species. Recorded restricted rather than banned or legal, because the permit regime plainly reaches it and pet keeping is not clearly ruled out.

DE.cite: 3 Del. Admin. Code 903-6.2, with Del. Code tit. 3 § 7201
DE.quote: Unless specifically exempt from the permitting requirement as presented in regulation 6.1, all persons who would own or have custody of an exotic animal must first obtain a permit issued by the Department.
DE.note: The Bengal is a hybrid of a wild mammal, which § 7201 names expressly alongside wild mammals themselves, and no cat appears on the exempt list. So an Individual permit is required and the filial generation does not enter into it, because the statute reaches the hybrid as such. The permit is a $25 Individual permit from the Department of Agriculture, issued where possession will be in the public interest, so this is a real route rather than a closed door.

CO.quote: Domestic cat (Felis catus) including hybrids with wild felines
CO.note: Colorado disposes of the entire hybrid cat question in five words. The domestic animal list clears Felis catus "including hybrids with wild felines", with no generation cutoff, no weight threshold and no registration, so an F1 Bengal sits in the same place as a housecat. Arizona reaches the opposite answer on an express hybrid clause, and Pennsylvania cannot answer it at all, which makes this among the cleanest hybrid rules on the map. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: "Dangerous animal" means a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, bear, hyena, wolf or coyote. Dangerous animal does not mean any herptiles included in the Herptiles-Herps Act.
IL.note: Illinois names 11 wild cats and stops. The Bengal is a cross with the Asian leopard cat, Prionailurus bengalensis, which is not one of them, and the statute has no hybrid clause, no generation cutoff and no weight threshold, so nothing in it reaches a Bengal at any filial generation. Worth reading the list carefully rather than the word leopard in it: the leopard named is Panthera pardus. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

OR.quote: Any member of the family Felidae not indigenous to Oregon, except the species Felis catus (domestic cat)
OR.note: Oregon has no hybrid clause anywhere in its exotic animal statute, which is what decides this. The definition names Felidae and excepts Felis catus, and the wildlife rules separately declare "Cat (all domestic breeds) — Felis catus" not wild, so a Bengal registered as a domestic breed sits on the exempt side of both. The statute goes further than silence: ORS 609.341(4)(a)(B) expressly contemplates breeding a small exotic feline with a domestic cat for retail sale of the offspring under an Agriculture permit, which is the Bengal and Savannah breeding programme described in a statute that then does nothing to the offspring. Compare Minnesota, where the same question turns on a hybrid sentence Oregon never wrote. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Category One Wild Animal" means, notwithstanding changes in taxonomic nomenclature, any wild animal, gamete or hybrid of any of the following: (A) A member within the family Felidae (including, but not limited to, lion, leopard, cheetah, jaguar, ocelot, jaguarundi cat, puma, lynx and bobcat) except Bengal cat pursuant to section 26-40a of the Connecticut General Statutes; (B) A member within the family Canidae (including, but not limited to, wolf and coyote); (C) A member within the family Ursidae ...; or (D) A member within the family Hominidae ...
CT.note: Connecticut writes the exception into the middle of the family listing: Felidae, "except Bengal cat pursuant to section 26-40a of the Connecticut General Statutes". It is the only species carved out of Category One by name, and there is no generation cutoff, weight threshold or registration attached to it. The clause also opens with "notwithstanding changes in taxonomic nomenclature", which forecloses the argument that a reclassification could pull the animal back in. Set against Minnesota, where a carve-out and a hybrid sentence in one definition contradict each other, this is what an unambiguous answer to the hybrid question looks like.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Bobcat/domestic cat hybrids ... Hybrids resulting from a cross between a Class II species and a domestic animal or Class III species
TN.note: Two things settle this. The Class I cat entry is "Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs, cougars--All species", and the Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal, Prionailurus bengalensis, is none of them, so it is Class III itself under the catch-all and its hybrid with a domestic cat is too. And Tennessee shows its hand two subdivisions later by putting bobcat/domestic cat hybrids in the no-permit class expressly, even though the bobcat is a native Class II animal. A state that deliberately drops a hybrid of its own native wildcat into Class III is not reaching an Asian leopard cat hybrid by implication.

TX.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means: (A) a lion; (B) a tiger; (C) an ocelot; (D) a cougar; (E) a leopard; (F) a cheetah; (G) a jaguar; (H) a bobcat; (I) a lynx; (J) a serval; (K) a caracal; (L) a hyena; (M) a bear; (N) a coyote; (O) a jackal; (P) a baboon; (Q) a chimpanzee; (R) an orangutan; (S) a gorilla; or (T) any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision.
TX.note: The ninth different answer to the Bengal question on this map, and it turns entirely on clause (T), which reaches a hybrid only of an animal "listed in this subdivision". The small cats on that list are specific: ocelot, bobcat, lynx, serval, caracal. Prionailurus bengalensis, the Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal, is none of them and appears nowhere in Texas law, so its hybrid is not caught. No generation cutoff, no weight test, no registry requirement. The sentence does catch a Savannah, because the serval is at clause (J), which puts the two hybrid breeds on opposite sides of one line.

MA.quote: No person shall possess, sell, trade, breed, import, export or release a wild canid hybrid or wild felid hybrid, except as otherwise provided by rules and regulations of the division. ... The provisions of this section shall not apply to an owner or person possessing a domesticated show or pet cat registered with a nationally or internationally recognized breeding association or registry which certifies the pedigree and registration of such cat to be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of three generations.
MA.note: The tenth Bengal answer on this map, and the only one that requires the registry paperwork rather than merely referring to it. § 77A prohibits possessing a wild felid hybrid outright, and 321 CMR 9.02(2)(e) confirms the route by making every wild-domestic mammal hybrid domestic EXCEPT wild canid and wild felid hybrids, which it sends back to § 77A. The exit is a cat registered with a national or international registry whose pedigree certifies no wild felid parentage for at least three generations, which lands on the same animal as Iowa's fourth filial generation but reaches it by counting backwards from the cat rather than forwards from the cross. Two conditions, not one: the generations alone are not enough without the registration, and the registration alone is not enough without the certified pedigree. MassWildlife applies the same test to the Savannah, saying it is domestic "only if it can be documented to be generations (F4) past the original mating with an African Serval".

grandfathered.detail: An owner in possession on 1 January 1994 who obtained a permit from the director on or before 31 July 1994 is outside the section.

FL.quote: Class III: All other wildlife not listed herein, except those for which a permit is not required pursuant to Rule 68A-6.003, F.A.C. ... Hybrids resulting from the cross between wildlife and domestic animal, which are substantially similar in size, characteristics and behavior so as to be indistinguishable from the wild animal shall be regulated as wildlife at the higher and more restricted class of the wild parent.
FL.note: The twelfth Bengal answer on this map, and the only one written as a resemblance test. 68A-6.002(1)(d) reaches hybrids of wildlife and domestic animals only where they are "substantially similar in size, characteristics and behavior so as to be indistinguishable from the wild animal", and then regulates them at the class of the wild parent. A Bengal sold as a pet is not indistinguishable from an Asian leopard cat, so the clause does not engage. And even where it did, the answer would be mild: Prionailurus bengalensis is on neither the Class I nor the Class II list, only the fishing cat represents that genus in Class II, so the wild parent is itself Class III and the worst case is the free personal use permit rather than a bar. No generation number appears anywhere, which leaves an early-generation animal to an argument about whether it looks like its wild parent.

GA.cite: R. 391-4-8-.04(1)(a)2(ii); DNR Guide to Legal Pets
GA.quote: The following wild animals are considered inherently dangerous to human beings and pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4 are subject to licensing and liability insurance requirements. (a) Mammals: ... 2. Order Carnivora: (i) Family Canidae: Genera Canis, Chrysocyon, Cuon, and Lycaon (wolves, jackals, dingos, etc.) - All species ...; (ii) Family Felidae (cats) - All species; (iii) Family Hyaenidae (hyenas) - All species; ...
GA.note: The fourteenth Bengal answer on this map and the bluntest. Georgia has no generation rule, no weight test and no registry carve-out. The inherently dangerous list is "Family Felidae (cats) - All species", and DNR states the hybrid position directly: "Hybrids or crosses between any combination of domestic animals, wildlife, or regulated wild animals and all subsequent generations are regulated in Georgia and may not be held without a license", followed by "Most exotic cat hybrids, such as a savannah cat, are not a legal pet in Georgia." The phrase "all subsequent generations" is what forecloses the argument every other state on this row leaves open.

NJ.quote: Carnivora Canidae--Nondomestic dogs / Ursidae--Bears / Felidae--Nondomestic cats
NJ.note: New Jersey writes the cat line as "Felidae--Nondomestic cats" and stops there. There is no hybrid provision anywhere in subchapter 4, no generation count of the sort New York and Massachusetts use, and no filial cutoff in the Division's published notice, so the whole question is carried by the word "nondomestic" doing work the rule never defines. A Bengal is Felis catus crossed to Prionailurus bengalensis, which makes it half of each category the line distinguishes. The statute above the rule does not help either, because N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3(j) excludes "domesticated companion animals ... as defined by the Fish and Game Council" and the Council has not defined that term by rule. Recorded as unread rather than guessed, because the two available guesses are a free pet and a species that may not be kept at all.

CA.note: The reptile list covers crocodilians, snapping turtles, venomous snakes and the Gila monster only.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the veiled chameleon is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles
DC.note: Lizards are absent from the permitted list entirely.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The reptile clause is a list of families and the veiled chameleon belongs to none of them: not Helodermatidae, not a venomous snake family, not Boidae, Pythonidae, Varanidae, Iguanidae, teiidae, Chelydridae or Crocodylia. Chamaeleonidae appears nowhere in the article.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: New Jersey is a closed-list state in the strict sense. 7:25-4.2(a) bars possession of any exotic or nongame species without a permit, 4.4 then names the handful that may be kept without one, and 4.5 sweeps everything else back in. The veiled chameleon appears on none of the Division's three lists, so it is not exempt under 4.4, not one of the families singled out in 4.3, and not potentially dangerous under 4.8. That leaves 4.5, and the permit it points to is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, which 4.7 conditions on diet, caging that prevents escape, lawful acquisition, veterinary care and freedom from disease. The Division's own handout tells readers to phone the permits office for anything the lists do not name, which is a fair signal that the catch-all is where these end up rather than an oversight. Chamaeleonidae is absent from 4.3, which does reach a long run of lizard families, so the chameleons are one of the groups that only 4.5 answers.

ME.note: Named by binomial on the unrestricted list, so no permit of any kind applies.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Chamaeleo calyptratus is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004. Worth noting that this species has established populations in south Florida and the state has still not listed it, which is a reminder that the prohibited list is a set of individual decisions rather than a rule about establishment.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the veiled chameleon is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No chameleon appears in any category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MA.quote: All true Chameleons (Chamaelenoidae) may be kept without a permit, except species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3).
MA.note: The true chameleons are cleared as a family, subject to the categorical bar, and Chamaeleo calyptratus is IUCN least concern so the bar does not reach it. The family is worth checking species by species in this state rather than relying on the group, because a great many chameleons are IUCN-listed and this one is not.

CO.quote: Any species of lizard native only to the tropical and subtropical region from the following families: Chamaeleonidae (chameleons)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. CPW files Chamaeleo calyptratus against this line. This entry moved chapters in 2026: the same family listing used to sit in Chapter W-11 § 1103(B) and now lives in Chapter W-7. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

OR.quote: Chameleons -- Chamaeleonidae -- All species;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. The whole family is cleared, so no chameleon question arises in Oregon. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

WA.note: Varanidae covers water and crocodile monitors only; no chameleons.

OH.note: The only lizard listed is the Komodo dragon.

VA.note: Chamaeleonidae is absent from the permit table.

AR.quote: Veiled Chameleon (Chamaeleo calyptratus)
AR.cite: Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.note: Named individually on the unrestricted list, so no permit is required.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians

KY.note: The only lizards restricted are gila monsters and beaded lizards, the Komodo dragon, and nothing else.

RI.quote: Old World Chameleons (Chameleonidae) may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;

MO.note: Not native to Missouri, so outside Class I, and not a deadly or dangerous reptile.

KS.note: Only snakes are named among the reptiles, and only venomous ones.

SC.quote: 15. reptiles

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous lizards not on the controlled or prohibited lists, including but not limited to the following families or subfamilies: ...(vi) Chamaeleonidae (chameleons);

WV.quote: The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: The only reptiles in the guidance are large constrictors, venomous snakes and crocodilians.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)

AL.note: Only tegus of the genus Salvator are named among the lizards.

IN.quote: (4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter or in the current administrative rules.

WY.quote: (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.

MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

LA.note: On neither the prohibited nor the restricted nonnative list. The restricted lizards are the Asian water monitor, brown basilisk, spiny-tailed iguana, curly-tailed lizard and Peter's rock agama.

OK.quote: monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license

HI.quote: The introduction into Hawaii of live animals or live non-domestic animals as defined in this chapter at any stage of development is prohibited except for those animals on the lists
HI.note: Chamaeleo calyptratus appears on no Hawaii list. The only chameleons named anywhere are Chamaeleo chamaeleon and Furcifer oustaleti, both on the restricted list for research and exhibition only. Veiled chameleons are established in the wild on Maui and Oahu, which is exactly the outcome the default rule exists to prevent.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The squamate half of the definition is exhaustively enumerated: varanidae limited to water and crocodile monitors, helodermatidae, the venomous snake families, and henophidia limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas and African rock pythons. Nothing here is among them.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The veiled chameleon is native to the Arabian Peninsula and does not appear on the Fish and Boat Commission's published list of Pennsylvania native species, so Chapter 79, which is built entirely around native species, does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The veiled chameleon is an Arabian species and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

VT.quote: Squamata | Iguania | Chamaelonidae | all species | Chameleons
VT.note: The whole family is unrestricted, so no chameleon needs a permit in Vermont.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Lizard | Chamaeleonidae | Chamaeleo calyptratus | Veiled chameleon | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The veiled chameleon is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The veiled chameleon is on none of it, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: The veiled chameleon is covered by the entry for chameleons is named on the exempt list at regulation 6.1, so it needs no permit at all. Delaware exempts lizards generously and exempts no snake, turtle or tortoise at all, which is the sharpest line in this state's rules.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The veiled chameleon is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A veiled chameleon is a lizard, so the breeder-source condition applies to it as much as to a Minnesota native. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. No chameleon is native to Maryland; the native lizards are three skinks, the eastern fence lizard and the six-lined racerunner. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The veiled chameleon is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Chamaeleo calyptratus is not indigenous to Texas, so 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O does not reach it, and the dangerous wild animal list at Health & Safety Code § 822.101(4) contains no reptile. Texas has no general exotic reptile permit: the only reptiles it regulates by name are the six controlled exotic snakes, the venomous species, and its own native herpetofauna through the nongame and threatened species subchapters.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Chamaeleo calyptratus is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the veiled chameleon is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. No chameleon is native to Utah and none appears on any division table. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

CA.note: Only Chelydridae among turtles.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the Russian tortoise is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it. The two chelonians Georgia licenses are the African helmeted turtle and the Chinese softshell, and its native gopher tortoise and box turtles are prohibited natives.

DC.note: Statute says 'turtles'; a tortoise is Testudines, so this is defensible rather than express.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: New York City draws its turtle line by size rather than by species: the reptile clause ends with "all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches". The Russian tortoise is not otherwise named, so an adult is lawful and a hatchling is not, and the animal grows out of the prohibition rather than into it. The four-inch figure is the same one the federal rule at 21 C.F.R. 1240.62 uses, and the reason is the same: small turtles are the ones children put in their mouths. This entry previously read as unrestricted, which is right for an adult and wrong for a hatchling. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: New Jersey is a closed-list state in the strict sense. 7:25-4.2(a) bars possession of any exotic or nongame species without a permit, 4.4 then names the handful that may be kept without one, and 4.5 sweeps everything else back in. The Russian tortoise appears on none of the Division's three lists, so it is not exempt under 4.4, not one of the families singled out in 4.3, and not potentially dangerous under 4.8. That leaves 4.5, and the permit it points to is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, which 4.7 conditions on diet, caging that prevents escape, lawful acquisition, veterinary care and freedom from disease.
