The Division's own handout tells readers to phone the permits office for anything the lists do not name, which is a fair signal that the catch-all is where these end up rather than an oversight. The only chelonians 4.4 exempts are the eastern painted turtle and the snapping turtle, so every tortoise sold as a pet in New Jersey is a permit animal.

ME.note: Maine's list mislabels it 'Greek Tortoise'. The binomial is Horsfield's/Russian; Greek is T. graeca.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the Russian tortoise is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. Native turtles are small game and cannot be possessed; an Asian tortoise is not a native turtle. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians

KY.note: On neither restricted list.

RI.quote: All exotic species of turtles may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit, except endangered species.
RI.note: The three exceptions are the Chaco tortoise, the genus Gopherus and the pancake tortoise. Testudo horsfieldii is none of them.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;

MO.note: Not native to Missouri, so outside Class I.

KS.note: Only snakes are named among the reptiles, and only venomous ones.

SC.quote: 15. reptiles

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of turtles with a carapace or shell length of more than 4 inches and not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(ix) Testudinidae (tortoises);
MT.note: The four inch floor is the federal small turtle rule written into state law. A hatchling under that size is a different question.

WV.quote: The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)

AL.note: No tortoise appears on the list and Testudo horsfieldii is not federally injurious.

IN.quote: (4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter or in the current administrative rules.

WY.quote: (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.

MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

LA.note: The turtle rules in § 101.G govern native turtles. Testudo horsfieldii is nonnative and appears on neither the prohibited nor the restricted list.

OK.quote: monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license

HI.cite: List of Conditionally Approved Animals, Family Testudinidae
HI.quote: FAMILY Testudinidae ... Testudo (all species in genus)
HI.note: A genuine surprise given how much Hawaii bans. The whole genus Testudo is conditionally approved, so Testudo horsfieldii may be imported and kept subject to the conditions the Department of Agriculture attaches, rather than being barred by the default rule the way most exotics are.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The squamate half of the definition is exhaustively enumerated: varanidae limited to water and crocodile monitors, helodermatidae, the venomous snake families, and henophidia limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas and African rock pythons. Nothing here is among them.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Tortoises (Genera: Agrionemys, Aldabrachelys, Chelonoidis, Centrochelys, Geochelone, Gopherus, Indotestudo, Manouria, Psuedotestudo, Stigmochelys, Testudo)
AR.note: Covered twice over: the Russian tortoise sits in Testudo under the usual treatment and in Agrionemys under the alternative one, and Arkansas lists both genera.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: No chelonian is on the dangerous wild animal list. The four-inch federal rule on selling small turtles still applies.

WA.quote: Class reptilia ... Order crocodilia, all species
WA.note: The only chelonian-adjacent entry is crocodilians. No turtle or tortoise is a potentially dangerous wild animal in Washington.

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The Russian tortoise is a Central Asian species and does not appear on the Fish and Boat Commission's published list of Pennsylvania native species, so Chapter 79, which is built entirely around native species, does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The Russian tortoise is Central Asian and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

VT.quote: Testudines | Testudinidae | Testudo/Agrionemys | horsfieldii | Russian tortoise (Captive Bred Only)
VT.note: Named to the species and unrestricted, but the Captive Bred Only marker is a real condition rather than a footnote. The list requires captive bred animals to arrive with a statement of origin or a certificate of veterinary inspection identifying the business of origin and the number of animals imported.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Turtle | Testudinidae | Testudo horsfieldii | Russian tortoise | II
NM.note: Group II on the Director's list: not known to be invasive or dangerous, but an importation permit is still required before the animal may be brought into New Mexico.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The Russian tortoise is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The Russian tortoise is on none of it, so no special licence is required. The only tortoises Arizona restricts are the genus Gopherus, which is its own desert tortoise.

DE.cite: 3 Del. Admin. Code 903-6.2, with Del. Code tit. 3 § 7201
DE.quote: Unless specifically exempt from the permitting requirement as presented in regulation 6.1, all persons who would own or have custody of an exotic animal must first obtain a permit issued by the Department.
DE.note: The Russian tortoise is a live reptile not native to Delaware and is not on the exempt list, so regulation 6.2 requires an Individual permit before anyone may bring one in, possess, sell or exhibit it. Delaware exempts no chelonian of any kind.  The permit is a $25 Individual permit from the Department of Agriculture, issued where possession will be in the public interest, so this is a real route rather than a closed door.

CO.cite: CPW, Wildlife and Animal Possession in Colorado, Regulated Wildlife
CO.quote: Any species of wildlife that is not specifically listed in Chapter W-11 as Domestic or Unregulated or in Chapter W-07 as Appendix A or Appendix B, the species is regulated wildlife and a CPW license is required. CPW will not issue a license for private possession (eg pet) of regulated wildlife.
CO.note: Testudinidae is on Appendix A, but only for tortoises native only to the tropical and subtropical region, and the Russian tortoise is a Central Asian steppe animal ranging far north of the 26 degree line. CPW's herpetofauna list records Testudo horsfieldii against Appendix A, C, 3 with the finding "native range is outside tropical/subtropical", and files the Greek tortoise, Hermann's tortoise and the leopard tortoise the same way, against the sulcata and the red-footed tortoise which do clear it. A tortoise being on Appendix A's family list is therefore not the answer in Colorado; the range test is.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The Russian tortoise is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: A person may not take, possess, or transport turtles without a resident angling license and a recreational turtle license. ... A person does not need the licenses specified under subdivision 1: ... (2) when buying a turtle at a retail outlet
MN.note: Turtles are the gap in the 2021 pet reptile rule. Section 97A.401, subd. 8 covers snakes, lizards and salamanders and stops there, so turtles stay under their own older regime, which is a licence requirement with a short list of exemptions rather than a source condition. Whether a Russian tortoise is a "turtle" for this section is not spelled out, since Minnesota never defines the word and its turtle rules are plainly written around aquatic natives. It does not matter much in practice: read broadly, the retail outlet exemption in subd. 2c covers a pet-shop animal anyway, and read narrowly the section does not reach it at all. Either way no licence is needed for one bought at retail, and the species is on neither invasive species list.

OR.quote: Tortoises -- Testudinidae -- All species;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Oregon clears the tortoises as a family with no exceptions and no range test, which is the opposite of how Colorado now does it. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No tortoise appears in any category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three. One caveat that applies to every Connecticut turtle on this map: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 26-78 addresses turtles separately from the regulation, and it could not be read this sitting because cga.ct.gov refuses every connection from this container. This entry rests on § 26-55-6, which is the comprehensive rule and mentions no turtle sale ban, and the point is flagged rather than assumed away.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. No tortoise is native to Maryland; the native testudines are pond and box turtles, softshells and the terrapin. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The Russian tortoise is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Testudo horsfieldii is Central Asian and appears in no Texas list. The tortoise to keep it separate from is the Texas tortoise, Gopherus berlandieri, which is listed as threatened under 31 TAC § 65.175 and cannot be taken, possessed or sold at all. The nongame subchapter and the threatened species subchapter both reach only species indigenous to Texas, so neither touches this one.

MA.quote: All species of turtles may be kept without a permit, up to a limit of 100 turtles and/or eggs, in any combination, of each species, except for the following species for which a permit is always required: 1. Species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3). 2. Argentina or Chaco Tortoise (Geochelone chilensis). 3. Gopher Tortoises (Gopherus polyphemus) and all other species in the genus Gopherus. 4. Pancake Tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri). 5. Spotted Turtle (Clemmys guttata). 6. Red-eared Slider (Trachemys scripta, including all subspecies and forms).
MA.note: The turtle allowance is generous and the categorical bar is what removes this species from it. Testudo horsfieldii is assessed by the IUCN as vulnerable, so 9.01(3)(b) applies and it cannot be exempted whatever the general clause says. Note that MassWildlife's own summary page lists only four tortoises as off limits and does not carry the rarity clause into its turtle table, while it does carry it into its snake and gecko tables; the regulation governs, and the page itself says its lists may not be all-inclusive. MassWildlife's own guidance is blunt about what that means in practice: permits for non-exempt wildlife "are issued only for certain scientific, educational, commercial, or other specific reasons" and "You will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet." The statute is less absolute, since § 23 contemplates "an individual license for an animal that is not on the special exemption list" and even sets a preference for captive-bred animals where wild depletion is an issue, so the licence exists on paper and the agency says it will not grant one for a pet.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Testudo horsfieldii is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Testudo horsfieldii is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004. Florida's tortoise restriction is aimed at its own: the gopher tortoise, Gopherus polyphemus, is on the imperiled list with its own protective provisions.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the Russian tortoise is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. The only tortoise Utah names is the Mojave desert tortoise, Gopherus agassizii, which is on the prohibited list and cannot be collected or possessed without a variance. Testudo horsfieldii is not it. The federal four inch sale rule, restated at R657-53-13(5), reaches hatchlings of any tortoise. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

CA.note: Restricted snakes are venomous families plus boomslang, twig snakes and Nerodia.

HI.note: All snakes prohibited.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The python clause is a family, not a list: "any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python". Python regius is a member of that family, so a ball python is prohibited in the five boroughs even though nothing about it resembles the examples. New York State names six large constrictors; the city bans the family. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: i. Pythons - Family Pythonidae;
NJ.note: The ball python is answered by name on the 4.3 permit list rather than by the catch-all. The list takes the whole family, "Pythons - Family Pythonidae", so it does not matter that Python regius is never named. The list is written by family as often as by species, and 4.3 is open-ended, "include, but are not limited to", so being on it settles the permit question but not being on it settles nothing. The permit is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, subject to the general possession criteria at 4.7. The contrast with the boa constrictor next door is the thing to hold on to: 4.4 exempts Boa constrictor by name while 4.3 puts every python on the permit list, so two snakes of similar size and temperament get opposite answers in the same state.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Python regius is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004. The prohibited list names six pythons and this is not one of them, which is a species-by-species line rather than a genus one.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the ball python is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. Nine constrictors are named and Python regius is not among them. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. Category Two names four pythons, the northern and southern African, the reticulated and the amethystine, and the ball python is not one of them. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MA.quote: All venomous snakes require a permit. The following snakes may be kept without a permit: 1. All species of boas and pythons (family Boidae), except those species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3), and except the African Rock Python (Python sebae), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus) and all species of Anaconda (Eunectes spp.), which require a permit.
MA.note: Boas and pythons are exempt as a family with three species pulled out by name, the African rock python, the reticulated python and every anaconda, and the ball python is none of them. The one edge worth naming: Python regius is assessed by the IUCN as near threatened, and 9.01(3)(b) bars exempting a species in the Red Book(s) without saying which categories count. Near threatened is the boundary the text does not draw, and MassWildlife lists ball pythons among the snakes that may be kept, so the practical answer is settled even though the wording is not.

OR.quote: Pythons and Boas -- Boidae -- All nonnative species (including those also classified as Loxocemidae spp.);
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Boidae is cleared at family level for nonnative species, with no length threshold anywhere in the rule. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

WA.note: Listed snakes are venomous families plus the boomslang.

OH.note: Restricted constrictors are the anacondas plus reticulated, Indian, Burmese, North and South African rock and amethystine pythons. Python regius is not among them.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. Pythonidae is not among the four venomous families named, and no python is a Maryland native. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

DE.quote: Giant snakes over 5 feet (anacondas, pythons, boas)
DE.note: Corrected from banned. Pythons do appear in these regulations, but only at 7.5.2.10, which lists giant snakes over five feet among the animals a Sales Permit holder may not breed. That is a breeding restriction on one permit class, not a prohibition on possession, and it carries a size qualifier the previous entry read past. The only animals the State Veterinarian may not permit at all are gila monsters, beaded lizards and komodo dragons. A ball python is a non-native reptile on no exempt list, so it needs an Individual permit. The permit is a $25 Individual permit from the Department of Agriculture, issued where possession will be in the public interest, so this is a real route rather than a closed door.

AR.quote: Ball Python (Python regius)
AR.cite: Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.note: Named individually on the unrestricted list. Arkansas clears the species rather than the family, so a python not on the list is a different question.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians

IA.quote: A member of the superfamily henophidia, which are limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas, and African rock pythons.
IA.note: Python regius is a henophidian but is not one of the three the statute limits itself to.

KY.quote: Venomous exotic snakes of the families Viperidae, Atractaspididae, Elapidae, Hydrophidae, and Colubridae, except for hognose snakes (Genus Heterodon);
KY.note: Only venomous snakes are inherently dangerous here. Constrictors are not listed at any size.

RI.quote: All species of boas and pythons (family Boidae), may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit except those species that are endangered, and except the Emerald Tree Boa (Corallus caninus), Green Tree Python (Chondropython spp.), African Rock Python (Python sebae), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus) and all species of Anaconda (Eunectes spp.).

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;

MO.quote: any deadly or dangerous reptile over eight feet long
MO.note: Python regius tops out well under the eight foot line and is not venomous.

KS.quote: all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The snake restriction turns on venom alone, so constrictors of any size sit outside it.

SC.quote: 15. reptiles

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous snakes not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(iv) Pythonidae (pythons);

WV.quote: (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes;
WV.note: Python regius does not reach six feet, which is the one place the statute gives a number rather than a category.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)

AL.quote: Any species of venomous reptile which has never naturally existed in the wild in Alabama including but not limited to venomous snakes of the families Viperidae, Atractaspididae, Elapidae, Hydrophiidae and Colubridae, except for hognose snakes (genus Heterodon);
AL.note: Not venomous, not a tegu, and not on the federal injurious list.

IN.quote: A permit is required under this rule for the following Class III wild animals: ...(4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter or in the current administrative rules.

WY.quote: The animals listed in this section may be imported or possessed without securing an importation/possession permit... (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.

MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian. No reptile appears anywhere in it.

LA.quote: The importation, private possession, selling, and/or purchasing of constrictor snakes in excess of eight feet... shall only be allowed via permit issued by the Department of Wildlife and Fisheries
LA.note: Python regius does not reach eight feet and is on neither the prohibited nor the restricted list, so it stays outside all three tiers.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided, monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license; except those which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma and which may be potentially injurious or detrimental to Oklahoma's wildlife, agriculture or public safety in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

ME.note: Named on the unrestricted snake list. Maine lists pythons species by species rather than clearing the family, so the ball python's presence says nothing about its larger relatives.

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The ball python is West African and does not appear on the Fish and Boat Commission's published list of Pennsylvania native species, so Chapter 79, which is built entirely around native species, does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The ball python is West African and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

VT.quote: Squamata | Serpentes | Boidae | All species of boas and pythons, except those listed in Appendix that require an importation and possession
VT.note: Boas and pythons are unrestricted as a group, and the Restricted list claws back eleven of them. The ball python is not among them.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Snake | Pythonidae | Python regius | Ball Python | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Worth contrasting with the reticulated python two rows down, which is Group IV. New Mexico sorts pythons by species rather than treating the family as one.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The ball python is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The ball python is on none of it, so no special licence is required. Pythonidae appears nowhere in the rule.

CO.quote: Any species of snake native only to the tropical and subtropical region from the following families: Pythonidae (giant snakes)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. The ball python is West and Central African and breeds nowhere outside the tropics, so it satisfies the "native only" qualifier that decides most of this appendix. CPW's herpetofauna list files Python regius against this line. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: Unless contrary to any other law or rule, nothing shall prohibit lawfully acquired possession of any of the Boidae family, such as boas, pythons, and anacondas, provided captive maintenance requirements from the Department as set forth in this Act are met. All boas, pythons, and anacondas referenced in this Act are exempt from the permit process, associated annual fee, and liability insurance coverage.
IL.note: Illinois clears the boas and pythons by name in statute rather than by leaving them off a list, which is a stronger position than most species here get. There is no length threshold anywhere in it. What the Act does attach is husbandry: § 15-10 requires any boa, python or anaconda not native to the United States to be kept in a strong, impact resistant, escape-proof enclosure regardless of length, and § 15-20 requires it to be out of public sight in an escape-proof enclosure during transport. The ball python is a python and squarely inside § 15-5. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A ball python is a snake, so it needs to have come from a permitted breeder or to have been held before 1 August 2021. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The ball python is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: Controlled exotic snake--Any live snake that is: (A) a venomous snake not indigenous to Texas; (B) any of the following: (i) African rock python (Python sebae); (ii) Asiatic rock python, (Python molurus); (iii) Burmese python (Python bivittatus); (iv) green anaconda, (Eunectes murinus); (v) reticulated python, (Python reticulatus); (vi) southern African python (Python natalensis); or (C) a hybrid of any species listed in this paragraph.
TX.note: The controlled exotic snake list is six constrictors by name plus nonnative venomous species, and Python regius is not among them. Texas named three pythons and left the rest of the genus alone, which is the clearest case on this map of a state legislating by species rather than by genus. Nothing else reaches a ball python: it is not indigenous to Texas, so the nongame caps do not apply.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Python regius is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list. Nebraska has no constrictor rule of any kind, which is a real contrast with the neighbouring states that legislate by species or by length.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the ball python is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it. Two pythons are named, the Indian and the Burmese, and Python regius is neither.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the ball python is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Python regius is on none of the division's tables. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

CA.note: California's restricted list covers named constrictors, chiefly the giant pythons and anacondas, and Boa constrictor is not among them. The order Squamata is not restricted as a whole the way order Rodentia is.

HI.note: Hawaii bans the entire snake suborder by name, which is unusually blunt even for Hawaii and reflects having no native snakes to protect. There is no permit route for a pet.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The clause reaches "any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda". Boa constrictor is the type genus of that family. New York State names the anacondas and leaves the boa alone; the city takes the whole family, which is a real difference in outcome for an ordinary pet snake. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: ... iii. Boa constrictor - Constrictor constrictor;
NJ.note: The boa constrictor is on the closed exempt list at 4.4, which is the only route to keeping an animal in New Jersey with no permit at all. It is listed under the disused name Constrictor constrictor. 4.4(b) attaches the one condition that survives exemption, that the animal "must be housed or caged in such a manner as to prevent liberation". New Jersey is unusual here. Most states that name large constrictors name them to restrict them, and this is one of the few that exempts one outright while requiring a permit for every python under 4.3(a)3.i and for the rest of Boidae under 4.3(a)3.iii. The exemption is for the boa constrictor specifically and not for boas generally, so a rosy boa or a sand boa does not come with it.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Boa constrictor is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004. All four anacondas are prohibited and the boa constrictor is not, so the two large constrictors most often grouped together sit on opposite sides of the Florida line.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the boa constrictor is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. All four anacondas are named and Boa constrictor is not, so the two are on opposite sides of the New York line. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. Category Two names three anacondas and four large pythons and no other boid, so there is no length test and no family-wide rule to catch a boa constrictor. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MA.quote: All venomous snakes require a permit. The following snakes may be kept without a permit: 1. All species of boas and pythons (family Boidae), except those species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3), and except the African Rock Python (Python sebae), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus) and all species of Anaconda (Eunectes spp.), which require a permit.
MA.note: Exempt under the family clearance, and the clearance is unusually explicit about size: MassWildlife summarises it as "All species of boas & pythons (family Boidae), regardless of size". Boa constrictor is IUCN least concern, so the categorical bar does not reach it either. Massachusetts is therefore more permissive on this animal than several states that cap constrictors by length.

CO.quote: Any species of snake native only to the tropical and subtropical region from the following families: Boidae (giant snakes)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. Boa constrictor and Boa imperator are both filed on Appendix A by CPW. The family listing alone does not settle a boa in Colorado, since the same family line puts the rosy boa and the rubber boa outside it on native range, but this species clears the qualifier. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

OR.quote: Pythons and Boas -- Boidae -- All nonnative species (including those also classified as Loxocemidae spp.);
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Cleared on the family entry, with no length threshold. Oregon has one native boid, the rubber boa, which is what the word nonnative is doing in the entry. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

WA.quote: A person shall not own, possess, keep, harbor, bring into the state, or have custody or control of a potentially dangerous wild animal
WA.note: The reptile half of the definition reaches crocodilians and venomous snakes. Constrictors are absent, at any length.

OH.note: Ohio's restricted snake list is constrictors of twelve feet or more plus the venomous families. A boa constrictor under twelve feet falls outside it, which makes length rather than species the test here.

DE.cite: 3 Del. Admin. Code 903-6.2, with Del. Code tit. 3 § 7201
DE.quote: Unless specifically exempt from the permitting requirement as presented in regulation 6.1, all persons who would own or have custody of an exotic animal must first obtain a permit issued by the Department.
DE.note: Resolved from unclear. The question was whether Delaware's list reached Boidae generally, and the answer is that the list in question is a breeding restriction on Sales Permit holders at 7.5.2.10, not a possession ban, and the only outright refusals are the gila monster, beaded lizard and komodo dragon. The boa constrictor is simply a non-native reptile that no exemption covers, so an Individual permit is required. The permit is a $25 Individual permit from the Department of Agriculture, issued where possession will be in the public interest, so this is a real route rather than a closed door.

AR.quote: Boa Constrictors (Genus Boa)
AR.cite: Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.note: Cleared by genus, which covers every Boa in the pet trade.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians

IA.quote: A member of the superfamily henophidia, which are limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas, and African rock pythons.
IA.note: Anaconda means Eunectes. Boa constrictor is a different genus and is outside the definition.

KY.quote: Venomous exotic snakes of the families Viperidae, Atractaspididae, Elapidae, Hydrophidae, and Colubridae, except for hognose snakes (Genus Heterodon);

RI.quote: All species of boas and pythons (family Boidae), may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit except those species that are endangered, and except the Emerald Tree Boa (Corallus caninus), Green Tree Python (Chondropython spp.), African Rock Python (Python sebae), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus) and all species of Anaconda (Eunectes spp.).
RI.note: Boa constrictor is not one of the five exceptions. The emerald tree boa is.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;

MO.quote: any deadly or dangerous reptile over eight feet long... unless he or she has registered such animals with the local law enforcement agency in the county in which the animal is kept
MO.note: A large female Boa constrictor can pass eight feet, which brings the registration duty into play. A smaller animal does not.

KS.quote: all non-native, venomous snakes.

SC.quote: 15. reptiles

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous snakes not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: (i) Boidae (boas);

WV.quote: (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes;
WV.note: Six feet is a low bar for a boa constrictor, so most adults would be caught if the list is adopted as guided.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Boa constrictor is not on the federal injurious list, which is why it survives a clause that catches the Burmese python.

IN.quote: (4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter or in the current administrative rules.

WY.quote: (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.

MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

LA.quote: The following restricted nonnative species may be in possession only via permit to be approved and monitored by the department... i. Boa constrictor (Boa constrictor);
LA.note: Restricted rather than prohibited, so a permit route exists, but a Restricted Snake Permit is required regardless of the animal's length and the facility is open to inspection.

OK.quote: monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: No snake appears on the permit table at all. Virginia's concern in this section is species whose release would harm native fish and wildlife.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: Permitted as a non-venomous snake. DC applies no length test, unlike Ohio and Louisiana.

ME.note: Named individually with no length or weight qualifier attached.

TX.quote: Controlled exotic snake--Any live snake that is: (A) a venomous snake not indigenous to Texas; (B) any of the following: (i) African rock python (Python sebae); (ii) Asiatic rock python, (Python molurus); (iii) Burmese python (Python bivittatus); (iv) green anaconda, (Eunectes murinus); (v) reticulated python, (Python reticulatus); (vi) southern African python (Python natalensis); or (C) a hybrid of any species listed in this paragraph.
TX.note: Boa constrictor is not on the six-name list, which covers the pythons, the green anaconda and the southern African python. The green anaconda is there and the boa is not, so the two large constrictors most often grouped together in secondary summaries are on opposite sides of the Texas line. Not indigenous, so the nongame caps do not apply either.

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The boa constrictor is a Central and South American species and does not appear on the Fish and Boat Commission's published list of Pennsylvania native species, so Chapter 79, which is built entirely around native species, does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The boa constrictor is a Central and South American species and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

VT.quote: Squamata | Serpentes | Boidae | All species of boas and pythons, except those listed in Appendix that require an importation and possession
VT.note: Not among the eleven boids clawed back on the Restricted list, which name the anacondas, the large Python species and a handful of sand boas and Australasian pythons.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Snake | Boidae | Boa constrictor imperator | Boa, Columbian Red Tail | III
NM.note: The Columbian red-tail is the boa that dominates the pet trade and it sits in Group III, needing an importation permit with specific provisions attached. The Peruvian and Argentine red-tails are Group III too. Two rows go the other way: Boa constrictor ssp, except as restricted in another group, covers the Central American and Hog Isle boas at Group I. So the answer turns on which boa, and the common one needs the permit. One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The boa constrictor is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The boa constrictor is on none of it, so no special licence is required. Boidae appears nowhere in the rule.

IL.quote: Unless contrary to any other law or rule, nothing shall prohibit lawfully acquired possession of any of the Boidae family, such as boas, pythons, and anacondas, provided captive maintenance requirements from the Department as set forth in this Act are met. All boas, pythons, and anacondas referenced in this Act are exempt from the permit process, associated annual fee, and liability insurance coverage.
IL.note: Illinois clears the boas and pythons by name in statute rather than by leaving them off a list, which is a stronger position than most species here get. There is no length threshold anywhere in it. What the Act does attach is husbandry: § 15-10 requires any boa, python or anaconda not native to the United States to be kept in a strong, impact resistant, escape-proof enclosure regardless of length, and § 15-20 requires it to be out of public sight in an escape-proof enclosure during transport. Boa constrictor is the animal § 15-5 is named for. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A boa constrictor is a snake, so it needs to have come from a permitted breeder or to have been held before 1 August 2021. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. The four snake families Maryland names are Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae and Crotolidae, all venomous. There is no constrictor length rule anywhere in the statute.
