Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The boa constrictor is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial. There is no constrictor length rule anywhere in this part.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Boa constrictor is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the boa constrictor is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it. No boid appears anywhere in the three tiers.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the boa constrictor is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Utah has a boid of its own, the northern rubber boa, Charina bottae, Controlled at Standard, and the rule handles it by species rather than by family, so nothing about Boidae attaches to Boa constrictor. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

NYC.quote: No person shall sell or give to another person, possess, harbor, keep, or yard wild or other animals identified in this section ... other than in: (i) a zoological park or aquarium ...; or (ii) a laboratory ...; or (iii) a veterinary hospital ...; or (iv) a temporary exhibit, performance or display that has been issued a permit by the Commissioner. ... For the purposes of this Code, a wild animal is deemed to be any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings and all such animals are hereby prohibited ... Such animals shall also include: (i) any animals specified by the Commissioner in regulations ...; (ii) any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule; and (iii) any of the following animals:
NYC.note: Named outright in a clause covering "Arachnida and Chilopoda: All venomous spiders, including, but not limited to, tarantula, black widow and solifugid; scorpion; all venomous arthropods including, but not limited to, centipede". Naming the tarantula beside the black widow is a stretch biologically, since no theraphosid has medically significant venom to a healthy adult, but the text leaves nothing to argue about. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

RI.quote: Nothing in this Part shall prohibit any person from possession of exotic animals or native animals of the class Insecta unless the animals of that class appear on the list of prohibited insects
RI.note: The blanket invertebrate exemption is written for the class Insecta. Spiders are Arachnida, so on the literal wording they stay inside the definition of exotic animal at § 3.6(A)(9), which covers any invertebrate that is not domestic, native or exempt.

MT.quote: A person may not import into the state, possess, or sell any exotic wildlife unless: (a) the importation, possession, or sale of the exotic wildlife is allowed by law or commission rule
MT.note: Not by name, but by omission. The arachnid entry at ARM 12.6.2205(3) clears two scorpions and no spiders, and under the white list an unclassified exotic species is not permitted. Montana is the one state where the emperor scorpion is expressly cleared and the tarantula is not.

DC.quote: a person shall not import into the District, possess... any living member of the animal kingdom, including those born or raised in captivity, except the following
DC.note: Same gap as the millipede. The seven permitted categories contain no invertebrate.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian. No invertebrate appears in it.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: The permit provision at § 50-16-20 lists furbearers, cervids, pigs, peccaries, bovids, coyote, bear and turkey. No invertebrate is in it, and Chapter 47-2 covers only big cats, bears and great apes.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: No invertebrate appears anywhere in the chapter.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No invertebrate is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. Counties may regulate animals dangerous to persons or property under § 153A-131.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: On neither Kentucky list, which are drawn around vertebrates and a few named pests.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: No invertebrate appears in the categories the board is directed to consider.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: Absent from the permit table, which covers vertebrates.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles. No invertebrate appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state
LA.note: Louisiana's exotic animal rules cover wild quadrupeds, big cats, primates, reptiles and amphibians. No invertebrate appears in either.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds... and those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri.
MO.note: The Wildlife Code classes cover birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians and cervids. No invertebrate is in any of them.

HI.quote: Any animal that is not on the lists of conditionally approved, restricted, or prohibited animals shall be prohibited until the board's review and determination for placement on one of these lists
HI.note: No theraphosid appears on any of the four lists. Hawaii's lists cover invertebrates in detail, down to leeches and brine shrimp, so the absence is a genuine gap rather than a category the rules ignore, and the default prohibition fills it.

WY.quote: "Cold-Blooded Wildlife" means all fish, amphibians, reptiles, mollusks, crustaceans, their viable gametes (eggs and sperm), fertilized eggs and any transgenic product or hybrid thereof.
WY.note: Wyoming divides its wildlife rules by body temperature, and the cold-blooded definition stops at crustaceans. An arachnid is in neither chapter, so the Game and Fish regulations simply do not reach it.

NH.quote: A permit to import wildlife shall be required for all species, including hybrids, designated as controlled as cited in Table 800.01.
NH.note: New Hampshire defines wildlife to include invertebrates, so a tarantula is within reach of the chapter in principle. The permit duty attaches to Table 800.1, which contains no invertebrate at all, and the prohibited invertebrates are aquatic pests: zebra mussels, two waterfleas, non-indigenous crayfish and the Asiatic clam. A tarantula is on none of the three lists, so nothing requires a permit.

ID.quote: No person may import into Idaho, export from Idaho, transport, possess or otherwise hold in captivity, propagate, sell or release into the wild any live wildlife, except those animals exempted by Idaho Code or these rules, without a corresponding import, export, transport, captive possession... license/permit from the Department.
ID.note: Idaho Code § 36-202(g) defines wildlife as any form of animal life, native or exotic, generally living in a state of nature, which on its face reaches an invertebrate. The conventional pets exemption is a closed list that names no invertebrate, and the contrast is deliberate: the agricultural animals definition two lines above says include but are not limited to, while this one does not. Read literally that means a captive possession license, which is almost certainly not how the Department treats a pet shop tarantula. Worth a phone call rather than an assumption.

AK.quote: "game" means any species of bird, reptile, and mammal, including a feral domestic animal, found or introduced in the state, except domestic birds and mammals
AK.note: An invertebrate is not game, so 5 AAC 92.029 does not reach it. Alaska's plant and animal import rules are aimed at agricultural pests, which is a separate regime from the live game permit.

ME.quote: Araneae (Spiders) ... Grammostola pulchra ... Grammostola pulchripes ... Grammostola rosea
ME.note: Three tarantulas are unrestricted and no others: the Brazilian black, the Chaco golden knee and the Chilean rose. Every Brachypelma, Aphonopelma, Caribena or Poecilotheria needs a permit. This is the sharpest species-level split in the matrix, and it turns entirely on which animal is in the enclosure.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: The unrestricted list has no invertebrate section, so whether a tarantula needs an exemption depends on whether the Game and Fish Commission's definition of wildlife reaches invertebrates at all. Most state game codes stop at vertebrates, but Arkansas's does list mussels among the aquatic wildlife it regulates, which cuts the other way.

CA.quote: (8) Class Crustacea   Crustaceans ... (9) Class Gastropoda   Slugs, Snails ... (10) Class Bivalvia   Bivalves
CA.note: Section 671 reaches invertebrates, but only three classes of them: crustaceans, gastropods and bivalves, all aquatic or agricultural concerns. No arachnid appears anywhere in the manual.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Chapter 935 lists no invertebrate. The only match for the word spider in the statute is the black spider monkey, which is a primate.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: The statute covers mammals and reptiles only, so no invertebrate is reached.

WI.cite: Wis. Admin. Code ch. NR 40; Wis. Stat. § 169.04(4)(b)
WI.note: No invertebrate kept as a pet appears on NR 40, whose terrestrial invertebrate entries are forest and soil pests such as the emerald ash borer and jumping worm. Non-native species are outside captive wildlife licensing.

PA.quote: Wild birds, wild mammals and facsimiles thereof, regardless of classification, whether protected or unprotected, including any part, product, egg or offspring thereof, or the dead body or parts thereof (excluding fossils), whether or not included in a manufactured product or in a processed food product.
PA.note: A tarantula is neither a bird nor a mammal, so it is not wildlife and the Game Commission has no authority over it. The Fish and Boat Commission's Chapter 79 covers reptiles and amphibians. Pennsylvania's two animal agencies divide the field between them and a terrestrial invertebrate falls in the gap, so no state possession rule applies.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: A tarantula is not a reptile or amphibian, so the herp order does not reach it, and it is not a cat, a bear or native game, so neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the captive game permit reaches it either. Michigan regulates terrestrial invertebrates through its invasive species list rather than any pet law, and no common pet invertebrate is on it.

VT.quote: All species of Invertebrates, except those listed in Appendix that require an importation and possession permit. Note: Importation of any invertebrate species also requires compliance with USDA regulations.
VT.note: A tarantula is covered by the blanket invertebrate entry, and the Restricted list claws back no terrestrial invertebrate at all. The USDA condition attaches to importing rather than to keeping.

NM.cite: Director's Species Importation List, 2023, and 19.35.7 NMAC
NM.quote: Any species of live non-domesticated animal not currently on the species importation list will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.
NM.note: A tarantula is not on the Director's list, and neither is any other terrestrial invertebrate: the roughly 1,300 rows are mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish. Read literally the default clause would designate it group IV and bar it, since it is a live non-domesticated animal. Read in context that looks wrong, because the rule is titled importation of live non-domesticated animals, birds and fish, its scope speaks of wildlife species, and its machinery is veterinary inspection certificates and disease testing built for vertebrates. The regulation never uses the word invertebrate. Recorded unclear rather than banned, because the definition arguably reaches the animal and plainly was not written with it in mind.

NV.quote: "Wildlife" means any wild mammal, wild bird, fish, reptile, amphibian, mollusk or crustacean found naturally in a wild state
NV.note: A tarantula is an arthropod, and Nevada's definition of wildlife lists mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks and crustaceans and stops there. Insects and arachnids are outside the Department of Wildlife's authority altogether, so neither the prohibited list nor the importation rule reaches one. A cleaner answer than New Mexico gives, where the same animals fall into a default clause written for vertebrates. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: "Wildlife" means all wild mammals, wild birds and the nests or eggs thereof, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans and fish, including their eggs or spawn.
AZ.note: A tarantula is an arthropod, and Arizona's definition of wildlife runs to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans and fish. Insects and arachnids are not in it, so Title 17 and the restricted live wildlife rule made under it do not reach one at all. Arizona and Nevada answer this the same clean way; New Mexico does not, which is why the same animals sit unclear there.

DE.quote: No person shall bring into this State, possess, sell or exhibit any live wild mammal or hybrid of a wild mammal or live reptile not native to or generally found in Delaware without first securing a permit under this chapter.
DE.note: The permit requirement reaches live wild mammals, hybrids of wild mammals and non-native reptiles only. A tarantula is an arthropod and falls outside the chapter entirely, as it does outside the exotic animal regulations made under it.

CO.quote: "Wildlife" means wild vertebrates, mollusks, and crustaceans, whether alive or dead, including any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof, that exist as a species in a natural wild state in their place of origin, presently or historically
CO.note: A tarantula is an arachnid, and Colorado's statutory definition of wildlife runs to wild vertebrates, mollusks and crustaceans and stops there. Everything CPW does about private possession, the licensing scheme in Chapter W-11, the prohibited list in Chapter W-0 and the new herpetofauna chapter, is built on that definition, so none of it reaches this animal. CPW's own species lists are divided into birds, mammals, herpetofauna and fish and marine animals, with no terrestrial invertebrate category at all, which is the same gap seen from the other side. Arizona and Nevada answer this the same clean way; New Mexico does not, which is why the same animals sit unclear there.

IL.quote: This Act shall apply only to the wild birds and parts of wild birds (including, but not limited to, their nests and eggs), and wild mammals and parts of wild mammals, which shall include their green hides, in the State of Illinois, or which may be brought into the State.
IL.note: A tarantula is an arachnid, and Illinois divides its animal law up in a way that leaves it out of every piece. The Wildlife Code says in its own words that it applies only to wild birds and wild mammals. The Herptiles-Herps Act covers reptiles and amphibians. The Fish and Aquatic Life Code covers aquatic life. The injurious species list at 17 Ill. Adm. Code 805 has a category for invertebrates, and it is headed "Fish, Mollusks and Aquatic Invertebrates". A terrestrial arthropod falls in the gap, the same way it does in Pennsylvania, so no state possession rule applies. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: "Wild animals" means all creatures, whether dead or alive, not human, wild by nature, endowed with sensation and power of voluntary motion, and includes mammals, birds, fish, amphibians, reptiles, crustaceans, and mollusks.
MN.note: A tarantula is an arachnid, and Minnesota's definition of wild animals lists seven groups, of which the only invertebrates are crustaceans and mollusks. That places it outside chapter 97A altogether, including the protected wild animal list and the possession bar built on it. The invasive species rules stop in the same place: the invertebrates designated under Minn. R. 6216.0250 are aquatic snails, rusty crayfish and the spiny waterflea. Minnesota is unusual in that its wild animal definition is broad enough to catch a ball python and still narrow enough to miss a tarantula.

OR.quote: Invertebrate species listed as approved may be imported, possessed, sold, purchased, exchanged, transported, or released in Oregon without a permit from the Department. This applies only to stock collected within the continental United States. ... Tarantulas, Family Theraphosidae (education, pet). ... Live invertebrates not on the list of approved invertebrates in any life stage may not be imported, possessed, sold, purchased, exchanged, transported, or released in the state unless a permit is first obtained from the Department.
OR.note: Oregon runs two closed lists, and this animal is on the second one. ORS 496.004(19) defines wildlife as fish, shellfish, amphibians, reptiles, feral swine, wild birds and wild mammals, so a terrestrial arthropod is outside the Fish and Wildlife rules entirely; the Department of Agriculture picks it up instead under its plant pest authority. Cleared at family level and marked for pet use, so no species question arises. The asterisked stock restriction on the two entries below it, the wolf spider and the orb weaver, which may come only from Pacific Northwest stock, does not apply to the tarantulas. The condition is a real one and easy to miss: the clearance applies only to stock collected within the continental United States, so an animal imported from abroad needs a Department permit even though the species is approved. Nothing on this list is unregulated; an invertebrate absent from it may not be possessed at all without a permit. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. A tarantula appears in none of them. This one is worth stating carefully, because Connecticut is unusual in that its definition of wild animal does reach invertebrates, and the section is titled importation, possession or liberation of wild birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates. So the answer here is not the jurisdictional gap that clears the same animal in Arizona, Nevada and Pennsylvania; Connecticut has the authority and has simply not used it against any terrestrial arthropod. The only invertebrates that could be caught are ones on the state endangered, threatened and special concern list, which is Connecticut's own beetles, dragonflies and mussels.

MD.quote: "Wildlife" means, except as provided in § 10-2A-01 of this title, every living creature, not human, wild by nature, endowed with sensation and power of voluntary motion. (2) "Wildlife" includes mammals, birds, amphibians, and reptiles which spend a majority of their life cycle on land
MD.note: A tarantula is worth reading carefully in Maryland, because the definition is broad rather than narrow. Unlike Arizona, Nevada and Oregon, whose wildlife definitions list vertebrate groups and stop, Maryland's opening words are "every living creature, not human, wild by nature", with the vertebrate list following as an inclusion rather than a limit. What saves the answer is the operative section rather than the definition: § 10-902 attaches its permit only to wildlife native to Maryland, and this species is not. Section 10-903 gives the Secretary a separate power to restrict non-native wildlife by regulation, and Maryland has used it for nonnative aquatic organisms at COMAR 08.02.19, a list of fish, crustaceans, molluscs and two plants, and for nothing terrestrial. Crim. Law § 10-621 reaches no invertebrate either. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: "Wildlife" means wild vertebrates, mollusks, crustaceans, and fish
TN.note: A tarantula is an arachnid, and Tennessee's definition of wildlife runs to wild vertebrates, mollusks, crustaceans and fish. Section 70-4-403 classifies "live wildlife", so the five classes never reach a terrestrial arthropod at all, and neither does the possession prohibition in § 70-4-401(a), which is written about wildlife. Arizona, Nevada and Colorado draw the line in almost the same words. It matters less here than in a closed-list state, since Tennessee's catch-all would have put the animal in the no-permit class in any event.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Texas regulates nongame wildlife through 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O, and the rule defines its own subject as "species of vertebrate wildlife". That is narrower than the statute it was written under: Parks & Wild. Code § 67.001 defines nongame as "those species of vertebrate and invertebrate wildlife indigenous to Texas". The department had the power to reach invertebrates and did not use it, so the tarantula sits outside the scheme entirely. The dangerous wild animal list is mammals only, and 31 TAC Chapter 57 Subchapter A, the harmful exotic species rule, covers fish, shellfish and aquatic plants and no terrestrial arthropod. This matters more here than in most states, because Texas has native Aphonopelma tarantulas: a native invertebrate is still outside the rule, since the vertebrate limit does the excluding rather than the origin test.

MA.quote: Species means an individual or individuals of any distinct non-domestic vertebrate animal population whose members interbreed when mature or are self-perpetuating through the production of viable offspring and can include any subspecies or variety of vertebrate animal.
MA.note: Massachusetts is a closed-list state, so the question worth asking first is whether the list applies at all, and for a tarantula it does not. M.G.L. c. 131, § 23 reaches "fish, birds, mammals, reptiles, or amphibians", and 321 CMR 9.01(2) defines the species the exemption list is made of as vertebrate populations. A terrestrial arthropod is outside the licensing scheme entirely rather than unlisted within it, which is a different answer from the one the closed list gives a mammal nobody put on it.

NE.quote: Wildlife means any member of any nondomesticated species of the animal kingdom, whether reared in captivity or not, including any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate and includes any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof or the dead body or parts thereof.
NE.note: Nebraska defines wildlife broadly enough to include a tarantula, since § 37-247 reaches "any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate". What it does not do is regulate one. The captivity prohibition at § 37-477(1) and at 166 NAC 8 § 001.01B is written about wild birds, wild mammals, nongame species in need of conservation and listed species, none of which is an arthropod; 166 NAC 10 covers only reptiles and amphibians; and the importation list at § 001.08A contains nothing but mammals and birds. The one loose end is that the list is headed "the following wildlife may be imported" and wildlife on the statutory definition includes arthropods, so a very literal reading of that heading would bar importing a tarantula. Nothing in the chapter turns that heading into a prohibition, and every operative sentence in it is about birds and mammals.

FL.quote: It is unlawful to introduce, multiply, possess, move, or release any arthropod, plant pest, biological control agent, noxious weed, or invasive plant regulated by the Department or the USDA except under permit issued by the Department unless a federal permit, PPQ 526, has been issued by the USDA with concurrence by the Department. No permit shall be issued nor concurrence with a federal permit, PPQ 526 made unless the Department has determined that the arthropod, plant pest, biological control agent, noxious weed, or invasive plant can be contained to prevent escape into the environment or that it will not pose a threat to agriculture, beneficial organisms, or the environment or become a public nuisance.
FL.note: Florida regulates invertebrates only in water. The prohibited list reaches the zebra and quagga mussels, the mitten crab and the Australian crayfish; the conditional list reaches more crayfish and the arapaima; and every invertebrate entry across both chapters is aquatic. Nothing in either names a terrestrial arthropod, and the captive wildlife chapter answers a tarantula no better, since its no-permit list covers reptiles, amphibians, mammals and birds and its class lists name no invertebrate at all. The rule that does reach arthropods here belongs to the agriculture department: 5B-57.004(1) bars possessing any arthropod "regulated by the Department or the USDA" without a permit. That is a federal test as much as a state one, and it is what puts the giant African millipede and the hissing cockroach into the permit tier while leaving this animal out of it, since neither a tarantula nor a scorpion is a plant pest.

NY.quote: Prohibited invasive species cannot be knowingly possessed with the intent to sell, import, purchase, transport or introduce. In addition, no person shall sell, import, purchase, transport, introduce or propagate prohibited invasive species. Regulated invasive species, on the other hand, are species which cannot be knowingly introduced into a free-living state, or introduced by a means that one should have known would lead to such an introduction, although such species shall be legal to possess, sell, buy, propagate and transport.
NY.note: New York has two ways to reach an invertebrate and neither takes in a tarantula. ECL § 11-0103(6)(a) defines wildlife as "wild game and all other animal life existing in a wild state, except fish, shellfish and crustacea", which is wide enough to include arthropods, but the closed wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses of vertebrates and Crocodylia and the dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 names none. The other route is Part 575, whose own definition of animal expressly includes "arthropods, insects, and their eggs, larvae or young", and whose invertebrate entries are the zebra mussel, the Asian longhorned beetle and their kind. Nothing on either list is a pet arthropod.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are considered inherently dangerous to human beings and pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4 are subject to licensing and liability insurance requirements. (a) Mammals: ... 2. Order Carnivora: (i) Family Canidae: Genera Canis, Chrysocyon, Cuon, and Lycaon (wolves, jackals, dingos, etc.) - All species ...; (ii) Family Felidae (cats) - All species; (iii) Family Hyaenidae (hyenas) - All species; ...
GA.note: Georgia regulates invertebrates in three places and none of them reaches a tarantula. The prohibited list at .03(1)(d) covers dreissenid mussels, giant African land snails and the marbled crayfish. The inherently dangerous list at .04(1)(d) is scorpions only, and it is species-specific: the fattail, bark and burrowing thicktail genera, the deathstalker, and one Scorpionidae species, Opistophthalmus glabrifons. The licence list at .05(1)(f) is molluscs, crayfishes and shrimps. Every entry across all three is either aquatic or venomous.

NJ.quote: "Nongame species" means any wildlife for which a legal hunting or trapping season has not been established in New Jersey or which has not been classified as an endangered species by statute or regulation of this State.
NJ.note: New Jersey never says what it does about invertebrates and the two obvious readings go opposite ways. 4.5 requires a permit for "any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species", and that last phrase is not limited by class: 4.1 defines a nongame species as any wildlife without a hunting season, and the enabling act at N.J.S.A. 23:2A-3 defines wildlife to include "or other wild animal", which reaches a spider. 4.17 confirms the Division does treat invertebrates as nongame wildlife, since it assigns conservation status to bivalves and insects. Pulling the other way, the possession statute at N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3(j) defines an exotic animal as a mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian, fish, mollusc or crustacean, which leaves out arachnids entirely, and not one of the Division's three published lists names a single invertebrate. Left unresolved rather than called either way.

UT.quote: "Wildlife" means: (a) crustaceans, including brine shrimp and crayfish; (b) mollusks; and (c) vertebrate animals living in nature, except feral animals.
UT.note: Utah answers the invertebrates at the level of the statute rather than the rule, and it answers them cleanly. Utah Code 23A-1-101(65) defines wildlife as crustaceans, molluscs, and "vertebrate animals living in nature, except feral animals". A tarantula is an arachnid, and an arachnid is none of the three, so the Division of Wildlife Resources has no authority over it, and its rules divide the same way: R657-53 reaches Amphibia and Reptilia, R657-3b birds and mammals, R657-3c aquatic animals. There is a trap in R657-3a worth naming, because reading it alone gives the wrong answer. Its own definition of "Animal" carries no class limit, and 3a-2(20)(b) says a prohibited species "also means a species or subspecies that has not gone through the division's species classification process", which on its face would make every unclassified arthropod prohibited. It does not, because 3a-1(1) makes the rule under Title 23A and the rule cannot reach further than the code's definition of wildlife does. Nor does the Department of Agriculture and Food fill the gap the way Florida's does. Utah's plant industry rules at R68 are commodity quarantines aimed at named pests, the Japanese beetle, the spongy moth and firewood, rather than a general permit for possessing an arthropod.

AL.quote: It shall be unlawful to take, capture, kill, or attempt to take, capture or kill; possess, sell, trade for anything of monetary value, or offer to sell or trade for anything of monetary value the following invertebrate species (or any parts or reproductive products of such species) without a scientific collection permit or written permit from the Commissioner, Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, which shall specifically state what the permittee may do with regard to said species:
AL.note: Alabama is one of the few states with an invertebrate rule at all, which makes the answer better grounded here than in most. 220-2-.98 is a closed list of protected native invertebrates, cave crayfish, freshwater mussels, aquatic snails and the American burying beetle, and protection there means a scientific collection permit or a written permit from the Commissioner. A tarantula is on none of it. The prohibited list at 220-2-.26 does reach two kinds of invertebrate, the giant African land snail by name and anything the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service lists as injurious crustacea or mollusk, a phrase the 2024 amendment added. Neither touches an arachnid.

IN.quote: Any invertebrate not identified in this rule is an exempted wild animal.
IN.note: Indiana answers this in one sentence, which no other state on this map does. 312 IAC 9-9 governs invertebrates in five short sections, covering crayfish, mussels and a list of endangered mussels and beetles, and 9-9-5 then says "any invertebrate not identified in this rule is an exempted wild animal". 312 IAC 9-1-6 defines an exempted wild animal as one "which is unprotected and may be taken or possessed at any time". A tarantula is not identified in the rule, so it is expressly unprotected rather than merely unmentioned.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided by law, no person may possess: 1. Any wildlife or parts thereof during the closed season for that particular wildlife species; 2. Any endangered or threatened species or parts thereof at any time; or 3. Any native bear or native cat that will grow to reach the weight of fifty (50) pounds or more. B. Persons exempt from provisions of paragraphs 1 and 2 of subsection A of this section are: ... 4. Persons possessing legally obtained wildlife, from a source other than the wild, as pets or for the purpose of training hunting dogs, except as provided for by law or under rules promulgated by the Wildlife Conservation Commission;
OK.note: Oklahoma reaches invertebrates and then lets a pet tarantula through. 800:25-25-3(a)(19) exempts "native invertebrates" from the licence requirements, carving out only crayfish and freshwater mussels, which shows the Department treats invertebrates as wildlife it could regulate. a pet tarantula is not native, so that clause is not the answer; the answer is that nothing else applies. The statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A) reaches wildlife in a closed season, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats, and a captive-bred pet is separately exempted by § 7-502(B)(4). The reptile and amphibian licence at 800:25-7-7(2) is written about reptiles and amphibians.

NYC.quote: No person shall sell or give to another person, possess, harbor, keep, or yard wild or other animals identified in this section ... other than in: (i) a zoological park or aquarium ...; or (ii) a laboratory ...; or (iii) a veterinary hospital ...; or (iv) a temporary exhibit, performance or display that has been issued a permit by the Commissioner. ... For the purposes of this Code, a wild animal is deemed to be any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings and all such animals are hereby prohibited ... Such animals shall also include: (i) any animals specified by the Commissioner in regulations ...; (ii) any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule; and (iii) any of the following animals:
NYC.note: The clause needs only one word for this animal: after the venomous spiders it says "scorpion", with no genus, no species and no venom threshold. Pandinus imperator is among the least dangerous scorpions kept as pets and is prohibited on the same word as a deathstalker. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

RI.quote: Nothing in this Part shall prohibit any person from possession of exotic animals or native animals of the class Insecta unless the animals of that class appear on the list of prohibited insects
RI.note: Same gap as the tarantula. Scorpions are arachnids, not insects.

MT.quote: Emperor scorpion - Pandinus imperator;
MT.note: Named individually, along with the Tanzanian redclaw. Those two are the entire arachnid list.

DC.quote: a person shall not import into the District, possess... any living member of the animal kingdom, including those born or raised in captivity, except the following
DC.note: No invertebrate category exists in the permitted list.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian. No invertebrate appears in it.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: The permit provision at § 50-16-20 lists furbearers, cervids, pigs, peccaries, bovids, coyote, bear and turkey. No invertebrate is in it, and Chapter 47-2 covers only big cats, bears and great apes.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: No invertebrate appears anywhere in the chapter.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No invertebrate is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. Counties may regulate animals dangerous to persons or property under § 153A-131.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: On neither Kentucky list, which are drawn around vertebrates and a few named pests.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: No invertebrate appears in the categories the board is directed to consider.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: Absent from the permit table, which covers vertebrates.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles. No invertebrate appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state
LA.note: No invertebrate appears in Louisiana's quadruped rule or its reptile and amphibian rule.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds... and those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri.
MO.note: No invertebrate appears in any of the three wildlife classes.

HI.quote: Any animal that is not on the lists of conditionally approved, restricted, or prohibited animals shall be prohibited until the board's review and determination for placement on one of these lists
HI.note: No scorpion appears on any list. The only matches for the word are scorpion fishes on the prohibited list, which are unrelated.

WY.quote: "Cold-Blooded Wildlife" means all fish, amphibians, reptiles, mollusks, crustaceans...
WY.note: Arachnids fall outside the cold-blooded definition and are not warm-blooded wildlife either, so neither chapter applies.

NH.quote: A permit to import wildlife shall be required for all species, including hybrids, designated as controlled as cited in Table 800.01.
NH.note: No scorpion is in the controlled table or among the five prohibited invertebrates, so no permit requirement attaches.

ID.quote: No person may import into Idaho... possess or otherwise hold in captivity... any live wildlife, except those animals exempted by Idaho Code or these rules, without a corresponding... captive possession... license/permit from the Department.
ID.note: Same gap as the tarantula. The venom test in the conventional pets definition is attached to reptiles and amphibians, so it says nothing either way about a scorpion, and no invertebrate category exists to fall into.

AK.quote: "game" means any species of bird, reptile, and mammal, including a feral domestic animal, found or introduced in the state, except domestic birds and mammals
AK.note: Not game, so no permit is required. Note that the venom qualifier on the clean list applies only to reptiles, and would not have reached a scorpion even if invertebrates were covered.

ME.note: The arachnid section runs to three tarantulas and one predatory mite. No scorpion appears in it, so the emperor scorpion is not unrestricted and needs a permit. Pandinus imperator is also on CITES Appendix II, though that is not what decides it here.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: Same open question as the tarantula: no invertebrate appears on the list in either direction.

CA.quote: (8) Class Crustacea   Crustaceans ... (9) Class Gastropoda   Slugs, Snails ... (10) Class Bivalvia   Bivalves
CA.note: The invertebrate classes California restricts are crayfish, mitten crabs, certain snails and slugs, apple snails, abalone and zebra mussels. Arachnids are not among them.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: No invertebrate is reached by Ohio's exotic animal law.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: Outside both classes the statute names.

WI.cite: Wis. Admin. Code ch. NR 40; Wis. Stat. § 169.04(4)(b)
WI.note: No invertebrate kept as a pet appears on NR 40, whose terrestrial invertebrate entries are forest and soil pests such as the emerald ash borer and jumping worm. Non-native species are outside captive wildlife licensing.

PA.quote: Wild birds, wild mammals and facsimiles thereof, regardless of classification, whether protected or unprotected, including any part, product, egg or offspring thereof, or the dead body or parts thereof (excluding fossils), whether or not included in a manufactured product or in a processed food product.
PA.note: The emperor scorpion is neither a bird nor a mammal, so it is not wildlife and the Game Commission has no authority over it. The Fish and Boat Commission's Chapter 79 covers reptiles and amphibians. Pennsylvania's two animal agencies divide the field between them and a terrestrial invertebrate falls in the gap, so no state possession rule applies.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The emperor scorpion is not a reptile or amphibian, so the herp order does not reach it, and it is not a cat, a bear or native game, so neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the captive game permit reaches it either. Michigan regulates terrestrial invertebrates through its invasive species list rather than any pet law, and no common pet invertebrate is on it.

VT.quote: All species of Invertebrates, except those listed in Appendix that require an importation and possession permit. Note: Importation of any invertebrate species also requires compliance with USDA regulations.
VT.note: The emperor scorpion is covered by the blanket invertebrate entry, and the Restricted list claws back no terrestrial invertebrate at all. The USDA condition attaches to importing rather than to keeping.

NM.cite: Director's Species Importation List, 2023, and 19.35.7 NMAC
NM.quote: Any species of live non-domesticated animal not currently on the species importation list will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.
NM.note: The emperor scorpion is not on the Director's list, and neither is any other terrestrial invertebrate: the roughly 1,300 rows are mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish. Read literally the default clause would designate it group IV and bar it, since it is a live non-domesticated animal. Read in context that looks wrong, because the rule is titled importation of live non-domesticated animals, birds and fish, its scope speaks of wildlife species, and its machinery is veterinary inspection certificates and disease testing built for vertebrates. The regulation never uses the word invertebrate. Recorded unclear rather than banned, because the definition arguably reaches the animal and plainly was not written with it in mind.

NV.quote: "Wildlife" means any wild mammal, wild bird, fish, reptile, amphibian, mollusk or crustacean found naturally in a wild state
NV.note: The emperor scorpion is an arthropod, and Nevada's definition of wildlife lists mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks and crustaceans and stops there. Insects and arachnids are outside the Department of Wildlife's authority altogether, so neither the prohibited list nor the importation rule reaches one. A cleaner answer than New Mexico gives, where the same animals fall into a default clause written for vertebrates. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: "Wildlife" means all wild mammals, wild birds and the nests or eggs thereof, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans and fish, including their eggs or spawn.
AZ.note: The emperor scorpion is an arthropod, and Arizona's definition of wildlife runs to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans and fish. Insects and arachnids are not in it, so Title 17 and the restricted live wildlife rule made under it do not reach one at all. Arizona and Nevada answer this the same clean way; New Mexico does not, which is why the same animals sit unclear there.

DE.quote: No person shall bring into this State, possess, sell or exhibit any live wild mammal or hybrid of a wild mammal or live reptile not native to or generally found in Delaware without first securing a permit under this chapter.
DE.note: The permit requirement reaches live wild mammals, hybrids of wild mammals and non-native reptiles only. The emperor scorpion is an arthropod and falls outside the chapter entirely, as it does outside the exotic animal regulations made under it.

CO.quote: "Wildlife" means wild vertebrates, mollusks, and crustaceans, whether alive or dead, including any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof, that exist as a species in a natural wild state in their place of origin, presently or historically
CO.note: The emperor scorpion is an arachnid, and Colorado's statutory definition of wildlife runs to wild vertebrates, mollusks and crustaceans and stops there. Everything CPW does about private possession, the licensing scheme in Chapter W-11, the prohibited list in Chapter W-0 and the new herpetofauna chapter, is built on that definition, so none of it reaches this animal. CPW's own species lists are divided into birds, mammals, herpetofauna and fish and marine animals, with no terrestrial invertebrate category at all, which is the same gap seen from the other side. Arizona and Nevada answer this the same clean way; New Mexico does not, which is why the same animals sit unclear there.

IL.quote: This Act shall apply only to the wild birds and parts of wild birds (including, but not limited to, their nests and eggs), and wild mammals and parts of wild mammals, which shall include their green hides, in the State of Illinois, or which may be brought into the State.
IL.note: The emperor scorpion is an arachnid, and Illinois divides its animal law up in a way that leaves it out of every piece. The Wildlife Code says in its own words that it applies only to wild birds and wild mammals. The Herptiles-Herps Act covers reptiles and amphibians. The Fish and Aquatic Life Code covers aquatic life. The injurious species list at 17 Ill. Adm. Code 805 has a category for invertebrates, and it is headed "Fish, Mollusks and Aquatic Invertebrates". A terrestrial arthropod falls in the gap, the same way it does in Pennsylvania, so no state possession rule applies. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: "Wild animals" means all creatures, whether dead or alive, not human, wild by nature, endowed with sensation and power of voluntary motion, and includes mammals, birds, fish, amphibians, reptiles, crustaceans, and mollusks.
MN.note: The emperor scorpion is an arachnid, and Minnesota's definition of wild animals lists seven groups, of which the only invertebrates are crustaceans and mollusks. That places it outside chapter 97A altogether, including the protected wild animal list and the possession bar built on it. The invasive species rules stop in the same place: the invertebrates designated under Minn. R. 6216.0250 are aquatic snails, rusty crayfish and the spiny waterflea. Minnesota is unusual in that its wild animal definition is broad enough to catch a ball python and still narrow enough to miss a tarantula.

OR.quote: Invertebrate species listed as approved may be imported, possessed, sold, purchased, exchanged, transported, or released in Oregon without a permit from the Department. This applies only to stock collected within the continental United States. ... Emperor scorpion, Pandinus imperator (education, pet). ... Live invertebrates not on the list of approved invertebrates in any life stage may not be imported, possessed, sold, purchased, exchanged, transported, or released in the state unless a permit is first obtained from the Department.
OR.note: Oregon runs two closed lists, and this animal is on the second one. ORS 496.004(19) defines wildlife as fish, shellfish, amphibians, reptiles, feral swine, wild birds and wild mammals, so a terrestrial arthropod is outside the Fish and Wildlife rules entirely; the Department of Agriculture picks it up instead under its plant pest authority. Named to the species and marked for pet use, in a scorpion section that runs to more than a dozen entries including the fat-tailed scorpions and the deathstalker. The condition is a real one and easy to miss: the clearance applies only to stock collected within the continental United States, so an animal imported from abroad needs a Department permit even though the species is approved. Nothing on this list is unregulated; an invertebrate absent from it may not be possessed at all without a permit. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. The emperor scorpion appears in none of them. This one is worth stating carefully, because Connecticut is unusual in that its definition of wild animal does reach invertebrates, and the section is titled importation, possession or liberation of wild birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates. So the answer here is not the jurisdictional gap that clears the same animal in Arizona, Nevada and Pennsylvania; Connecticut has the authority and has simply not used it against any terrestrial arthropod. The only invertebrates that could be caught are ones on the state endangered, threatened and special concern list, which is Connecticut's own beetles, dragonflies and mussels.

MD.quote: "Wildlife" means, except as provided in § 10-2A-01 of this title, every living creature, not human, wild by nature, endowed with sensation and power of voluntary motion. (2) "Wildlife" includes mammals, birds, amphibians, and reptiles which spend a majority of their life cycle on land
MD.note: The emperor scorpion is worth reading carefully in Maryland, because the definition is broad rather than narrow. Unlike Arizona, Nevada and Oregon, whose wildlife definitions list vertebrate groups and stop, Maryland's opening words are "every living creature, not human, wild by nature", with the vertebrate list following as an inclusion rather than a limit. What saves the answer is the operative section rather than the definition: § 10-902 attaches its permit only to wildlife native to Maryland, and this species is not. Section 10-903 gives the Secretary a separate power to restrict non-native wildlife by regulation, and Maryland has used it for nonnative aquatic organisms at COMAR 08.02.19, a list of fish, crustaceans, molluscs and two plants, and for nothing terrestrial. Crim. Law § 10-621 reaches no invertebrate either. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: "Wildlife" means wild vertebrates, mollusks, crustaceans, and fish
TN.note: The emperor scorpion is an arachnid, and Tennessee's definition of wildlife runs to wild vertebrates, mollusks, crustaceans and fish. Section 70-4-403 classifies "live wildlife", so the five classes never reach a terrestrial arthropod at all, and neither does the possession prohibition in § 70-4-401(a), which is written about wildlife. Arizona, Nevada and Colorado draw the line in almost the same words. It matters less here than in a closed-list state, since Tennessee's catch-all would have put the animal in the no-permit class in any event.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Texas regulates nongame wildlife through 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O, and the rule defines its own subject as "species of vertebrate wildlife". That is narrower than the statute it was written under: Parks & Wild. Code § 67.001 defines nongame as "those species of vertebrate and invertebrate wildlife indigenous to Texas". The department had the power to reach invertebrates and did not use it, so Pandinus imperator sits outside the scheme entirely. The dangerous wild animal list is mammals only, and 31 TAC Chapter 57 Subchapter A, the harmful exotic species rule, covers fish, shellfish and aquatic plants and no terrestrial arthropod.

MA.quote: Species means an individual or individuals of any distinct non-domestic vertebrate animal population whose members interbreed when mature or are self-perpetuating through the production of viable offspring and can include any subspecies or variety of vertebrate animal.
MA.note: Massachusetts is a closed-list state, so the question worth asking first is whether the list applies at all, and for the emperor scorpion it does not. M.G.L. c. 131, § 23 reaches "fish, birds, mammals, reptiles, or amphibians", and 321 CMR 9.01(2) defines the species the exemption list is made of as vertebrate populations. A terrestrial arthropod is outside the licensing scheme entirely rather than unlisted within it, which is a different answer from the one the closed list gives a mammal nobody put on it.

NE.quote: Wildlife means any member of any nondomesticated species of the animal kingdom, whether reared in captivity or not, including any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate and includes any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof or the dead body or parts thereof.
NE.note: Nebraska defines wildlife broadly enough to include the emperor scorpion, since § 37-247 reaches "any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate". What it does not do is regulate one. The captivity prohibition at § 37-477(1) and at 166 NAC 8 § 001.01B is written about wild birds, wild mammals, nongame species in need of conservation and listed species, none of which is an arthropod; 166 NAC 10 covers only reptiles and amphibians; and the importation list at § 001.08A contains nothing but mammals and birds. The one loose end is that the list is headed "the following wildlife may be imported" and wildlife on the statutory definition includes arthropods, so a very literal reading of that heading would bar importing a tarantula. Nothing in the chapter turns that heading into a prohibition, and every operative sentence in it is about birds and mammals.

FL.quote: It is unlawful to introduce, multiply, possess, move, or release any arthropod, plant pest, biological control agent, noxious weed, or invasive plant regulated by the Department or the USDA except under permit issued by the Department unless a federal permit, PPQ 526, has been issued by the USDA with concurrence by the Department. No permit shall be issued nor concurrence with a federal permit, PPQ 526 made unless the Department has determined that the arthropod, plant pest, biological control agent, noxious weed, or invasive plant can be contained to prevent escape into the environment or that it will not pose a threat to agriculture, beneficial organisms, or the environment or become a public nuisance.
FL.note: Florida regulates invertebrates only in water. The prohibited list reaches the zebra and quagga mussels, the mitten crab and the Australian crayfish; the conditional list reaches more crayfish and the arapaima; and every invertebrate entry across both chapters is aquatic. Nothing in either names a terrestrial arthropod, and the captive wildlife chapter answers the emperor scorpion no better, since its no-permit list covers reptiles, amphibians, mammals and birds and its class lists name no invertebrate at all. The rule that does reach arthropods here belongs to the agriculture department: 5B-57.004(1) bars possessing any arthropod "regulated by the Department or the USDA" without a permit. That is a federal test as much as a state one, and it is what puts the giant African millipede and the hissing cockroach into the permit tier while leaving this animal out of it, since neither a tarantula nor a scorpion is a plant pest.

NY.quote: Prohibited invasive species cannot be knowingly possessed with the intent to sell, import, purchase, transport or introduce. In addition, no person shall sell, import, purchase, transport, introduce or propagate prohibited invasive species. Regulated invasive species, on the other hand, are species which cannot be knowingly introduced into a free-living state, or introduced by a means that one should have known would lead to such an introduction, although such species shall be legal to possess, sell, buy, propagate and transport.
NY.note: New York has two ways to reach an invertebrate and neither takes in the emperor scorpion. ECL § 11-0103(6)(a) defines wildlife as "wild game and all other animal life existing in a wild state, except fish, shellfish and crustacea", which is wide enough to include arthropods, but the closed wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses of vertebrates and Crocodylia and the dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 names none. The other route is Part 575, whose own definition of animal expressly includes "arthropods, insects, and their eggs, larvae or young", and whose invertebrate entries are the zebra mussel, the Asian longhorned beetle and their kind. Nothing on either list is a pet arthropod.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are considered inherently dangerous to human beings and pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4 are subject to licensing and liability insurance requirements. (a) Mammals: ... 2. Order Carnivora: (i) Family Canidae: Genera Canis, Chrysocyon, Cuon, and Lycaon (wolves, jackals, dingos, etc.) - All species ...; (ii) Family Felidae (cats) - All species; (iii) Family Hyaenidae (hyenas) - All species; ...
GA.note: Georgia regulates invertebrates in three places and none of them reaches the emperor scorpion. The prohibited list at .03(1)(d) covers dreissenid mussels, giant African land snails and the marbled crayfish. The inherently dangerous list at .04(1)(d) is scorpions only, and it is species-specific: the fattail, bark and burrowing thicktail genera, the deathstalker, and one Scorpionidae species, Opistophthalmus glabrifons. The licence list at .05(1)(f) is molluscs, crayfishes and shrimps. Every entry across all three is either aquatic or venomous. This is the one to check rather than assume, because scorpions are the only arachnids Georgia names. Pandinus imperator is a Scorpionidae, the same family as the one listed species, and it is not that species, so it falls outside.

NJ.quote: "Nongame species" means any wildlife for which a legal hunting or trapping season has not been established in New Jersey or which has not been classified as an endangered species by statute or regulation of this State.
NJ.note: Same unresolved question as the tarantula, and worth noting that New Jersey does not treat venom as its own trigger the way it does for reptiles. 4.8(a) lists venomous lizards and venomous snakes by family and says nothing about venomous invertebrates, so the emperor scorpion is not potentially dangerous under the rule. It then falls into the same gap: 4.5 reaches "nongame species", which 4.1 and the enabling act define broadly enough to include an arachnid, while the possession statute at N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3(j) does not reach arachnids at all and no Division list names one.

UT.quote: "Wildlife" means: (a) crustaceans, including brine shrimp and crayfish; (b) mollusks; and (c) vertebrate animals living in nature, except feral animals.
UT.note: Utah answers the invertebrates at the level of the statute rather than the rule, and it answers them cleanly. Utah Code 23A-1-101(65) defines wildlife as crustaceans, molluscs, and "vertebrate animals living in nature, except feral animals". The emperor scorpion is an arachnid, and an arachnid is none of the three, so the Division of Wildlife Resources has no authority over it, and its rules divide the same way: R657-53 reaches Amphibia and Reptilia, R657-3b birds and mammals, R657-3c aquatic animals. There is a trap in R657-3a worth naming, because reading it alone gives the wrong answer. Its own definition of "Animal" carries no class limit, and 3a-2(20)(b) says a prohibited species "also means a species or subspecies that has not gone through the division's species classification process", which on its face would make every unclassified arthropod prohibited. It does not, because 3a-1(1) makes the rule under Title 23A and the rule cannot reach further than the code's definition of wildlife does. Venom changes nothing here. Utah does treat venom as a trigger, at R657-53-9(1)(a) for non-native squamates and at R657-53-12 for native venomous reptiles, but both provisions are inside the herp rule and neither reaches an invertebrate.

AL.quote: It shall be unlawful to take, capture, kill, or attempt to take, capture or kill; possess, sell, trade for anything of monetary value, or offer to sell or trade for anything of monetary value the following invertebrate species (or any parts or reproductive products of such species) without a scientific collection permit or written permit from the Commissioner, Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, which shall specifically state what the permittee may do with regard to said species:
AL.note: Same answer as the tarantula and for the same two rules. Worth adding that Alabama does treat venom as a trigger, at 220-2-.26(1), and the clause is written for reptiles: it bans venomous species that have never naturally existed in the wild in Alabama and then names five snake families. Nothing in it reaches an invertebrate, so the scorpion's sting is not what the rule is about.

IN.quote: Any invertebrate not identified in this rule is an exempted wild animal.
IN.note: Indiana answers this in one sentence, which no other state on this map does. 312 IAC 9-9 governs invertebrates in five short sections, covering crayfish, mussels and a list of endangered mussels and beetles, and 9-9-5 then says "any invertebrate not identified in this rule is an exempted wild animal". 312 IAC 9-1-6 defines an exempted wild animal as one "which is unprotected and may be taken or possessed at any time". The emperor scorpion is not identified in the rule, so it is expressly unprotected rather than merely unmentioned. Venom is not a trigger for an invertebrate here. 312 IAC 9-11-8(a)(4) makes venomous reptiles a Class III wild animal and 9-5-8 bars possessing a dangerous reptile outright, but both are written about reptiles and neither reaches an arachnid.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided by law, no person may possess: 1. Any wildlife or parts thereof during the closed season for that particular wildlife species; 2. Any endangered or threatened species or parts thereof at any time; or 3. Any native bear or native cat that will grow to reach the weight of fifty (50) pounds or more. B. Persons exempt from provisions of paragraphs 1 and 2 of subsection A of this section are: ... 4. Persons possessing legally obtained wildlife, from a source other than the wild, as pets or for the purpose of training hunting dogs, except as provided for by law or under rules promulgated by the Wildlife Conservation Commission;
OK.note: Oklahoma reaches invertebrates and then lets the emperor scorpion through. 800:25-25-3(a)(19) exempts "native invertebrates" from the licence requirements, carving out only crayfish and freshwater mussels, which shows the Department treats invertebrates as wildlife it could regulate. the emperor scorpion is not native, so that clause is not the answer; the answer is that nothing else applies. The statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A) reaches wildlife in a closed season, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats, and a captive-bred pet is separately exempted by § 7-502(B)(4). The reptile and amphibian licence at 800:25-7-7(2) is written about reptiles and amphibians. Venom is not a trigger anywhere in the Oklahoma code for an invertebrate. Rattlesnakes get their own season, their own five-day permit and their own sale rules, and the venomous families named at 800:25-25-3(c) are all reptiles.

GA.quote: (c) Reptiles: 1. Order Squamata: (i) Family Pythonidae - Python molurus (Indian rock python); (ii) Family Pythonidae - Python bivittatus (Burmese python); (iii) Family Teidae - Salvator merianae (Argentine black-and-white tegu); (iv) Family Varanidae - Varanus niloticus (Nile monitor); 2. Order Testudines: (i) Family Pelomedusidae - Pelomedusa subrufa (African helmeted turtle); (ii) Family Trionychidae (softshell turtles) - Pelodiscus sinensis (Chinese softshell turtle); 3. The species listed in subparagraph (c) shall only be licensed for scientific, educational, or public exhibition purposes consistent with O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4; provided, however, that such species possessed on or before the effective date of this rule may be held as a pet without a license or permit provided that the owner tags and registers all individuals with the Georgia DNR Law Enforcement Division within 12 months following the effective date of this rule;
GA.note: Georgia names six reptiles in its licence rule and then closes the pet route on all of them in the same subparagraph: they "shall only be licensed for scientific, educational, or public exhibition purposes". Salvator merianae is named by its current binomial rather than as Tupinambis, which is the post-2012 name and forecloses a taxonomy argument. This entry previously read as restricted; the correct reading is that no pet licence exists. The grandfathering is unusually generous in kind and unusually short in time: an animal held on or before the effective date may be kept as a pet with no licence at all, provided the owner tagged and registered it with DNR Law Enforcement within twelve months of that date.

grandfathered.before: the effective date of the rule
grandfathered.detail: An animal possessed on or before the effective date may be held as a pet without a licence if tagged and registered with Georgia DNR Law Enforcement within 12 months of that date.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The clause covers "any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu", using the lower-case spelling the Code prints. Salvator merianae is the black and white tegu, named and family-caught both. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

FL.quote: Live specimens of the following species, including their taxonomic successors, subspecies, or hybrids or eggs thereof may be possessed only pursuant to permit issued by the Executive Director except as provided in Rule 68-5.007, F.A.C. ... (4) Non-native reptiles: (a) Yellow anaconda ... (e) Indian or Burmese python (Python molurus). (f) Reticulated python (Python reticulatus). (g) Northern African python (Python sebae). (h) Southern African python (Python natalensis). (i) Amethystine python (Morelia amethistinus). (j) Scrub python (Morelia kinghorni). (k) Green anaconda (Eunectes murinus). (l) Nile monitor (Varanus niloticus). (m) Green iguana (Iguana iguana) (n) Tegus (genera Salvator and Tupinambis, all species)
FL.note: The entry reads "Tegus (genera Salvator and Tupinambis, all species)", which is written to survive the 2012 split that moved the Argentine black and white tegu from Tupinambis to Salvator.
