MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland writes its cat clause as the whole family with one species excepted, so the serval is caught by the same six words that catch a lion. There is no permit anywhere in this section: the exemptions run to zoos, sanctuaries, research and licensed exhibitors, and for private keepers there is only the closed 2006 notification window. Enforcement is unusually direct, with immediate seizure available on probable cause and the costs of care falling on the keeper unless a court finds the seizure unjustified. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

grandfathered.detail: Lawful possession on or before 31 May 2006 may continue, but only if the keeper gave written notification to the local animal control authority by 1 August 2006, with the number and type of animals and a photograph or a description of a tattoo or microchip. That window is long closed.

NM.quote: Mammal | Cat, wild | Felidae | Leptailurus serval | Serval | IV
NM.note: Resolved from unclear, and now confirmed rather than assumed. Named outright in Group IV. Group IV importation is prohibited for the general public and allowed only for scientific study, department approved restoration, zoological display, temporary events, use as a service animal, or by a qualified expert. One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

TN.quote: Class I--This class includes all species inherently dangerous to humans. ... The following is a listing of animals considered inherently dangerous: (A) Mammals: (i) Primates--Gorillas, orangutans, chimpanzees, gibbons, siamangs, mandrills, drills, baboons, Gelada baboons; (ii) Carnivores: (a) Wolves--All species; (b) Bears--All species; and (c) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs, cougars--All species;
TN.note: The Class I cat entry names six kinds and the serval is none of them: lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and cougars, each "all species". Leptailurus serval is not a Panthera, an Acinonyx or a Puma, and the statute names no other felid. On the statute alone the serval is Class III under the catch-all and needs no permit, and Tennessee reinforces that reading two subdivisions later by putting bobcat hybrids in Class III expressly. What could not be checked is the commission's own rules. Section 70-4-403(1) gives the commission, with the commissioner of agriculture, express power to add or delete species from the Class I list by regulation, and Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 1660-01-18 is where such an addition would sit. That chapter could not be read here: publications.tnsosfiles.com returns 403 to this container on every path, and Tennessee's official code is behind LexisNexis. Recorded unclear on that gap rather than on the statute, which is the improvement over the previous note here; the statute itself is readable and does not reach this animal. What rides on it is more than paperwork. Section 70-4-404(c)(1) closed personal possession of Class I wildlife in 1991: the permit it describes is for people who already held the animal on 25 June 1991, "no new animals shall be brought into possession under authority of a personal possession permit", and the subsection ends by saying it "shall not be construed to authorize new personal possession of Class I wildlife". TWRA restates it in one line on its permits page: "Personal possession of any Class 1 species is not allowed." So an addition by rule would not mean a $150 permit for a private keeper. It would mean no.

ID.quote: Serval (Felis serval).
ID.note: Listed under small felidae. Only the large felidae and primate lists carry the extra requirement that the facility be AZA accredited.

IA.quote: A member of the family felidae of the order carnivora, including but not limited to lions, tigers, cougars, leopards, cheetahs, ocelots, and servals. However, a dangerous wild animal does not include a domestic cat.

grandfathered.detail: An owner in possession on 1 July 2007 could keep the animal after implanting an electronic identification device within sixty days and registering with the department by 31 December 2007. No new route exists.

KY.quote: Lions, jaguars, leopards, or tigers (Genus Panthera); Lynx (Genus Lynx);
KY.note: The inherently dangerous list names Panthera, Lynx, cheetah, clouded leopard and snow leopard. Leptailurus serval is on neither that list nor the prohibited list, so possession is lawful, though a transportation permit is needed to bring one into the state and a city or county may prohibit it under KRS 65.877.

RI.quote: no permits shall be granted by the Department to a private person authorizing the import, and/or possession of any exotic wild animals of the order Carnivora, or hybrids thereof, for which there is no USDA conditionally licensed or unconditionally licensed rabies vaccine
RI.note: There is no USDA licensed rabies vaccine for servals, so the permit route is closed to private owners. § 3.7(A) restricts possession to researchers, USDA licensed exhibitors and AZA facilities.

NH.quote: 5   Serval, African
NH.note: The permittee category is 5, exhibitor, with no category 1. A private individual cannot be issued a possession permit for one.

MO.quote: if he or she keeps any lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, Canada lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, hyena, wolf, bear, nonhuman primate, coyote, any deadly, dangerous, or poisonous reptile, or any deadly or dangerous reptile over eight feet long
MO.note: The cat list runs to eleven species and the serval is not one of them. Nor is it Missouri wildlife, so 3 CSR 10-9 does not reach it either.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: Six cats by name, all of them large. Leptailurus serval is none of them, which makes Kansas one of the few states where a serval is not regulated at state level.

SC.quote: Family Felidae, Genus panthera—all lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cougars, cheetahs, snow leopards, and clouded leopards;
SC.note: The ban is drawn at one genus. Leptailurus serval is outside it, and a serval is not a South Carolina furbearer, so the § 50-16-20 import permit does not apply either.

MT.quote: Serval cat - Leptailurus serval;
MT.note: Montana is one of very few states that classifies the serval as noncontrolled by name. The caracal, by contrast, sits on the controlled list and needs a permit.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: Big cats are the second item the board is pointed at. Whether a serval counts as a big cat is exactly the kind of question the missing list was meant to answer.

AK.quote: The department may not issue a permit for the capture, possession, import, or export of any game animal, including a hybrid of a game animal and a species listed in (b) of this section, for use as a pet
AK.note: The only cat on the clean list is Felis catus.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section: (1) Of the order Carnivora, all nondomestic members of the following families: (a) Felidae;
SD.note: A possession permit costs ten dollars an animal and must be renewed annually by 1 January.

AL.quote: black bear (Ursus americanus), mountain lion (Felis concolor), bobcat (Felis rufus)
AL.note: The only cats named are Alabama's own two, and only when brought in from outside the state. Leptailurus serval is not on the list and is not federally injurious.

IN.quote: A permit is required under this rule for the following Class II wild animals: ...(11) Serval (Leptailurus serval).
IN.note: Class II, not Class III, so the permit is applied for within five days of taking possession rather than obtained in advance. A Class II wild animal is defined as one that may pose a threat to human safety.

ND.quote: The board of animal health may require a license for nontraditional livestock maintained within this state.
ND.note: Nontraditional livestock is defined as any wildlife held in confinement, which reaches a serval. Whether a licence is actually required turns on board rules, and the chapter of the administrative code that used to carry the species categories has been repealed. Ask the state veterinarian.

WY.quote: A permit may be authorized upon approval for other warm-blooded wildlife unless otherwise specified in this regulation.
WY.note: Not on the prohibited list at Section 11 and not on either the domestic or the domesticated list, so it lands in the discretionary permit category. May be authorised is not the same as shall be issued.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The cat entry is drawn by genus and Leptailurus is not among them.

LA.quote: the following big exotic cats: i. tigers; ii. lions; iii. leopards (including, but not limited to snow leopard and clouded leopard); iv. jaguars; v. cheetahs; vi. cougars or mountain lions (Felis concolor); vii. all subspecies of the above listed exotic cats; viii. hybrids resulting from cross breeding of the above listed exotic cats.
LA.note: The list is six cats. Leptailurus serval is not among them, and the hybrid clause attaches only to the six.

OK.quote: (4) Cats (except native cats and bears).
OK.note: The exemption is written for cats generally and carves out only native cats. Leptailurus serval is not native to Oklahoma.

NE.quote: (1) No person shall keep in captivity in this state any wild birds, any wild mammals, any nongame wildlife in need of conservation as determined by the commission under section 37-805, or any wildlife determined to be an endangered or threatened species ... without first having obtained a permit. (2) Except as provided in subsection (3) of this section, no person shall keep in captivity in this state any wolf, any skunk, or any member of the families Felidae and Ursidae. This subsection shall not apply to (a) the species Felis domesticus, (b) any zoo, park, refuge, wildlife area, or nature center owned or operated by a city, village, state, or federal agency or any zoo accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums or the Zoological Association of America, or (c) any person who holds a captive wildlife permit ... and who raises Canada Lynx (Lynx canadensis) or bobcats (Lynx rufus) solely for the purpose of producing furs.
NE.note: Nebraska bans the whole of Felidae by statute, not by regulation, and there is no permit behind it. The three exceptions are Felis domesticus, public and accredited zoos, and a captive wildlife permit holder raising Canada lynx or bobcats for fur, which is the only commercial route and does not reach a serval. This is one of the shortest routes to a no on this map: no list to check, no species name, just the family.

grandfathered.detail: A person legally holding such an animal on 1 March 1986 may keep it for its lifetime under § 37-477(3), and may not trade, sell or dispose of it without the commission's written permission.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches it. § 153A-131 hands the question to counties, several of which have used it.

HI.note: Listed under the cat family on Part A using the older name Felis serval rather than Leptailurus. Research and exhibition only.

ME.quote: Carnivora (Carnivores)   Mustela putorius furo   Domestic Ferret
ME.note: Same one-line carnivore list. The serval is not on it.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: No felid appears anywhere on the unrestricted list.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Except as otherwise listed, all species are presumed prohibited. All species not listed will require an assessment before collection, importation, or possession will be authorized.
UT.note: Not listed anywhere in Table 3b-1, and the table's default is inverted: unlisted birds and mammals are 'presumed prohibited' and require a division assessment before possession will be authorized. So this is neither cleared nor expressly banned, it is an application to DWR with no published answer. Worth noting the prohibited column's big cat entry lists Panthera, Acinonyx, Uncia and Puma by name under the federal Big Cat Public Safety Act, and the serval is not among them, so it falls to the unlisted default rather than the big cat ban.

PA.quote: In the family Felidae . Species and subspecies, except species which are commonly called house cats which may be possessed but not released into the wild.
PA.note: The Felidae line is a whole-family prohibition with one exception, house cats, and a serval is not a house cat. The route out is the exotic wildlife possession permit under 34 Pa.C.S. § 2963 and 58 Pa. Code Ch. 147 Subchapter N, and it is written around facilities rather than pet homes: a separate permit for each animal, and a new applicant must document two years of hands-on work with the species at a recognized or approved facility, with a letter of reference from its owner or manager. The 2005 Joint State Government Commission report on exotic wildlife in Pennsylvania lists the serval among the lesser cats given minimum cage specifications, which confirms the Commission treats it as exotic wildlife rather than leaving it to the catch-all.

VT.cite: Unrestricted Wild Animal List, July 2025, and Regulation 881
VT.quote: Species not found on the Restricted, Unrestricted or Domestic species lists are considered Restricted.
VT.note: The serval is on neither the Unrestricted nor the Restricted list, and Vermont treats that absence as a restriction rather than a gap. The only cats on the Unrestricted list are wild-domestic hybrids of the fourth generation or later. A serval is not a hybrid. A permit exists on paper but not for a pet: Regulation 881 says the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for keeping or possessing a wild animal in captivity except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes. So restricted here means a private keeper cannot have one, not that there is paperwork to fill in.

DE.cite: 3 Del. Admin. Code 903-6.2, with Del. Code tit. 3 § 7201
DE.quote: Unless specifically exempt from the permitting requirement as presented in regulation 6.1, all persons who would own or have custody of an exotic animal must first obtain a permit issued by the Department.
DE.note: The serval is a live wild mammal and is not on the exempt list, so regulation 6.2 requires an Individual permit. The permit is a $25 Individual permit from the Department of Agriculture, issued where possession will be in the public interest, so this is a real route rather than a closed door. Delaware's outright refusals at 4.7 are only the gila monster, the beaded lizard and the komodo dragon, so no mammal is barred from permitting by name. County and municipal ordinances are the more likely obstacle for a cat or a canid of this size.

CO.cite: CPW, Wildlife and Animal Possession in Colorado, Regulated Wildlife
CO.quote: Any species of wildlife that is not specifically listed in Chapter W-11 as Domestic or Unregulated or in Chapter W-07 as Appendix A or Appendix B, the species is regulated wildlife and a CPW license is required. CPW will not issue a license for private possession (eg pet) of regulated wildlife.
CO.note: The serval is a wild felid, not Felis catus, so the domestic-cat line that clears Bengal hybrids does not reach it, and Leptailurus serval appears on neither the unregulated list nor the prohibited list. That leaves it regulated. Colorado has no pet licence to issue. Chapter W-11 § 1104 offers commercial wildlife park licences, which require commercial status, and a non-commercial wildlife park licence that § 1104(B)(2) closed to new entrants: it is available only to someone who held one already or held exotic mammals lawfully before 1 January 1983. The chapter introduction states the effect plainly, that "noncommercial (pet) possession of regulated mammals has been prohibited by these regulations since 1983". The contrast inside a single sentence of § 1103(A) is the thing to notice: a serval hybrid is a domestic cat in Colorado, and a serval is not.

MA.quote: The purpose of 321 CMR 9.01 is to list those species which are exempt from the licensing provisions of M.G.L. c. 131, § 23, and which may be imported, possessed, maintained, propagated, bought, sold, exchanged or offered for sale without a license or permit from the Division. Species not listed, or which are expressly listed as "require(s) a permit", are not exempt from the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131, § 23.
MA.note: The mammal exemption list is thirteen entries and the serval is not one of them, which in a closed-list state is the whole answer. 9.01(1) says species not listed "are not exempt from the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131, § 23", and 9.02(2)(c) adds that any vertebrate taxon not on the domestic list is presumed wild. No felid appears on the exemption list at all, and the domestic list carries only Felis catus, so Massachusetts reaches every exotic cat by omission rather than by naming one. MassWildlife's own guidance is blunt about what that means in practice: permits for non-exempt wildlife "are issued only for certain scientific, educational, commercial, or other specific reasons" and "You will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet." The statute is less absolute, since § 23 contemplates "an individual license for an animal that is not on the special exemption list" and even sets a preference for captive-bred animals where wild depletion is an issue, so the licence exists on paper and the agency says it will not grant one for a pet.

FL.quote: Class II: ... 15. Servals (Leptailurus serval) 16. European and Canadian lynx (Lynx lynx) 17. Bobcats (Lynx rufus) 18. Caracals (Caracal caracal) ... 24. Wolves, coyotes, jackals (family Canidae) ...
FL.note: Named at Class II item 15, between the lynxes and the caracals, so the serval is one of the few animals Florida answers by name rather than by class. A Permit to Possess Class II Wildlife for Personal Use costs $140 a year, requires the applicant to be 18, and requires documented experience: FWC asks for a logged experience record along with facility and caging standards under 68A-6.004 and 68A-6.010. That is a real barrier rather than a fee, and it is the difference between Class II and the free Class III permit. Class I, one tier up, cannot be held as a personal pet at all.

NJ.quote: Carnivora Canidae--Nondomestic dogs / Ursidae--Bears / Felidae--Nondomestic cats ... The potentially dangerous species shall not be kept as a pet, for hobby purposes or in situations, which, in the judgment of the Department, could adversely affect the health of the animal or which could constitute a hazard to the public.
NJ.note: Leptailurus serval is a nondomestic cat and 4.8(a) takes Felidae on that basis without naming a species. What turns the listing into a ban is 4.9(a)3, which says the potentially dangerous species "shall not be kept as a pet, for hobby purposes", so the permit at 4.8(b) exists for zoos, researchers and exhibitors and not for keepers. The Division puts the same point in one sentence in its notice: potentially dangerous species "may not be kept as pets or for hobby purposes for any reason".

CA.quote: Domesticated races of chinchillas of the species Chinchilla laniger are not restricted

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia licenses whole taxonomic orders and then writes short exception lists inside them, so being named in one of those lists is the whole answer here. Chinchilla is excepted by name.

NYC.quote: In addition to domesticated dogs and cats, an animal may be kept, possessed, harbored or sold in the City of New York provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law, including federal, state and local laws regulating domestic animals and livestock or protecting wildlife and endangered species. Such animals include, but are not limited to, gerbil, hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and fowl or small birds such as parakeet, parrot, canary and finch.
NYC.note: Not named anywhere in the article. The clause to check is (b)(14), "All large rodents", whose thirteen examples are all considerably bigger, and the chinchilla is not among them. § 161.01(c) is the article's short affirmative list, and it is written as examples rather than as a closed set: "an animal may be kept ... provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law", followed by gerbil, hamster, guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and small birds. So the question in New York City is always whether something else in § 161.01(b) reaches the animal.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: New Jersey is a closed-list state in the strict sense. 7:25-4.2(a) bars possession of any exotic or nongame species without a permit, 4.4 then names the handful that may be kept without one, and 4.5 sweeps everything else back in. The chinchilla appears on none of the Division's three lists, so it is not exempt under 4.4, not one of the families singled out in 4.3, and not potentially dangerous under 4.8. That leaves 4.5, and the permit it points to is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, which 4.7 conditions on diet, caging that prevents escape, lawful acquisition, veterinary care and freedom from disease. The Division's own handout tells readers to phone the permits office for anything the lists do not name, which is a fair signal that the catch-all is where these end up rather than an oversight. It sits awkwardly next to the exempt list, which names the hamster, the gerbil, the guinea pig and laboratory mice and rats, all farmed pet rodents of the same kind. The chinchilla was simply not added, and 4.4 is closed, so the omission decides it.

ME.note: Named by binomial on the unrestricted list.

MA.quote: List of Mammals. (a) The following mammals may be kept without a permit: 1. Four-toed (African pygmy) hedgehog (Erinaceus albiventris) (= Atelerix pruneri) 2. Chinchilla (Chinchilla spp.) derived from captive stock. 3. Deer Mouse and White-footed Mouse 4. Degu (Octodon degus) 5. Egyptian Spiny Mouse 6. House Mouse 7. Jerboas 8. Norway Rat 9. Paca 10. Southern Flying Squirrel (Glaucomys volans) 11. Striped hamster ... 12. Sugar Glider (Petaurus breviceps) 13. American Bison
MA.note: The entry reads "Chinchilla (Chinchilla spp.) derived from captive stock", and the qualifier is doing real work. Wild chinchillas are IUCN-listed as endangered, which under 9.01(3)(b) means the species cannot be exempted at all, and the Division answered that by exempting the captive-bred form specifically. A keeper is asked for provenance rather than paperwork: there is no permit and no registry, but the animal has to be captive stock. This is also the clearest evidence on the face of the rule of how the Division reads the categorical bar, since it exempted a species whose wild population is listed by writing the captive qualifier into the entry.

CO.quote: Domesticated races of chinchillas (Chinchilla laniger)
CO.note: On the domestic animal list, so exempted from Parks and Wildlife Commission regulations outright. Colorado names the domesticated race of the long-tailed chinchilla specifically, and CPW files Chinchilla laniger against this line. Its close relative the degu is on no list at all and is regulated wildlife, so the two sit at opposite ends of this map in Colorado. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

WA.quote: A person shall not own, possess, keep, harbor, bring into the state, or have custody or control of a potentially dangerous wild animal
WA.note: No rodent appears in the enumerated definition.

OH.note: No rodent appears on either Ohio list.

MI.note: None of Michigan's three relevant acts reaches a rodent, domesticated or otherwise.

IL.quote: "Dangerous animal" means a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, bear, hyena, wolf or coyote. Dangerous animal does not mean any herptiles included in the Herptiles-Herps Act.
IL.note: Illinois runs a closed list of 15 named mammals plus a blanket bar on primates, and it has no catch-all clause, no size test and no dangerousness test. An animal that is not on the list and is not native Illinois wildlife is simply outside the statute. No rodent appears on it, and the chinchilla is not a native Illinois wild mammal. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: all members of the Felidae family including, but not limited to, lions, tigers, cougars, leopards, cheetahs, ocelots, and servals, but not including domestic cats or cats recognized as a domestic breed, registered as a domestic breed, and shown as a domestic breed by a national or international multibreed cat registry association; (2) bears; and (3) all nonhuman primates
MN.note: Minnesota's regulated animal definition is three groups and nothing else: the cat family, bears, and non-human primates. No rodent is in it.

NV.quote: Domesticated races of chinchillas

VA.note: The rodent section of the table names the prairie dog and a handful of ground squirrels. Chinchilla lanigera is not among them.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. No rodent appears in the eight clauses, and the chinchilla is not native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

NM.quote: Mammal | Rodent | Chinchillidae | Chinchilla laniger | Chinchilla, Long-tailed | I | Except Chinchilla brevicaudata boliviana
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Resolved from unclear. The long-tailed chinchilla of the pet trade is Group I, and the exception named is the short-tailed Bolivian chinchilla, which is federally endangered and sits in Group IV.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

VT.quote: Rodentia | Hystricomorpha | Chinchillidae | Chinchilla | all species | Chinchillas
VT.note: Resolved. Named at genus level on the Unrestricted list, so no permit is needed.

TN.note: Tennessee names the ferret and the chinchilla together in their own subdivision of the no-permit class, rather than leaving them to be inferred. Class III wildlife needs no wildlife permit and no supplier documentation, since § 70-4-401(b) reaches only Class I and Class II.

NC.quote: A county may by ordinance regulate, restrict, or prohibit the possession or harboring of animals which are dangerous to persons or property.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches the chinchilla, and it is a hard animal to characterise as dangerous to persons or property, so a county ordinance is unlikely to catch it either.

All Ratites, All Waterfowl, All Peafowl, All Game Birds, All Cage and Aviary Birds

IA.note: Not a canid, hyaenid, felid, ursid, rhino, elephant, primate or swine, which is the whole of the mammal half of the definition.

Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.note: Listed under 'Domestic mammals and mammalian livestock not covered under this rule', so R657-3b does not reach it and no certificate of registration arises.

PA.quote: Unless otherwise provided in this section or the act, it is unlawful for a person to import, possess, sell, offer for sale or release within this Commonwealth the following wild animals or wild birds or the eggs of the birds or a crossbreed or hybrid of the wild animals or wild birds, which are similar in appearance
PA.note: The chinchilla appears in none of the eleven categories the Game Commission prohibits, which run to cats, canids, bears, raccoons, nutria, skunks, primates, listed species, the monk parakeet, and wildlife taken from the wild or captive bred out of state. Read literally, § 137.1(a)(11) bars possessing any wildlife captive bred in another state, and 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines wild animals as every mammal except horses, cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, so the text reaches far wider than the Game Commission applies it. The Commission draws its line at undomesticated species, which is why hedgehogs and sugar gliders are pursued and long domesticated pets are not.

AZ.quote: Order Erinaceomorpha, all species, except members of the genus Atelerix, which are not restricted. Common name: longeared and pygmy hedgehogs; Order Lagomorpha, all species, except members of the genus Oryctolagus containing domestic rabbits, which are not wildlife and are not restricted; Order Rodentia, the families Capromyidae, Castoridae, Dipodidae, Echimyidae, Erethizontidae, Geomyidae, Sciuridae
AZ.note: Arizona restricts rodents by family rather than as an order, and the seven families named are Capromyidae, Castoridae, Dipodidae, Echimyidae, Erethizontidae, Geomyidae and Sciuridae. The chinchilla is Chinchillidae, which is not among them, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Chinchillas appear by name on the exempt mammal list, so no permit is required.

OR.quote: Pursuant to the definition of "wildlife," the following species are not subject to these rules because they are not "wild" ... (7) Chinchilla — Chinchilla laniger.
OR.note: This is the strongest position an animal can hold in Oregon. ORS 496.004(19) leaves it to the commission to define which mammals count as wild, and this rule is that definition: the 32 species on it are declared not wild and fall outside the wildlife rules altogether, rather than being permitted by them. Oregon names the domesticated chinchilla directly, and separately prohibits the Argentine plains viscacha, its wild relative in the same family. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: A member within the order Rodentia, except for guinea pig (Cavia porcellus), gerbil (Meriones unguiculatus), chinchilla (Chinchilla lanigera), rat (Rattus norvegicus), mouse (Mus musculus), hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), dwarf hamster (genera Phodopus and Cricetulus), Patagonia mara (Dolichotis patagonum) and American beaver (Castor canadensis)
CT.note: Connecticut puts the whole order Rodentia in Category Two, which bars private possession, and then excepts nine species. The chinchilla, Chinchilla lanigera is one of them, so it is named in the regulation rather than merely absent from it. Named to the species, and to the species rather than the genus: Chinchilla chinchilla, the short-tailed chinchilla, is not excepted.

TX.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means: (A) a lion; (B) a tiger; (C) an ocelot; (D) a cougar; (E) a leopard; (F) a cheetah; (G) a jaguar; (H) a bobcat; (I) a lynx; (J) a serval; (K) a caracal; (L) a hyena; (M) a bear; (N) a coyote; (O) a jackal; (P) a baboon; (Q) a chimpanzee; (R) an orangutan; (S) a gorilla; or (T) any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision.
TX.note: Chinchilla lanigera is Andean and appears in no Texas list. The fur-bearing animal definition at Parks & Wild. Code § 71.001(1) is worth checking here because chinchillas are farmed for fur, and it does not name them: it is a closed list of eleven native fur-bearers.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Named at (14)(l), with no captive-stock qualifier of the kind Massachusetts and Nebraska attach. Florida asks nothing about provenance for this animal.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the chinchilla is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species.

CA.quote: Domesticated races of guinea pigs of the species Cavia porcellus are not restricted

Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia licenses whole taxonomic orders and then writes short exception lists inside them, so being named in one of those lists is the whole answer here. Cavia is excepted by name.

DC.quote: Domesticated rodents and rabbits
DC.note: One of the seven permitted categories, and the guinea pig is squarely inside it. The same sentence is why a hamster is fine in DC and a hedgehog is not, since a hedgehog is not a rodent.

NYC.quote: In addition to domesticated dogs and cats, an animal may be kept, possessed, harbored or sold in the City of New York provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law, including federal, state and local laws regulating domestic animals and livestock or protecting wildlife and endangered species. Such animals include, but are not limited to, gerbil, hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and fowl or small birds such as parakeet, parrot, canary and finch.
NYC.note: Named in § 161.01(c). Worth pairing with the large rodent clause at (b)(14), which prohibits the paca, the viscacha and the capybara, all caviomorphs like this one, so the line here is size rather than relatedness. § 161.01(c) is the article's short affirmative list, and it is written as examples rather than as a closed set: "an animal may be kept ... provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law", followed by gerbil, hamster, guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and small birds. So the question in New York City is always whether something else in § 161.01(b) reaches the animal.

It is named by species, Cavia porcellus, which is the domesticated animal and not one of the wild cavies. 4.4(b) attaches the one condition that survives exemption, that the animal "must be housed or caged in such a manner as to prevent liberation".

MI.note: None of Michigan's three relevant acts reaches a domesticated rodent.

AZ.note: Arizona restricts rodents by family rather than as an order, and the seven families named are Capromyidae, Castoridae, Dipodidae, Echimyidae, Erethizontidae, Geomyidae and Sciuridae. The guinea pig is Caviidae, which is not among them, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Guinea pigs appear by name on the exempt mammal list, so no permit is required.

CO.quote: Domesticated races of guinea pigs (Cavia porcellus)
CO.note: Named to the species on the domestic animal list. The capybara, its much larger relative in the same family, is not, which is why the two land on opposite sides of this map in Colorado. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: "Dangerous animal" means a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, bear, hyena, wolf or coyote. Dangerous animal does not mean any herptiles included in the Herptiles-Herps Act.
IL.note: Illinois runs a closed list of 15 named mammals plus a blanket bar on primates, and it has no catch-all clause, no size test and no dangerousness test. An animal that is not on the list and is not native Illinois wildlife is simply outside the statute. No rodent appears on it. Illinois has no exotic mammal permit scheme at all for an animal off the list, so there is nothing to apply for and nothing to comply with at state level. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: all members of the Felidae family including, but not limited to, lions, tigers, cougars, leopards, cheetahs, ocelots, and servals, but not including domestic cats or cats recognized as a domestic breed, registered as a domestic breed, and shown as a domestic breed by a national or international multibreed cat registry association; (2) bears; and (3) all nonhuman primates
MN.note: Minnesota's regulated animal definition is three groups and nothing else: the cat family, bears, and non-human primates. No rodent is in it. Minnesota has no general exotic mammal licence, so an animal outside those three groups and off the invasive lists is simply unregulated at state level.

OR.quote: Pursuant to the definition of "wildlife," the following species are not subject to these rules because they are not "wild" ... (13) Guinea pig — Cavia porcellus.
OR.note: This is the strongest position an animal can hold in Oregon. ORS 496.004(19) leaves it to the commission to define which mammals count as wild, and this rule is that definition: the 32 species on it are declared not wild and fall outside the wildlife rules altogether, rather than being permitted by them. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: A member within the order Rodentia, except for guinea pig (Cavia porcellus), gerbil (Meriones unguiculatus), chinchilla (Chinchilla lanigera), rat (Rattus norvegicus), mouse (Mus musculus), hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), dwarf hamster (genera Phodopus and Cricetulus), Patagonia mara (Dolichotis patagonum) and American beaver (Castor canadensis)
CT.note: Connecticut puts the whole order Rodentia in Category Two, which bars private possession, and then excepts nine species. The guinea pig, Cavia porcellus is one of them, so it is named in the regulation rather than merely absent from it. Named to the species, and the Patagonian mara is excepted a few words later, so two caviomorphs are cleared while the capybara, a third, is not.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. No rodent appears in the eight clauses, and the guinea pig is not native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TX.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means: (A) a lion; (B) a tiger; (C) an ocelot; (D) a cougar; (E) a leopard; (F) a cheetah; (G) a jaguar; (H) a bobcat; (I) a lynx; (J) a serval; (K) a caracal; (L) a hyena; (M) a bear; (N) a coyote; (O) a jackal; (P) a baboon; (Q) a chimpanzee; (R) an orangutan; (S) a gorilla; or (T) any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision.
TX.note: Cavia porcellus is a domesticated South American rodent. It is not indigenous to Texas, so the nongame possession caps do not reach it, and no rodent is on the dangerous wild animal list.

MA.quote: Domestic animals as listed in 321 CMR 9.02(3) shall be exempt from the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131, § 23, and may be possessed, propagated, maintained, imported, bought, sold, or otherwise disposed of ... Any vertebrate taxa not listed in 321 CMR 9.02 shall be presumed to be wild and shall be subject to the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131.
MA.note: Cavia porcellus is on the domestic animal list. The presumption in 9.02(2)(c) is what makes that listing necessary rather than obvious: an unlisted vertebrate is presumed wild here, so a domesticated species that nobody listed would be in the permit tier.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Named at (14)(i), and again at 68A-6.003(12) for sale without a permit. The contrast with the degu, an animal of similar size and origin that is not on either list, is what makes this a naming exercise rather than a principle.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the guinea pig is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: Named: "any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana". Florida added this species to its prohibited list in 2021 for ecological reasons; New York City reached it decades earlier under a rule about animals capable of inflicting harm. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: ... ii. Common iguana - Iguana iguana;
NJ.note: The green iguana is on the closed exempt list at 4.4, which is the only route to keeping an animal in New Jersey with no permit at all. It is listed as the "Common iguana - Iguana iguana". 4.4(b) attaches the one condition that survives exemption, that the animal "must be housed or caged in such a manner as to prevent liberation". This is the outlier on the reptile side of the exempt list. New Jersey lets the green iguana be kept freely while requiring a permit for a leopard gecko and a bearded dragon, which is the opposite of the ranking most keepers would draw by difficulty of care.

FL.quote: Live specimens of the following species, including their taxonomic successors, subspecies, or hybrids or eggs thereof may be possessed only pursuant to permit issued by the Executive Director except as provided in Rule 68-5.007, F.A.C. ... (4) Non-native reptiles: (a) Yellow anaconda ... (e) Indian or Burmese python (Python molurus). (f) Reticulated python (Python reticulatus). (g) Northern African python (Python sebae). (h) Southern African python (Python natalensis). (i) Amethystine python (Morelia amethistinus). (j) Scrub python (Morelia kinghorni). (k) Green anaconda (Eunectes murinus). (l) Nile monitor (Varanus niloticus). (m) Green iguana (Iguana iguana) (n) Tegus (genera Salvator and Tupinambis, all species)
FL.note: Iguana iguana was added to the prohibited list in the 2021 rulemaking, which is recent enough that a lot of secondary material still describes Florida as the easiest state in the country for this animal. The transitional provisions in 68-5.007(1)(a)2 are unusually specific about it, letting a Class III exhibition or sale licensee who documented green iguanas on a 2018 or 2019 application keep exhibiting them, without importing any. The grandfathering is narrow and personal: under 68-5.007 a permit for personal possession may be issued only to someone in lawful possession before the species was listed, for the remainder of that animal's life, with the animal PIT-tagged, and no additional specimens may ever be acquired. A surviving spouse or beneficiary can be permitted to keep the animal out, but nobody new can start.

grandfathered.detail: Only a person in lawful possession before the species was listed may hold one, for that animal's life, under a Conditional/Prohibited/Nonnative Species permit, with the animal PIT-tagged and no further specimens acquired.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians

IA.quote: A member of the order squamata which is any of the following:
IA.note: The subparagraphs that follow are an exhaustive list of squamate families: varanidae, atractaspidae, helodermatidae, the venomous snake families, and superfamily henophidia. Iguanidae is not among them.

KY.note: On neither restricted list.

RI.quote: The following Iguanid Lizards (Iguanidae) may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit: Basilisks (Basiliscus spp.), Collared and Leopard Lizards (Crotaphytus spp.), Common or Green Iguanas (Iguana i. iguana)

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;

MO.note: Not native to Missouri and not over the eight foot line in § 578.023.

KS.note: Only snakes are named among the reptiles, and only venomous ones.

SC.quote: 15. reptiles

MT.quote: (xv) Iguanidae (iguanas);

WV.quote: The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)

AL.note: Only tegus of the genus Salvator are named among the lizards. Florida bans this species, Alabama does not.

IN.quote: (4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter or in the current administrative rules.

WY.quote: (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.

MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

LA.quote: v. Green Iguana (Iguana iguana);

grandfathered.detail: Registration within 365 days of the rule taking effect, no breeding, no further acquisition.

OK.quote: monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: No lizard fits any of the seven permitted categories, so DC bars the green iguana without ever having listed it as invasive the way Florida and Louisiana did.

HI.note: Part A lists the genus, so the green iguana is covered even though the common name column reads club tail iguana. Research and exhibition only. The species is also already loose on several islands.

ME.quote: All Species in Genus Ctenosaura (Spiny-tailed Iguanas)
ME.note: The only iguanas cleared are the spiny-tailed Ctenosaura. Iguana iguana is not on the list, so the common green iguana needs a permit in Maine while its less commonly kept relative does not.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Iguanine Lizards (in part) (Genera: Basiliscus, Ctenosaura, Cyclura, Iguana)
AR.note: Genus Iguana is cleared, so the green iguana needs no permit. The in part qualifier means other iguanian genera were deliberately left off rather than overlooked.

CA.quote: Class Reptilia   Reptiles: (A) Order Crocodilia ... (G) Family Helodermatidae
CA.note: No iguanid is restricted in California. The state's reptile concerns in section 671 are venom and crocodilians rather than invasiveness.

OH.quote: (14) Komodo dragons
OH.note: Outside both lists in Chapter 935.

WA.quote: Family varanidae, only water monitors and crocodile monitors
WA.note: Iguanidae appears nowhere in the statute. The reptile side of RCW 16.30 is venomous snakes, crocodilians and two monitors.

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The green iguana is Central and South American and does not appear on the Fish and Boat Commission's published list of Pennsylvania native species, so Chapter 79, which is built entirely around native species, does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The green iguana is Central and South American and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

VT.cite: Unrestricted Wild Animal List, July 2025, and Regulation 881
VT.quote: Species not found on the Restricted, Unrestricted or Domestic species lists are considered Restricted.
VT.note: The green iguana is on neither the Unrestricted nor the Restricted list, and Vermont treats that absence as a restriction rather than a gap. Vermont's Unrestricted list works through the lizard families one at a time, agamids, chameleons, geckos, skinks, teiids, anguids, lacertids, four named monitors and four iguanian families, and Iguanidae is not among them. A permit exists on paper but not for a pet: Regulation 881 says the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for keeping or possessing a wild animal in captivity except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes. So restricted here means a private keeper cannot have one, not that there is paperwork to fill in.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Lizard | Iguanidae | Iguana iguana | Iguana, Green Common | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The green iguana is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The green iguana is on none of it, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: The green iguana is covered by the entry for iguanas is named on the exempt list at regulation 6.1, so it needs no permit at all. Delaware exempts lizards generously and exempts no snake, turtle or tortoise at all, which is the sharpest line in this state's rules.

CO.quote: Any species of lizard native only to the tropical and subtropical region from the following families: Iguanidae (iguanas)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. CPW files Iguana iguana against this line. The green iguana is neotropical from Mexico south to Paraguay, inside the band the chapter draws. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The green iguana is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A green iguana is a lizard, so the breeder-source condition applies to it as much as to a Minnesota native. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Iguanid lizards -- Iguanaidae -- All nonnative species except: Crotaphytus spp., Gambelia spp., Sceloporus spp., Uta spp., Phrynosoma spp.;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Iguana iguana is a nonnative iguanid and none of the five excepted genera, which are all Oregon natives. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. Iguanidae appears in no category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. No iguanid is native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The green iguana is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Iguana iguana is not indigenous to Texas, so 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O does not reach it, and the dangerous wild animal list at Health & Safety Code § 822.101(4) contains no reptile. Texas has no general exotic reptile permit: the only reptiles it regulates by name are the six controlled exotic snakes, the venomous species, and its own native herpetofauna through the nongame and threatened species subchapters. Florida is where this animal is restricted, as an established invasive. Texas has no prohibited nonnative reptile list to put it on.

MA.quote: The following Iguanid Lizards (Iguanidae) may be kept without a permit: Basilisks (Basiliscus spp.) Collared and Leopard Lizards (Crotaphytus spp.) Common or Green Iguanas (Iguana i. iguana) False or Spring-tailed Iguanas (Ctenosaurus spp.) Tree Iguanas (Liolaemus spp.) New World Chameleons (Anolis spp. and Ctenotus spp.) Spiny Lizards (Sceloporus spp.) Tree and Bush Lizards (Urosaurus spp.) Diving Lizards (Uranoscodon spp.) Zebra-tailed Lizards (Callisaurus spp.)
MA.note: Named as "Common or Green Iguanas (Iguana i. iguana)", using the trinomial for the nominate subspecies. The iguanid entry is a closed list rather than a family clearance, so an iguanid not on it is not exempt, which makes the naming here the whole answer. Iguana iguana is IUCN least concern.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Iguana iguana is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the green iguana is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. New York names twelve reptiles and the green iguana is not among them, which is a sharp contrast with Florida, where it was added to the prohibited list in 2021. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the green iguana is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it. Notable by comparison with Florida, which prohibited this species in 2021: Georgia names four squamates in its licence rule and the green iguana is not among them.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the green iguana is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. The desert iguana, Dipsosaurus dorsalis, is a Utah animal at Limited, and Iguana iguana is not it. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

CA.quote: Family Chelyridae-Snapping Turtles: All species (D)

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia).
