All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The clause is "all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle", so both species are named and the family is taken. New York State allows a licensed snapping turtle season with a twelve-inch minimum; the city prohibits the animal outright. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: ... v. Snapping turtles-Chelydra serpentina;
NJ.note: The snapping turtle is on the closed exempt list at 4.4, which is the only route to keeping an animal in New Jersey with no permit at all. It is one of only two turtles on the list, with the eastern painted turtle. 4.4(b) attaches the one condition that survives exemption, that the animal "must be housed or caged in such a manner as to prevent liberation". It is exempt because it is a New Jersey animal with a harvest season rather than because it is an easy pet, and 7:25-6.22 runs that season with a twelve inch minimum carapace length and a daily limit of one. So possession is unpermitted but taking one is not unregulated.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: Snapping turtles are not native to Idaho, so the carve out for native wildlife captured from the wild does not apply.

IA.quote: It is unlawful for a person, except as otherwise expressly provided, to take, capture, or kill fish, frogs, or turtles except during the open season established by the commission.
IA.note: Chelydra serpentina is native here and taking one from the wild falls under the licence, season and possession limit rules. Subsection 2 exempts snapping turtles from the noncommercial season only, not from the rest.

RI.quote: The possession of native turtles is restricted to those institutions identified within § 3.7(C) of this Part... Turtles considered native to Rhode Island and which possession as pets is prohibited include the following: ...Snapping Turtle (Chelydra serpentina),
RI.note: Possession is limited to the Department, USFWS, AZA zoos, research institutions and USDA licensed exhibitors.

NH.quote: 1,5   Snapping turtle   Chelydra serpentina
NH.note: Category 1 is an individual, so unlike the serval this one is open to a private keeper who holds a permit to possess wildlife.

MO.quote: those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri
MO.note: Chelydra serpentina is a native nonvenomous reptile and so falls in Class I.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: Alaska has no native turtles, so nothing in the rule pulls it back out.

LA.quote: No person shall collect or possess more than 10 restricted turtles, as listed in Paragraph G.3 herein, in any combination, with no individual species to exceed two per person at any time... i. Snapping Turtle—Chelydra serpentina;
LA.note: Two per person, a basic recreational fishing licence to collect, no commercial use of native turtles, and captive breeding is unlawful without department approval.

OK.quote: monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license
OK.note: The exemption is written for reptiles not indigenous to Oklahoma. Chelydra serpentina is native here, so it falls outside it.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is drawn family by family and is entirely mammalian. Mississippi restricts no reptile under this rule at any size.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit, and its only other exotic pet statute reaches genus Panthera, non-native bears and great apes.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: That sentence, plus tattooing for mountain lions and wolves and rulemaking for primates, is the whole of North Dakota's prohibition list. No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The only reptiles Kansas regulates are non-native venomous snakes. Constrictors, lizards and turtles are untouched at any size.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: On neither the prohibited species list nor the inherently dangerous list. The only reptiles on either are gila monsters, beaded lizards, the Komodo dragon, crocodilians and venomous snakes other than hognose.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: The only reptiles the statute points the board at are constrictors over six feet, venomous snakes and crocodilians. Nothing here falls in those categories.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: Turtles are one of the seven permitted categories.

HI.note: Named on Part A, research and exhibition only.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: Chelydra serpentina is native to eastern Wyoming, but the native-species trigger in Section 9(c) applies only to animals imported for commercial use, so captive-bred stock kept as a pet falls to the Section 10 catch-all. Taking one from the wild is a separate question governed by the nongame regulation referenced in Section 9(b).

MT.quote: "Exotic wildlife" means a wildlife species that is not native to Montana.
MT.note: The common snapping turtle is native to eastern Montana, which puts it outside the exotic wildlife lists entirely. Section 87-5-116 covers commercial taking of native reptiles, not private possession.

ME.note: Chelydra serpentina is native to Maine and does not appear on the list of unrestricted species, which is the ordinary pattern: the list is aimed at exotics and native wildlife is handled under the general permit requirement.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Additionally, persons may possess and hold captive fish, bullfrogs, mussels, aquatic turtles, alligators and other aquatic wildlife in compliance with Code Chapters 26.00, 27.00, 29.00, 30.00, 31.00, 32.00, 33.00, 34.00, 35.00, and Addenda Chapters I1.00, J1.00, and V1.00.
AR.note: The unrestricted list expressly hands aquatic turtles to a different set of chapters rather than answering for them, and the common snapping turtle is native to Arkansas and commercially harvested there. The answer exists, but not in this document.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Not a dangerous wild animal. Chelydra serpentina is native to Ohio and is a regulated species for taking and for commercial harvest under the Division of Wildlife's rules, which is a separate regime from Chapter 935 and worth checking before collecting one.

WA.quote: Class reptilia ... Order crocodilia, all species
WA.note: Not a potentially dangerous wild animal. The common snapping turtle is not native to Washington and has established in a few places after releases, which the department treats as an invasive problem rather than a possession one.

WI.quote: A person may possess a live native snapping turtle for the purpose of harvest authorized under s. NR 19.275 (4), 21.13 (4), or 22.13 (4) for no more than 7 days.
WI.note: Wisconsin treats the snapping turtle as a harvestable native rather than a pet. Collecting or possessing native turtles requires a small game hunting or fishing approval, and the recreated rule caps live possession at 7 days tied to an authorized harvest. Wisconsin repealed and recreated NR 16.12(3) effective 1 January 2027 (CR 25-092). Until then the rule allows taking or possessing up to 5 individuals of each non-listed native species. From that date possession of live native reptiles and amphibians is prohibited outright except under narrow exemptions, of which the one that matters to keepers is NR 16.12(3)(k): captive-bred colour variants acquired from a legal source. A wild-type native animal will no longer be keepable.

UT.cite: Utah DWR reptile and amphibian species tables, non-controlled non-native
UT.quote: Common snapping turtle - Chelydra serpentina
UT.note: Utah puts established non-natives in a deliberately permissive column: 'they may be collected or possessed in any number without a permit', precisely because the division treats them as problematic for native wildlife. Note the one-way rule that applies to every herp here, native or not: once removed from the wild it may not be released back.

PA.quote: Common snapping turtle ( Chelydra serpentina ) | July 1 to October 31 | 15 | 30
PA.note: The only turtle in the table with a real open season, and personal possession of up to 30 needs no permit. Three conditions bind. The animal has to be taken in season, taking requires a fishing license, and § 79.5 requires an annual permit before anyone may take, catch, kill or possess snapping turtles for sale, barter or trade. Then § 79.10(a) bars importing a native species from another jurisdiction, so a Pennsylvania snapping turtle has to come from your own lawful take rather than a seller in another state.

MI.quote: A fishing license is required to take amphibians and reptiles for personal use.
MI.note: Not protected, and the only turtle here with an open season. The conditions are specific: the season runs July 15 to September 15, the limit is two a day and four in total, and a fishing license is required to take one. Buying one is not an option, because reptiles and amphibians may not be bought, sold or offered for sale in Michigan, so a snapping turtle has to come from your own lawful take.

VT.cite: Unrestricted Wild Animal List, July 2025, and Regulation 881
VT.quote: Species not found on the Restricted, Unrestricted or Domestic species lists are considered Restricted.
VT.note: The snapping turtle is on neither the Unrestricted nor the Restricted list, and Vermont treats that absence as a restriction rather than a gap. Chelydra is on neither list, so despite being native to Vermont it cannot be kept. A permit exists on paper but not for a pet: Regulation 881 says the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for keeping or possessing a wild animal in captivity except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes. So restricted here means a private keeper cannot have one, not that there is paperwork to fill in.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Turtle | Chelydridae | Chelydra serpentina serpentina | Eastern Snapping Turtle | II
NM.note: Group II on the Director's list: not known to be invasive or dangerous, but an importation permit is still required before the animal may be brought into New Mexico. Both the eastern and Florida snapping turtles are Group II.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (8) Snapping Turtles................ All species in the family Chelydridae
NV.note: Named at family level on the prohibited list, so importation, transportation and possession are all unlawful and no subspecies argument helps. The only permits available under this section go to accredited zoos and aquariums, universities and government agencies for research, other scientific institutions, commercial aquaculture, and tax-exempt nonprofits exhibiting wildlife for education, none of which is a pet route. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Named at family level, so every snapping turtle is restricted live wildlife and needs the appropriate special licence under R12-4-409(A) or a lawful exemption. The exemptions at R12-4-407 are about transit, fairs and circuses, photography, advertising, veterinary care and registered research facilities, none of which is a pet route, so a private keeper has no practical way in. Arizona restricts only two turtle groups and this is one of them, the other being its own gopher tortoises.

DE.note: The snapping turtle is native to Delaware, so it is not exotic and the Agriculture permit chapter does not reach it. What applies instead is DNREC's native wildlife regime, under which native reptiles are not available for private ownership. The narrow carve-out Delaware does allow, a captive-bred native snake in an aberrant colour morph held under permit, is written for snakes and does not help a turtle.

CO.quote: W-07, Appendix A, C: Family Chelydridae not approved in regulation
CO.note: Chelydridae appears nowhere in Chapter W-7. Appendix A's turtle block lists five families and this is not one of them, Appendix B is three snake genera, and Appendix C, the wild-collection list, does not include it either. Under § 701 anything the chapter does not allow is unlawful to possess, so a snapping turtle is regulated wildlife with no pet licence available. The snapping turtle is native to Colorado's eastern plains, which is the context for the one route the chapter does leave: § 704(B)(7)(a) lets someone who lawfully held a snapping turtle collected on or before 1 May 2026 keep it for the animal's life, on filing a CPW Legacy Report by 30 July 2026.

grandfathered.detail: A snapping turtle legally collected on or before 1 May 2026 may be kept and transported within Colorado for the life of the animal if a CPW Legacy Report was filed by 30 July 2026. No new wild capture is allowed.

IL.quote: Bullfrogs and common snapping turtles may be taken only June 15 through October 15. There is no closed season on all other non-listed native herptiles. The daily harvest limit for bullfrogs is eight, with a possession limit of 16. The daily harvest limit for common snapping turtles is two, with a possession limit of four.
IL.note: Illinois pulls the common snapping turtle out of the general herptile cap and gives it its own regime, the only reptile besides the bullfrog treated this way. It is a native taxon under § 885.40, and it is the only one with a closed season: a sport fishing licence, take only between 15 June and 15 October, two a day and four in possession. Bowfishing for it is barred in sixteen named southern counties, and § 30-10 bars collecting wild turtles for turtle races in the seven counties where ranavirus has been documented. The alligator snapping turtle is a different animal and is state endangered. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: A person may not take, possess, or transport turtles without a resident angling license and a recreational turtle license. ... A person does not need the licenses specified under subdivision 1: ... (2) when buying a turtle at a retail outlet
MN.note: Turtles are the gap in the 2021 pet reptile rule. Section 97A.401, subd. 8 covers snakes, lizards and salamanders and stops there, so turtles stay under their own older regime, which is a licence requirement with a short list of exemptions rather than a source condition. The snapping turtle is the one animal on this map that Minnesota treats as its own harvestable native turtle. It and the western painted turtle are the only two a recreational turtle licence covers, and the only two native turtles that may be sold as pets, under a turtle seller's licence. Minn. R. 6256.0500 sets the size floor at a shell length greater than 12 inches. A retail purchase is exempt from the licence requirement, and taking one from the wild needs both an angling licence and a recreational turtle licence, for personal use only.

OR.quote: Snapping turtle — Chelydridae — All species and hybrids;
OR.note: The whole family is prohibited, so the alligator snapping turtle goes with the common one. Chelydridae appears nowhere on the noncontrolled list, which clears eight other turtle families. OAR 635-056-0150 allows someone who held the animal before the commission listed it to keep it for its life, on proof of lawful prior possession, with no transfer, sale or transport inside Oregon and no release. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. The common snapping turtle is a Connecticut native but is not among the eight herptiles in Category Three, and DEEP's fact sheet shows it as unlisted rather than of special concern, so it is not Category Four either. Taking one from the wild is a separate question governed by DEEP's harvest regulations rather than by this section. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three. One caveat that applies to every Connecticut turtle on this map: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 26-78 addresses turtles separately from the regulation, and it could not be read this sitting because cga.ct.gov refuses every connection from this container. This entry rests on § 26-55-6, which is the comprehensive rule and mentions no turtle sale ban, and the point is flagged rather than assumed away.

MD.quote: A person may not catch a snapping turtle from the waters of the State by the use of a hook and line, trot line, bow and arrow, spear, gig or gig iron, or any other device capable of piercing any part of a turtle.
MD.note: The snapping turtle is a Maryland native and appears on none of the three native herptile lists, which looks like an omission until you notice which agency has it: Maryland treats the species as a fishery, under the Fisheries Service and Natural Resources Article §§ 4-218 and 4-738 rather than the wildlife article. This chapter governs taking one from the wild, with prohibited gear, a season, a prescribed way of measuring the carapace and a harvest permit card. What it does not do is set up a pet possession permit, so a captive animal is not reached by the herptile chapter and a wild-caught one runs through the fisheries rules instead. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The snapping turtle is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial. The point that decides every native reptile in Tennessee is the exception clause in Class II, which reads "native species, except those listed in other classes". A native nonpoisonous reptile IS listed in another class, at (3)(A), so it is excluded from Class II and lands in Class III with no permit. The supplier documentation requirement in § 70-4-401(b) follows Class I and Class II and does not reach it either. Commercial harvest from the wild is regulated separately; the classification decides possession.

TX.quote: A person without a nongame or nongame dealer’s permit may: (A) possess six or fewer specimens of a species of nongame wildlife listed in §65.331(e) of this title, provided the person does not engage in commercial activity involving the nongame wildlife; and (B) possess 25 or fewer specimens of a species of nongame wildlife listed in §65.331(d) of this title, provided the person does not engage in commercial activity involving the nongame wildlife.
TX.note: The common snapping turtle, Chelydra serpentina, is on the § 65.331(e) list: six without a permit, no commercial activity. Do not read across from the alligator snapping turtle, Macrochelys temminckii, which Texas lists as threatened under 31 TAC § 65.175, where § 65.171(b)(2) bars taking, possessing, transporting, importing, exporting or selling it altogether. Two snapping turtles, two entirely different answers, and the name is what runs them together. The cap reaches captive-bred animals: § 65.325(a) says nongame wildlife "includes captive-bred nongame wildlife", so a pet shop receipt does not lift it.

MA.quote: All species of turtles may be kept without a permit, up to a limit of 100 turtles and/or eggs, in any combination, of each species, except for the following species for which a permit is always required: 1. Species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3). 2. Argentina or Chaco Tortoise (Geochelone chilensis). 3. Gopher Tortoises (Gopherus polyphemus) and all other species in the genus Gopherus. 4. Pancake Tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri). 5. Spotted Turtle (Clemmys guttata). 6. Red-eared Slider (Trachemys scripta, including all subspecies and forms).
MA.note: Chelydra serpentina is not one of the five named exceptions, is IUCN least concern and is not on the Massachusetts list, so it falls under the general turtle allowance: no permit, and a cap of 100 turtles or eggs of the species in any combination. The cap is written for dealers rather than keepers and no pet owner will meet it. The separate rule to know is about acquisition: MassWildlife allows taking two snapping turtles from the wild in Massachusetts as personal pets under 321 CMR 3.05, and animals taken that way may not be sold, bartered or exchanged, or released back.

NE.quote: 003.05 SNAPPING TURTLES: 003.05A It shall be unlawful to take snapping turtles except by hand, hand net, hook and line, bow and arrow or gaff. 003.05B It shall be unlawful to sell, offer for sale, trade or barter for any snapping turtle. ... 003.05E The take of any turtle(s) exceeding the daily bag limits shall be released immediately.
NE.note: Nebraska answers this animal in its fishing regulations rather than its wildlife ones, which is why it is easy to miss. 166 NAC 10 excludes game species from its herp rules, and the snapping turtle is handled at 164 NAC 6 alongside fish, bullfrogs and mussels, with a daily bag limit and a possession limit set annually by the Commission, take restricted to hand, hand net, hook and line, bow or gaff, and a fishing permit behind all of it. The clause that matters most to a keeper is § 003.05B: it is unlawful to sell, offer for sale, trade or barter any snapping turtle, so there is no lawful in-state commerce in one at any number.

FL.quote: (6) Turtles. (a) Take and possession ... 1. No person shall take more than one turtle per day unless authorized by permit ... 4. No person shall take Escambia map turtles (Graptemys ernsti), cooters (Pseudemys spp.), striped mud turtles (Lower Keys population) (Kinosternon baurii) or snapping turtles (Chelydra spp.) from the wild. ... 8. No person shall possess more than two Escambia map turtles (Graptemys ernsti), two box turtles of Florida native species ... or two loggerhead musk turtles (Sternotherus minor). ... (c) Sale - No person shall buy, sell, or possess for sale turtles, their eggs or parts thereof, that have been taken from the wild.
FL.note: Wild take is barred outright. 68A-25.002(6)(a)4 says no person shall take Escambia map turtles, cooters, Lower Keys striped mud turtles "or snapping turtles (Chelydra spp.)" from the wild, and (6)(c) bars buying or selling any turtle taken from the wild. What is not barred is possession: the common snapping turtle is not on the imperiled list at 68A-27.003, is not among the species capped at two, and is a nonvenomous unprotected reptile for the purposes of 68A-6.003(14)(a), so a lawfully acquired captive-bred animal needs no permit. The alligator snapping turtle is the opposite: 68A-25.002(6)(a)5 bars taking, possessing, transporting or selling any Macrochelys at all.

NY.cite: ECL § 11-0103(2)(c); DEC reptile and amphibian seasons
NY.quote: "Small game" means black, gray and fox squirrels, European hares, varying hares, cottontail rabbits, native frogs, native salamanders, native turtles, native lizards, native snakes, coyotes, red fox (Vulpes vulpes) and gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus) except captive bred red fox or gray fox, raccoon, opossum, or weasel, skunk, bobcat, lynx, muskrat, mink, except mink born in captivity, fisher, otter, beaver, sable and marten but does not include coydogs. ... No person shall, at any time of the year, buy, sell, offer or expose for sale, transport, or have in his possession any fish protected by law, game, protected wildlife ... whether taken within the state or coming from without the state, except as permitted by the Fish and Wildlife Law.
NY.note: The one native New York reptile with an open season, which is why it is the only one a private person can lawfully hold. Taking requires a hunting licence, runs 15 July to 30 September statewide, and is limited to a firearm or a bow. The carapace must measure twelve inches or longer in a straight line, the daily bag is five and the season bag is thirty. Everything else about New York natives flows from the same definition and comes out the other way: native turtles are small game, and the snapping turtle is the only one the department opened a season for.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the common snapping turtle is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it. The turtle Georgia does protect is the alligator snapping turtle, Macrochelys, which is on the prohibited natives list; Chelydra serpentina is not, and freshwater turtles are among the natives DNR lists as takeable.

AL.quote: Nothing in this regulation prohibits the taking for personal use of up to two legal turtles per day by hand, dip net or hook and line from the wild in this state, to include public and private waters.
AL.note: Two turtles matter in Alabama and only one of them is this one. 220-2-.92(1)(c) protects the alligator snapping turtle, Macrochelys temminckii, which needs a scientific collection permit or a written permit from the Commissioner. The common snapping turtle, Chelydra serpentina, is not on that list, nor on any other. What does reach it is the turtle rule at 220-2-.142, which bars taking or possessing any wild turtle for commercial purposes and then allows taking up to two a day for personal use. That is a take limit rather than a possession cap, so a captive-bred or lawfully acquired snapping turtle is unrestricted.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: The common snapping turtle is native to Indiana, which is what decides it, and Indiana's native rule is unusual in reaching a purchased animal. 9-5-7(c) lists the eastern snapping turtle, Chelydra serpentina serpentina, among the 99 taxa whose sale it governs, and 9-5-7(a) says the section applies "regardless of place of origin", so a captive-bred animal from an out-of-state breeder is caught by it just as a wild-caught one is. Selling, offering for sale or transporting for sale is barred; possessing is not, subject to 9-5-6(f)'s cap of four live animals of any one native species. Two exits exist. 9-5-7(f) exempts a captive-bred animal with albinistic, leucistic or xanthic colour morphology, on the same logic New Jersey uses for corn snake morphs, that a morph is visibly not a wild-caught animal. And 9-5-9 provides a reptile captive breeding licence under which sales are lawful. Indiana adds a wild-take regime on top for this species specifically: 9-5-6(c) allows four a day of the snapping turtle and the two softshells combined, only between July 1 and March 31, and only at twelve inches or more of carapace length. The alligator snapping turtle is a separate entry on the same list and a different animal.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: ... viii. Tokay gecko - Gekko gecko;
NJ.note: The tokay gecko is on the closed exempt list at 4.4, which is the only route to keeping an animal in New Jersey with no permit at all. It is named by species, Gekko gecko. 4.4(b) attaches the one condition that survives exemption, that the animal "must be housed or caged in such a manner as to prevent liberation". The pairing with 4.3 is what makes this one worth reading twice: the permit list at 4.3(a)3.xiv takes "Geckos - Family Gekkonidae other than Tokay Gecko", carving this one animal out of the family so that the exemption survives. Every other gecko in the trade needs a permit and the tokay does not.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians

KY.note: On neither restricted list.

RI.quote: All Gekkos (Gekkonidae) may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit except the Big Bend Gekko (Coleonyx reticulatus).

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;

MO.note: Not native to Missouri, so outside Class I.

KS.note: Only snakes are named among the reptiles, and only venomous ones.

SC.quote: 15. reptiles

MT.quote: (xiii) Gekkonidae (geckos);

WV.quote: The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)

AL.note: Only tegus of the genus Salvator are named among the lizards.

IN.quote: (4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter or in the current administrative rules.

WY.quote: (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.

MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

LA.note: On neither the prohibited nor the restricted nonnative list.

OK.quote: monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The squamate half of the definition is exhaustively enumerated: varanidae limited to water and crocodile monitors, helodermatidae, the venomous snake families, and henophidia limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas and African rock pythons. Nothing here is among them.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: No lizard fits any of the seven permitted categories.

HI.note: Named on Part A, research and exhibition only.

ME.quote: Infraorder Gekkota*   all species in infraorder Gekkota
ME.note: Cleared at infraorder level, so every gecko is unrestricted. The asterisk footnote does not bite here: Gekko gecko went onto CITES Appendix II in 2019, and the footnote only removes Appendix I species.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Tokay Gecko (Gecko gecko)
AR.note: Named individually. The binomial is misspelled in the list, which prints Gecko gecko rather than Gekko gecko, but the common name removes any doubt.

CA.quote: Class Reptilia   Reptiles: (A) Order Crocodilia ... (G) Family Helodermatidae
CA.note: No gecko appears on the restricted list. The only lizard California restricts is the reticulate Gila monster.

OH.quote: (14) Komodo dragons
OH.note: Outside both lists in Chapter 935.

WA.quote: Family varanidae, only water monitors and crocodile monitors
WA.note: No gecko family appears in the statute.

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The tokay gecko is Southeast Asian and does not appear on the Fish and Boat Commission's published list of Pennsylvania native species, so Chapter 79, which is built entirely around native species, does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The tokay gecko is Southeast Asian and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

VT.quote: Squamata | Scleroglossa | Gekkonidae | all species | Geckos
VT.note: Covered by the family-wide gecko entry and absent from the Restricted list.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Lizard | Gekkonidae | Gekko gecko | Tokay Gecko | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The tokay gecko is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The tokay gecko is on none of it, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: The tokay gecko is covered by the entry for geckos is named on the exempt list at regulation 6.1, so it needs no permit at all. Delaware exempts lizards generously and exempts no snake, turtle or tortoise at all, which is the sharpest line in this state's rules.

CO.quote: Any species from the families Diplodactylidae (eyelash geckos), Eublepharidae (eyelid geckos), or Gekkonidae (geckos) except Mediterranean house geckos (Hemidactylus turcicus)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. The geckos are handled in the appendix's Other Species block, which CPW introduces as species that are not native only to tropic or subtropic regions, so the native-range qualifier that governs the family lists does not apply to them. Three gecko families are cleared with a single exception, the Mediterranean house gecko. CPW files Gekko gecko against this line. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The tokay gecko is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A tokay gecko is a lizard, so the breeder-source condition applies to it as much as to a Minnesota native. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Geckos -- Gekkonidae and Eublepharidae -- All species;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Gekko gecko is a Gekkonidae in any taxonomy, so nothing turns on the family question here. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No gecko appears in any category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. No gecko is native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The tokay gecko is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Gekko gecko is not indigenous to Texas, so 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O does not reach it, and the dangerous wild animal list at Health & Safety Code § 822.101(4) contains no reptile. Texas has no general exotic reptile permit: the only reptiles it regulates by name are the six controlled exotic snakes, the venomous species, and its own native herpetofauna through the nongame and threatened species subchapters.

MA.quote: All Geckos (Gekkonidae) may be kept without a permit except for those species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3) and the Big Bend Gecko (Coleonyx reticulatus) which require a permit.
MA.note: Cleared by the family listing. Gekko gecko is IUCN least concern, which is the point to check in this state rather than the animal's reputation for biting: the gecko clearance is subject only to the categorical bar and to the Big Bend gecko.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Gekko gecko is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Gekko gecko is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the tokay gecko is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the tokay gecko is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The reptile clause is a list of families and the tokay gecko belongs to none of them: not Helodermatidae, not a venomous snake family, not Boidae, Pythonidae, Varanidae, Iguanidae, teiidae, Chelydridae or Crocodylia. No gecko family is named, and the tokay's reputation for biting is not the kind of harm the opening standard is aimed at.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the tokay gecko is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Gekko gecko is south-east Asian and on none of the division's tables. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

CA.quote: Genus Ambystoma (nonnative tiger salamander group)-(D)

ID.quote: Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho
ID.note: Captive bred stock is a conventional pet. Ambystoma mavortium is native to Idaho, so one taken from the wild in the state is wildlife and falls outside the definition.

RI.quote: All persons other than a bona fide researcher, or a licensed pet shops and their transportation agents are prohibited from possessing any species of exotic amphibians unless they are kept indoors as pets in a manner that will prevent their escape or liberation into the wild. Keeping of these animals in any type of outdoor enclosure is prohibited.
RI.note: Rhode Island's native amphibian list does not include the tiger salamander, so it is an exotic amphibian: keepable, but indoors only, and only a pet shop or researcher may import one.

NH.quote: Amphibians, exotic;
NH.note: The controlled table covers the four Ambystoma species native to New Hampshire. The tiger salamander is not one of them, so it counts as an exotic amphibian.

MO.quote: those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri
MO.note: Ambystoma tigrinum is native to Missouri, which puts it in Class I rather than outside the Wildlife Code.

SC.quote: 16. amphibians.

OK.quote: monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license
OK.note: Ambystoma is native to Oklahoma, so the non-indigenous exemption does not reach it.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian, so no amphibian is reached by it.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: No amphibian appears anywhere in the chapter. The prohibitions are skunks and raccoons.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No amphibian is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. No amphibian is reached by it, and § 153A-131 leaves the rest to counties.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only. A free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

VA.quote: Ambystomatidae   All species, except Ambystoma mexicanum   All mole salamanders, except Mexican axolotl
VA.note: The mole salamander family is on the permit table with a single exception for the axolotl, so the tiger salamander needs the special permit.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: Not a dangerous wild animal. Salamanders appear in Iowa Code only in the bait provisions, which govern selling them for fish bait rather than keeping one.

LA.quote: Persons engaged in herpetological research shall possess a Scientific Research and Collecting Permit prior to removal of native reptiles or amphibians from the wild.
LA.note: Ambystoma is native to Louisiana, so taking one from the wild falls under the collecting rules rather than the nonnative lists. Captive bred stock is a different question the rule does not address directly.

KY.quote: Except as established in Section 5 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport into Kentucky, or possess the following exotic wildlife that are considered potentially injurious to native ecosystems:
KY.note: The only amphibians on either Kentucky list are the giant or cane toad and the African clawed frog. Ambystoma appears on neither, though the species is native to Kentucky so the native wildlife rules in 301 KAR 1 are a separate question.

WV.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means a mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian or aquatic animal, including a hybrid, that is dangerous to humans, other animals or the environment due to its inherent nature and capability to do significant harm.
WV.note: The definition can reach an amphibian in principle, but the categories the board is pointed at are bears, big cats, canids, primates, large constrictors, venomous snakes and crocodilians. A salamander is not plausibly any of them.

DC.quote: a person shall not import into the District, possess, display, offer for sale, trade, barter, exchange, or adoption, or give as a household pet, any living member of the animal kingdom, including those born or raised in captivity, except the following
DC.note: Amphibians appear nowhere in the permitted list, so the salamander is barred alongside the axolotl.

HI.note: Conditionally approved, which is the opposite of what Hawaii's reputation would suggest. Part A restricts two other Ambystoma species, so the genus is split across two lists and the species name is what decides it.

WY.quote: An importation/possession permit shall not be issued for importation or possession of the live cold-blooded wildlife in this section... (a) Injurious wildlife listed in 50 CFR § 16.
WY.note: Wyoming adopts the federal injurious wildlife list wholesale, and 50 CFR 16.14 covers every species in the genus Ambystoma. That makes the tiger salamander one of the few animals Wyoming will not permit at all, and the ban follows from a federal disease rule about Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans rather than from anything Wyoming decided about salamanders.

MT.quote: "Exotic wildlife" means a wildlife species that is not native to Montana.
MT.note: Ambystoma tigrinum is native to Montana, so the exotic wildlife permit regime does not reach it at all. The only statute that singles out native amphibians is § 87-5-116, and that restricts taking them for commercial purposes rather than keeping one.

AK.quote: "game" means any species of bird, reptile, and mammal, including a feral domestic animal, found or introduced in the state, except domestic birds and mammals
AK.note: The permit rule at 5 AAC 92.029 applies to live game, and the statutory definition of game stops at birds, reptiles and mammals. An amphibian is not game, so the strictest clean list in the country simply does not apply to it.

ME.quote: Amphibia (Amphibians)   Captive Bred Origin Only ... Anura (Frogs And Toads)
ME.note: Maine's amphibian section contains one order, Anura, and every entry in it is a frog or a toad. There is no Caudata order at all, so no salamander or newt of any species is unrestricted in Maine. The whole section is also limited to captive bred origin.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Additionally, persons may possess and hold captive fish, bullfrogs, mussels, aquatic turtles, alligators and other aquatic wildlife...
AR.note: The unrestricted list has sections for birds, mammals, reptiles and snakes and no amphibian section at all. The only amphibian it mentions is the bullfrog, and that by deferring to other chapters. Ambystoma tigrinum is also native to Arkansas.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: No amphibian appears in Chapter 935. Ambystoma tigrinum is native to Ohio, so taking one from the wild falls under the Division of Wildlife's native amphibian rules, and federal law separately bars moving any Ambystoma across a state line.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals, whether bred in the wild or in captivity, and any or all hybrids thereof: (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: The statute reaches two classes, mammals and reptiles. No amphibian is covered. Ambystoma tigrinum is native to eastern Washington, so wild collection engages the department's native amphibian rules, and federal law bars shipping any Ambystoma across a state line.

WI.quote: A person may possess native northern leopard frogs of the species Lithobates pipiens, mudpuppies of the species Necturus maculosus, and eastern tiger salamanders of the species Ambystoma tigrinum provided that such species are possessed for the purpose of purchase and sale under the authority of a Class A captive wild animal farm license
WI.note: The eastern tiger salamander is a Wisconsin native and is singled out by name. Under the current rule it falls within the 5-per-species native cap; from 1 January 2027 the recreated rule routes it through a Class A captive wild animal farm licence instead. Wisconsin repealed and recreated NR 16.12(3) effective 1 January 2027 (CR 25-092). Until then the rule allows taking or possessing up to 5 individuals of each non-listed native species. From that date possession of live native reptiles and amphibians is prohibited outright except under narrow exemptions, of which the one that matters to keepers is NR 16.12(3)(k): captive-bred colour variants acquired from a legal source. A wild-type native animal will no longer be keepable.

UT.cite: Utah DWR species tables, controlled species
UT.quote: Tiger salamander - Ambystoma mavortium - Standard possession (3 daily/9 total, per species)
UT.note: A Utah native and a controlled species. Taking one from the wild requires the orientation course and a collection permit, caps at 3 daily and 9 in total possession, and carries a mandatory online report within 72 hours.

PA.quote: Native species not listed in this subsection | No closed season | 1 | 1
PA.note: Ambystoma tigrinum sits on the Fish and Boat Commission's own native species list even though it is considered extirpated here, because § 79.1 defines a native species by whether it occurs historically in Pennsylvania rather than whether it still does. It is not tabled by name, so the catch-all line applies and the limit is one animal, and § 79.10(a) bars importing a native species from another jurisdiction. Check what you are actually buying, because most pet-trade tiger salamanders are the barred tiger salamander, Ambystoma mavortium, a western species absent from Pennsylvania's native list and therefore outside Chapter 79.

MI.quote: Reptiles and amphibians may not be bought, sold or offered for sale.
MI.note: The eastern tiger salamander is Michigan native and, unlike the small-mouthed and marbled salamanders, is not on the protected list. So it may be taken with a fishing license, up to ten amphibians in total, but it may not be bought or sold, which rules out a shop or a breeder. Check what you are buying, because the barred tiger salamander, Ambystoma mavortium, is a western species outside this order entirely and is the one usually sold in the trade.

VT.quote: Amphibians | Caudata | Ambystomatidae | Ambystoma | all species | Mole salamanders
VT.note: The whole genus is on the Restricted list, so both the eastern tiger salamander and the barred tiger salamander sold in the trade are caught. Unlike Pennsylvania and Michigan, the species being native or not makes no difference here. A permit exists on paper but not for a pet: Regulation 881 says the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for keeping or possessing a wild animal in captivity except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes. So restricted here means a private keeper cannot have one, not that there is paperwork to fill in.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Salamander | Ambystomatidae | Ambystoma tigrinum | Eastern Tiger Salamander | II
NM.note: Group II on the Director's list: not known to be invasive or dangerous, but an importation permit is still required before the animal may be brought into New Mexico. The barred tiger salamander that fills the pet trade is listed separately at Group II as well, so both answers land in the same place. The Sonora and California tiger salamanders are Group IV as federally listed animals.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: Unprotected amphibians are all species of amphibians which are not classified as game, protected, threatened, sensitive or endangered amphibians.
NV.note: The tiger salamander is indigenous to Nevada, so the nonindigenous clearance does not reach it and the classification rule decides instead. Nevada's protected amphibians are three frogs and four toads, none of them a salamander, so the tiger salamander is unprotected and the possession restriction at NAC 503.093, which applies only to protected wildlife, does not bite. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: The species Bufo horribilis, Bufo marinus, Bufo schneideri ... All species of the genus Rana ... All species of the genus Xenopus
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted amphibian list is three genera and species groups, the giant and marine toads, the genus Rana and the genus Xenopus. Ambystoma is not among them, so the tiger salamander needs no special licence. One Arizona-specific caveat: this species occurs in the wild here, and taking one alive from the wild is a separate question governed by R12-4-404 and R12-4-405 and the take limits in Commission Order 43, which need a valid hunting licence. The clearance above is about keeping a captive-bred animal, not about collecting one. The Sonora tiger salamander is also federally endangered, which is a separate federal constraint on that subspecies.

DE.note: The eastern tiger salamander is native to Delaware and is state endangered there. Amphibians sit outside the Agriculture permit chapter, which names only mammals, their hybrids and reptiles, so DNREC's native wildlife rules are the whole answer and they do not make native wildlife available as pets. The barred tiger salamander sold in the trade is a western species and would fall outside the native rules, but it is also outside the Agriculture chapter, which is why the axolotl comes out legal here.

CO.quote: Any species from the order Urodela (salamanders and newts) except tiger salamanders (Ambystoma tigrinum/mavortium)
CO.note: Colorado clears the salamanders at order level and then carves this one species pair straight back out, which is why the axolotl is free here and the tiger salamander is not. The route that remains is a wild-collection licence, not a pet-shop purchase: Appendix C(J) lists the western tiger salamander, and § 704 lets a Colorado resident take, possess and transport one only under a Resident Herpetofauna Collection and Possession License, which requires passing a CPW education course, is capped at four animals a year and twelve at once, bars propagation, and requires reporting each take within seven days. Non-residents have no route at all, and CPW's list records that any acquisition of a western tiger salamander other than licensed wild collection or legacy possession is not allowed. Colorado is also where the ranavirus work on the bait-salamander trade was done, which is the concern this rule sits against.

grandfathered.detail: A western tiger salamander legally collected from the wild on or before 1 May 2026 may be kept for life if a CPW Legacy Report was filed by 30 July 2026.

IL.quote: The possession limit for herptiles (excluding common snapping turtles and bullfrogs) is no more than 4 total per species. ... In no case shall a person possess more than 8 indigenous amphibian or reptiles in total.
IL.note: The eastern tiger salamander, Ambystoma tigrinum is on the § 885.40 list of Illinois native herptile taxa, which is what puts it inside the cap rather than outside it. No licence is needed to keep one, but three conditions ride along: no more than 4 of the species and no more than 8 indigenous herptiles in total, a sport fishing licence to collect any native taxon from the wild, and a $50 Herpetoculture Permit to breed or to sell. Non-residents may not possess herptiles collected from the wild in Illinois at all except under a scientific collection permit. It is not on the state endangered or threatened list, unlike the Jefferson, silvery and spotted dusky salamanders and the mudpuppy, so the ordinary cap is the whole of it. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. The eastern tiger salamander is a Minnesota native, and it is the animal the DNR's own summary of the rule is aimed at, since the department describes the restriction as reaching wild collected Minnesota salamanders. It is not on the state endangered or threatened list; the listed amphibian is Blanchard's cricket frog. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Tiger salamander — Ambystomatidae — Ambystoma tigrinum All nonnative sub-species;
OR.note: Prohibited by name, and the reason is next door: eastern Oregon has its own tiger salamander population, and the rule bars the nonnative subspecies that would hybridise with it. Oregon lists nineteen caudates as prohibited and four as noncontrolled, and the axolotl is on the short list while this species is on the long one. OAR 635-056-0150 allows someone who held the animal before the commission listed it to keep it for its life, on proof of lawful prior possession, with no transfer, sale or transport inside Oregon and no release. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. Ambystoma tigrinum is not a Connecticut species, so neither the Category Three native list nor the state endangered and threatened list reaches it. Connecticut is at the opposite end from Oregon here, which prohibits every nonnative subspecies of the same animal by name to protect its own population.
