So no permit, no cap and no list. Worth flagging because this animal is restricted in most of the states around it: Nebraska has no controlled-snake list, no size rule and no invasive-species listing that reaches it.

GA.quote: (c) Reptiles: 1. Order Squamata: (i) Family Pythonidae - Python molurus (Indian rock python); (ii) Family Pythonidae - Python bivittatus (Burmese python); (iii) Family Teidae - Salvator merianae (Argentine black-and-white tegu); (iv) Family Varanidae - Varanus niloticus (Nile monitor); 2. Order Testudines: (i) Family Pelomedusidae - Pelomedusa subrufa (African helmeted turtle); (ii) Family Trionychidae (softshell turtles) - Pelodiscus sinensis (Chinese softshell turtle); 3. The species listed in subparagraph (c) shall only be licensed for scientific, educational, or public exhibition purposes consistent with O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4; provided, however, that such species possessed on or before the effective date of this rule may be held as a pet without a license or permit provided that the owner tags and registers all individuals with the Georgia DNR Law Enforcement Division within 12 months following the effective date of this rule;
GA.note: Georgia names six reptiles in its licence rule and then closes the pet route on all of them in the same subparagraph: they "shall only be licensed for scientific, educational, or public exhibition purposes". Python bivittatus is named, and so is Python molurus separately, so the split between the Indian and Burmese pythons is handled on both sides. The grandfathering is unusually generous in kind and unusually short in time: an animal held on or before the effective date may be kept as a pet with no licence at all, provided the owner tagged and registered it with DNR Law Enforcement within twelve months of that date.

grandfathered.before: the effective date of the rule
grandfathered.detail: An animal possessed on or before the effective date may be held as a pet without a licence if tagged and registered with Georgia DNR Law Enforcement within 12 months of that date.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: Named among the examples in the Pythonidae clause and caught by the family in any event. This is the one python on this row where the state and the city agree. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: i. Pythons - Family Pythonidae;
NJ.note: The Burmese python is answered by name on the 4.3 permit list rather than by the catch-all. It is covered by the family entry "Pythons - Family Pythonidae". The list is written by family as often as by species, and 4.3 is open-ended, "include, but are not limited to", so being on it settles the permit question but not being on it settles nothing. The permit is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, subject to the general possession criteria at 4.7. New Jersey does not put the giant constrictors in a separate tier the way many states now do, so the Burmese python and the ball python are read off the same line. The federal Lacey Act injurious listing still bars importing one across state lines, which is a separate question from whether New Jersey will permit one already here.

UT.quote: (a) A species of the Order Squamata (snakes and lizards) is classified as a prohibited species if: (i) it is venomous; (ii) not native to Utah; and (iii) a bite from which may cause substantial physical injury to humans ordinarily requiring medical treatment. (b) Species of the Order Crocodilia (crocodiles, gharials, caimans, and alligators) are classified as prohibited.
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the Burmese python is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Utah writes its prohibited categories by hazard rather than by size: venomous non-native squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, with no giant constrictor tier of the sort Florida and several other states now run. What does reach this species is federal, since the Lacey Act injurious listing bars importing one or moving it across state lines, which is a separate question from whether Utah will let you keep one already here. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

MA.quote: List of Mammals. (a) The following mammals may be kept without a permit: 1. Four-toed (African pygmy) hedgehog (Erinaceus albiventris) (= Atelerix pruneri) 2. Chinchilla (Chinchilla spp.) derived from captive stock. 3. Deer Mouse and White-footed Mouse 4. Degu (Octodon degus) 5. Egyptian Spiny Mouse 6. House Mouse 7. Jerboas 8. Norway Rat 9. Paca 10. Southern Flying Squirrel (Glaucomys volans) 11. Striped hamster ... 12. Sugar Glider (Petaurus breviceps) 13. American Bison
MA.note: Named at 9.01(12)(a)(4). Massachusetts is one of the few states that thought about the degu specifically rather than leaving it to a rodent catch-all, which matters here because the list is closed and a rodent that is not on it cannot be kept.

CO.cite: CPW, Wildlife and Animal Possession in Colorado, Regulated Wildlife
CO.quote: Any species of wildlife that is not specifically listed in Chapter W-11 as Domestic or Unregulated or in Chapter W-07 as Appendix A or Appendix B, the species is regulated wildlife and a CPW license is required. CPW will not issue a license for private possession (eg pet) of regulated wildlife.
CO.note: Absent from both lists, so regulated. CPW's mammal list names Octodon degus and files it as regulated wildlife. Colorado has no pet licence to issue. Chapter W-11 § 1104 offers commercial wildlife park licences, which require commercial status, and a non-commercial wildlife park licence that § 1104(B)(2) closed to new entrants: it is available only to someone who held one already or held exotic mammals lawfully before 1 January 1983. The chapter introduction states the effect plainly, that "noncommercial (pet) possession of regulated mammals has been prohibited by these regulations since 1983". The chinchilla, another South American caviomorph rodent kept as a pet, is named on the domestic animal list; the degu never was.

grandfathered.detail: The pre-1983 non-commercial wildlife park licence in § 1104(B)(2) is the only possession route the chapter leaves open for a regulated mammal.

MI.note: None of Michigan's three relevant acts reaches a rodent. Worth knowing because Colorado does require a permit for a degu, so the two states differ.

ID.quote: South American Rodents. All South American rodents except guinea pigs and chinchillas.
ID.note: Octodon degus is a Chilean rodent and is not one of the two exceptions, so it is a deleterious exotic animal needing a possession permit.

KY.note: On neither restricted list. Kentucky bans prairie dogs and the Gambian pouched rat by name, so the rodent list is specific rather than general.

RI.quote: Degu (Octodon degus),

NH.quote: Degaus (Octodon degus);
NH.note: Spelled Degaus in the rule as filed.

MO.note: Not Missouri wildlife and not on the dangerous wild animal list.

KS.note: Outside the definition of a dangerous regulated animal.

SC.note: Outside every group named in the import permit provision.

MT.quote: Degu (bush-tailed rat) - Octodon degus;

WV.quote: that is dangerous to humans, other animals or the environment due to its inherent nature and capability to do significant harm

AK.quote: The department may not issue a permit for the capture, possession, import, or export of any game animal... for use as a pet
AK.note: The clean list clears the guinea pig, the cavy, the chinchilla and two gerbils. The degu is not among them.

SD.quote: A permit from the board is required to import nondomestic animals.
SD.note: No rodent appears on the possession permit list.

AL.quote: Any of the following from any area outside the state of Alabama; ...species of skunk, wild rodent, or strain of wild turkey
AL.note: Wild rodent is not defined anywhere in the rule. A pet degu is captive bred, but Octodon degus is a wild species with no domesticated lineage behind it, unlike the hamster or the guinea pig. Ask the Division of Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries before buying.

IN.note: Not referenced in the rule.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.

WY.quote: A permit may be authorized upon approval for other warm-blooded wildlife unless otherwise specified in this regulation.
WY.note: The domesticated list clears the chinchilla, the guinea pig, the gerbil, the hamster, the mouse and the rat, but not the degu.

MS.note: No rodent appears on the list.

LA.note: Not among the listed animals.

OK.quote: The following wildlife species are exempt from import and export permits, commercial wildlife breeders licenses, noncommercial wildlife breeders licenses and commercial hunting area license requirements
OK.note: The list clears chinchillas, gerbils, guinea pigs, hamsters, mice and rats but not the degu, so it stays inside the permit and breeder licence regime rather than being banned.

NE.quote: 001.08A Importation: the following wildlife may be imported: Alpaca ... Chinchilla, Chinchilla spp. ... Coatimundi ... Degu, Octodon spp. ... Fox, Vulpes spp. ... Genet ... Gerbil, Gerbillus spp. ... Guinea pig, Cavia porcellus ... Eurasian Hedgehogs, Erinaceus spp. ... Jerboa, greater ... Sugar Glider(s), Petaurus spp. ... Wallabies ... All Ratites, All Waterfowl, All Peafowl, All Game Birds, All Cage and Aviary Birds
NE.note: Listed as "Degu, Octodon spp." Nebraska is one of a small number of states that name this animal at all, and it matters here because the importation list is closed: an unlisted exotic rodent has no route in.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches it. § 153A-131 hands the question to counties, several of which have used it.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: Absent from the permit table, so no special permit applies.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: Not a canid, hyaenid, felid, ursid, rhino, elephant, primate or swine, which is the whole of the mammal half of the definition.

DC.quote: Domesticated rodents and rabbits
DC.note: The rodent category is limited to domesticated ones. A degu is a wild species bred in captivity rather than a domesticated one, which puts it in the same position as the capybara and outside the category.

HI.quote: Any animal that is not on the lists of conditionally approved, restricted, or prohibited animals shall be prohibited until the board's review and determination for placement on one of these lists
HI.note: Octodon is on no Hawaii list. The contrast with the chinchilla and the guinea pig, both conditionally approved, is a good illustration that Hawaii's lists work species by species rather than by how domesticated an animal looks.

ME.note: Named individually, which is worth noting because the degu is barred outright in California and Georgia and is a legal grey area in several other states.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: Octodon degus is absent while the chinchilla, guinea pig and hamsters are all named, so the omission looks deliberate rather than accidental.

CA.quote: Order Rodentia-Hamsters, Field Mice, Voles, Muskrats, Gerbils, Squirrels, Chipmunks, Woodchucks, and Prairie Dogs. All species (D), except: ... b. Domesticated races of golden hamsters ... and dwarf hamsters of the Genus Phodopus ... d. Domesticated races of guinea pigs of the species Cavia porcellus ... e. Domesticated races of chinchillas of the species Chinchilla laniger
CA.note: California restricts the whole order and then names five exceptions. Octodon degus is not one of them, which is why the degu is barred here while the chinchilla, a close relative and also a South American caviomorph, is expressly cleared. Section 671.1 permits exist but are not issued for pet keeping.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Ohio does not maintain an approved species list, so a rodent that is not a dangerous wild animal needs no clearance. This is the opposite of California, where the degu is barred by falling inside a restricted order.

WA.quote: (a) Class mammalia (i) Order carnivora ... (iii) Order primates ... (iv) Order proboscidae
WA.note: Washington keeps no approved species list, so a rodent that is not a potentially dangerous wild animal needs no clearance.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Except as otherwise listed, all species are presumed prohibited. All species not listed will require an assessment before collection, importation, or possession will be authorized.
UT.note: Not listed anywhere in Table 3b-1, and the table's default is inverted: unlisted birds and mammals are 'presumed prohibited' and require a division assessment before possession will be authorized. So this is neither cleared nor expressly banned, it is an application to DWR with no published answer.

PA.quote: Game or wild held captive . Game or wildlife held in captivity or captive bred in another state or nation.
PA.note: The degu is named nowhere in Pennsylvania law. What arguably reaches it is this catch-all, which bars possessing wildlife captive bred in another state, read together with 34 Pa.C.S. § 102, where wild animals means every mammal except horses, cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. That is the same reading the Game Commission uses to ban hedgehogs and sugar gliders, and it is an agency interpretation of a definition rather than a rule anyone wrote about this species. Recorded unclear rather than banned because no text names the animal.

VT.quote: Rodentia | Hystricomorpha | Octodontidae | Octodon | all species | Degus
VT.note: Named at genus level. Worth contrasting with Colorado, which does require a permit for a degu.

NM.quote: Any species of live non-domesticated animal not currently on the species importation list will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.
NM.note: The degu appears nowhere on the Director's list, and New Mexico's default clause is the operative rule: an unlisted live non-domesticated animal is designated group IV until the director decides otherwise. Group IV importation is prohibited for the general public and allowed only for scientific study, department approved restoration, zoological display, temporary events, use as a service animal, or by a qualified expert. One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: it is unlawful, except by the written consent and approval of the Department, for any person at any time to receive, bring or have brought or shipped into this State, or remove from one stream or body of water in this State to any other...any aquatic life or wildlife
NV.note: The degu is on neither Nevada list. That is not the same as being unregulated, which is the point earlier research could not settle: NRS 503.597 makes it unlawful to bring any wildlife into the state without the written consent and approval of the Department, and NAC 503.140 is the Commission's list of exemptions from exactly that. An animal off both lists therefore needs Department approval. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: Order Erinaceomorpha, all species, except members of the genus Atelerix, which are not restricted. Common name: longeared and pygmy hedgehogs; Order Lagomorpha, all species, except members of the genus Oryctolagus containing domestic rabbits, which are not wildlife and are not restricted; Order Rodentia, the families Capromyidae, Castoridae, Dipodidae, Echimyidae, Erethizontidae, Geomyidae, Sciuridae
AZ.note: Arizona restricts rodents by family rather than as an order, and the seven families named are Capromyidae, Castoridae, Dipodidae, Echimyidae, Erethizontidae, Geomyidae and Sciuridae. The degu is Octodontidae, which is not among them, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Degus appear by name on the exempt mammal list, so no permit is required. Worth noting because Delaware names the degu specifically, which few states do, and Colorado goes the other way and requires a permit for one.

IL.quote: "Dangerous animal" means a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, bear, hyena, wolf or coyote. Dangerous animal does not mean any herptiles included in the Herptiles-Herps Act.
IL.note: Illinois runs a closed list of 15 named mammals plus a blanket bar on primates, and it has no catch-all clause, no size test and no dangerousness test. An animal that is not on the list and is not native Illinois wildlife is simply outside the statute. No rodent appears on it. The degu is not on the Part 805 injurious species list either, which is where Illinois puts the exotic mammals it does want to keep out, among them the raccoon dog, the multimammate rat and the brushtail possum. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: all members of the Felidae family including, but not limited to, lions, tigers, cougars, leopards, cheetahs, ocelots, and servals, but not including domestic cats or cats recognized as a domestic breed, registered as a domestic breed, and shown as a domestic breed by a national or international multibreed cat registry association; (2) bears; and (3) all nonhuman primates
MN.note: Minnesota's regulated animal definition is three groups and nothing else: the cat family, bears, and non-human primates. No rodent is in it, and the degu is on neither the prohibited nor the regulated invasive species list.

OR.quote: Degus -- Octodontidae -- Octodon All species;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Cleared at genus level. Oregon is unusually specific about which rodents it will and will not have: the same rule clears the mara, the paca, the agoutis and the dwarf hamsters, and the prohibited list names the capybara, the prairie dogs and the plains viscacha. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: A member within the order Rodentia, except for guinea pig (Cavia porcellus), gerbil (Meriones unguiculatus), chinchilla (Chinchilla lanigera), rat (Rattus norvegicus), mouse (Mus musculus), hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), dwarf hamster (genera Phodopus and Cricetulus), Patagonia mara (Dolichotis patagonum) and American beaver (Castor canadensis)
CT.note: Connecticut regulates rodents the opposite way round from most states: rather than naming the ones it bars, it puts the whole order Rodentia in Category Two and then excepts nine, the guinea pig, gerbil, chinchilla, rat, mouse, hamster, dwarf hamsters, Patagonian mara and American beaver. The degu is not among them. The exception list names every small rodent that is commonly sold, including both hamster groups, which makes the degu's absence hard to read as accidental. Subsection (b)(3) allows possession of a Category Two animal only by a vet treating it, a municipal park, zoo, marine mammal park, aquarium, nature centre, museum, exhibitor, laboratory or research facility. There is no private permit.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. No rodent appears in the eight clauses, and the degu is not native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q).
TN.note: Tennessee's catch-all sits in the no-permit class rather than the permit class, which is the single fact that decides most questions here: an animal that appears nowhere in Classes I, II, IV or V is Class III and needs no wildlife permit. The degu is not on the Class I list, is not native to Tennessee, and is not among the three Class IV species. The rodent subdivision names seven kinds and the catch-all covers the rest.

TX.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means: (A) a lion; (B) a tiger; (C) an ocelot; (D) a cougar; (E) a leopard; (F) a cheetah; (G) a jaguar; (H) a bobcat; (I) a lynx; (J) a serval; (K) a caracal; (L) a hyena; (M) a bear; (N) a coyote; (O) a jackal; (P) a baboon; (Q) a chimpanzee; (R) an orangutan; (S) a gorilla; or (T) any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision.
TX.note: Octodon degus is Chilean, so the nongame rules do not reach it, and the dangerous wild animal list contains no rodent. Texas asks nothing about it.

FL.quote: Class III: All other wildlife not listed herein, except those for which a permit is not required pursuant to Rule 68A-6.003, F.A.C. ... Hybrids resulting from the cross between wildlife and domestic animal, which are substantially similar in size, characteristics and behavior so as to be indistinguishable from the wild animal shall be regulated as wildlife at the higher and more restricted class of the wild parent.
FL.note: Class III in Florida is a residual category, "all other wildlife not listed herein, except those for which a permit is not required", and the degu lands in it by not being anywhere else. That means a Permit to Possess Class III Wildlife for Personal Use, which costs nothing, runs two years, and requires the applicant to be 16. The thing to notice is what it is not on: 68A-6.003(14) exempts 22 categories from any permit at all, and this animal is not among them. This is the sharpest illustration of how the exemption list works, because the chinchilla is on it at (l) and the degu is not. Two South American caviomorph rodents of similar size and similar husbandry, and one needs a permit because a list written years ago named the other.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the degu is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's licence rule works by taxonomic order rather than by species, which is what catches the degu. Octodon is not among the six excepted genera and DNR names the degu specifically. The excepted list is what makes the point: the guinea pig, chinchilla, gerbil and hamster are all legal because someone wrote their genera down, and the degu is not because nobody did. The reason a licence does not help is in the statute rather than the rule. O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4(b)(1) says wild animal licences "will be issued only to persons engaged in the wholesale or retail wild animal business or persons exhibiting wild animals to the public", and permits only for scientific or educational purposes, for a capuchin monkey held by a person with a permanent disability, or to a pond owner for grass carp. There is no pet category anywhere in it, which is why the rule has to write an express pet exception where it wants one, as it does for the European ferret and the sugar glider.

NYC.quote: In addition to domesticated dogs and cats, an animal may be kept, possessed, harbored or sold in the City of New York provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law, including federal, state and local laws regulating domestic animals and livestock or protecting wildlife and endangered species. Such animals include, but are not limited to, gerbil, hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and fowl or small birds such as parakeet, parrot, canary and finch.
NYC.note: Not named anywhere in the article, and it clears the large rodent clause on the same reasoning as the chinchilla: it is a caviomorph, like the prohibited paca and viscacha, but it is rat-sized. § 161.01(c) is the article's short affirmative list, and it is written as examples rather than as a closed set: "an animal may be kept ... provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law", followed by gerbil, hamster, guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and small birds. So the question in New York City is always whether something else in § 161.01(b) reaches the animal.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: New Jersey is a closed-list state in the strict sense. 7:25-4.2(a) bars possession of any exotic or nongame species without a permit, 4.4 then names the handful that may be kept without one, and 4.5 sweeps everything else back in. The degu appears on none of the Division's three lists, so it is not exempt under 4.4, not one of the families singled out in 4.3, and not potentially dangerous under 4.8. That leaves 4.5, and the permit it points to is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, which 4.7 conditions on diet, caging that prevents escape, lawful acquisition, veterinary care and freedom from disease. The Division's own handout tells readers to phone the permits office for anything the lists do not name, which is a fair signal that the catch-all is where these end up rather than an oversight.

DC.quote: a person shall not import into the District, possess, display, offer for sale, trade, barter, exchange, or adoption, or give as a household pet, any living member of the animal kingdom, including those born or raised in captivity, except the following
DC.note: The seven permitted categories are dogs, cats, domesticated rodents and rabbits, captive-bred common cage birds, non-venomous snakes, fish and turtles, ferrets and racing pigeons. No amphibian fits any of them, so the axolotl is barred by omission.

HI.cite: List of Conditionally Approved Animals, Family Ambystomidae
HI.note: Named individually on the conditionally approved list, so importation and possession are allowed subject to Department of Agriculture conditions. A rare yes from a state that bans most exotics by default.

RI.quote: All persons other than a bona fide researcher, or a licensed pet shop and their transportation agents are prohibited from possessing any species of exotic amphibians unless they are kept indoors as pets in a manner that will prevent their escape or liberation into the wild.
RI.note: Treated as an exotic amphibian: indoors only, and importation limited to pet shops and researchers.

NH.quote: Amphibians, exotic;
NH.note: Exotic amphibians are non-controlled for possession. The controlled table covers New Hampshire's own Ambystoma species, and the axolotl is Mexican.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of salamanders not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: (i) Ambystomatidae (mole salamanders);
MT.note: Cleared by family on the statutory noncontrolled list, which matters in Montana because anything not classified cannot be imported at all.

CA.quote: Genus Ambystoma (nonnative tiger salamander group)-(D)
CA.note: Ambystoma mexicanum sits in the listed genus. The parenthetical describes the group the restriction was aimed at rather than narrowing it, and none of the permit types in § 671.1 covers pet keeping, so there is no route.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian, so no amphibian is reached by it.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: Amphibians are exempted as a class from the import permit in the same sentence as reptiles.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: No amphibian appears anywhere in the chapter. The prohibitions are skunks and raccoons.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No amphibian is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. No amphibian is reached by it, and § 153A-131 leaves the rest to counties.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: On neither Kentucky list. The only amphibians named are the cane toad and the African clawed frog, both as injurious species.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: No amphibian appears in the categories the board is directed to consider.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition covers canids, hyenas, felids, bears, rhinos, elephants, primates, crocodilians, some squamates and swine. No amphibian appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only. A free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

VA.quote: Ambystomatidae   All species, except Ambystoma mexicanum   All mole salamanders, except Mexican axolotl
VA.note: One of the few places in the country where the axolotl is written into a rule as an exception rather than a target. Virginia restricts every other mole salamander and carves this one out by binomial and by common name.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state
LA.note: The prohibited amphibians are the Cuban treefrog, the cane toad and the African clawed frog. The axolotl is not among them.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds... native to the continental United States, and those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri.
MO.note: Mexican, so not native to Missouri and outside Class I. Missouri's own Ambystoma species are a different question.

WY.quote: An importation/possession permit shall not be issued for importation or possession of the live cold-blooded wildlife in this section... (a) Injurious wildlife listed in 50 CFR § 16.
WY.note: Ambystoma mexicanum is inside the same federal genus listing, so Wyoming will not issue a permit. Section 8 is absolute: it does not offer a permit route, it forecloses one.

ID.quote: Conventional Pets. Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders.
ID.note: A non-venomous amphibian that is not Idaho native wildlife, so it is a conventional pet and § 200.06 exempts it from any Department permit. Idaho's approach is unusually readable: one definition does the work that other states spread over three lists.

AK.quote: "game" means any species of bird, reptile, and mammal, including a feral domestic animal, found or introduced in the state, except domestic birds and mammals
AK.note: Outside the definition of game, so outside the clean list. This is the reverse of the usual pattern, where Alaska is the hardest state to satisfy.

ME.quote: Amphibia (Amphibians)   Captive Bred Origin Only ... Anura (Frogs And Toads)
ME.note: Same gap as the tiger salamander: the amphibian list is frogs and toads only. The axolotl is also IUCN Critically Endangered, which the footnote would catch even if a salamander order existed.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Additionally, persons may possess and hold captive fish, bullfrogs, mussels, aquatic turtles, alligators and other aquatic wildlife...
AR.note: No amphibian section exists on the unrestricted list, so a non-native salamander is neither exempted nor addressed. Note separately that federal law at 50 CFR 16.14 bars bringing any Ambystoma across a state line.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Outside Chapter 935 and not native to Ohio. The federal injurious wildlife listing of the genus Ambystoma is the constraint that matters, and it bites on importing or shipping one rather than on keeping it.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: Amphibians are outside the statute. As with every state, the live constraint on the axolotl is federal: 50 CFR 16.14 lists the whole genus as injurious wildlife.

WI.note: Non-native, so NR 16.12's native amphibian rules do not reach it. Worth not confusing with the eastern tiger salamander, a Wisconsin native in the same genus that NR 16.12 does restrict.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The axolotl is Mexican and is absent from the Fish and Boat Commission's native species list, so Chapter 79 does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework. Worth noting that the answer turns on the species and not the genus, because its Pennsylvania native congener the tiger salamander is covered by that chapter and is limited to one animal.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The axolotl is Mexican and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit. The answer turns on the species and not the genus, because Michigan's own tiger salamander is covered by this order and may not be bought or sold.

VT.quote: Amphibians | Caudata | Ambystomatidae | Ambystoma | all species | Mole salamanders
VT.note: Salamanders and newts are unrestricted as a group, and then the entire genus Ambystoma is clawed back, which catches the axolotl even though it is a laboratory and pet animal that has not existed in the wild in any meaningful way for decades. A permit exists on paper but not for a pet: Regulation 881 says the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for keeping or possessing a wild animal in captivity except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes. So restricted here means a private keeper cannot have one, not that there is paperwork to fill in.

NM.quote: Any species of live non-domesticated animal not currently on the species importation list will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.
NM.note: Fifteen Ambystoma appear on the list and the axolotl is not among them, so the default clause designates it group IV. That is a harsh result for a laboratory animal that has effectively no wild population, and it sits oddly beside the tiger salamander two rows away at group II. Group IV importation is prohibited for the general public and allowed only for scientific study, department approved restoration, zoological display, temporary events, use as a service animal, or by a qualified expert. One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (qq) Nonindigenous species of amphibians, except: (1) Bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana); and (2) Species listed in NAC 503.110;
NV.note: Nonindigenous amphibians are cleared as a class, with only bullfrogs and the species on the prohibited list carved out. The prohibited amphibians are clawed frogs and the giant marine toads, so the axolotl is clear. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: The species Bufo horribilis, Bufo marinus, Bufo schneideri ... All species of the genus Rana ... All species of the genus Xenopus
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted amphibian list is three genera and species groups, the giant and marine toads, the genus Rana and the genus Xenopus. Ambystoma is not among them, so the axolotl needs no special licence.

DE.quote: No person shall bring into this State, possess, sell or exhibit any live wild mammal or hybrid of a wild mammal or live reptile not native to or generally found in Delaware without first securing a permit under this chapter.
DE.note: A quirk of Delaware's drafting decides this one. The permit requirement covers wild mammals, their hybrids and reptiles, and amphibians are simply not in it. The axolotl is also not native to Delaware, so the DNREC native wildlife rules do not reach it either. It falls between the two regimes and needs no permit.

CO.quote: Any species from the order Urodela (salamanders and newts) except tiger salamanders (Ambystoma tigrinum/mavortium)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. The salamanders are cleared at order level in the appendix's Other Species block, which CPW introduces as species that are not native only to tropic or subtropic regions, so the axolotl does not have to satisfy the range test that governs the family lists. The single carve-out is for tiger salamanders, and the axolotl is a different Ambystoma. Its own conservation status does the rest of the work in practice: the species is CITES Appendix II and effectively extinct in the wild, so what circulates is captive stock. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The axolotl is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. Nor is it a medically significant amphibian: § 885.48 lists those by name and they are toxic toads and frogs. Part 805 injurious species would be the other place to look, and § 805.10 excludes herptiles from that Part expressly, sending them here. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. The axolotl is a salamander, so the same condition applies. Nothing else in Minnesota reaches it: it is not on either invasive species list, and the DNR's frog importation permit list at Minn. R. 6256.0300 is frogs and toads only. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Axolotl -- Ambystomatidae -- Ambystoma mexicanum;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Oregon lists only four caudates as Noncontrolled and the axolotl is the first of them. Its close relative is on the opposite list: Ambystoma tigrinum, all nonnative subspecies, is prohibited. Two Ambystoma, one cleared by name and one banned by name, in the same division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. The four amphibians in Category Three are Fowler's toad, the northern dusky salamander, the gray treefrog, the eastern newt and the wood frog, all Connecticut natives, and no amphibian appears in Category Two at all. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. Ambystoma mexicanum is not native to Maryland. Its congener the eastern tiger salamander is, and is on the tier that may not be possessed at all, so the two Ambystoma come out at opposite ends of the same chapter. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The axolotl is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial. Only poisonous amphibians are Class I, and the axolotl is not one.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Ambystoma mexicanum is endemic to the Xochimilco canals in Mexico City, so it is not indigenous to Texas and the nongame rules do not reach it, even though its close relative the tiger salamander is capped at 25. The other rule worth ruling out is 31 TAC Chapter 57 Subchapter A, the harmful or potentially harmful exotic species list, which is long but covers only fish, shellfish and aquatic plants and names no amphibian at all.

MA.quote: List of Amphibians. All amphibians may be kept without a permit except species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3).
MA.note: The class-wide amphibian clearance is subject to 9.01(3), and Ambystoma mexicanum is assessed by the IUCN as critically endangered, which makes it categorically non-exempt. The axolotl is the sharpest case for that clause anywhere on this map: the wild population is confined to the Xochimilco canals and is genuinely near extinction, while the captive population is enormous, entirely laboratory-derived and in no sense taken from the wild. The regulation draws no distinction, and unlike the chinchilla entry it writes no captive-stock exception here. MassWildlife's own guidance is blunt about what that means in practice: permits for non-exempt wildlife "are issued only for certain scientific, educational, commercial, or other specific reasons" and "You will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet." The statute is less absolute, since § 23 contemplates "an individual license for an animal that is not on the special exemption list" and even sets a preference for captive-bred animals where wild depletion is an issue, so the licence exists on paper and the agency says it will not grant one for a pet.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Ambystoma mexicanum is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list. The contrast with the tiger salamander is sharp and entirely about geography: the Mexican species is unregulated here and the native one cannot lawfully be possessed at all, because the chapter reaches natives and then lists the ones that may be collected.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Ambystoma mexicanum is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004. The two flatwoods salamanders are the only Ambystoma on Florida's imperiled list, and both are natives.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the axolotl is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The contrast with the tiger salamander is complete: the Mexican species is unregulated here and its New York relative is endangered and cannot be held at all. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the axolotl is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it. The only amphibian in the licence rule is the cane toad genus Rhinella.

NYC.quote: No person shall sell or give to another person, possess, harbor, keep, or yard wild or other animals identified in this section ... other than in: (i) a zoological park or aquarium ...; or (ii) a laboratory ...; or (iii) a veterinary hospital ...; or (iv) a temporary exhibit, performance or display that has been issued a permit by the Commissioner. ... For the purposes of this Code, a wild animal is deemed to be any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings and all such animals are hereby prohibited ... Such animals shall also include: (i) any animals specified by the Commissioner in regulations ...; (ii) any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule; and (iii) any of the following animals:
NYC.note: No amphibian clause exists anywhere in § 161.01(b). The twenty-four categories cover mammals, birds, reptiles, insects, arachnids and centipedes, and skip amphibians entirely. The clause to check instead is (b)(ii), which imports species protected or endangered under federal, state or local law, and although Ambystoma mexicanum is critically endangered in the wild it is not listed under the US Endangered Species Act or by New York State, so nothing imports. Its New York relative, the eastern tiger salamander, is state-endangered and is prohibited through that route. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: Due to the difficulties in determining morphological differences among several species, the following may not be kept as pets or for hobby purposes, nor may they be sold in New Jersey: grey tree frogs (all species), larval salamanders, water dogs, dino dogs, mud puppies, axolotls.
NJ.note: The axolotl is named outright in the Division's restricted species notice, in the sentence that bans grey tree frogs, larval salamanders, water dogs, dino dogs, mud puppies and axolotls from being kept, held for hobby purposes or sold. The reason given is enforcement rather than the animal: a neotenic salamander cannot reliably be told from the larva of a protected native one by looking at it, and New Jersey has two listed Ambystoma of its own. There is a second and independent route to the same answer, since the notice treats an IUCN Red List entry as an endangered listing and Ambystoma mexicanum is Critically Endangered there, which 4.10(a) turns into a bar on issuing a permit. Note that the express ban lives in the notice and not in the rule text, which is the sort of thing that gets missed by reading the code alone.

UT.quote: Any amphibian or reptile listed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service as endangered or threatened pursuant to the federal Endangered Species Act shall have a zero daily and total possession limit
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the axolotl is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Two things that catch this species elsewhere do not catch it here. R657-53-9(1)(d) gives a zero limit only to a species listed under the federal Endangered Species Act, and Ambystoma mexicanum is IUCN Critically Endangered without being on that list, so Utah's hook never engages. And the January 2025 federal salamander rule is an injurious wildlife listing, which restricts importation and shipment rather than possession. The one genuine add-on is R657-53-4(3)(h), which bars transporting or propagating an amphibian without complying with Title 4 Chapter 37 of the Utah Code and the Department of Agriculture and Food's rules under it, an aquaculture regime that sits outside the wildlife division entirely. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: This is what an incorporation by reference does when the federal list moves. Alabama bans possessing any amphibian the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service lists as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act, and the salamander rule effective January 2025 put genus Ambystoma on that list. Nothing in Alabama changed and the answer did. The distinction that saves the axolotl in most states, that an injurious listing restricts importation and interstate shipment rather than possession, does not help here, because Alabama has adopted the federal list as its own possession bar. The state's own native protection at 220-2-.92 would not have reached this animal, since Ambystoma mexicanum is Mexican and that clause covers native salamanders.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana splits its reptiles cleanly and The axolotl lands on the free side of the split. 312 IAC 9-5 governs reptiles and amphibians native to Indiana, and it is the rule that does the real work: 9-5-1(b) makes every native a protected wild animal, 9-5-6(f) caps possession at four per species, and 9-5-7 bars selling one regardless of where it came from, against a list of 99 taxa named by binomial. The axolotl is on none of them. The other rule, 312 IAC 9-11, requires a permit only for Class I animals, which is the cottontail and three squirrels, Class II, which is Indiana's furbearers and a named run of small wild cats, and Class III, which is purebred wolves, bears, wild cats, venomous reptiles and crocodilians at least five feet long. Nothing there reaches it either. Worth being precise about the salamanders, because Indiana lists eight Ambystoma by binomial on its native list and Ambystoma mexicanum is not among them. Indiana also does not adopt the federal injurious wildlife list as a possession bar, which is what turns the same animal into a banned one in Alabama.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided, monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license; except those which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma and which may be potentially injurious or detrimental to Oklahoma's wildlife, agriculture or public safety in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations.
OK.note: This one turns on how the carve-out in 800:25-25-3(c) is joined. Non-indigenous reptiles and amphibians are exempt except those "which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma AND which may be potentially injurious or detrimental ... in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations". The second limb is now satisfied, because the January 2025 federal salamander rule put genus Ambystoma on the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service injurious wildlife list, which is a Department of the Interior regulation. The first is not: Ambystoma mexicanum is an obligate neotene from two high-altitude lakes in the Valley of Mexico and could not establish in Oklahoma. Both limbs are required, so the exemption holds. Compare Alabama, which adopts the injurious list flat as its own possession bar and therefore bans the same animal outright.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: Turtles are one of the seven permitted categories, and the clause turns on keeping the animal for pleasure rather than commercially.

HI.quote: Terrapene (all species in genus except T. coahuila)
HI.note: The whole genus is conditionally approved apart from the Coahuilan box turtle, which sits on the restricted Part B list instead.

RI.quote: The possession of native turtles is restricted to those institutions identified within § 3.7(C) of this Part... Box Turtle (Terrapene carolina),
RI.note: Native to Rhode Island, so possession is limited to the Department, USFWS, AZA zoos, research institutions and USDA licensed exhibitors. Not a pet species here.

LA.quote: Box Turtles—Terrapene sp.
LA.note: A restricted turtle. No more than ten restricted turtles in total and no more than two of any one species, and § 101.G.2.a.ii separately caps native box turtles at two regardless of species. A basic recreational fishing licence is needed to collect one.

NH.quote: 5   Eastern box turtle   Terrapene carolina carolina
NH.note: Permittee category 5 is an exhibitor, with no category 1 for an individual, so a private keeper cannot be permitted for one.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is drawn family by family and is entirely mammalian. Mississippi restricts no reptile under this rule at any size.

SC.quote: A person shall not possess more than 2 eastern box turtles (Terrapene carolina).
SC.note: This entry read legal on § 50-16-60, which clears reptiles as a class from the import permit. Regulation 123-151.4(I) says that section does not privilege a native reptile, and the eastern box turtle gets its own subsection. 123-151.4(D) caps possession at two, and anyone who held more on 28 September 2020 had ninety days to register them by species, wild-caught and captive-born alike, with no further turtles acquirable until the number drops below the cap. Registered turtles are assigned a unique identification number and must be shell notched with it, the keeper must file an affidavit confirming the notching, and permit holders file an annual report. On top of that 123-151.3(A) bars selling, buying or re-homing one at all. Two is also the aggregate cap for diamondback terrapins, against ten for native turtles generally.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: That sentence, plus tattooing for mountain lions and wolves and rulemaking for primates, is the whole of North Dakota's prohibition list. No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The only reptiles Kansas regulates are non-native venomous snakes. Constrictors, lizards and turtles are untouched at any size.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: On neither the prohibited species list nor the inherently dangerous list. The only reptiles on either are gila monsters, beaded lizards, the Komodo dragon, crocodilians and venomous snakes other than hognose.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: The only reptiles the statute points the board at are constrictors over six feet, venomous snakes and crocodilians. Nothing here falls in those categories.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The squamate half of the definition is exhaustively enumerated: varanidae limited to water and crocodile monitors, helodermatidae, the venomous snake families, and henophidia limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas and African rock pythons. Nothing here is among them.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds (including ring-necked pheasants and gray partridge) native to the continental United States, and those species of mammals (except bison and those listed in 3 CSR 10-9.240 and 3 CSR 10-9.250) and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri.
MO.note: Both the three-toed and the ornate box turtle are native to Missouri, which puts them in Class I. Permits issue only for species on the Approved Confined Wildlife Species List.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: The ornate box turtle reaches southeastern Wyoming, so the same split applies: no permit for captive-bred stock kept privately, while the nongame regulation governs collecting one.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of turtles with a carapace or shell length of more than 4 inches and not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ... (v) Emydidae (pond turtles)
MT.note: Box turtles are Emydidae, so the family is cleared, but every category on this list is gated on being tropical and subtropical, and both the eastern and the ornate box turtle are temperate North American animals. The qualifier looks deliberate, since a temperate species could survive a Montana release in a way a tropical one could not. Ask Fish, Wildlife and Parks before buying.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: No Terrapene is native to Idaho, so the captured from the wild in Idaho carve-out does not bite, and a box turtle is a conventional pet needing no permit.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: Alaska's clean list is almost entirely species by species, then clears the whole of Class Reptilia in one line so long as the animal is not venomous. A box turtle needs no permit.

ME.note: No Terrapene appears anywhere on the list. The only match for the words box turtle is the Amboina box turtle, which is a Cuora and a different animal. The eastern box turtle is also a species of special concern in Maine, so its own native status is part of the picture.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Additionally, persons may possess and hold captive fish, bullfrogs, mussels, aquatic turtles, alligators and other aquatic wildlife in compliance with Code Chapters 26.00, 27.00, 29.00, 30.00, 31.00, 32.00, 33.00, 34.00, 35.00...
AR.note: Both the three-toed and the ornate box turtle are native to Arkansas, and a terrestrial native turtle is neither on the unrestricted list nor inside the aquatic wildlife carve-out. Arkansas's native wildlife rules govern, and this document does not reach them.

CA.quote: Family Chelyridae-Snapping Turtles: All species (D)
CA.note: Snapping turtles are the only restricted family in Testudines, so a box turtle is unrestricted. The spelling Chelyridae in the regulation is a long-standing typo for Chelydridae.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Chapter 935 does not reach it. The eastern box turtle is native to Ohio and taking one from the wild is governed by the Division of Wildlife rather than by the exotic animal law.

WA.quote: Class reptilia ... Order crocodilia, all species
WA.note: No Terrapene is native to Washington and none is listed, so nothing in RCW 16.30 applies.

WI.cite: Wis. Stat. § 29.604; Wis. Admin. Code ch. NR 27
WI.note: Wisconsin's only native box turtle, the ornate box turtle, is a state Endangered species, so it may not be taken or possessed without an endangered and threatened species permit, and those are issued for education, research and conservation rather than pet keeping. The eastern box turtle is not a Wisconsin native and would instead be a non-native reptile under § 169.04.
