Its Sahelian range sits inside the band, unlike the Russian, Greek, Hermann's and leopard tortoises, which CPW files as regulated on the same family listing. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The sulcata tortoise is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: A person may not take, possess, or transport turtles without a resident angling license and a recreational turtle license. ... A person does not need the licenses specified under subdivision 1: ... (2) when buying a turtle at a retail outlet
MN.note: Turtles are the gap in the 2021 pet reptile rule. Section 97A.401, subd. 8 covers snakes, lizards and salamanders and stops there, so turtles stay under their own older regime, which is a licence requirement with a short list of exemptions rather than a source condition. Whether a sulcata is a "turtle" for this section is not spelled out, since Minnesota never defines the word and its turtle rules are plainly written around aquatic natives. It does not matter much in practice: read broadly, the retail outlet exemption in subd. 2c covers a pet-shop animal anyway, and read narrowly the section does not reach it at all. Either way no licence is needed for one bought at retail, and the species is on neither invasive species list.

OR.quote: Tortoises -- Testudinidae -- All species;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. The whole family is cleared, so the sulcata needs nothing. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No tortoise appears in any category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three. One caveat that applies to every Connecticut turtle on this map: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 26-78 addresses turtles separately from the regulation, and it could not be read this sitting because cga.ct.gov refuses every connection from this container. This entry rests on § 26-55-6, which is the comprehensive rule and mentions no turtle sale ban, and the point is flagged rather than assumed away.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. No tortoise is native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The sulcata tortoise is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Centrochelys sulcata is African. Nothing in the nongame rules reaches it, because they apply only to wildlife indigenous to Texas, and no Texas list names it. The state’s own tortoise, Gopherus berlandieri, is threatened and off limits entirely, which is a useful contrast: Texas restricts the tortoise it has and not the ones it does not.

MA.quote: All species of turtles may be kept without a permit, up to a limit of 100 turtles and/or eggs, in any combination, of each species, except for the following species for which a permit is always required: 1. Species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3). 2. Argentina or Chaco Tortoise (Geochelone chilensis). 3. Gopher Tortoises (Gopherus polyphemus) and all other species in the genus Gopherus. 4. Pancake Tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri). 5. Spotted Turtle (Clemmys guttata). 6. Red-eared Slider (Trachemys scripta, including all subspecies and forms).
MA.note: Centrochelys sulcata is IUCN endangered, which makes it categorically non-exempt under 9.01(3)(b) and takes it out of the turtle allowance. Massachusetts is a genuinely unusual answer for this animal: most states that restrict the sulcata do it for size or for the burrowing, and this one does it through a conservation listing that has nothing to do with either. MassWildlife's own guidance is blunt about what that means in practice: permits for non-exempt wildlife "are issued only for certain scientific, educational, commercial, or other specific reasons" and "You will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet." The statute is less absolute, since § 23 contemplates "an individual license for an animal that is not on the special exemption list" and even sets a preference for captive-bred animals where wild depletion is an issue, so the licence exists on paper and the agency says it will not grant one for a pet.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Centrochelys sulcata is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the sulcata tortoise is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the sulcata tortoise is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: New York City draws its turtle line by size rather than by species: the reptile clause ends with "all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches". The sulcata tortoise is not otherwise named, so an adult is lawful and a hatchling is not, and the animal grows out of the prohibition rather than into it. The four-inch figure is the same one the federal rule at 21 C.F.R. 1240.62 uses, and the reason is the same: small turtles are the ones children put in their mouths. A sulcata passes four inches within its first year and then reaches a size no New York City apartment can hold, so the legal constraint is the least of the problems here. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: New Jersey is a closed-list state in the strict sense. 7:25-4.2(a) bars possession of any exotic or nongame species without a permit, 4.4 then names the handful that may be kept without one, and 4.5 sweeps everything else back in. The sulcata tortoise appears on none of the Division's three lists, so it is not exempt under 4.4, not one of the families singled out in 4.3, and not potentially dangerous under 4.8. That leaves 4.5, and the permit it points to is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, which 4.7 conditions on diet, caging that prevents escape, lawful acquisition, veterinary care and freedom from disease. The Division's own handout tells readers to phone the permits office for anything the lists do not name, which is a fair signal that the catch-all is where these end up rather than an oversight. 4.7 conditions the permit on housing that lets the animal "perform the normal behavior patterns of its species", which is a real question for an animal that reaches a hundred pounds and digs, rather than a formality.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the sulcata tortoise is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Centrochelys sulcata is IUCN Endangered but carries no federal Endangered Species Act listing, which is what R657-53-9(1)(d) turns on when it gives a zero limit to any species the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has listed as endangered or threatened. Utah reads the federal list rather than the IUCN one, which is the opposite of the choice Massachusetts and New Jersey made. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Alabama works from a prohibited list rather than a permitted one, so the question is only whether the sulcata tortoise is on it, and it is not. 220-2-.26(1) reaches non-native venomous reptiles, tegus, mongooses, wild rabbits and hares, a block of mammals when they come from outside the state, a run of fish, and everything the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act. The other half of Alabama is 220-2-.92, which protects native nongame species, and that one is about Alabama's own wildlife. The only tortoise Alabama protects is its own gopher tortoise, Gopherus polyphemus. Centrochelys sulcata is IUCN Endangered and carries no federal Endangered Species Act listing, and Alabama's rule reads the injurious wildlife list rather than the endangered one, so neither reaches it.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana splits its reptiles cleanly and The sulcata tortoise lands on the free side of the split. 312 IAC 9-5 governs reptiles and amphibians native to Indiana, and it is the rule that does the real work: 9-5-1(b) makes every native a protected wild animal, 9-5-6(f) caps possession at four per species, and 9-5-7 bars selling one regardless of where it came from, against a list of 99 taxa named by binomial. The sulcata tortoise is on none of them. The other rule, 312 IAC 9-11, requires a permit only for Class I animals, which is the cottontail and three squirrels, Class II, which is Indiana's furbearers and a named run of small wild cats, and Class III, which is purebred wolves, bears, wild cats, venomous reptiles and crocodilians at least five feet long. Nothing there reaches it either. Indiana lists fifteen native turtles on the sale list and no tortoise, since it has none.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided, monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license; except those which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma and which may be potentially injurious or detrimental to Oklahoma's wildlife, agriculture or public safety in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations.
OK.note: Oklahoma exempts non-indigenous reptiles and amphibians as a class rather than species by species. 800:25-25-3(c) clears them from import and export requirements and from both wildlife breeder licences, and the sulcata tortoise is squarely inside it. The carve-out at the end of the same sentence has two limbs joined by "and", so it bites only on a species that is biologically capable of establishing a self-sustaining population in the wild of Oklahoma AND is injurious under federal rules; neither is true here. What remains is the statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A), which reaches closed-season wildlife, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats. Not one of the three touches the sulcata tortoise. The box turtle clause at 800:15-9-3(3) reaches terrestrial turtles "commonly known as box turtles", which is a common-name limit rather than a habit-based one, so an African tortoise is not swept in with it.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: Hognose snakes are rear-fanged with a mild saliva toxin, which raises the question of whether the non-venomous qualifier reaches them. Every venomous reptile law we read draws its line well above hognose, so this reads as permitted.

HI.note: Hawaii bans the entire snake suborder with no exception for harmless species, having no native snakes to protect.

KY.quote: Venomous exotic snakes of the families Viperidae, Atractaspididae, Elapidae, Hydrophidae, and Colubridae, except for hognose snakes (Genus Heterodon);
KY.note: Kentucky is the state that settles the argument in writing. Colubridae is listed among the venomous families and the hognose is then carved straight back out by genus, which is as close to an official answer on rear-fanged snakes as any state gives.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;
NH.note: New Hampshire names the western hognose as the single exception to its venomous reptile exclusion, so the species most often kept as a pet is cleared by name even if the venomous label is applied to it. The native eastern hognose is separately controlled at exhibitor level.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous snakes not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(v) Colubridae (modern snakes);
MT.note: Montana clears Colubridae as nonvenomous, which places the hognose on the permitted side of the line.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Heterodon is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004. Both Florida hognose species are unprotected and neither appears at 68A-27.003, which is a contrast with Massachusetts and Nebraska, where the eastern hognose is listed.

AR.cite: Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.note: Arkansas names permitted species individually. The list clears several colubrids and reaches no venomous family that would sweep in the hognose.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is drawn family by family and is entirely mammalian. Mississippi restricts no reptile under this rule at any size.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit, and its only other exotic pet statute reaches genus Panthera, non-native bears and great apes.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: That sentence, plus tattooing for mountain lions and wolves and rulemaking for primates, is the whole of North Dakota's prohibition list. No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The only reptiles Kansas regulates are non-native venomous snakes. Constrictors, lizards and turtles are untouched at any size.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: The only reptiles the statute points the board at are constrictors over six feet, venomous snakes and crocodilians. Nothing here falls in those categories.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The squamate half of the definition is exhaustively enumerated: varanidae limited to water and crocodile monitors, helodermatidae, the venomous snake families, and henophidia limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas and African rock pythons. Nothing here is among them.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state
LA.note: The prohibited and restricted nonnative lists name crocodilians, tegus, two monitors, the green iguana, several snakes and some frogs. No hognose is among them. Louisiana's only mention of Heterodon is the native eastern hog-nosed snake on its checklist of native species.

MO.quote: those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri
MO.note: Both the eastern and the western hognose are native to Missouri and neither is venomous for the purposes of the Class II list, so they fall in Class I.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: Neither hognose is venomous for the purposes of Section 9(a), which is aimed at front-fanged species, and neither is on the Section 8 prohibited list. Both are native to Wyoming, so wild collection is governed separately from keeping captive-bred animals.

RI.quote: Snakes of the family Colubridae, as follows may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit: ... (xvi) Western Hognose Snake (Heterodon nasicus)
RI.note: Rhode Island is unusually precise here, and the two hognoses land on opposite sides. The western hognose is named on the no-permit list, while the eastern hog-nosed snake is treated as a native species whose possession as a pet is prohibited outright. Which hognose you are buying is the whole question.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: No hognose is native to Idaho. The rule's test is non-venomous or non-dangerous, phrased in the alternative, so even the rear-fanged mild toxicity that gets the hognose argued about elsewhere does not matter here: it clears on the second limb regardless.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: The clean list's only reptile test is venom. The hognose is rear-fanged with mild saliva toxicity and is not treated as a venomous snake, so it clears.

ME.note: Only the western hognose is named. The eastern hog-nosed snake is native to Maine and is not on the list, so which species you are buying decides the answer, the same split Rhode Island draws.

CA.quote: Family Colubridae-Colubrids: 1. Dispholidus typus (Boomslang) (D) 2. Genus Thelotornis (Bird, twig, or vine snakes) (D) 3. Genus Nerodia (watersnakes) (D)
CA.note: California restricts exactly three colubrid groups, two of them dangerously venomous rear-fanged African species and one, Nerodia, for invasiveness. Heterodon is on none of them.

OH.quote: "Restricted snake" means any of the following: (1) All of the following constricting snakes that are twelve feet or longer ... (2) Species of the following families: (a) Atractaspididae; (b) Elapidae; (c) Viperidae; (3) Boomslang snakes; (4) Twig snakes.
OH.note: The restricted snake list is three venomous families plus two named rear-fanged species plus eight large constrictors. The hognose is none of them. The eastern hognose is native to Ohio, so wild collection is a Division of Wildlife question.

WA.quote: Family colubridae, only dispholidus typus
WA.note: The only colubrid Washington restricts is the boomslang. The hognose is unaffected.

WI.quote: A person may take or possess up to 5 individuals or eggs of each species of native amphibian, lizard and snake that are not endangered or threatened
WI.note: The eastern hognose is a Wisconsin native, listed by DNR as Common rather than threatened, so it falls under the general native-herp cap rather than the endangered species rules. Wisconsin repealed and recreated NR 16.12(3) effective 1 January 2027 (CR 25-092). Until then the rule allows taking or possessing up to 5 individuals of each non-listed native species. From that date possession of live native reptiles and amphibians is prohibited outright except under narrow exemptions, of which the one that matters to keepers is NR 16.12(3)(k): captive-bred colour variants acquired from a legal source. A wild-type native animal will no longer be keepable.

PA.quote: Eastern Hog-nosed Snake ( Heterodon platirhinos ) | No open season | 0 | 0
PA.note: The condition is which hognose. The eastern hognose is Pennsylvania native, gets no open season and a zero limit, and cannot be imported from another jurisdiction under § 79.10(a), so it can be neither taken nor bought. The western hognose, Heterodon nasicus, which is what the pet trade almost always sells, is not on the Commission's native species list and so falls outside Chapter 79 entirely. Nearly every hognose in a Pennsylvania shop is lawful and the one in the field is not.

MI.quote: Reptiles and amphibians may not be bought, sold or offered for sale.
MI.note: The eastern hog-nosed snake is Michigan native and is not on the protected list, so it may be taken, but only on conditions. A fishing license is required, the limit is three a day and six in total across snakes, lizards and turtles combined, and the quoted sale ban means you cannot lawfully buy one in Michigan or sell the one you have. Personal collection is the only lawful route. The western hognose that dominates the pet trade is not a Michigan species at all, so it sits outside this order and is simply legal, which makes the answer depend entirely on which hognose is in the tank.

VT.quote: Squamata | Serpentes | Colubridae | All species of colubrids, except those listed in Appendix that require an importation and possession permit
VT.note: Heterodon appears nowhere on the Restricted list, so both the eastern and the western hognose are unrestricted.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Snake | Colubridae | Heterodon nasicus nasicus | Western Hognose Snake | III
NM.note: Group III, which is a permit with strings: the list defines the group as animals presenting minimal or manageable concerns that require specific provisions to be met before an importation permit issues. All three Heterodon on the list sit here, the western, eastern and Mexican hognose alike, so unlike most states the answer does not turn on which hognose you have. One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The hognose snake is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The four colubrids Arizona claws back are the brown tree snake, boomslang, keelback and twig snake, and Heterodon is not among them. One Arizona-specific caveat: this species occurs in the wild here, and taking one alive from the wild is a separate question governed by R12-4-404 and R12-4-405 and the take limits in Commission Order 43, which need a valid hunting licence. The clearance above is about keeping a captive-bred animal, not about collecting one. The Mexican hognose reaches southeastern Arizona.

DE.cite: Del. Code tit. 7, c. 7, with Del. Code tit. 3 § 7201
DE.note: The condition is which hognose. The eastern hognose is native to Delaware, so it is DNREC's and native reptiles are not available for private ownership, subject only to the captive-bred aberrant colour morph carve-out held under permit. The western hognose that dominates the pet trade is not a Delaware species, which makes it a non-native reptile needing an Individual permit from Agriculture instead. Neither route is simply open, but they are different routes.

CO.quote: Any captive-bred species from the genus Heterodon except the Eastern hog-nosed snake (Heterodon platirhinos), Lystrophis, or Leioheterodon (hognose snakes)
CO.note: Captive-bred western hognose is on Appendix B, needing documentation under § 703(B) but no licence, and CPW files Heterodon nasicus (captive bred) against exactly this line. Two things fall outside it. The eastern hognose is excluded by name. And a hognose taken from the wild in Colorado is not covered: CPW files that as legacy possession only, lawful if held on or before 1 May 2026 and reported by 30 July 2026, with no new wild capture allowed. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: THREATENED AMPHIBIANS AND REPTILES OF ILLINOIS ... Snakes ... Plains Hog-nosed Snake Heterodon nasicus
IL.note: The species the pet trade sells as the western hognose is Heterodon nasicus, and Illinois lists it as a threatened species. 520 ILCS 10/3 then makes it unlawful to possess any animal on the Illinois List unless otherwise authorized by law, with no captive-bred carve-out written into the statute, so a Department endangered or threatened species possession permit is the route, applied for through the Office of Resource Conservation, with a separate Herptile Endangered and Threatened Species Propagation Permit at $150 a year on top if the animal is to be bred or sold. The eastern hognose, Heterodon platirhinos, is the other Illinois native and is not listed, so it sits under the ordinary 4-per-species and 8-total cap instead. Which hognose it is decides the answer here, and the pet trade animal is the listed one. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. Both hognose species are Minnesota natives, so the wild-collection reading and the breeder-source reading point the same way. Neither is listed as endangered or threatened in Minnesota; the DNR's listed snakes are the eastern massasauga, the timber rattlesnake and the western ratsnake. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Hognose snake -- Colubridae -- Heterodon nasicus;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Oregon clears one hognose by species and no others. The western hognose, Heterodon nasicus, is the pet-trade animal and is named. The eastern hognose, H. platirhinos, is on no list at all, which under OAR 635-056-0130(1) means it may not be possessed. A rule written to a single binomial is one to read exactly. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: Eastern Hog-nosed Snake ... State Species of Special Concern
CT.note: Which hognose it is decides the answer, and the split runs the opposite way from Illinois. Connecticut's own eastern hog-nosed snake, Heterodon platirhinos, is a State Species of Special Concern, which makes it a Category Four Wild Animal needing a permit to import or possess. The western hognose, H. nasicus, is the animal the pet trade sells, is not a Connecticut species, and appears in none of the four categories, so it is unrestricted. Illinois lists the western and leaves the eastern alone; Connecticut does the reverse.

MD.quote: Notwithstanding Natural Resources Article, §4-902, Annotated Code of Maryland, a person without a reptile and amphibian permit may possess only one of each individual reptile or amphibian, live or dead, listed in Regulation .03B of this chapter. A person may not take wood turtles, spotted turtles, or diamond-backed terrapins, including their eggs, from the wild. ... All turtles shall have a carapace length of at least 4 inches.
MD.note: Which hognose it is decides the answer, and Maryland makes the split a matter of degree rather than of kind. The eastern hog-nosed snake, Heterodon platirhinos, is a Maryland native on the middle tier, so one per person with no permit. The western hognose, H. nasicus, is the animal the pet trade sells, is not on any of the three native lists, and is therefore outside the chapter entirely and unrestricted. Illinois and Connecticut each list one hognose and leave the other alone too, and no two of the three states pick the same one. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The hognose snake is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial. The point that decides every native reptile in Tennessee is the exception clause in Class II, which reads "native species, except those listed in other classes". A native nonpoisonous reptile IS listed in another class, at (3)(A), so it is excluded from Class II and lands in Class III with no permit. The supplier documentation requirement in § 70-4-401(b) follows Class I and Class II and does not reach it either. Both the eastern and the western hognose are nonvenomous, so which species it is makes no difference here. That is unusual: Illinois, Connecticut and Maryland all split the two, and no two of them split it the same way.

TX.quote: A person without a nongame or nongame dealer’s permit may: (A) possess six or fewer specimens of a species of nongame wildlife listed in §65.331(e) of this title, provided the person does not engage in commercial activity involving the nongame wildlife; and (B) possess 25 or fewer specimens of a species of nongame wildlife listed in §65.331(d) of this title, provided the person does not engage in commercial activity involving the nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Both Texas hognose species are on the § 65.331(d) list by name, the western Heterodon nasicus and the eastern H. platirhinos, so whichever one a keeper has, the answer is 25 without a permit and no commercial activity. The cap reaches captive-bred animals: § 65.325(a) says nongame wildlife "includes captive-bred nongame wildlife", so a pet shop receipt does not lift it. The western hognose is the ordinary pet-trade animal and is squarely native to Texas, so the captive-bred qualification is the one that matters here.

MA.quote: Snakes of the family Colubridae, as follows: ... Garter and Ribbon Snakes (Thamnophis spp.) ... Kingsnakes and Milk Snakes (Lampropeltis spp.) ... North American Ratsnakes (Pantherophis spp.) except the Black Ratsnake (Pantherophis alleghaniensis other than albinistic and leucistic individuals) which requires a permit ... Western Hognose Snake (Heterodon nasicus)
MA.note: Massachusetts answers the two hognose species differently, and the common name hides it. The colubrid list clears the Western Hognose Snake, Heterodon nasicus, by name and by name only, so the ordinary pet-trade hognose is exempt. The eastern hognose, Heterodon platirhinos, is a Massachusetts species of special concern on the 321 CMR 10.90 list, which makes it categorically non-exempt under 9.01(3)(c) and puts it in the permit tier that MassWildlife says is not issued for pets. Both animals are IUCN least concern, so this split comes entirely from the state list.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Both Nebraska hognose species are on the three-per-species list at § 001.03A4, the plains hognose Heterodon nasicus and the eastern hognose H. platirhinos. That is unusually even-handed: most states on this map treat the two differently, because the eastern is the one that tends to be listed. Nebraska caps them identically. The route that matters for a pet is § 001.03A2: an animal legally bought or consigned from outside Nebraska may be possessed without regard to numbers, provided the keeper can produce proof of lawful acquisition, a bill of sale or a consignment record. So the cap is on collecting, and the receipt is what lifts it.

NY.quote: "Small game" means black, gray and fox squirrels, European hares, varying hares, cottontail rabbits, native frogs, native salamanders, native turtles, native lizards, native snakes, coyotes, red fox (Vulpes vulpes) and gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus) except captive bred red fox or gray fox, raccoon, opossum, or weasel, skunk, bobcat, lynx, muskrat, mink, except mink born in captivity, fisher, otter, beaver, sable and marten but does not include coydogs. ... No person shall, at any time of the year, buy, sell, offer or expose for sale, transport, or have in his possession any fish protected by law, game, protected wildlife ... whether taken within the state or coming from without the state, except as permitted by the Fish and Wildlife Law.
NY.note: Caught twice over. The eastern hognose snake is on the § 3.3 native snake list with no open season, and it is separately listed as a species of special concern on DEC's Part 182 list, which is named directly in the definition of protected wildlife at ECL § 11-0103(6)(c). The western hognose, the ordinary pet-trade animal, is not a New York species, so the answer turns on which hognose a keeper actually has, and the state list only reaches one of them. The chain runs through a definition nobody expects. ECL § 11-0103(2)(c) puts "native frogs, native salamanders, native turtles, native lizards, native snakes" inside the definition of SMALL GAME, which makes them game, which makes them protected wildlife under § 11-0103(6)(c). § 11-0107(2) then bars possessing protected wildlife "whether taken within the state or coming from without the state, except as permitted by the Fish and Wildlife Law", so a captive-bred animal bought in another state is in the same position as one caught in a New York yard. And the only possession licence, § 11-0515, is issued for "propagation, banding, scientific or exhibition purposes", which is not a pet.

GA.cite: DNR Guide to Legal Pets; O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4(b)(1)
GA.quote: By Georgia Law, most native species of wildlife cannot be held without permits or licenses. These licenses are not issued for the purpose of holding native wildlife as pets. These restrictions apply to the various species of animal, regardless of the origin or morphology. ... The following list of species native to Georgia may not be held as a pet regardless of its origin or morphology.
GA.note: Georgia handles its own wildlife separately from the wild animal rule, and the sentence that matters is "These restrictions apply to the various species of animal, regardless of the origin or morphology." A captive-bred animal from an out-of-state breeder is in the same position as one caught in a Georgia yard, and a colour morph is too. Both Georgia hognose snakes, the eastern and the southern, is on DNR's list of native species that may not be held as a pet. Licences exist under O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4 and DNR says in terms that they "are not issued for the purpose of holding native wildlife as pets". The western hognose, the ordinary pet-trade animal, is not a Georgia species and is not on the list, so which hognose a keeper has decides this cell.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The one animal on this map that the Colubridae clause is plainly written for. It reaches "all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized", and the hognose is the textbook rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded colubrid whose bite produces local envenomation. The words "even if devenomized" show the clause is aimed at exactly this category rather than at front-fanged species, which the previous sentence already covers. The eastern hognose is also a New York species of special concern, so § 161.01(b)(ii) reaches it independently through the state's protected wildlife scheme. The western hognose, the ordinary pet-trade animal, escapes the state route and not the colubrid one. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: The two hognoses reach the permit from opposite directions. The eastern hognose, Heterodon platirhinos, is native to New Jersey and appears on the 4.17 nongame table as secure-stable, so it is a nongame species and 4.5 catches it. The western hognose, Heterodon nasicus, is not native, so it is an exotic reptile and 4.5 catches it too. Neither is on the closed exempt list at 4.4, whose only colubrids are the garter snake and the ribbon snake. For the native one there is the further point that taking it from the wild is separately illegal, so the permit has to sit on a captive-bred animal.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the hognose snake is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Neither Heterodon species appears on any Utah table, which is the point worth checking rather than assuming, because Utah does list a long run of native colubrids at Standard and Limited and a keeper could reasonably expect a hognose among them. The rear-fanged question does not arise either: R657-53-9(1)(a) reaches a venomous non-native squamate only where a bite "may cause substantial physical injury to humans ordinarily requiring medical treatment". The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

AL.quote: Snake, Southern Hognose Heterodon simus
AL.note: Which hognose decides this, and Alabama says so twice. 220-2-.92(1)(c) protects the southern hognose, Heterodon simus, by name, so possessing that species needs a scientific collection permit or a written permit from the Commissioner. The eastern hognose, H. platirhinos, is also an Alabama animal and is not on the list, and the western hognose, H. nasicus, is the pet trade species and is not native here at all. Both of those are unrestricted. The other half is a nice piece of drafting: 220-2-.26(1) bans venomous reptiles that have never naturally existed in the wild in Alabama and then writes an express exception, "except for hognose snakes (genus Heterodon)", which settles the rear-fanged argument that leaves this animal ambiguous in several other states.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: The hognose snake is native to Indiana, which is what decides it, and Indiana's native rule is unusual in reaching a purchased animal. 9-5-7(c) lists the eastern hog-nosed snake, Heterodon platirhinos, among the 99 taxa whose sale it governs, and 9-5-7(a) says the section applies "regardless of place of origin", so a captive-bred animal from an out-of-state breeder is caught by it just as a wild-caught one is. Selling, offering for sale or transporting for sale is barred; possessing is not, subject to 9-5-6(f)'s cap of four live animals of any one native species. Two exits exist. 9-5-7(f) exempts a captive-bred animal with albinistic, leucistic or xanthic colour morphology, on the same logic New Jersey uses for corn snake morphs, that a morph is visibly not a wild-caught animal. And 9-5-9 provides a reptile captive breeding licence under which sales are lawful. Which hognose matters. The eastern is the Indiana animal and is on the list; the western, Heterodon nasicus, is the pet trade species, is not native here, and is not on it. The rear-fanged question never arises, because 9-5-8 and 9-11-8(a)(4) reach a venomous reptile and Indiana has not treated a hognose as one.

OK.quote: No closed season. All reptiles except those listed in (3) and (5) of this section shall have a year-round season. (2) Bag limit. The bag limit is 6 per day or in possession for each species allowed in section (1) of this section.
OK.note: The hognose snake is an Oklahoma animal, which moves it out of the exemption at 800:25-25-3(c), since that clause is written for species "not indigenous to Oklahoma". What applies instead is the reptile and amphibian part at 800:25-7. Two provisions matter to a keeper. 7-7(2)(A) requires a resident or nonresident hunting licence of anyone "taking or attempting to take reptiles and amphibians or possessing reptiles or amphibians" that are land dwelling, which is a possession hook and not merely a collecting one. And 7-8 gives every reptile a year-round season except a closed list of twelve, with a limit of "6 per day or in possession for each species". Recorded as conditional on those two rather than as a permit, because there is no application and no discretion: a hunting licence is sold over the counter. 29 O.S. § 7-502(B)(4) separately exempts anyone possessing legally obtained wildlife "from a source other than the wild, as pets" from the statutory possession bar, which is why a captive-bred animal is not caught by the closed-season rule. Both the eastern and the plains hognose reach Oklahoma, so unlike most states the answer does not turn on which species you have. Neither is on the closed list at 7-8(5), and Oklahoma does not treat a rear-fanged colubrid as venomous anywhere in the part: the venomous species it does single out are the four rattlesnakes, which get their own March to June season and their own five-day permit.

DC.quote: Captive-bred species of common cage birds, including chickens
DC.note: Captive-bred is doing real work here, and every African grey legally sold in the United States is captive-bred because the Wild Bird Conservation Act has barred commercial import of wild-caught birds since 1992.

HI.note: Named by binomial on the conditionally approved list.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the entry at (14)(q), which is the single word "Parrots", sitting in a list that separately names shell parakeets, canaries, lovebirds, cockatiels, finches, myna birds and toucans. The African grey is a parrot on any reading. Nothing in the Florida rules distinguishes species by conservation status, so unlike Massachusetts the CITES Appendix I listing changes only where the bird can lawfully come from, not whether it can be kept.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian. No bird appears in it.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: The only bird needing an import permit is turkey of the genus Meleagris, and the pet trade exemption separately clears parrots.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: No bird prohibition exists in the chapter. The only bird provision is a seven dollar annual licence fee for species the board requires to be licensed.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No bird is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. Your county code is the operative layer.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: The permit-exempt list clears parrots, lovebirds, budgerigars, macaws and parakeets, excepting only the monk parakeet.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: No bird category appears in the guidance at all.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles. No bird appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: Nondomestic birds are handled by ARSD 12:68:13 rather than the mammal permit list here.

VA.quote: Psittaciformes   Psittacidae   Myiopsitta monachus   Monk parakeet*
VA.note: The only parrot on the permit table is the monk parakeet. No other psittacine appears, so the African grey needs no state permit.

LA.quote: This commission regulation prohibits importation and private possession, and otherwise regulates certain wild quadrupeds, big exotic cats, and non-human primates as provided herein.
LA.note: The quadruped regulation reaches mammals only. No bird is listed.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds (including ring-necked pheasants and gray partridge) native to the continental United States
MO.note: The bird half of Class I is limited to species native to the continental United States. Psittacus erithacus is African.

WY.quote: Live warm-blooded wildlife listed in this section... may be imported, possessed or transported without a permit... (b) Birds: (i) Cage and aviary birds.
WY.note: Chapter 10 defines cage and aviary birds as exotic captive-reared birds such as parrots which are adapted to live and breed in a cage or would not survive in the wild in the state. An African grey is squarely within that, so no permit and no veterinary certificate are required by the Department.

NH.quote: A permit to import wildlife shall not be required for any person to import wildlife designated as non-controlled... (6) The following birds: ... c. Parrots (Psittaciformes)
NH.note: The non-controlled list names the whole order, so every parrot is covered. New Hampshire readopted this rule in April 2026, which makes it one of the most recently confirmed entries in the matrix.

RI.quote: Psittacidae (Parrots and their allies) except for Myiopsitta monachus (Monk Parakeet), which requires a permit
RI.note: The parrot family is permit-free with a single carve-out for the monk parakeet, which is the pattern in most states that regulate parrots at all.

MT.quote: The following noncontrolled exotic wildlife may not be released or transplanted in the state but may be possessed or sold as pets in Montana without a permit: (a) tropical and subtropical birds in the order Passeriformes, including but not limited to birds in the families: ... (xi) Psittacidae (parrots)
MT.note: Noncontrolled, so no permit is needed. The drafting is odd, since parrots are Psittaciformes rather than Passeriformes, but the family is named outright and the list is expressly not exhaustive.

ID.quote: non-poultry birds
ID.note: The bird category is drawn by exclusion rather than by listing families, so every parrot is a conventional pet. Idaho does not carve out the monk parakeet the way most states do.

AK.quote: Parrot, parakeet, cockatiel, macaw, and other members of the Family Psittacidae   not prohibited by federal or international law
AK.note: Psittacidae is on the clean list, but Alaska attaches a qualifier no other state does: not prohibited by federal or international law. That matters here, because the African grey was moved to CITES Appendix I in 2017. Appendix I bars commercial international trade rather than domestic keeping, so a captive-bred bird already in the country is fine, but paperwork is worth having.

ME.quote: Order Psittaciformes*   All Species in Order Psittaciformes (Parrots)   Except for: Myiopsitta monachus; Cyanoliseus patagonus; Enicognathus leptorhynchus; Enicognathus ferrugineus; Family Strigopidae
ME.note: The whole parrot order is cleared, but the asterisk carries the footnote that removes anything on CITES Appendix I or listed by the IUCN as Endangered. The African grey is both: it moved to Appendix I on 2 January 2017 and was assessed Endangered in 2016, months before this list was published. So the one parrot most people think of is outside the clearance while a macaw is inside it.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Congo African Grey Parrot, Timneh African Grey Parrot (Psittacus erithacus, P. timneh)
AR.note: Both greys are named individually, including the Timneh, which was split off as its own species in 2012. Arkansas is the useful contrast with Maine here: same bird, same CITES Appendix I status, and Arkansas simply names it while Maine's footnote strips it out.

CA.quote: Family Psittacidae-Parrots, Parakeets: Myiopsitta monachus (Monk or Quaker parakeet) (D)
CA.note: The only parrot California restricts is the monk parakeet. Every other psittacine, the African grey included, is outside section 671.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Birds are outside Chapter 935 entirely.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: Birds fall outside both the statute and the deleterious exotic wildlife rule.

WI.note: Meets Wisconsin's unregulated pet bird definition: psittacine, non-native, not federally endangered and not migratory. Only the monk parakeet is carved back out, by NR 40. Out-of-state birds need a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Parrots - Family Psittacidae - All species not native to North America
UT.note: Utah clears the whole parrot family by one line, provided the species is not native to North America. Unlike Wisconsin and a number of other states, Utah draws no monk parakeet carve-out, so the Quaker sits in the same noncontrolled column as the African grey and the cockatoo.

PA.quote: All migratory birds as defined in 50 CFR by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service of the Department of the Interior, game birds and any other birds designated by the commission, including, but not limited to, grouse, partridge, pheasant, quail and wild turkey.
PA.note: The Game Code reaches a bird only if it is a wild bird, and that definition is a closed set of three: federally listed migratory birds, game birds, and any other birds the Commission designates. The African grey is none of them. The Commission has used its designation power on exactly one pet parrot, the monk parakeet at 58 Pa. Code § 137.1(a)(9), which shows it designates by name rather than by category. Parrots are not covered as a group.

MI.quote: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection is required for the import of exotic, circus and zoo animals, native wild animals, domestic rabbits, nonnative rodents, nonnative reptiles and amphibians, and non-poultry birds
MI.note: The African grey is named in no Michigan statute or order. The Large Carnivore Act covers cats and bears, the captive game permit covers native game, and the herp order covers reptiles and amphibians, so nothing reaches a pet parrot. The only requirement is the certificate of veterinary inspection for a non-poultry bird moved into the state.

NM.quote: Bird | Parrot | Psittacidae | Psittacus sp. | Parrots, African Greys | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Named at genus level.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (h) Parrots;
NV.note: Cleared by name, and absent from the three-species prohibited bird list. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: The following species within the family Phasianidae ... All species listed under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act listed under 50 CFR 10.13
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted bird list is a handful of quail, grouse and turkeys plus everything covered by the federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act. No psittacine appears, and the only parrot the state names anywhere is the thick-billed parrot, a native species. The African grey is neither, so no licence is required.

DE.quote: No person shall bring into this State, possess, sell or exhibit any live wild mammal or hybrid of a wild mammal or live reptile not native to or generally found in Delaware without first securing a permit under this chapter.
DE.note: The permit requirement names live wild mammals, hybrids of wild mammals and non-native reptiles, and stops there. Birds are absent from the operative text despite the chapter's title mentioning them, and the Department of Agriculture's own guidance states that all birds and fish are exempt from the permitting process. The African grey therefore needs nothing.

CO.quote: All Psitticine birds
CO.note: The unregulated wildlife list clears the parrots as a group, with the regulation's own misspelling of psittacine. Unregulated means no CPW licence is required, not that nothing applies: importation and health requirements still do. One parrot is carved out elsewhere and it is not this one. The monk parakeet sits on the Chapter W-0 prohibited list, and CPW's bird list restates this line as "All Psitticine birds (except Monk Parakeet/Quaker Parrot)". CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: This Act shall apply only to the wild birds and parts of wild birds (including, but not limited to, their nests and eggs), and wild mammals and parts of wild mammals, which shall include their green hides, in the State of Illinois, or which may be brought into the State.
IL.note: The Wildlife Code then lists the protected birds family by family, running from loons through finches and covering essentially the native and migratory avifauna. Psittacidae is not among them, so no parrot is a protected species in Illinois. The Part 805 injurious bird list is four species long, the pink starling, the dioch, the Java sparrow and the red-whiskered bulbul, and the African grey is not one of them. Federal CITES Appendix I paperwork is the constraint that actually bites on this species, and it is not a state matter. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: "Protected wild animals" means big game, small game, game fish, native rough fish, minnows, leeches, chubs, frogs, turtles, clams, mussels, wolf, mourning doves, bats, snakes, salamanders, lizards, any animal species listed as endangered, threatened, or of special concern in Minnesota Rules, chapter 6134, and wild animals that are protected by a restriction in the time or manner of taking, other than a restriction in the use of artificial lights, poison, or motor vehicles.
MN.note: The protected list is worth reading in full for Minnesota, because it names five herptile categories and then almost nothing among birds beyond game birds and mourning doves. The African grey falls outside it, so § 97A.501's possession bar does not apply. No parrot appears on either invasive species list. Federal CITES Appendix I paperwork is the live constraint for this species and is not a Minnesota matter.

OR.quote: Pursuant to the definition of "wildlife," the following species are not subject to these rules because they are not "wild" ... (28) Parrots, Parakeets, Lories, and Cockatoos — Psittaciforme (All species).
OR.note: The whole order Psittaciformes is declared not wild, so the African grey is outside the wildlife rules entirely. Federal CITES Appendix I paperwork is the live constraint on this species and is not an Oregon matter. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No parrot is regulated here except the monk parakeet. Federal CITES Appendix I paperwork is the live constraint on this species and is not a Connecticut matter.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. The statute reaches no bird, and the African grey is not native Maryland wildlife. Federal CITES Appendix I paperwork is the live constraint on this species and is not a Maryland matter. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Avian species not otherwise listed, excluding North American game birds, ostriches and cassowary
TN.note: Covered by the avian catch-all. Federal CITES Appendix I paperwork is the live constraint on this species and is not a Tennessee matter.

TX.quote: (a) Except as provided by this code, no person may: (1) catch, kill, injure, pursue, or possess, dead or alive, or purchase, sell, expose for sale, transport, ship, or receive or deliver for transportation, a bird that is not a game bird ... (d) Canaries, parrots, and other exotic nongame birds may be sold, purchased, and kept as domestic pets.
TX.note: Psittacus erithacus is a parrot, which subsection (d) clears by name for sale, purchase and keeping. The state layer is the easy half here. The federal Wild Bird Conservation Act bars commercial import of wild-caught birds and CITES Appendix I has covered this species since 2017, so a lawfully sold African grey in Texas is a captive-bred one with paperwork, and that paperwork is what a buyer should be checking rather than a state list.

MA.quote: List of Birds. (a) The following groups of birds are prohibited without a permit: 1. Species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3). 2. Migratory birds listed in the Code of Federal Regulations, 50 CFR 10.13. 3. Any other bird native to the United States and Canada. (b) Except for species listed in 321 CMR 9.01(11)(a), the birds or groups of birds may be kept without a permit: ... 6. Psittacidae (parrots and their allies)
MA.note: The family exemption for Psittacidae is expressly subject to 9.01(11)(a), and clause 1 pulls out anything categorically non-exempt under 9.01(3). Psittacus erithacus is assessed by the IUCN as endangered, so it falls inside 9.01(3)(b) and outside the parrot clearance.
