This is the clearest illustration on this map of why the categorical bar has to be read before the group listing: on the group listing alone an African grey is an ordinary pet parrot in Massachusetts, and it is not. MassWildlife's own guidance is blunt about what that means in practice: permits for non-exempt wildlife "are issued only for certain scientific, educational, commercial, or other specific reasons" and "You will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet." The statute is less absolute, since § 23 contemplates "an individual license for an animal that is not on the special exemption list" and even sets a preference for captive-bred animals where wild depletion is an issue, so the licence exists on paper and the agency says it will not grant one for a pet.

NE.quote: Cage and Aviary Birds - Means those captive-reared birds, not native to Nebraska, such as parrots, exotic finches, and canaries, which are adapted to live and breed in a cage. For purposes of this regulation, the monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus) is not a cage and aviary bird.
NE.note: Cleared by the last line of the importation list, "All Cage and Aviary Birds", which the chapter defines as captive-reared birds not native to Nebraska such as parrots, exotic finches and canaries. The African grey is squarely inside that. The definition also carries the state's one carve-out, for the monk parakeet, so the sentence that clears this bird is the same sentence that bans that one. Nebraska adds nothing to the federal position, so the constraint that actually bites is CITES Appendix I and the Wild Bird Conservation Act, which together mean a lawfully sold bird is captive-bred with paperwork.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the African grey is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The federal layer is the operative one for this species: CITES Appendix I and the Wild Bird Conservation Act mean a lawfully sold bird is captive-bred with paperwork.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the African grey is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it. The bird section of the licence rule is long and covers raptors, corvids, owls, weavers and starlings, and no psittacine other than the prohibited monk parakeet.

NYC.quote: In addition to domesticated dogs and cats, an animal may be kept, possessed, harbored or sold in the City of New York provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law, including federal, state and local laws regulating domestic animals and livestock or protecting wildlife and endangered species. Such animals include, but are not limited to, gerbil, hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and fowl or small birds such as parakeet, parrot, canary and finch.
NYC.note: A parrot, and named as a permitted category in § 161.01(c). The constraint on this species is federal rather than municipal: CITES Appendix I and the Wild Bird Conservation Act. § 161.01(c) is the article's short affirmative list, and it is written as examples rather than as a closed set: "an animal may be kept ... provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law", followed by gerbil, hamster, guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and small birds. So the question in New York City is always whether something else in § 161.01(b) reaches the animal.

NJ.quote: Birds: ... vi. African gray parrot - Psittacus erithacus; ... NJ Fish & Wildlife classifies any animal as endangered when it is listed on any relevant State or Federal endangered species list, including but not limited to the US Fish and Wildlife Service Endangered Species List, IUCN Red List, and the New Jersey Endangered Species List.
NJ.note: Two documents the Division publishes point opposite ways at this one bird. The 4.3 permit list names the African gray parrot, Psittacus erithacus, as a species a permit may be issued for, which would make it an ordinary permit animal. The restricted species notice then says the Division classifies any animal as endangered when it appears on the IUCN Red List, and Psittacus erithacus has been Endangered there since the 2016 assessment, which would put it under the notice's rule that endangered species may not be kept as pets for any reason. The 4.3 list is old enough to still call macaws permit species "except endangered forms", so the tension looks like a list that was never revisited rather than a deliberate exception. Recorded as unresolved because a keeper cannot tell from the published documents which one the permits office applies.

AL.quote: All nongame birds are protected under the provisions of this regulation except crows, and non-native species including starlings, house sparrows, Eurasian collared doves, rock pigeons.
AL.note: Alabama protects birds by a blanket rather than a list, and the blanket is written so that it misses every pet parrot. 220-2-.92(1)(d) says all nongame birds are protected "except crows, and non-native species including starlings, house sparrows, Eurasian collared doves, rock pigeons". The four named non-natives are examples of the exception, not its limit, so an African grey is outside the protection as a non-native bird. On the other side, 220-2-.26(1) names no bird species at all and reaches birds only through the Lacey Act injurious list, which contains no psittacine. The species' IUCN Endangered listing has no purchase in Alabama, which reads the federal injurious list rather than any conservation list.

IN.quote: A permit is required under this rule for the following Class III wild animals: (1) Wolves that are purebred. (2) Bears (all species). (3) Wild cats (all species), except feral cats and cats listed in section 7 of this rule. (4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.
IN.note: Indiana's permit rule is a closed list of three classes and no bird appears in any of them. Class I is the cottontail and three squirrels, Class II is the state's furbearers plus a named run of small wild cats, and Class III is purebred wolves, bears, wild cats, venomous reptiles and crocodilians at least five feet long. 312 IAC 9-4 governs birds and is written about native and migratory species rather than the pet trade. The African grey's IUCN Endangered listing has no purchase here, since Indiana's rules turn on its own class lists and on federal endangered listings rather than on the IUCN one.

OK.quote: The following list of birds shall be exempt from import and export requirements ... (1) Cockatoos, cockatiels, canaries, macaws and exotic finches. (2) Psittacine birds (parrots, parakeets and budgerigars).
OK.note: Oklahoma names the pet birds twice over. 800:25-25-3(b)(1) exempts "Cockatoos, cockatiels, canaries, macaws and exotic finches" and (b)(2) then exempts "Psittacine birds (parrots, parakeets and budgerigars)" as a group, which takes Psittacus erithacus. The exemption from import and export requirements is qualified for birds brought in from outside the United States, which need documentation, and the rule then says that once such a bird reaches its destination in Oklahoma it "shall be considered a domesticated species" and is exempt from breeder licence requirements. The IUCN Endangered listing that complicates this species in Massachusetts and New Jersey has no purchase here, because Oklahoma's bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A)(2) reaches endangered or threatened species as designated under state and federal law rather than by the IUCN.

VT.cite: Vermont Domestic Species List, August 2010; Regulation 881; 10 V.S.A. § 4709
VT.quote: Birds Psittaciformes Psittacidae Agapornis personatus Masked lovebird Captive Bred Only ... Melopsittacus undulatus Budgerigar Captive Bred Only ... Psittacula eupatria Alexandrine parakeet-blue form Captive Bred Only
VT.note: Vermont is an inverted-list state and the African grey falls through all three of its lists. 10 V.S.A. § 4709 bars bringing in, transporting or possessing any live wild bird or animal without authorisation, and the Unrestricted Wild Animal List closes the loop by saying a species found on none of the Restricted, Unrestricted or Domestic lists is considered Restricted. the African grey is on none of them: the Unrestricted list's birds are the rock dove, the European buzzard, a run of estrildid finches and the canary, with no psittacine at all, and the Domestic Species List's psittacine section is a closed list of about thirty species that names the budgerigar, the cockatiel, the lovebirds, the rosellas, the conures and Psittacula, and stops. What makes Restricted a ban rather than paperwork is Regulation 881: "the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for the keeping or possession of any wild animal in captivity, except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes". There is no pet category to apply under. The Domestic list was published in August 2010, six years before the IUCN moved Psittacus erithacus to Endangered, so its absence is not a conservation judgment. It is one of the most commonly kept parrots in the country and Vermont has never listed it.

DC.quote: a person shall not import into the District, possess... any living member of the animal kingdom, including those born or raised in captivity, except the following
DC.note: No invertebrate category exists in the permitted list, so every millipede, spider and scorpion is outside it. DC bans by omission rather than by name.

RI.quote: Nothing in this Part shall prohibit any person from possession of exotic animals or native animals of the class Insecta unless the animals of that class appear on the list of prohibited insects
RI.note: The blanket invertebrate exemption is written for the class Insecta. A millipede is a myriapod, so on the literal wording it stays inside the definition of exotic animal and needs a permit, exactly like the tarantula and the scorpion.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian. No invertebrate appears in it.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: The permit provision at § 50-16-20 lists furbearers, cervids, pigs, peccaries, bovids, coyote, bear and turkey. No invertebrate is in it, and Chapter 47-2 covers only big cats, bears and great apes.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: No invertebrate appears anywhere in the chapter.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No invertebrate is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. Counties may regulate animals dangerous to persons or property under § 153A-131.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: On neither Kentucky list, which are drawn around vertebrates and a few named pests.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: No invertebrate appears in the categories the board is directed to consider.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: Absent from the permit table, which covers vertebrates.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles. No invertebrate appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state
LA.note: No invertebrate appears in either of Louisiana's exotic animal rules.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds... and those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri.
MO.note: No invertebrate appears in any of the three wildlife classes.

HI.quote: Any animal that is not on the lists of conditionally approved, restricted, or prohibited animals shall be prohibited until the board's review and determination for placement on one of these lists
HI.note: No myriapod appears on any Hawaii list, so the default prohibition applies. Hawaii's concern with invertebrates is unusually close, given what introduced ones have already done to the islands.

WY.quote: "Cold-Blooded Wildlife" means all fish, amphibians, reptiles, mollusks, crustaceans...
WY.note: A myriapod is outside both chapters. Wyoming's silence here is structural rather than an oversight: the Game and Fish Commission's authority runs to wildlife as Title 23 defines it.

NH.quote: A permit to import wildlife shall be required for all species, including hybrids, designated as controlled as cited in Table 800.01.
NH.note: The prohibited invertebrate list is entirely aquatic and the controlled table has no invertebrate entries, so a millipede is unregulated here despite the broad definition of wildlife.

MT.quote: A person may not import into the state, possess, or sell any exotic wildlife unless: (a) the importation, possession, or sale of the exotic wildlife is allowed by law or commission rule
MT.note: Montana defines wildlife to end with the phrase or other wild animal, which reaches an invertebrate, and it runs a white list rather than a black list. The statutory noncontrolled list has no myriapod, and the commission's rule at ARM 12.6.2205 clears two scorpions and one hermit crab and nothing else. Absence is the answer here, and the answer is no.

ID.quote: No person may import into Idaho... possess or otherwise hold in captivity... any live wildlife, except those animals exempted by Idaho Code or these rules, without a corresponding... captive possession... license/permit from the Department.
ID.note: A millipede is animal life and is not on the conventional pets list, so the same literal reading applies. Idaho's deleterious exotic animal rules at IDAPA 02.04.27 do not mention myriapods either, so nothing prohibits one outright.

AK.quote: "game" means any species of bird, reptile, and mammal, including a feral domestic animal, found or introduced in the state, except domestic birds and mammals
AK.note: A myriapod is not game and needs no permit from Fish and Game.

ME.quote: Diplopoda (Millipedes) ... Spirostreptus gigas   Giant African Millipede
ME.note: Maine gives millipedes their own class section and names the giant African millipede twice, under Spirostreptus gigas and Mardonius parilis acuticonus. The species usually sold under that name today is Archispirostreptus gigas, which is the same animal under a later genus.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: No myriapod is named, and the list's scope is birds, mammals, reptiles and snakes, so nothing here settles it.

CA.quote: (8) Class Crustacea   Crustaceans ... (9) Class Gastropoda   Slugs, Snails ... (10) Class Bivalvia   Bivalves
CA.note: No myriapod is restricted. Note that agricultural inspection at the state border is a separate regime from Fish and Wildlife's restricted species list.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Outside Chapter 935 entirely.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: Not reached by RCW 16.30 or by the deleterious exotic wildlife rule.

WI.cite: Wis. Admin. Code ch. NR 40; Wis. Stat. § 169.04(4)(b)
WI.note: No invertebrate kept as a pet appears on NR 40, whose terrestrial invertebrate entries are forest and soil pests such as the emerald ash borer and jumping worm. Non-native species are outside captive wildlife licensing.

PA.quote: Wild birds, wild mammals and facsimiles thereof, regardless of classification, whether protected or unprotected, including any part, product, egg or offspring thereof, or the dead body or parts thereof (excluding fossils), whether or not included in a manufactured product or in a processed food product.
PA.note: The giant African millipede is neither a bird nor a mammal, so it is not wildlife and the Game Commission has no authority over it. The Fish and Boat Commission's Chapter 79 covers reptiles and amphibians. Pennsylvania's two animal agencies divide the field between them and a terrestrial invertebrate falls in the gap, so no state possession rule applies.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The giant African millipede is not a reptile or amphibian, so the herp order does not reach it, and it is not a cat, a bear or native game, so neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the captive game permit reaches it either. Michigan regulates terrestrial invertebrates through its invasive species list rather than any pet law, and no common pet invertebrate is on it.

VT.quote: All species of Invertebrates, except those listed in Appendix that require an importation and possession permit. Note: Importation of any invertebrate species also requires compliance with USDA regulations.
VT.note: The giant African millipede is covered by the blanket invertebrate entry, and the Restricted list claws back no terrestrial invertebrate at all. The USDA condition attaches to importing rather than to keeping.

NM.cite: Director's Species Importation List, 2023, and 19.35.7 NMAC
NM.quote: Any species of live non-domesticated animal not currently on the species importation list will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.
NM.note: The giant African millipede is not on the Director's list, and neither is any other terrestrial invertebrate: the roughly 1,300 rows are mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish. Read literally the default clause would designate it group IV and bar it, since it is a live non-domesticated animal. Read in context that looks wrong, because the rule is titled importation of live non-domesticated animals, birds and fish, its scope speaks of wildlife species, and its machinery is veterinary inspection certificates and disease testing built for vertebrates. The regulation never uses the word invertebrate. Recorded unclear rather than banned, because the definition arguably reaches the animal and plainly was not written with it in mind.

NV.quote: "Wildlife" means any wild mammal, wild bird, fish, reptile, amphibian, mollusk or crustacean found naturally in a wild state
NV.note: The giant African millipede is an arthropod, and Nevada's definition of wildlife lists mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks and crustaceans and stops there. Insects and arachnids are outside the Department of Wildlife's authority altogether, so neither the prohibited list nor the importation rule reaches one. A cleaner answer than New Mexico gives, where the same animals fall into a default clause written for vertebrates. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: "Wildlife" means all wild mammals, wild birds and the nests or eggs thereof, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans and fish, including their eggs or spawn.
AZ.note: The giant African millipede is an arthropod, and Arizona's definition of wildlife runs to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans and fish. Insects and arachnids are not in it, so Title 17 and the restricted live wildlife rule made under it do not reach one at all. Arizona and Nevada answer this the same clean way; New Mexico does not, which is why the same animals sit unclear there.

DE.quote: No person shall bring into this State, possess, sell or exhibit any live wild mammal or hybrid of a wild mammal or live reptile not native to or generally found in Delaware without first securing a permit under this chapter.
DE.note: The permit requirement reaches live wild mammals, hybrids of wild mammals and non-native reptiles only. The giant African millipede is an arthropod and falls outside the chapter entirely, as it does outside the exotic animal regulations made under it.

CO.quote: "Wildlife" means wild vertebrates, mollusks, and crustaceans, whether alive or dead, including any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof, that exist as a species in a natural wild state in their place of origin, presently or historically
CO.note: The giant African millipede is a myriapod, and Colorado's statutory definition of wildlife runs to wild vertebrates, mollusks and crustaceans and stops there. Everything CPW does about private possession, the licensing scheme in Chapter W-11, the prohibited list in Chapter W-0 and the new herpetofauna chapter, is built on that definition, so none of it reaches this animal. CPW's own species lists are divided into birds, mammals, herpetofauna and fish and marine animals, with no terrestrial invertebrate category at all, which is the same gap seen from the other side. Arizona and Nevada answer this the same clean way; New Mexico does not, which is why the same animals sit unclear there.

IL.quote: This Act shall apply only to the wild birds and parts of wild birds (including, but not limited to, their nests and eggs), and wild mammals and parts of wild mammals, which shall include their green hides, in the State of Illinois, or which may be brought into the State.
IL.note: The giant African millipede is a myriapod, and Illinois divides its animal law up in a way that leaves it out of every piece. The Wildlife Code says in its own words that it applies only to wild birds and wild mammals. The Herptiles-Herps Act covers reptiles and amphibians. The Fish and Aquatic Life Code covers aquatic life. The injurious species list at 17 Ill. Adm. Code 805 has a category for invertebrates, and it is headed "Fish, Mollusks and Aquatic Invertebrates". A terrestrial arthropod falls in the gap, the same way it does in Pennsylvania, so no state possession rule applies. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: "Wild animals" means all creatures, whether dead or alive, not human, wild by nature, endowed with sensation and power of voluntary motion, and includes mammals, birds, fish, amphibians, reptiles, crustaceans, and mollusks.
MN.note: The giant African millipede is a myriapod, and Minnesota's definition of wild animals lists seven groups, of which the only invertebrates are crustaceans and mollusks. That places it outside chapter 97A altogether, including the protected wild animal list and the possession bar built on it. The invasive species rules stop in the same place: the invertebrates designated under Minn. R. 6216.0250 are aquatic snails, rusty crayfish and the spiny waterflea. Minnesota is unusual in that its wild animal definition is broad enough to catch a ball python and still narrow enough to miss a tarantula.

OR.quote: Invertebrate species listed as approved may be imported, possessed, sold, purchased, exchanged, transported, or released in Oregon without a permit from the Department. This applies only to stock collected within the continental United States. ... Giant African millipede, Archispirostreptus gigas (education, pet). ... Live invertebrates not on the list of approved invertebrates in any life stage may not be imported, possessed, sold, purchased, exchanged, transported, or released in the state unless a permit is first obtained from the Department.
OR.note: Oregon runs two closed lists, and this animal is on the second one. ORS 496.004(19) defines wildlife as fish, shellfish, amphibians, reptiles, feral swine, wild birds and wild mammals, so a terrestrial arthropod is outside the Fish and Wildlife rules entirely; the Department of Agriculture picks it up instead under its plant pest authority. Named to the species and marked for pet use, alongside five other millipedes. Oregon is one of the few states that answers this animal by name in either direction. The condition is a real one and easy to miss: the clearance applies only to stock collected within the continental United States, so an animal imported from abroad needs a Department permit even though the species is approved. Nothing on this list is unregulated; an invertebrate absent from it may not be possessed at all without a permit. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. The giant African millipede appears in none of them. This one is worth stating carefully, because Connecticut is unusual in that its definition of wild animal does reach invertebrates, and the section is titled importation, possession or liberation of wild birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates. So the answer here is not the jurisdictional gap that clears the same animal in Arizona, Nevada and Pennsylvania; Connecticut has the authority and has simply not used it against any terrestrial arthropod. The only invertebrates that could be caught are ones on the state endangered, threatened and special concern list, which is Connecticut's own beetles, dragonflies and mussels.

MD.quote: "Wildlife" means, except as provided in § 10-2A-01 of this title, every living creature, not human, wild by nature, endowed with sensation and power of voluntary motion. (2) "Wildlife" includes mammals, birds, amphibians, and reptiles which spend a majority of their life cycle on land
MD.note: The giant African millipede is worth reading carefully in Maryland, because the definition is broad rather than narrow. Unlike Arizona, Nevada and Oregon, whose wildlife definitions list vertebrate groups and stop, Maryland's opening words are "every living creature, not human, wild by nature", with the vertebrate list following as an inclusion rather than a limit. What saves the answer is the operative section rather than the definition: § 10-902 attaches its permit only to wildlife native to Maryland, and this species is not. Section 10-903 gives the Secretary a separate power to restrict non-native wildlife by regulation, and Maryland has used it for nonnative aquatic organisms at COMAR 08.02.19, a list of fish, crustaceans, molluscs and two plants, and for nothing terrestrial. Crim. Law § 10-621 reaches no invertebrate either. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: "Wildlife" means wild vertebrates, mollusks, crustaceans, and fish
TN.note: The giant African millipede is a myriapod, and Tennessee's definition of wildlife runs to wild vertebrates, mollusks, crustaceans and fish. Section 70-4-403 classifies "live wildlife", so the five classes never reach a terrestrial arthropod at all, and neither does the possession prohibition in § 70-4-401(a), which is written about wildlife. Arizona, Nevada and Colorado draw the line in almost the same words. It matters less here than in a closed-list state, since Tennessee's catch-all would have put the animal in the no-permit class in any event.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Texas regulates nongame wildlife through 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O, and the rule defines its own subject as "species of vertebrate wildlife". That is narrower than the statute it was written under: Parks & Wild. Code § 67.001 defines nongame as "those species of vertebrate and invertebrate wildlife indigenous to Texas". The department had the power to reach invertebrates and did not use it, so Archispirostreptus gigas sits outside the scheme entirely. The dangerous wild animal list is mammals only, and 31 TAC Chapter 57 Subchapter A, the harmful exotic species rule, covers fish, shellfish and aquatic plants and no terrestrial arthropod. The federal layer is the one to check for this animal: giant African millipedes are restricted at the border by USDA APHIS as a plant pest, which is a separate question from Texas law.

MA.quote: Species means an individual or individuals of any distinct non-domestic vertebrate animal population whose members interbreed when mature or are self-perpetuating through the production of viable offspring and can include any subspecies or variety of vertebrate animal.
MA.note: Massachusetts is a closed-list state, so the question worth asking first is whether the list applies at all, and for the giant African millipede it does not. M.G.L. c. 131, § 23 reaches "fish, birds, mammals, reptiles, or amphibians", and 321 CMR 9.01(2) defines the species the exemption list is made of as vertebrate populations. A terrestrial arthropod is outside the licensing scheme entirely rather than unlisted within it, which is a different answer from the one the closed list gives a mammal nobody put on it.

NE.quote: Wildlife means any member of any nondomesticated species of the animal kingdom, whether reared in captivity or not, including any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate and includes any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof or the dead body or parts thereof.
NE.note: Nebraska defines wildlife broadly enough to include the giant African millipede, since § 37-247 reaches "any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate". What it does not do is regulate one. The captivity prohibition at § 37-477(1) and at 166 NAC 8 § 001.01B is written about wild birds, wild mammals, nongame species in need of conservation and listed species, none of which is an arthropod; 166 NAC 10 covers only reptiles and amphibians; and the importation list at § 001.08A contains nothing but mammals and birds. The one loose end is that the list is headed "the following wildlife may be imported" and wildlife on the statutory definition includes arthropods, so a very literal reading of that heading would bar importing a tarantula. Nothing in the chapter turns that heading into a prohibition, and every operative sentence in it is about birds and mammals. The restriction that does exist for this animal is federal: USDA APHIS treats it as a plant pest at the border.

FL.quote: It is unlawful to introduce, multiply, possess, move, or release any arthropod, plant pest, biological control agent, noxious weed, or invasive plant regulated by the Department or the USDA except under permit issued by the Department unless a federal permit, PPQ 526, has been issued by the USDA with concurrence by the Department. No permit shall be issued nor concurrence with a federal permit, PPQ 526 made unless the Department has determined that the arthropod, plant pest, biological control agent, noxious weed, or invasive plant can be contained to prevent escape into the environment or that it will not pose a threat to agriculture, beneficial organisms, or the environment or become a public nuisance.
FL.note: Florida answers this animal through its agriculture department, not FWC, and the wildlife chapters give no hint of it. 5B-57.004(1) makes it unlawful to possess any arthropod "regulated by the Department or the USDA" without a permit from the Division of Plant Industry, unless a federal PPQ 526 has already issued with the Department's concurrence. Archispirostreptus gigas moves interstate under exactly that federal permit, which is what brings it inside the sentence. The permit standard is containment: the Department must find the animal can be contained to prevent escape into the environment, which in practice means secure enclosure rather than a fee. Nothing in Chapter 68-5 or Chapter 68A-6 names it, so an entry resting on those chapters alone would read this as unrestricted.

NY.quote: Prohibited invasive species cannot be knowingly possessed with the intent to sell, import, purchase, transport or introduce. In addition, no person shall sell, import, purchase, transport, introduce or propagate prohibited invasive species. Regulated invasive species, on the other hand, are species which cannot be knowingly introduced into a free-living state, or introduced by a means that one should have known would lead to such an introduction, although such species shall be legal to possess, sell, buy, propagate and transport.
NY.note: New York has two ways to reach an invertebrate and neither takes in the giant African millipede. ECL § 11-0103(6)(a) defines wildlife as "wild game and all other animal life existing in a wild state, except fish, shellfish and crustacea", which is wide enough to include arthropods, but the closed wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses of vertebrates and Crocodylia and the dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 names none. The other route is Part 575, whose own definition of animal expressly includes "arthropods, insects, and their eggs, larvae or young", and whose invertebrate entries are the zebra mussel, the Asian longhorned beetle and their kind. Nothing on either list is a pet arthropod. The live constraint on this animal is a federal USDA APHIS plant pest permit rather than anything New York does.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are considered inherently dangerous to human beings and pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4 are subject to licensing and liability insurance requirements. (a) Mammals: ... 2. Order Carnivora: (i) Family Canidae: Genera Canis, Chrysocyon, Cuon, and Lycaon (wolves, jackals, dingos, etc.) - All species ...; (ii) Family Felidae (cats) - All species; (iii) Family Hyaenidae (hyenas) - All species; ...
GA.note: Georgia regulates invertebrates in three places and none of them reaches the giant African millipede. The prohibited list at .03(1)(d) covers dreissenid mussels, giant African land snails and the marbled crayfish. The inherently dangerous list at .04(1)(d) is scorpions only, and it is species-specific: the fattail, bark and burrowing thicktail genera, the deathstalker, and one Scorpionidae species, Opistophthalmus glabrifons. The licence list at .05(1)(f) is molluscs, crayfishes and shrimps. Every entry across all three is either aquatic or venomous. The federal USDA APHIS plant pest permit is the live constraint on this animal.

NYC.quote: No person shall sell or give to another person, possess, harbor, keep, or yard wild or other animals identified in this section ... other than in: (i) a zoological park or aquarium ...; or (ii) a laboratory ...; or (iii) a veterinary hospital ...; or (iv) a temporary exhibit, performance or display that has been issued a permit by the Commissioner. ... For the purposes of this Code, a wild animal is deemed to be any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings and all such animals are hereby prohibited ... Such animals shall also include: (i) any animals specified by the Commissioner in regulations ...; (ii) any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule; and (iii) any of the following animals:
NYC.note: The article reaches invertebrates in two clauses and both turn on venom. Clause (12) is "All venomous insects", with bees other than non-aggressive honey bees, hornets and wasps as its examples. Clause (13) is "Arachnida and Chilopoda: All venomous spiders ...; scorpion; all venomous arthropods including, but not limited to, centipede". The giant African millipede is neither venomous nor a chilopod, so neither clause applies. The distinction that saves it is a taxonomic one the Code happens to get right: centipedes are Chilopoda and venomous, millipedes are Diplopoda and defend themselves with benzoquinone secretions rather than venom. The live constraint on this animal is the federal USDA plant pest permit. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: "Nongame species" means any wildlife for which a legal hunting or trapping season has not been established in New Jersey or which has not been classified as an endangered species by statute or regulation of this State.
NJ.note: The same invertebrate gap as the tarantula: 4.5 reaches "nongame species", 4.1 defines that as any wildlife without a hunting season, and the enabling act's definition of wildlife ends in "or other wild animal", while the possession statute at N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3(j) covers only vertebrates plus molluscs and crustaceans and no Division list names an invertebrate. Archispirostreptus gigas carries a separate federal problem regardless of how New Jersey reads its own rule, since USDA APHIS treats non-native millipedes as regulated organisms requiring a PPQ 526 permit to move interstate, which is the restriction that actually bites on this species in most states.

UT.quote: "Wildlife" means: (a) crustaceans, including brine shrimp and crayfish; (b) mollusks; and (c) vertebrate animals living in nature, except feral animals.
UT.note: Utah answers the invertebrates at the level of the statute rather than the rule, and it answers them cleanly. Utah Code 23A-1-101(65) defines wildlife as crustaceans, molluscs, and "vertebrate animals living in nature, except feral animals". A millipede is a myriapod, and a myriapod is none of the three, so the Division of Wildlife Resources has no authority over it, and its rules divide the same way: R657-53 reaches Amphibia and Reptilia, R657-3b birds and mammals, R657-3c aquatic animals. There is a trap in R657-3a worth naming, because reading it alone gives the wrong answer. Its own definition of "Animal" carries no class limit, and 3a-2(20)(b) says a prohibited species "also means a species or subspecies that has not gone through the division's species classification process", which on its face would make every unclassified arthropod prohibited. It does not, because 3a-1(1) makes the rule under Title 23A and the rule cannot reach further than the code's definition of wildlife does. The restriction that actually bites on this species is federal rather than Utah's: USDA APHIS treats non-native millipedes as regulated organisms, so moving one across state lines needs a PPQ 526 permit whatever Utah says.

AL.quote: It shall be unlawful to take, capture, kill, or attempt to take, capture or kill; possess, sell, trade for anything of monetary value, or offer to sell or trade for anything of monetary value the following invertebrate species (or any parts or reproductive products of such species) without a scientific collection permit or written permit from the Commissioner, Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, which shall specifically state what the permittee may do with regard to said species:
AL.note: Not on the protected native invertebrate list at 220-2-.98 and not on the prohibited list at 220-2-.26, so Alabama has nothing to say about it. The restriction that does reach this species is federal: USDA APHIS treats non-native millipedes as regulated organisms, so moving one across a state line needs a PPQ 526 permit whatever Alabama says. Alabama's own arthropod quarantines sit with the Department of Agriculture and Industries and are aimed at named crop pests rather than at possession.

IN.quote: Any invertebrate not identified in this rule is an exempted wild animal.
IN.note: Indiana answers this in one sentence, which no other state on this map does. 312 IAC 9-9 governs invertebrates in five short sections, covering crayfish, mussels and a list of endangered mussels and beetles, and 9-9-5 then says "any invertebrate not identified in this rule is an exempted wild animal". 312 IAC 9-1-6 defines an exempted wild animal as one "which is unprotected and may be taken or possessed at any time". A millipede is not identified in the rule, so it is expressly unprotected rather than merely unmentioned. The live restriction on this species is federal rather than Indiana's: USDA APHIS treats non-native millipedes as regulated organisms, so moving one across a state line needs a PPQ 526 permit.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided by law, no person may possess: 1. Any wildlife or parts thereof during the closed season for that particular wildlife species; 2. Any endangered or threatened species or parts thereof at any time; or 3. Any native bear or native cat that will grow to reach the weight of fifty (50) pounds or more. B. Persons exempt from provisions of paragraphs 1 and 2 of subsection A of this section are: ... 4. Persons possessing legally obtained wildlife, from a source other than the wild, as pets or for the purpose of training hunting dogs, except as provided for by law or under rules promulgated by the Wildlife Conservation Commission;
OK.note: Oklahoma reaches invertebrates and then lets the giant African millipede through. 800:25-25-3(a)(19) exempts "native invertebrates" from the licence requirements, carving out only crayfish and freshwater mussels, which shows the Department treats invertebrates as wildlife it could regulate. the giant African millipede is not native, so that clause is not the answer; the answer is that nothing else applies. The statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A) reaches wildlife in a closed season, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats, and a captive-bred pet is separately exempted by § 7-502(B)(4). The reptile and amphibian licence at 800:25-7-7(2) is written about reptiles and amphibians. The restriction that does reach this species is federal: USDA APHIS treats non-native millipedes as regulated organisms, so moving one across a state line needs a PPQ 526 permit.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Corn snake is not on the federal injurious wildlife list this rule points to.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: The clean list's only reptile test is venom.

AZ.note: Arizona's restricted live wildlife rule reaches crocodilians, elapids, burrowing asps, boomslangs, twig snakes, keelbacks and the brown tree snake. A common colubrid like the corn snake is not on it, and it is not an Arizona native, so no separate wild-collection rule applies either.

CA.note: California's restricted colubrid entries are boomslang, twig snakes and Nerodia. Corn snake is not California native, so the state's separate native-reptile take rules (Title 14 CCR §§ 40-43) don't reach it either.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No Pantherophis appears in any category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes

DE.note: Corrected from legal. The previous entry cleared this snake against a banned list that does not exist in the form described. The real point is that the corn snake is native to Delaware, so it is not exotic, the Agriculture permit chapter does not reach it, and DNREC's native wildlife rules do. Those rules do not make native wildlife available as pets, with one carve-out that matters here: a captive-bred native snake in an aberrant colour morph may be held under permit. Since the pet trade in this species is almost entirely captive-bred colour morphs, most animals offered for sale can qualify where a wild-type one cannot. Hence conditional rather than banned, which is where the garter snake sits.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Pantherophis guttatus is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004. One caveat that applies to nobody buying a captive-bred animal: the Lower Keys population of the red rat snake, which is this species, has its own Species Conservation Measures incorporated into 68A-25.002, so a wild Keys animal is a different question from a pet.

GA.cite: DNR Guide to Legal Pets; O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4(b)(1)
GA.quote: By Georgia Law, most native species of wildlife cannot be held without permits or licenses. These licenses are not issued for the purpose of holding native wildlife as pets. These restrictions apply to the various species of animal, regardless of the origin or morphology. ... The following list of species native to Georgia may not be held as a pet regardless of its origin or morphology.
GA.note: Georgia handles its own wildlife separately from the wild animal rule, and the sentence that matters is "These restrictions apply to the various species of animal, regardless of the origin or morphology." A captive-bred animal from an out-of-state breeder is in the same position as one caught in a Georgia yard, and a colour morph is too. The corn snake is on DNR's list of native species that may not be held as a pet. Licences exist under O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4 and DNR says in terms that they "are not issued for the purpose of holding native wildlife as pets". Georgia is the state on this map where the corn snake, the archetypal beginner pet snake, cannot be kept at all, and the origin-and-morphology sentence is what makes captive-bred and morph animals no different.

HI.note: Hawaii bans the entire snake suborder by name.

IA.note: The squamate half of Iowa's dangerous wild animal definition is exhaustively enumerated: monitors, helodermatids, the venomous families, and henophidia limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas and African rock pythons. A corn snake is in none of them.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians

IL.quote: Any hybrid, intergrade, cross, or morphological variation of any listed herptile shall be treated as an endangered or threatened herptile under this Part. Examples of these include, but are not limited to: scaleless corn snakes, root beer corn snakes, creamsicle/dreamsicle corn snakes, and Slowinski/Kisatchie rat snakes.
IL.note: This entry previously read the corn snake as an Illinois native subject to the possession cap. It is not: Pantherophis guttatus is absent from the § 885.40 native taxa list, which carries emoryi, obsoletus and ramspotti/vulpinus but not guttatus, so an ordinary corn snake is a non-native herptile and needs no licence. What does reach it is newer and narrower. Illinois lists the Great Plains ratsnake, Pantherophis emoryi, as endangered, and this subsection, added effective 31 July 2025, treats any hybrid, cross or morphological variation of a listed herptile as endangered too, then names the common pet-trade lines that carry emoryi ancestry: creamsicle, dreamsicle, root beer and scaleless corn snakes. Those need an endangered species possession permit; a normal corn snake does not. It is an unusually specific rule, and a keeper is unlikely to find it by looking up the species. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana's native list carries three Pantherophis, the gray ratsnake, the eastern foxsnake and the western foxsnake, all by binomial. Pantherophis guttatus is not among them, because the corn snake's range stops south of Indiana. So the sale bar in 9-5-7 and the four-animal cap in 9-5-6(f) both miss it, and 312 IAC 9-11's three permit classes contain no colubrid. Worth contrasting with Georgia and New Jersey, where the corn snake is native and the answer is very different.

KS.quote: all non-native, venomous snakes.

KY.quote: Venomous exotic snakes of the families Viperidae, Atractaspididae, Elapidae, Hydrophidae, and Colubridae, except for hognose snakes (Genus Heterodon);
KY.note: The Colubridae entry on Kentucky's restricted list is limited to venomous rear-fanged colubrids. A corn snake is not venomous, so it was never inside the clause to begin with.

LA.note: Not among the individually-named restricted nonnative species (which include Boa constrictor by exact binomial). Corn snake is Louisiana native; we did not separately verify Louisiana's wild-take rules for the native population, only that ordinary possession of a lawfully acquired animal is not on the restricted list.

MD.quote: Except as provided in §§D—F of this regulation, a person without a reptile and amphibian permit may not possess more than four of each individual reptile or salamander, live or dead, listed in Regulation .03A of this chapter. The individual reptiles or salamanders may have been: (1) Obtained from the wild; (2) Captively produced; or (3) Legally obtained outside of Maryland.
MD.note: The cornsnake, which Maryland lists as Elaphe guttata guttata is on Maryland's first tier of native species, which means no permit but a hard cap of four. Read the second sentence: the cap applies whether the animal came from the wild, from captive breeding, or lawfully from outside Maryland, so buying a captive-bred one out of state does not lift it. Above four, or to breed or sell at all, a reptile and amphibian permit is needed. Colour mutations bred in captivity are exempt from the cap under Regulation .04E, with the burden of proving the mutation on the owner, and Regulation .16 bars using any listed species in a competition. This entry previously read as unrestricted on the strength of the venomous snake clause in the criminal statute. That clause is accurate and is not the rule: the corn snake is a Maryland native and the possession chapter is where it is answered. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A corn snake is a snake, so it needs to have come from a permitted breeder or to have been held before 1 August 2021. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous snakes not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(v) Colubridae (modern snakes);

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in North Dakota's captivity-prohibition chapter.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Pantherophis guttatus is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list. The distinction is real rather than semantic here. Nebraska's ratsnakes, the Great Plains ratsnake P. emoryi, the western black ratsnake P. obsoleta and the western fox snake P. ramspotti, are all on the three-per-species collecting list, and the pet corn snake is a southeastern species that is none of them.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;
NH.note: Corn snake is not New Hampshire native, so it falls cleanly within the general exotic-reptile allowance.

NJ.quote: Wild phase corn snakes are classified as endangered in the State of New Jersey and may not be possessed as pets or for hobby purposes, nor may they be sold, for any reason. The only corn snake color morphs that are legal to possess as pets and/or sold in New Jersey include the following: red albino (amelanistic), butter, blizzard, candy cane, creamsicle, lavender, pearl, snow, and sun glow.
NJ.note: New Jersey is the state where the corn snake is endangered. 4.13(b)7 lists the corn snake, Elaphe guttata guttata, on the state endangered list, which under 4.10(a) means no permit may issue for it and under 4.15(b) means it may not be kept as a pet. The Division then carves out captive colour morphs, because a morph is visibly not a wild phase animal and so cannot be laundered from the Pine Barrens population. Its notice names nine that may be kept and sold: red albino, butter, blizzard, candy cane, creamsicle, lavender, pearl, snow and sun glow. That makes this conditional rather than a permit: a normal-looking corn snake is barred outright, one of the nine named morphs is allowed, and anything else in a trade that has produced hundreds of morph names is not addressed by the list. Previously recorded here as a plain permit under 4.5, which missed the endangered listing entirely.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the corn snake is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The § 3.3 native snake list names the black rat snake, Pantherophis alleghaniensis, and not this species, which is a southeastern animal and not a New York one. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

OH.note: Ohio's restricted snake list is three venomous families plus two named rear-fanged species plus eight large constrictors twelve feet or longer. A corn snake is none of those.

OK.quote: monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license
OK.note: Corn snake is not indigenous to Oklahoma, so it clears under this exemption.

OR.quote: Milk, Pine, Corn, Rat, Garter snakes -- Colubridae -- All nonnative species of Milk, Pine, Corn, Rat, Garter;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. The corn snake is a nonnative colubrid of a named kind, so the entry reaches it directly. The word nonnative is load-bearing across this whole entry, which is why the garter snake comes out differently. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

PA.note: Corrected. The previous entry left this unclear on the view that the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework might reach snakes. It cannot: 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines wildlife as wild birds and wild mammals, so every reptile is outside the Game Code. The corn snake is also absent from the Fish and Boat Commission's native species list, Pennsylvania's native ratsnake being Pantherophis alleghaniensis, so Chapter 79 does not reach it either. Nothing regulates it.
PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.

SC.quote: Corn snakes reproduced in captivity and under 20 inches in total length are allowed
SC.note: South Carolina's 2021 native-reptile law (Act 177) generally bars sale/possession of native reptiles, but carves out captive-bred corn snakes under 20 inches total length as an allowed pet-trade exception. We could not confirm the exact regulation subsection number for this specific size cutoff beyond the Chapter 123-150s series; the substance is corroborated by SCDNR's own herp regulations page describing the general native-species possession scheme.

SD.note: South Dakota's possession-permit list covers mammals only; reptiles are handled under separate Game, Fish and Parks rules, though a free entry permit applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The corn snake is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial. The point that decides every native reptile in Tennessee is the exception clause in Class II, which reads "native species, except those listed in other classes". A native nonpoisonous reptile IS listed in another class, at (3)(A), so it is excluded from Class II and lands in Class III with no permit. The supplier documentation requirement in § 70-4-401(b) follows Class I and Class II and does not reach it either. This entry previously carried a documentation condition drawn from § 70-4-401(b). That subsection reaches Class I and Class II wildlife, and a native nonvenomous reptile is neither.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: This one needs the species checked rather than the common name. The § 65.331(d) nongame list names two Texas ratsnakes that are easy to confuse with this animal, "Great Plains rat snake (Elaphe emoryi)" and "Slowinski’s cornsnake (Elaphe slowinskii)", both using the older Elaphe genus. Pantherophis guttatus itself, the pet-trade corn snake, is an animal of the southeastern United States whose range stops east of Texas, so it is not indigenous and the nongame rules do not reach it at all. The distinction is real rather than semantic: P. slowinskii was split out of P. guttatus in 2002, and it is the split that leaves the pet species outside the Texas list.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the corn snake is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. The near miss is worth naming: Utah's own Pantherophis is the Great Plains ratsnake, P. emoryi, which sits on the Limited table at two a day and four in total. Pantherophis guttatus is a different species and is on no Utah table, so it does not inherit that cap. This entry previously cited R657-3, a rule that no longer exists. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

VA.note: No snake appears on Virginia's special permit table at all.

WA.quote: Family colubridae, only dispholidus typus
WA.note: The only colubrid Washington restricts is the boomslang.

WV.quote: Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes;
WV.note: A corn snake, at a couple feet, is nowhere near the six-foot constrictor threshold.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The corn snake is a southeastern species and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

VT.quote: Squamata | Serpentes | Colubridae | All species of colubrids, except those listed in Appendix that require an importation and possession permit
VT.note: Colubrids are unrestricted as a group. The Restricted list reaches the North American ratsnake as Elaphe obsoleta but not the corn snake, which was Elaphe guttata and is now Pantherophis guttatus, so the corn snake stays clear.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Snake | Colubridae | Pantherophis guttatus | Red Cornsnake | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The corn snake is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

CO.quote: Any captive-bred species from the genus Pantherophis (cornsnakes, ratsnakes, and foxsnakes) except the Great Plains ratsnake (Pantherophis emoryi)
CO.note: Two conditions, both real. The animal must be captive-bred, and § 703(B) requires documentation that reasonably identifies it, a receipt or bill of sale, a donation certificate, an importation health certificate or proof it was bred from lawfully possessed parents. No licence and no fee, but a wild-caught corn snake and an undocumented one are both outside the exemption. Colorado carved the Great Plains ratsnake out of the genus because it is a native species. Anyone who held a Pantherophis on 1 May 2026 could satisfy the documentation requirement instead by filing a CPW Legacy Report under § 703(C). CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

MA.quote: Snakes of the family Colubridae, as follows: ... Garter and Ribbon Snakes (Thamnophis spp.) ... Kingsnakes and Milk Snakes (Lampropeltis spp.) ... North American Ratsnakes (Pantherophis spp.) except the Black Ratsnake (Pantherophis alleghaniensis other than albinistic and leucistic individuals) which requires a permit ... Western Hognose Snake (Heterodon nasicus)
MA.note: The colubrid list clears "North American Ratsnakes (Pantherophis spp.)" with one exception, the black ratsnake, Pantherophis alleghaniensis, other than albinistic and leucistic individuals. That exception is not about the pet trade: P. alleghaniensis is listed as endangered in Massachusetts at 321 CMR 10.90, and the colour-morph carve-out is there because an albino animal is visibly not wild-caught. Pantherophis guttatus is IUCN least concern and unlisted here, so the corn snake is clear.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The reptile clause is a list of families and the corn snake belongs to none of them: not Helodermatidae, not a venomous snake family, not Boidae, Pythonidae, Varanidae, Iguanidae, teiidae, Chelydridae or Crocodylia. The only colubrid provision reaches "all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members" of that family, and Pantherophis guttatus is none of those things. It is not a New York native either, so the state protected wildlife route at § 161.01(b)(ii) does not reach it. That makes the corn snake one of very few snakes lawful in the five boroughs.

RI.quote: North American Rat Snakes (Pantherophis spp.) except the Central Rat Snake (P. alleghaniensis) (other than albinistic and leucistic individuals) which requires a permit
RI.note: Rhode Island clears the genus and then carves out one species, its own native eastern ratsnake, so the corn snake sits inside the clearance and needs no exotic animal possession permit. It is also absent from the native-snake list at § 3.17(A)(4)(b)(3), which is what would otherwise pull it under the § 3.7(C) bar on keeping native wildlife. The parenthetical exempting albinistic and leucistic P. alleghaniensis shows the Division writes morph exceptions when it means to, so the absence of any morph condition here is deliberate.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Reptiles, Snakes
AR.quote: New World Colubrid Snakes (in part) (Genera: Bogertophis, Drymarchon, Drymobius, Lampropeltis, Pantherophis, Phrynonax, Pituophis, Pseudelaphe, Senticolis, Spilotes) except species native to Arkansas
AR.note: The genus clearance is qualified by nativity, so the answer is which Pantherophis Arkansas has.
