NY.quote: "Small game" means black, gray and fox squirrels, European hares, varying hares, cottontail rabbits, native frogs, native salamanders, native turtles, native lizards, native snakes, coyotes, red fox (Vulpes vulpes) and gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus) except captive bred red fox or gray fox, raccoon, opossum, or weasel, skunk, bobcat, lynx, muskrat, mink, except mink born in captivity, fisher, otter, beaver, sable and marten but does not include coydogs. ... No person shall, at any time of the year, buy, sell, offer or expose for sale, transport, or have in his possession any fish protected by law, game, protected wildlife ... whether taken within the state or coming from without the state, except as permitted by the Fish and Wildlife Law.
NY.note: The common garter snake is the fifth name on the § 3.3 list of native snakes, and subdivision (b) of that section reads in full "Open season. None." This entry previously read as requiring a permit, which understates it: no licence issued under § 11-0515 covers keeping one as a pet, so there is nothing to apply for. The chain runs through a definition nobody expects. ECL § 11-0103(2)(c) puts "native frogs, native salamanders, native turtles, native lizards, native snakes" inside the definition of SMALL GAME, which makes them game, which makes them protected wildlife under § 11-0103(6)(c). § 11-0107(2) then bars possessing protected wildlife "whether taken within the state or coming from without the state, except as permitted by the Fish and Wildlife Law", so a captive-bred animal bought in another state is in the same position as one caught in a New York yard. And the only possession licence, § 11-0515, is issued for "propagation, banding, scientific or exhibition purposes", which is not a pet.

OH.note: Ohio's restricted-snake list is three venomous families plus two named rear-fanged species plus large constrictors twelve feet and up. A garter snake is none of them.

OK.quote: No closed season. All reptiles except those listed in (3) and (5) of this section shall have a year-round season. (2) Bag limit. The bag limit is 6 per day or in possession for each species allowed in section (1) of this section.
OK.note: This entry read legal on 800:25-25-3, the exemption list, which is the wrong rule for a snake that lives in Oklahoma: subsection (c) exempts reptiles "not indigenous to Oklahoma" and Thamnophis sirtalis is indigenous. What applies instead is the reptile and amphibian part at 800:25-7. Two provisions matter to a keeper. 7-7(2)(A) requires a resident or nonresident hunting licence of anyone "taking or attempting to take reptiles and amphibians or possessing reptiles or amphibians" that are land dwelling, which is a possession hook and not merely a collecting one. And 7-8 gives every reptile a year-round season except a closed list of twelve, with a limit of "6 per day or in possession for each species". Recorded as conditional on those two rather than as a permit, because there is no application and no discretion: a hunting licence is sold over the counter. 29 O.S. § 7-502(B)(4) separately exempts anyone possessing legally obtained wildlife "from a source other than the wild, as pets" from the statutory possession bar, which is why a captive-bred animal is not caught by the closed-season rule. One gartersnake is on the closed list and it is not this one: 7-8(5)(G) closes the season on the wandering gartersnake, Thamnophis elegans vagrans.

OR.quote: Milk, Pine, Corn, Rat, Garter snakes -- Colubridae -- All nonnative species of Milk, Pine, Corn, Rat, Garter;
OR.note: The clearance is written for nonnative garter snakes only, and the common garter snake, Thamnophis sirtalis, is an Oregon native. So which animal it is decides the answer: a nonnative Thamnophis is cleared outright, and an Oregon one is not covered by this entry at all. Native wildlife falls outside this division, which by its own title governs nonnative wildlife, and lands instead under the ODFW protected wildlife and holding rules in OAR 635 division 44. Note also that the entry has been rewritten since it was last read here; it previously carved out Boiga irregularis, Lampropeltis getula, L. zonata and Pituophis catenifer, and now reads as a positive list of the five snake kinds. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

PA.note: Corrected from legal. The common garter snake is Pennsylvania native and is not tabled by name, so the catch-all line caps possession at one animal. Two further rules bind that the previous entry missed. § 79.10(a) makes it unlawful to transport or import a native species into Pennsylvania from another jurisdiction, so an out-of-state garter snake is not an option, and § 79.9 bars selling or buying a reptile taken from Pennsylvania and its progeny. The designated color morphs at § 79.12 are the exception, exempt from the possession limit and sellable by registered propagators. Note that two Pennsylvania gartersnakes, the short-headed gartersnake and the eastern ribbonsnake, are tabled separately at zero.
PA.quote: Native species not listed in this subsection | No closed season | 1 | 1

RI.note: Rhode Island's exempt Colubridae list names sixteen groups of pet-trade snakes by genus, and Thamnophis is not one of them. The regulation states directly that possession of native snakes is restricted to institutions, meaning typical pet ownership of a Rhode Island garter snake isn't permitted.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit.

SD.note: South Dakota's possession-permit list covers mammals only; reptiles fall under separate Game, Fish & Parks rules rather than this permit scheme.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The garter snake is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial. The point that decides every native reptile in Tennessee is the exception clause in Class II, which reads "native species, except those listed in other classes". A native nonpoisonous reptile IS listed in another class, at (3)(A), so it is excluded from Class II and lands in Class III with no permit. The supplier documentation requirement in § 70-4-401(b) follows Class I and Class II and does not reach it either. This entry previously read as requiring a Class II wildlife possession permit. It does not: the Class II definition excepts native species listed in other classes, and every nonvenomous native reptile is listed at (3)(A). A Class II personal possession permit costs $10 an animal under § 70-4-404(d)(1)(B), and there is no Class III equivalent because none is needed.

TX.quote: A person without a nongame or nongame dealer’s permit may: (A) possess six or fewer specimens of a species of nongame wildlife listed in §65.331(e) of this title, provided the person does not engage in commercial activity involving the nongame wildlife; and (B) possess 25 or fewer specimens of a species of nongame wildlife listed in §65.331(d) of this title, provided the person does not engage in commercial activity involving the nongame wildlife.
TX.note: The § 65.331(d) list names three Texas garter snakes, the western blackneck, the checkered and the western ribbon, and it does not name Thamnophis sirtalis. The common gartersnake is instead on the § 65.331(e) list, which drops it to the lower cap: six without a permit, and no selling, offering for sale, exchanging or bartering at all. This entry previously read as unrestricted, citing the dangerous wild animal statute, which contains no reptile. The rule that answers a native Texas snake is the nongame subchapter, and within it the two lists give different answers to two garter snakes. The cap reaches captive-bred animals: § 65.325(a) says nongame wildlife "includes captive-bred nongame wildlife", so a pet shop receipt does not lift it.

UT.cite: Utah Admin. Code R657-53-7(3)(a); species tables, Standard possession
UT.quote: Standard possession (3 daily/9 total, per species) ... Common gartersnake Thamnophis sirtalis
UT.note: This entry read legal before, on R657-53-5's list of activities allowed without a wildlife document. That is right for a captive-bred animal and wrong for a Utah one, and the common gartersnake is a Utah animal. Thamnophis sirtalis is on the division's Standard possession table, which makes it a Controlled species: taking one from the wild needs the herpetology collection permit, which costs ten dollars and requires passing an online orientation course first, and the limit is three a day and nine in total. The terrestrial gartersnake is on the same table and the black-necked gartersnake is at Limited, two and four. A captive-bred or out-of-state garter snake is a different animal in law: R657-53-8(1)(a) and (c) lift both out of the possession limit entirely, and no certificate of registration attaches to possessing one. So the answer turns on where the snake came from rather than what it is.

VA.note: Virginia's special-permit table works species by species and contains no reptile relevant to a garter snake.

VT.quote: Squamata | Serpentes | Colubridae | Thamnophis | all species | Garter snakes, ribbon snakes
VT.note: Resolved from a previous unclear entry now that the lists are in hand. Colubrids are unrestricted as a family and then the entire genus Thamnophis is clawed back on the Restricted list, so every garter snake and ribbon snake is restricted. A permit exists on paper but not for a pet: Regulation 881 says the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for keeping or possessing a wild animal in captivity except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes.

WA.quote: Family colubridae, only dispholidus typus
WA.note: The only colubrid Washington restricts is the boomslang.

WI.note: Wisconsin lets residents possess up to five individuals of each non-protected native species, garter snakes included, without a permit, but native reptiles generally may not be bought or sold within the state, so a Wisconsin-kept pet has to come from your own lawful collecting rather than a breeder or shop. Wisconsin repealed and recreated NR 16.12(3) effective 1 January 2027 (CR 25-092). Until then the rule allows taking or possessing up to 5 individuals of each non-listed native species. From that date possession of live native reptiles and amphibians is prohibited outright except under narrow exemptions, of which the one that matters to keepers is NR 16.12(3)(k): captive-bred colour variants acquired from a legal source. A wild-type native animal will no longer be keepable.

WV.note: The only reptiles West Virginia's dangerous-wild-animal guidance points at are large constrictors, venomous snakes, and crocodilians.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: Not venomous, and not on Wyoming's Section 8 prohibited list.

MI.quote: Reptiles and amphibians may not be bought, sold or offered for sale.
MI.note: The common garter snake is Michigan native and is not on the protected list, so it may be taken, but only on conditions. A fishing license is required, the limit is three a day and six in total across snakes, lizards and turtles combined, and the quoted sale ban means you cannot lawfully buy one in Michigan or sell the one you have. Personal collection is the only lawful route. Note that Butler's garter snake, a separate Michigan species, is on the protected list and may not be taken or possessed at all, so the answer turns on which garter snake you have.

NYC.quote: No person shall sell or give to another person, possess, harbor, keep, or yard wild or other animals identified in this section ... other than in: (i) a zoological park or aquarium ...; or (ii) a laboratory ...; or (iii) a veterinary hospital ...; or (iv) a temporary exhibit, performance or display that has been issued a permit by the Commissioner. ... For the purposes of this Code, a wild animal is deemed to be any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings and all such animals are hereby prohibited ... Such animals shall also include: (i) any animals specified by the Commissioner in regulations ...; (ii) any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule; and (iii) any of the following animals:
NYC.note: Caught by the clause most readings of this article skip. Before its 24 numbered categories, § 161.01(b)(ii) prohibits "any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule". New York State makes native frogs, salamanders, turtles, lizards and snakes small game and therefore protected wildlife, and ECL § 11-0107(2) bars possessing protected wildlife whether taken in the state or brought in from outside it. The common garter snake is a New York native, so the state prohibition becomes a city one through that sentence. The colubrid clause at (b)(10) is worth checking separately and probably does not reach it: that clause takes "all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae", and while Thamnophis does have a Duvernoy's gland, it is not a venomous snake in any ordinary sense. The state route is the clean one. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: Alaska's clean list turns entirely on venom.

AL.quote: Snake, All Native King Lampropeltis spp.
AL.note: The line to read is "Snake, All Native King  Lampropeltis spp.", and it is doing two things at once. The scientific name is the entire genus, which would take a California kingsnake with it; the common name limits that to native ones, and Lampropeltis californiae is a west coast animal that has never occurred in Alabama. Every other reptile on the list pairs one common name with one binomial, so the qualifier on this line is deliberate and it is what decides the answer. Recorded legal on that reading. It is worth knowing that the same line makes the milk snake a permit animal here, because Lampropeltis triangulum is native, so two snakes from one genus get opposite answers off one sentence.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: New World Colubrid Snakes (in part) (Genera: Bogertophis, Drymarchon, Drymobius, Lampropeltis, Pantherophis, Phrynonax, Pituophis, Pseudelaphe, Senticolis, Spilotes) except species native to Arkansas
AR.note: Named on the unrestricted list by genus; the native-species exception in that entry doesn't reach the California kingsnake since it isn't an Arkansas species.

AZ.note: The California kingsnake's range reaches into parts of Arizona, so the same hunting/fishing-license framework that governs wild take of native reptiles applies there, but simple possession of a lawfully-acquired one isn't restricted, and it isn't on Arizona's no-open-season list.

CA.note: Not on the Fish & Game Code § 671 restricted species list, so owning one is unrestricted. Wild collection of a California kingsnake specifically requires a sportfishing license and is capped at a 4-per-day bag/possession limit; unlike the common garter snake, there are no county-level closures for this species.

CO.quote: Any captive-bred species from the genus Lampropeltis (kingsnakes and milksnakes) except the Western milksnakes (Lampropeltis gentilis/Lampropeltis triangulum gentilis) and Speckled kingsnake (Lampropeltis holbrooki/Lampropeltis getula holbrooki)
CO.note: The California kingsnake is neither of the two excluded natives, so it is on Appendix B and needs no licence, but it does now need two things it did not need before 1 May 2026: it must be captive-bred, and § 703(B) requires documentation identifying the animal, a receipt or bill of sale, a donation certificate, an importation health certificate or proof of lawful parentage. CPW files Lampropeltis californiae against this line. Anyone holding one on 1 May 2026 could file a CPW Legacy Report under § 703(C) instead. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No Lampropeltis appears in any category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: A California kingsnake fits this exemption from DC's general wild-animal ban squarely.

DE.note: A live reptile not native to or generally found in Delaware needs a permit from the Department of Agriculture before it may be brought into the state, possessed, sold, or exhibited. The California kingsnake, a Pacific coast species, is exotic to Delaware.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Lampropeltis californiae is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004. The Lampropeltis that Florida does regulate is the short-tailed snake, L. extenuata, which has its own conservation measures; the California kingsnake is untouched.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the California kingsnake is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it. Georgia's own kingsnakes, the black, eastern, mole and scarlet, are on the prohibited natives list, and Lampropeltis californiae is not a Georgia species.

HI.note: Hawaii's snake ban reaches every species in the suborder, kingsnakes included, with no pet-keeping permit available.

IA.note: The squamate half of Iowa's 'dangerous wild animal' definition is exhaustively enumerated (monitors, helodermatids, venomous families, a short list of giant constrictors); a kingsnake is none of them.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: Idaho's test is venom, not species.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The California kingsnake is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. Illinois does have native Lampropeltis, the prairie, speckled and eastern black kingsnakes and the red and eastern milksnakes, and those are capped. Lampropeltis californiae is not one of them. This entry previously cited the dangerous animal statute, which says in terms that it does not reach herptiles at all. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana lists two kingsnakes on its native sale list, the prairie kingsnake, Lampropeltis calligaster, and the eastern black kingsnake, Lampropeltis nigra, and it names them by binomial rather than taking the genus. The California kingsnake, Lampropeltis californiae, is a west coast animal and is on neither entry, so the sale bar and the four-animal possession cap in 9-5-6(f) both miss it. The eastern milksnake is on the same list and is a Lampropeltis too, which is why this map answers the two differently. Nothing in 312 IAC 9-11 reaches a colubrid either.

KS.note: The only reptiles Kansas regulates are non-native venomous snakes.

KY.note: Kentucky's inherently-dangerous-wildlife list reaches Colubridae only when the snake is venomous.

LA.note: Louisiana's prohibited nonnative reptile list is built around crocodilians, tegus, monitors, the green iguana, and a short list of large or venomous snakes; ordinary colubrids like the kingsnake aren't on it.

MA.quote: Snakes of the family Colubridae, as follows: ... Garter and Ribbon Snakes (Thamnophis spp.) ... Kingsnakes and Milk Snakes (Lampropeltis spp.) ... North American Ratsnakes (Pantherophis spp.) except the Black Ratsnake (Pantherophis alleghaniensis other than albinistic and leucistic individuals) which requires a permit ... Western Hognose Snake (Heterodon nasicus)
MA.note: Cleared by the same genus-wide entry for Lampropeltis. Because the clearance is written to the genus rather than to a species list, the 2009 split of Lampropeltis californiae out of L. getula changes nothing here, which is the opposite of what the same split does in Texas, where the state list names L. getula specifically.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. Maryland does have native Lampropeltis, the eastern kingsnake and the mole kingsnake, both on the four-per-species list. The California kingsnake is Lampropeltis californiae and is not among them, and Regulation .03D provides that the scientific name controls where both are given, which settles it. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

ME.cite: Unrestricted Species list, Serpentes (Captive Bred Origin Only)
ME.quote: All Species in Genus Lampropeltis (Kingsnakes And Milk Snakes) Except for: Lampropeltis herrerae; Lampropeltis triangulum triangulum
ME.note: The whole genus is cleared except two named species, neither of which is the California kingsnake.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A California kingsnake is a snake, so it needs to have come from a permitted breeder or to have been held before 1 August 2021. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

MO.note: Class I, Missouri's permit tier for nonvenomous reptiles, reaches only species native to Missouri. The California kingsnake isn't one, so it falls outside that requirement.

MS.note: Mississippi's inherently-dangerous list is entirely mammalian; no reptile is restricted at any size.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous snakes not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(v) Colubridae (modern snakes);
MT.note: Colubridae is cleared as nonvenomous.

NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic-animal statute covers venomous reptiles. Everything else is left to county ordinance.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in North Dakota's captive wildlife chapter.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Lampropeltis californiae is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list. The two Nebraska kingsnakes are treated far more strictly than this one: the prairie kingsnake and the speckled kingsnake are both nongame species in need of conservation at 166 NAC 10 § 001.02, where possession without a scientific collection permit is unlawful. The California kingsnake, not being native, is untouched.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;
NH.note: An exotic, nonvenomous reptile like the California kingsnake clears New Hampshire's noncontrolled list.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: ... iv. King Snakes - Lampropeltis spp.;
NJ.note: This entry previously read legal, cited to 4.8(a), on the reasoning that an ordinary colubrid is not a potentially dangerous species. That is true and it is not the question. New Jersey does not work by a dangerous list with everything else free; 4.2(a) bars possession of any exotic or nongame species without a permit and 4.4 is a short closed list of exemptions that does not include kingsnakes. Worse, the kingsnake is not even left to the 4.5 catch-all, because 4.3(a)3.iv names the genus outright as "King Snakes - Lampropeltis spp.". Lampropeltis californiae is squarely inside it.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Snake | Colubridae | Lampropeltis getula californiae | California Kingsnake | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Resolved from unclear. Named to the subspecies, and all seven Lampropeltis getula subspecies on the list are Group I.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.note: Nevada's unprotected-reptile category covers most kingsnakes, though the state singles out California kingsnakes lacking a continuous banded/ringed pattern from head to vent as the specific unprotected form, so pattern can matter for certain individuals.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the California kingsnake is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The § 3.3 native snake list names the eastern milk snake, a Lampropeltis, and the California kingsnake is a different species that does not occur in New York. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

OH.note: Ohio's restricted-snake list is three venomous families plus two named rear-fanged species plus large constrictors twelve feet and up. A kingsnake is none of them.

OK.note: Non-indigenous reptiles are exempt from Oklahoma's import, breeder's-license, and permit requirements outright, and the California kingsnake isn't indigenous to Oklahoma.

OR.quote: Kingsnakes and gopher (bull) snakes -- Colubridae -- Individuals of Lampropeltis getula, L. zonata and Pituophis catenifer that are morphologically distinct from native species.
OR.note: Oregon clears these snakes individual by individual rather than by species, and the test is appearance: an animal must be morphologically distinct from the native species, which in practice means a recognisable colour or pattern morph rather than a wild-type-looking snake. Wild-caught, native-looking kingsnakes and their offspring are not covered. The entry is also written under the older taxonomy in which the California kingsnake was Lampropeltis getula californiae; it has since been raised to L. californiae, which Oregon does not name, so the animal depends on being read as part of L. getula. Two layers of imprecision on one line. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

PA.note: Fish and Boat Commission possession rules apply only to species native to Pennsylvania. The California kingsnake isn't one, so it isn't reached by that chapter at all.

RI.quote: Kingsnakes and Milk Snakes
RI.note: Named directly on Rhode Island's exempt Colubridae list.

SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit.

SD.note: South Dakota's possession-permit list covers mammals only; reptiles fall under separate Game, Fish & Parks rules.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The California kingsnake is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial. The California kingsnake is not a Tennessee native, so the Class II question never arises for it.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: The § 65.331(d) list names "Speckled or desert kingsnake (Lampropeltis getula)", which is the Texas native, and Lampropeltis californiae was split out of L. getula in 2009. The California kingsnake’s range runs from California and Baja east to western Arizona and Utah and does not reach Texas, so it is not indigenous and the nongame rules do not apply. Texas is one of several states where this animal is answered by the fact that the state’s own kingsnake is a different species.

UT.cite: Utah Admin. Code R657-53-7(3)(b); species tables, Limited possession
UT.quote: Limited possession (2 daily and yearly/4 total, per species) ... California kingsnake Lampropeltis californiae
UT.note: This entry read legal before, and Lampropeltis californiae is in fact on Utah's Limited possession table, which is the tightest controlled tier the rule has: two a day, two a year, and four in total, on a herpetology collection permit obtained after an orientation course. The Arizona mountain kingsnake and the western milk snake are on the same table. What the earlier reading got right is the other half: R657-53-8(1)(a) and (c) take captive-bred animals and animals legally obtained outside Utah out of the possession limits altogether, and the only possession certificate of registration in the rule is R657-53-12 for native venomous reptiles. So a captive-bred kingsnake from a breeder is unrestricted and a Utah-caught one is capped at four.

VA.note: Virginia's special-permit table works species by species and contains no reptile relevant to a kingsnake.

VT.quote: Squamata | Serpentes | Colubridae | All species of colubrids, except those listed in Appendix that require an importation and possession permit
VT.note: Resolved. Colubrids are unrestricted as a family, and the only Lampropeltis on the Restricted list is the eastern milk snake subspecies. The California kingsnake is not named, so it is clear.

WA.quote: Family colubridae, only dispholidus typus
WA.note: The only colubrid Washington restricts is the boomslang.

WI.note: As a non-native species, the California kingsnake sits outside Wisconsin's native-reptile possession cap and can be kept the way corn snakes and ball pythons are, without a DNR license. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit and health paperwork.

WV.note: The only reptiles West Virginia's dangerous-wild-animal guidance points at are large constrictors, venomous snakes, and crocodilians.

WY.note: Not venomous, and not on Wyoming's Section 8 prohibited list.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The California kingsnake is a western species and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit. Michigan's native kingsnake relative is the eastern milk snake, which is covered; the California kingsnake is not.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The reptile clause is a list of families and the California kingsnake belongs to none of them: not Helodermatidae, not a venomous snake family, not Boidae, Pythonidae, Varanidae, Iguanidae, teiidae, Chelydridae or Crocodylia. A nonvenomous colubrid with no Duvernoy's gland, and not a New York species, so neither the colubrid clause nor the state protection clause applies. Its New York relative, the eastern milk snake, is prohibited through the state route.

AK.quote: Parrot, parakeet, cockatiel, macaw, and other members of the Family Psittacidae   not prohibited by federal or international law
AK.note: Cockatoos are on Alaska's clean list, but the 'not prohibited by federal or international law' qualifier matters: several cockatoo species, including the Moluccan and yellow-crested cockatoo, are CITES Appendix I, which bars commercial international trade even though it doesn't touch domestic keeping of an already-captive-bred bird.

AL.note: Parrots, cockatiels, conures, and macaws are generally legal in Alabama. Species listed under CITES or the Migratory Bird Treaty Act may need import/export paperwork, but that doesn't reach ordinary possession of a captive-bred bird.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Cockatoos: Lesser Sulphur-crested or Yellow-crested, Sulphur-crested, Umbrella or White, Salmon-crested or Moluccan, Goffin's (Cacatua sulphurea, C. galerita, C. alba, C. moluccensis, C. goffiniana)
AR.note: Five named cockatoo species, including two that are CITES Appendix I (yellow-crested and Moluccan), are on Arkansas's unrestricted list outright, a useful contrast with states like Maine that carve CITES-I birds back out of an otherwise blanket parrot clearance.

AZ.note: Most cockatoos are legal pets in Arizona; the state's live-wildlife statute (A.R.S. § 17-306) is aimed at native and dangerous wildlife rather than common cage birds.

CA.quote: Family Psittacidae-Parrots, Parakeets: Myiopsitta monachus (Monk or Quaker parakeet) (D)
CA.note: The only parrot California's restricted species list reaches is the monk parakeet. Every cockatoo species is outside section 671.

CO.quote: All Psitticine birds
CO.note: The unregulated wildlife list clears the parrots as a group, so no CPW licence is required for a cockatoo. Unregulated is not unmonitored: importation and health requirements still apply, and § 1103(B) is expressly subject to the Chapter W-0 prohibited list. That list reaches exactly one parrot, the monk parakeet, and CPW restates this line as "All Psitticine birds (except Monk Parakeet/Quaker Parrot)". CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. The only psittacine anywhere in the regulation is the monk parakeet, which is Category Two. Cockatoos are untouched.

DC.quote: Captive-bred species of common cage birds, including chickens
DC.note: Every cockatoo sold in the US pet trade is captive-bred, so this exemption from DC's general wild-animal ban applies the same way it does for the African grey parrot.

DE.note: Delaware exempts birds entirely from its exotic-animal permit system; only mammals and non-native reptiles are reached by that Title 3 permit requirement.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the entry at (14)(q), which is the single word "Parrots", sitting in a list that separately names shell parakeets, canaries, lovebirds, cockatiels, finches, myna birds and toucans. Cockatoos are parrots for this purpose, and Florida attaches no species test.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the cockatoo is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it. Only one parrot appears anywhere in the rule, the monk parakeet, and it is on the prohibited list rather than the licence list.

HI.quote: White cockatoos (Umbrella, Moluccan, Sulphur-crested, Little Corella, etc.)
HI.note: Cockatoos are named on Hawaii's conditionally approved list, alongside the galah, gang-gang, black cockatoos, and palm cockatoo, so keeping one is possible but requires an import permit, pre-departure quarantine, health certification, and permanent ID before the bird ever lands in the state.

IA.note: Iowa's dangerous-wild-animal definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles; no bird appears in it.

ID.quote: non-poultry birds
ID.note: Idaho's clean-list bird category is drawn by exclusion, not by naming families, so every parrot including cockatoos is a conventional pet.

IL.quote: This Act shall apply only to the wild birds and parts of wild birds (including, but not limited to, their nests and eggs), and wild mammals and parts of wild mammals, which shall include their green hides, in the State of Illinois, or which may be brought into the State.
IL.note: The Wildlife Code's protected species list is native and migratory birds by family and does not include the parrots, so a cockatoo is outside it. The closed dangerous animal list at 720 ILCS 5/48-10 is mammals and primates only and does not reach birds at all. The one parrot Illinois names anywhere is the monk parakeet, and even that clause bars only release and propagation for release. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

IN.note: No bird appears in any of Indiana's three Wild Animal Possession Permit classes.

KS.note: Kansas regulates six big cats, bears, and non-native venomous snakes; no bird is in the definition.

KY.note: Kentucky's permit-exempt list clears parrots, lovebirds, budgerigars, macaws, and parakeets by name, excepting only the monk parakeet.

LA.note: Louisiana's quadruped regulation reaches mammals only; no bird is listed.

MA.quote: List of Birds. (a) The following groups of birds are prohibited without a permit: 1. Species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3). 2. Migratory birds listed in the Code of Federal Regulations, 50 CFR 10.13. 3. Any other bird native to the United States and Canada. (b) Except for species listed in 321 CMR 9.01(11)(a), the birds or groups of birds may be kept without a permit: ... 6. Psittacidae (parrots and their allies)
MA.note: Cockatoos are parrots for the purpose of the family exemption, so the answer turns entirely on the species and on 9.01(3)(b). The common pet cockatoos split both ways: the umbrella (Cacatua alba) and Moluccan (C. moluccensis) are IUCN endangered and the sulphur-crested group includes critically endangered species, all of which are categorically non-exempt, while the Major Mitchell's (C. leadbeateri) and long-billed corella (C. tenuirostris) are least concern and clear the bar. Goffin's (C. goffiniana) is near threatened, which is where the language runs out: the statute bars listing an animal "in any category" of the IUCN Red Data Books and MassWildlife paraphrases that as "any rarity category", and whether near threatened counts is not answered anywhere in the text. Check the species before assuming this is a bird question rather than a permit one.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. The statute reaches no bird, and no cockatoo is native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

ME.quote: All Species in Order Psittaciformes (Parrots) Except for: Myiopsitta monachus; Cyanoliseus patagonus; Enicognathus leptorhynchus; Enicognathus ferrugineus; Family Strigopidae *Except if listed on: IUCN Red List (Endangered, Critically Endangered, or Extinct in the Wild) OR CITES Appendix I
ME.note: Maine clears the whole parrot order but then strips back out anything on CITES Appendix I or the IUCN's Endangered/Critically Endangered tiers. That carve-out catches several of the most commonly kept pet cockatoos: the Moluccan and yellow-crested cockatoos are CITES Appendix I, and the umbrella cockatoo is IUCN Endangered even though it's only CITES Appendix II. Smaller, more secure species like the cockatiel or galah would still clear the list; the larger, more iconic cockatoos generally need Maine's captivity permit instead.

MN.quote: "Protected wild animals" means big game, small game, game fish, native rough fish, minnows, leeches, chubs, frogs, turtles, clams, mussels, wolf, mourning doves, bats, snakes, salamanders, lizards, any animal species listed as endangered, threatened, or of special concern in Minnesota Rules, chapter 6134, and wild animals that are protected by a restriction in the time or manner of taking, other than a restriction in the use of artificial lights, poison, or motor vehicles.
MN.note: The protected list is worth reading in full for Minnesota, because it names five herptile categories and then almost nothing among birds beyond game birds and mourning doves. The cockatoo falls outside it, so § 97A.501's possession bar does not apply. The invasive species rules do not reach it either: Minn. R. 6216.0250 designates no bird as a prohibited invasive species, and the three regulated invasive birds are the Egyptian goose, mute swan and Sichuan pheasant.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds (including ring-necked pheasants and gray partridge) native to the continental United States
MO.note: The bird half of Missouri's Class I is limited to species native to the continental United States. No cockatoo is.

MS.note: Mississippi's inherently-dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

MT.quote: The following noncontrolled exotic wildlife may not be released or transplanted in the state but may be possessed or sold as pets in Montana without a permit: ...(xi) Psittacidae (parrots)
MT.note: Psittacidae is named outright on Montana's noncontrolled list, cockatoos included.

NC.note: No bird provision exists in North Carolina's only statewide exotic-animal statute; it covers venomous reptiles.

ND.note: No bird prohibition exists in North Dakota's chapter beyond a modest annual license fee for species the board designates.

NE.quote: Cage and Aviary Birds - Means those captive-reared birds, not native to Nebraska, such as parrots, exotic finches, and canaries, which are adapted to live and breed in a cage. For purposes of this regulation, the monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus) is not a cage and aviary bird.
NE.note: Cleared by the last line of the importation list, "All Cage and Aviary Birds", which the chapter defines as captive-reared birds not native to Nebraska such as parrots, exotic finches and canaries. A cockatoo is squarely inside that. The definition also carries the state's one carve-out, for the monk parakeet, so the sentence that clears this bird is the same sentence that bans that one. Unlike Massachusetts, Nebraska attaches no conservation-status test to the listing, so the species does not change the answer here.

NH.quote: Parrots (Psittaciformes)
NH.note: The whole order is named on New Hampshire's noncontrolled list.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: This entry previously read legal, cited to 4.8(a), because the potentially dangerous table lists three parrots and no cockatoo among them. That reads the rule backwards. The three parrots on 4.8(a), the ring-necked parakeets, Myiopsitta and the Patagonian conure, are there as escape-and-establish agricultural pests, and being off that table only means a bird is not banned. The exempt list at 4.4 is what decides whether a bird is free, and its nine entries are the budgerigar, cockatiel, peafowl, rock dove, canary, house sparrow, European starling, zebra finch and society finch. No cockatoo, so 4.5 requires a permit. One caveat on top: the Division treats an IUCN Red List entry as an endangered listing, and several cockatoos in the trade carry one, the umbrella cockatoo as Endangered and the Moluccan as Vulnerable, so the answer may be harder than a permit depending on species.

NM.quote: Bird | Cockatoo | Cacatuidae | Cacatua sp. | Cockatoo | I | all species except as restricted in another group
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Resolved from unclear. The genus is Group I with a carve-out, and the carve-out is real: the white or umbrella, Philippine and yellow-crested cockatoos each appear separately in Group IV as federally endangered. Check the species, not just the genus.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.note: Companion parrot species, cockatoos included, are not on Nevada's prohibited-species list and need no state permit.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and a cockatoo is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. No bird appears on the wild animal list at all, and the only bird New York restricts on this map is the monk parakeet, which is regulated rather than prohibited under Part 575.

OH.note: Birds are outside Ohio's dangerous-wild-animal chapter entirely.

OK.note: Oklahoma's noncontrolled exotic-species exemption names cockatoos outright, along with cockatiels, macaws, canaries, and other psittacine birds.

PA.note: Conclusion unchanged, reasoning corrected. The previous entry said the Game Code does not reach birds at all, which is wrong: 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines wildlife as wild birds and wild mammals, and the Commission has designated the monk parakeet at 58 Pa. Code § 137.1(a)(9). The reason a cockatoo is lawful is narrower. Wild birds is a closed set of federally listed migratory birds, game birds, and birds the Commission designates, and no cockatoo is any of the three.
PA.quote: All migratory birds as defined in 50 CFR by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service of the Department of the Interior, game birds and any other birds designated by the commission, including, but not limited to, grouse, partridge, pheasant, quail and wild turkey.

RI.quote: Psittacidae (Parrots and their allies) except for Myiopsitta monachus (Monk Parakeet), which requires a permit
RI.note: The whole parrot family, cockatoos included, is permit-free with a single carve-out for the monk parakeet.

SC.note: The only bird South Carolina's import permit reaches is turkeys of genus Meleagris; the pet-trade exemption separately clears parrots.

SD.note: Nondomestic birds are handled by ARSD 12:68:13 rather than the mammal-only possession-permit list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Avian species not otherwise listed, excluding North American game birds, ostriches and cassowary
TN.note: The bird subdivision is written as a catch-all with three exclusions, none of which is a parrot. Class III needs no wildlife permit.

TX.quote: (a) Except as provided by this code, no person may: (1) catch, kill, injure, pursue, or possess, dead or alive, or purchase, sell, expose for sale, transport, ship, or receive or deliver for transportation, a bird that is not a game bird ... (d) Canaries, parrots, and other exotic nongame birds may be sold, purchased, and kept as domestic pets.
TX.note: Cockatoos are parrots in the ordinary sense subsection (d) uses, and the sentence reaches "other exotic nongame birds" in any event. Nothing in Texas law distinguishes them from any other pet parrot.

UT.quote: Parrots Family Psittacidae All species not native to North America
UT.note: Classified as noncontrolled, and a certificate of registration is not required to possess any noncontrolled bird.

VA.quote: Psittaciformes   Psittacidae   Myiopsitta monachus   Monk parakeet*
VA.note: The only parrot on Virginia's permit table is the monk parakeet.

VT.cite: Vermont Domestic Species List, August 2010; Regulation 881; 10 V.S.A. § 4709
VT.quote: Birds Psittaciformes Psittacidae Nymphicus hollandicus Cockatiel Captive Bred Only
VT.note: Vermont is an inverted-list state and the cockatoo falls through all three of its lists. 10 V.S.A. § 4709 bars bringing in, transporting or possessing any live wild bird or animal without authorisation, and the Unrestricted Wild Animal List closes the loop by saying a species found on none of the Restricted, Unrestricted or Domestic lists is considered Restricted. the cockatoo is on none of them: the Unrestricted list's birds are the rock dove, the European buzzard, a run of estrildid finches and the canary, with no psittacine at all, and the Domestic Species List's psittacine section is a closed list of about thirty species that names the budgerigar, the cockatiel, the lovebirds, the rosellas, the conures and Psittacula, and stops. What makes Restricted a ban rather than paperwork is Regulation 881: "the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for the keeping or possession of any wild animal in captivity, except for bona fide scientific or educational purposes". There is no pet category to apply under. This entry read unclear because the Domestic Species List could not be read; it can be now. The list does carry one cacatuid, the cockatiel, Nymphicus hollandicus, which is in the same family as the cockatoos and is the bird people most often assume settles the question. No Cacatua appears anywhere. So Vermont allows the cockatiel and not the cockatoo, off a list that names each species individually.

WA.note: Birds fall outside both the potentially-dangerous-animal statute and the deleterious exotic wildlife rule.

WI.cite: Wis. Stat. § 169.04; DATCP pet bird rules
WI.note: A cockatoo meets Wisconsin's definition of an unregulated 'pet bird': psittacine, non-native, not federally endangered, not a migratory species. The one psittacine Wisconsin does prohibit is the monk parakeet, as an invasive species. Importing one from out of state still calls for a DATCP animal import permit and health certificate.

WV.note: No bird category appears in West Virginia's dangerous-wild-animal guidance at all.

WY.quote: Live warm-blooded wildlife listed in this section... may be imported, possessed or transported without a permit... (b) Birds: (i) Cage and aviary birds.
WY.note: Chapter 10 defines cage and aviary birds as exotic captive-reared birds such as parrots that are adapted to live in a cage; a cockatoo qualifies.

MI.quote: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection is required for the import of exotic, circus and zoo animals, native wild animals, domestic rabbits, nonnative rodents, nonnative reptiles and amphibians, and non-poultry birds
MI.note: Cockatoos is named in no Michigan statute or order. The Large Carnivore Act covers cats and bears, the captive game permit covers native game, and the herp order covers reptiles and amphibians, so nothing reaches a pet parrot. The only requirement is the certificate of veterinary inspection for a non-poultry bird moved into the state.

OR.quote: Pursuant to the definition of "wildlife," the following species are not subject to these rules because they are not "wild" ... (28) Parrots, Parakeets, Lories, and Cockatoos — Psittaciforme (All species).
OR.note: Oregon disposes of the whole parrot order in one line, cockatoos named in it. No psittacine appears on the prohibited bird list, which runs to seven species and is aimed at the Egyptian goose, a thick-knee, two kingfishers and three European passerines. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

NYC.quote: In addition to domesticated dogs and cats, an animal may be kept, possessed, harbored or sold in the City of New York provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law, including federal, state and local laws regulating domestic animals and livestock or protecting wildlife and endangered species. Such animals include, but are not limited to, gerbil, hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and fowl or small birds such as parakeet, parrot, canary and finch.
NYC.note: Cleared by "parrot" in § 161.01(c) and outside the (b)(11) prohibition on predatory or large birds, which is aimed at eagles, hawks, owls, vultures, emus, rheas and ostriches. § 161.01(c) is the article's short affirmative list, and it is written as examples rather than as a closed set: "an animal may be kept ... provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law", followed by gerbil, hamster, guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and small birds. So the question in New York City is always whether something else in § 161.01(b) reaches the animal.

CA.note: Section 671's Testudines entries reach only Chelydridae (snapping turtles). No tortoise family is restricted, and California's own tortoise rules concern the native desert tortoise (Gopherus agassizii) as a protected species, not an exotic-possession restriction.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the red-footed tortoise is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

MA.quote: All species of turtles may be kept without a permit, up to a limit of 100 turtles and/or eggs, in any combination, of each species, except for the following species for which a permit is always required: 1. Species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3). 2. Argentina or Chaco Tortoise (Geochelone chilensis). 3. Gopher Tortoises (Gopherus polyphemus) and all other species in the genus Gopherus. 4. Pancake Tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri). 5. Spotted Turtle (Clemmys guttata). 6. Red-eared Slider (Trachemys scripta, including all subspecies and forms).
MA.note: Falls under the general turtle allowance: no permit, capped at 100 of the species in any combination of animals and eggs, which is a dealer-scale limit rather than a keeper-scale one. The categorical bar is worth checking here and comes out clean on the current IUCN checklist, which carries no assessment for Chelonoidis carbonarius; the older 1996 assessment was published under Geochelone carbonaria and is not on the current list. That makes this a thinner answer than the other tortoises on this row, and a reassessment would move it into the permit tier without any change to Massachusetts law.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: New Jersey is a closed-list state in the strict sense. 7:25-4.2(a) bars possession of any exotic or nongame species without a permit, 4.4 then names the handful that may be kept without one, and 4.5 sweeps everything else back in. The red-footed tortoise appears on none of the Division's three lists, so it is not exempt under 4.4, not one of the families singled out in 4.3, and not potentially dangerous under 4.8. That leaves 4.5, and the permit it points to is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, which 4.7 conditions on diet, caging that prevents escape, lawful acquisition, veterinary care and freedom from disease. The Division's own handout tells readers to phone the permits office for anything the lists do not name, which is a fair signal that the catch-all is where these end up rather than an oversight.

VA.note: No tortoise, Chelonoidis, or Testudinidae entry appears in the nonnative-animal permit table. Subsection (H) allows possession of nonnative animals not listed in the table, subject to general law.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the red-footed tortoise is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: A tortoise is a turtle in the taxonomic sense the category uses (Order Testudines), the same reading applied to the sulcata and Russian tortoise.

RI.quote: All exotic species of turtles may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit, except endangered species.
RI.note: The three tortoises pulled back out are the Chaco tortoise, the genus Gopherus and the pancake tortoise. Chelonoidis carbonarius is none of them and is not federally endangered.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Chelonoidis carbonarius is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Chelonoidis carbonarius is South American and is not indigenous to Texas, so the nongame possession caps do not apply. The turtle and tortoise restrictions in this state are all aimed at native species, and the only tortoise among them is the threatened Texas tortoise.

LA.note: Absent from Louisiana's prohibited and restricted nonnative-reptile lists (which do name the savannah and Nile monitor). The native-turtle registration requirement at § 101.G governs Louisiana's own species and does not reach this South American tortoise.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of turtles with a carapace or shell length of more than 4 inches and not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(ix) Testudinidae (tortoises);
MT.note: Cleared by family, above the four-inch floor, the same basis already used for the sulcata and Russian tortoise.

MS.note: Mississippi's inherently-dangerous list is drawn family by family and is entirely mammalian; no reptile is restricted under this rule at any size.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in North Dakota's captive-wildlife chapter or current administrative rules.

KS.note: Kansas's only exotic-pet statute reaches six named cats, bears, and non-native venomous snakes. Tortoises are untouched at any size.

NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic-animal statute covers venomous reptiles and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

KY.note: On neither the prohibited species list nor the inherently-dangerous list, which among reptiles names only gila monsters, beaded lizards, the Komodo dragon, crocodilians and venomous snakes other than hognose.

WV.note: The only reptiles the statute points the board at are constrictors over six feet, venomous snakes and crocodilians.

IA.note: The squamate/reptile half of Iowa's dangerous-wild-animal definition is exhaustively enumerated (certain monitors, helodermatids, venomous snakes, three named giant constrictors). No tortoise is among them.

SD.note: South Dakota's possession-permit list covers mammals only (carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants, primates); reptiles fall under Game, Fish and Parks rules instead.

MO.note: Not native to Missouri, so outside Class I, and not a deadly or dangerous reptile over eight feet under § 578.023.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: Non-venomous and not on the prohibited list, so no permit is required for personal use; the reptile must remain confined and never be released.

NH.quote: (4) Non-venomous reptiles, except the following: a. Indigenous reptile species listed in Table 800.1...
NH.note: No tortoise appears anywhere in the controlled table, so this non-native species clears the non-controlled category outright.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: A conventional pet under the reptile category, no size or weight qualifier attached.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: No permit required; the clean list sets no size limit on reptiles.

OH.note: Not a dangerous wild animal and not native to Ohio, so nothing in Chapter 935 reaches it.

WA.quote: Class reptilia ... Order crocodilia, all species
