WA.note: Not listed. Washington's reptile concerns under this chapter are venom and crocodilians rather than size or origin.

ME.note: Maine's own tortoise clearance list (documented in this site's sulcata-tortoise research) names the Russian, Greek, Hermann's, leopard, red-footed and yellow-footed tortoises by common name. The red-footed tortoise is expressly included; the exact binomial spelling used on Maine's PDF was not independently re-verified this round because the source PDF resisted text extraction, so double-check the primary document (maine.gov/ifw/docs/unrestrictedspecies.pdf) before publishing.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Tortoises (Genera: Agrionemys, Aldabrachelys, Chelonoidis, Centrochelys, Geochelone, Gopherus, Indotestudo, Manouria, Psuedotestudo, Stigmochelys, Testudo)
AR.note: Confirmed directly from the current AGFC PDF (revised 11/1/22). Genus Chelonoidis is named outright, which covers the red-footed tortoise without ambiguity.

HI.cite: List of Conditionally Approved Animals, Family Testudinidae
HI.quote: Chelonoidis (all species in genus except C. elephantopus)
HI.note: Confirmed directly from the HDOA conditional-animal-list PDF. Unlike the sulcata (which moved out of Geochelone entirely into the unlisted genus Centrochelys, leaving its status genuinely unclear), the red-footed tortoise's current genus Chelonoidis is named outright on this list, with only the Galapagos tortoise (C. elephantopus, separately restricted) carved out. Chelonoidis carbonarius is squarely covered.

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The red-footed tortoise is South American and does not appear on the Fish and Boat Commission's published list of Pennsylvania native species, so Chapter 79, which is built entirely around native species, does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The red-footed tortoise is South American and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

VT.quote: Testudines | Testudinidae | Geochelone | carbonaria | Red-footed tortoise (Captive Bred Only)
VT.note: Unrestricted under its older name Geochelone carbonaria, now Chelonoidis carbonarius, and subject to the same Captive Bred Only condition, which requires a statement of origin or certificate of veterinary inspection on import. Only three chelonians are on the whole Unrestricted list, so this is a narrow permission.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Turtle | Testudinidae | Geochelone carbonaria | Tortoise, Red-foot | II
NM.note: Group II on the Director's list: not known to be invasive or dangerous, but an importation permit is still required before the animal may be brought into New Mexico. Listed under the older genus Geochelone, now Chelonoidis.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The red-footed tortoise is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The red-footed tortoise is on none of it, so no special licence is required. The only restricted tortoises are the genus Gopherus.

DE.cite: 3 Del. Admin. Code 903-6.2, with Del. Code tit. 3 § 7201
DE.quote: Unless specifically exempt from the permitting requirement as presented in regulation 6.1, all persons who would own or have custody of an exotic animal must first obtain a permit issued by the Department.
DE.note: The red-footed tortoise is a live reptile not native to Delaware and is not on the exempt list, so regulation 6.2 requires an Individual permit before anyone may bring one in, possess, sell or exhibit it. Delaware exempts no chelonian of any kind.  The permit is a $25 Individual permit from the Department of Agriculture, issued where possession will be in the public interest, so this is a real route rather than a closed door.

CO.quote: Any species of turtle native only to the tropical and subtropical region from the following families: Testudinidae (tortoises)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. CPW files Chelonoidis carbonarius against this line. Its South American range is entirely inside the band Chapter W-7 § 700(G) draws. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The red-footed tortoise is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: A person may not take, possess, or transport turtles without a resident angling license and a recreational turtle license. ... A person does not need the licenses specified under subdivision 1: ... (2) when buying a turtle at a retail outlet
MN.note: Turtles are the gap in the 2021 pet reptile rule. Section 97A.401, subd. 8 covers snakes, lizards and salamanders and stops there, so turtles stay under their own older regime, which is a licence requirement with a short list of exemptions rather than a source condition. Whether a red-footed tortoise is a "turtle" for this section is not spelled out, since Minnesota never defines the word and its turtle rules are plainly written around aquatic natives. It does not matter much in practice: read broadly, the retail outlet exemption in subd. 2c covers a pet-shop animal anyway, and read narrowly the section does not reach it at all. Either way no licence is needed for one bought at retail, and the species is on neither invasive species list.

OR.quote: Tortoises -- Testudinidae -- All species;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. The whole family is cleared. Worth contrasting with the turtles a few lines above, where Oregon excepts nine genera from the Emydidae clearance and prohibits most of them outright. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No tortoise appears in any category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three. One caveat that applies to every Connecticut turtle on this map: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 26-78 addresses turtles separately from the regulation, and it could not be read this sitting because cga.ct.gov refuses every connection from this container. This entry rests on § 26-55-6, which is the comprehensive rule and mentions no turtle sale ban, and the point is flagged rather than assumed away.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. No tortoise is native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The red-footed tortoise is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Chelonoidis carbonarius is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: New York City draws its turtle line by size rather than by species: the reptile clause ends with "all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches". The red-footed tortoise is not otherwise named, so an adult is lawful and a hatchling is not, and the animal grows out of the prohibition rather than into it. The four-inch figure is the same one the federal rule at 21 C.F.R. 1240.62 uses, and the reason is the same: small turtles are the ones children put in their mouths. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the red-footed tortoise is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Chelonoidis carbonarius is CITES Appendix II but not federally listed, so R657-53-9(1)(d)'s zero limit for Endangered Species Act listings does not reach it. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Alabama works from a prohibited list rather than a permitted one, so the question is only whether the red-footed tortoise is on it, and it is not. 220-2-.26(1) reaches non-native venomous reptiles, tegus, mongooses, wild rabbits and hares, a block of mammals when they come from outside the state, a run of fish, and everything the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act. The other half of Alabama is 220-2-.92, which protects native nongame species, and that one is about Alabama's own wildlife. Chelonoidis carbonarius is CITES Appendix II, which governs international trade and not Alabama possession.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana splits its reptiles cleanly and The red-footed tortoise lands on the free side of the split. 312 IAC 9-5 governs reptiles and amphibians native to Indiana, and it is the rule that does the real work: 9-5-1(b) makes every native a protected wild animal, 9-5-6(f) caps possession at four per species, and 9-5-7 bars selling one regardless of where it came from, against a list of 99 taxa named by binomial. The red-footed tortoise is on none of them. The other rule, 312 IAC 9-11, requires a permit only for Class I animals, which is the cottontail and three squirrels, Class II, which is Indiana's furbearers and a named run of small wild cats, and Class III, which is purebred wolves, bears, wild cats, venomous reptiles and crocodilians at least five feet long. Nothing there reaches it either.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided, monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license; except those which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma and which may be potentially injurious or detrimental to Oklahoma's wildlife, agriculture or public safety in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations.
OK.note: Oklahoma exempts non-indigenous reptiles and amphibians as a class rather than species by species. 800:25-25-3(c) clears them from import and export requirements and from both wildlife breeder licences, and the red-footed tortoise is squarely inside it. The carve-out at the end of the same sentence has two limbs joined by "and", so it bites only on a species that is biologically capable of establishing a self-sustaining population in the wild of Oklahoma AND is injurious under federal rules; neither is true here. What remains is the statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A), which reaches closed-season wildlife, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats. Not one of the three touches the red-footed tortoise.

HI.note: Part A is headed FOR RESEARCH AND EXHIBITION, so a listed animal has no pet route: a university or a licensed exhibitor can hold one and a private keeper cannot. The inland bearded dragon is the species the pet trade actually sells, and Hawaii names it directly, alongside the Australian and Nullarbor bearded dragons. The official list misspells the species as vittaceps for vitticeps.

CA.note: California's restricted reptile list runs to crocodilians, snapping turtles, venomous snakes and the Gila monster, and nothing else. No agamid is restricted, so the most popular pet lizard in the country is unregulated here.

PA.note: The inland bearded dragon is Australian and is absent from the Fish and Boat Commission's list of Pennsylvania native species. Pennsylvania's Chapter 79 regulates native reptiles and amphibians only, and the Game and Wildlife Code reaches wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so a non-native reptile falls outside both agencies.

MI.note: The inland bearded dragon is Australian and is not a Michigan species. Michigan's Fisheries Order 224.21 reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR captive game permit reaches a reptile, so nothing in Michigan restricts it. Bringing one in calls for a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules.

VT.quote: Squamata | Iguania | Agamidae | all species | Agamas
VT.note: The whole agamid family is unrestricted, so the bearded dragon needs no permit.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Lizard | Agamidae | Pogona vitticepts | Bearded dragon | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. The list misspells the species, printing vitticepts for vitticeps.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The inland bearded dragon is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The bearded dragon is on none of it, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: The bearded dragon is covered by the entry for bearded dragons is named on the exempt list at regulation 6.1, so it needs no permit at all. Delaware exempts lizards generously and exempts no snake, turtle or tortoise at all, which is the sharpest line in this state's rules.

CO.quote: Any species of lizard native only to the tropical and subtropical region from the following families: Agamidae (chisel-teeth lizards)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. CPW files Pogona vitticeps against this line, treating the central bearded dragon's Australian interior range as falling inside the tropical and subtropical band. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The bearded dragon is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A bearded dragon is a lizard, so the breeder-source condition applies to it as much as to a Minnesota native. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Bearded dragons -- Agamidae -- Pogona All species;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Cleared at genus level. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. Agamidae appears in no category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. Agamidae is not represented among Maryland natives. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The bearded dragon is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Pogona vitticeps is not indigenous to Texas, so 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O does not reach it, and the dangerous wild animal list at Health & Safety Code § 822.101(4) contains no reptile. Texas has no general exotic reptile permit: the only reptiles it regulates by name are the six controlled exotic snakes, the venomous species, and its own native herpetofauna through the nongame and threatened species subchapters.

MA.quote: The following Agamid Lizards (Agamidae) may be kept without a permit: Dragon Lizards (Amphibolorus spp.) Forest, Garden and Bloodsucker Lizards (Calotes spp.) Sailfin Lizards (Hydrosaurus spp.) Bearded Dragons (Pogona spp.) Water Dragon (Physignathus spp.) Frilled Lizards (Chlamydosaurus spp.) Uromastyx Lizards (Uromastyx spp.)
MA.note: Named as a genus, "Bearded Dragons (Pogona spp.)". Like the iguanids, the agamid entry is a closed list rather than a family clearance, so the naming matters: an agamid outside these seven genera is not exempt. Pogona vitticeps is IUCN least concern.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Pogona vitticeps is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Pogona vitticeps is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the bearded dragon is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the bearded dragon is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The reptile clause is a list of families and the bearded dragon belongs to none of them: not Helodermatidae, not a venomous snake family, not Boidae, Pythonidae, Varanidae, Iguanidae, teiidae, Chelydridae or Crocodylia. Agamidae appears nowhere in the article, which is a notable gap given that Iguanidae, Varanidae and Teiidae are all taken as families.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: New Jersey is a closed-list state in the strict sense. 7:25-4.2(a) bars possession of any exotic or nongame species without a permit, 4.4 then names the handful that may be kept without one, and 4.5 sweeps everything else back in. The bearded dragon appears on none of the Division's three lists, so it is not exempt under 4.4, not one of the families singled out in 4.3, and not potentially dangerous under 4.8. That leaves 4.5, and the permit it points to is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, which 4.7 conditions on diet, caging that prevents escape, lawful acquisition, veterinary care and freedom from disease. The Division's own handout tells readers to phone the permits office for anything the lists do not name, which is a fair signal that the catch-all is where these end up rather than an oversight. Agamidae is missing from 4.3, which does list the collared lizard, the chuckwalla, the alligator lizard, the skinks and the geckos, so Pogona vitticeps ends up in the catch-all rather than on the named list. It is the single most common pet lizard in the country and New Jersey requires a permit for it.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the bearded dragon is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Pogona vitticeps is on none of the division's tables, which list Utah animals. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Alabama works from a prohibited list rather than a permitted one, so the question is only whether the bearded dragon is on it, and it is not. 220-2-.26(1) reaches non-native venomous reptiles, tegus, mongooses, wild rabbits and hares, a block of mammals when they come from outside the state, a run of fish, and everything the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act. The other half of Alabama is 220-2-.92, which protects native nongame species, and that one is about Alabama's own wildlife.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana splits its reptiles cleanly and The bearded dragon lands on the free side of the split. 312 IAC 9-5 governs reptiles and amphibians native to Indiana, and it is the rule that does the real work: 9-5-1(b) makes every native a protected wild animal, 9-5-6(f) caps possession at four per species, and 9-5-7 bars selling one regardless of where it came from, against a list of 99 taxa named by binomial. The bearded dragon is on none of them. The other rule, 312 IAC 9-11, requires a permit only for Class I animals, which is the cottontail and three squirrels, Class II, which is Indiana's furbearers and a named run of small wild cats, and Class III, which is purebred wolves, bears, wild cats, venomous reptiles and crocodilians at least five feet long. Nothing there reaches it either.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided, monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license; except those which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma and which may be potentially injurious or detrimental to Oklahoma's wildlife, agriculture or public safety in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations.
OK.note: Oklahoma exempts non-indigenous reptiles and amphibians as a class rather than species by species. 800:25-25-3(c) clears them from import and export requirements and from both wildlife breeder licences, and the bearded dragon is squarely inside it. The carve-out at the end of the same sentence has two limbs joined by "and", so it bites only on a species that is biologically capable of establishing a self-sustaining population in the wild of Oklahoma AND is injurious under federal rules; neither is true here. What remains is the statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A), which reaches closed-season wildlife, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats. Not one of the three touches the bearded dragon.

WI.quote: A person is exempt from holding a license or other approval as required under this chapter to possess live nonnative wild animals that are not endangered or threatened species, except for any of the following: 1. Pheasants ... 2. Nonnative wild birds of the family anatidae that are migratory birds. 3. Nonnative wild animals that are harmful wild animals.
WI.note: Wisconsin runs its captive wildlife chapter on an exemption rather than a list, and the bearded dragon is exempt by class. 169.04(1)(b) bars possessing any live wild animal without a licence, and then 169.04(4)(b) exempts every nonnative wild animal that is not endangered or threatened, with three carve-outs: hunting-preserve game birds, nonnative migratory waterfowl, and harmful wild animals. Harmful wild animals under 169.11(1)(a) are cougars, bears, wild swine and feral swine plus anything the department adds by rule, and no lizard has been added. The other rule to know about is NR 40, the invasive species chapter, which runs on a separate authority and lists no pet reptile.

NC.quote: Wild Animals. - Game animals; fur-bearing animals; feral swine; and all other wild mammals except marine mammals found in coastal fishing waters. In addition, this definition includes members of the following groups which are on the federal list of endangered or threatened species: wild amphibians, wild reptiles except sea turtles inhabiting and depending upon coastal fishing waters, and wild invertebrates except invertebrates declared to be pests under the Structural Pest Control Act of North Carolina of 1955 or the North Carolina Pesticide Law of 1971.
NC.note: North Carolina answers this in its definitions rather than its permit sections, and the answer is that the Wildlife Resources Commission has no jurisdiction. § 113-129(15) defines wild animals as game animals, fur-bearing animals, feral swine and other wild mammals, and then extends only to "wild amphibians, wild reptiles ... and wild invertebrates" that are "on the federal list of endangered or threatened species". The bearded dragon is not federally listed, so it is not a wild animal in North Carolina at all and the captivity licence at § 113-272.5 has nothing to attach to. § 14-417 reaches venomous reptiles and large constrictors, and § 153A-131 lets counties regulate dangerous animals, which is where any local restriction would come from.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: 1. tropical fishes 2. rats and mice 3. rabbits ... 15. reptiles 16. amphibians. The provisions of this section do not privilege the import or possession of a species otherwise protected or regulated by other provisions of this title.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts the bearded dragon from its one import permit and then has nothing else to say. § 50-16-20(A) requires a permit only for furbearers, cervids, non-domestic pigs and bovids, coyote, bear, turkey, and marine or freshwater species not already found here. § 50-16-60 separately exempts a list of pet-trade animals from the permit requirement, and reptiles and amphibians are on it as whole classes. The one Restricted Nonnative Wildlife designation the state has made, at Regulation 123-152, is the Argentine black and white tegu.

OH.quote: "Restricted snake" means any of the following: ... (c) Reticulated pythons; (d) Indian pythons; (e) Burmese pythons; (f) North African rock pythons; (g) South African rock pythons; (h) Amethystine pythons.
OH.note: Ohio's two restrictive schemes both miss the bearded dragon. § 935.01(C) lists the dangerous wild animals, which are big cats, bears, primates, hyenas, elephants and the like, and § 935.01(L) lists the restricted snakes, which are venomous species and six named giant pythons. Neither reaches a lizard. The other scheme is the propagating licence at § 1533.71, which covers game birds, game quadrupeds, reptiles, amphibians and fur-bearing animals and is about propagating rather than keeping.

RI.quote: The following Agamid Lizards (Agamidae) may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit: Amphibolorus spp., Calotes spp., Hydrosaurus spp., Pogona spp., Water Dragon (Physignathus spp.)
RI.note: The whole genus Pogona is named, so no exotic animal possession permit and no importation permit. Rhode Island reserves its lizard permits for the Gila monster, beaded lizards and all monitors at § 3.17(A)(4)(c)(1); nothing else in the lizard section needs one.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Reptiles, Geckos and Lizards
AR.quote: Bearded Dragon (Genus Pogona)
AR.note: The genus is named twice over: the Austral-Asian Agamid Lizards entry also lists Pogona among Chlamydosaurus, Hydrosaurus and Intellagama. Either way it is exempt from Codes 09.02, 09.07 and 09.10, so no possession, breeding or importation permit.

ME.note: Named by species rather than by genus, so no asterisk and no conservation-status filter. The whole Reptilia section of the list sits under the heading "Captive Bred Origin Only", which is the condition on the clearance: a wild-caught animal of the same species is not unrestricted and falls back to § 7.06(4), under which an uncategorised animal may not be possessed at all.

MO.quote: Except for federally-designated endangered species and species listed in 3 CSR 10-4.117 and 3 CSR 10-9.240, the following may be bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit: Asian clams (Corbicula species) taken from impoundments that are not waters of the state; bison; amphibians, reptiles, and mammals not native to Missouri except those mammals located in a licensed big game hunting preserve; and those birds (except ring necked pheasants and gray partridge) not native to the continental United States.
MO.note: Missouri sorts by nativity rather than by species list, and a bearded dragon is a reptile not native to Missouri, so the clearance covers buying, selling, possessing, transporting and exhibiting one without any permit. The two carve-outs from the clearance do not reach it: 3 CSR 10-4.117 is the prohibited species rule and is fish, crayfish and aquatic plants, and 3 CSR 10-9.240 Class II wildlife is the state's venomous natives plus the mountain lion, wolf and black bear.

ID.quote: Conventional Pets. Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders.
ID.note: A bearded dragon is a non-venomous, non-dangerous reptile and is not native Idaho wildlife, so it is a conventional pet. Section 200.06 then says no Department permit is needed to import, export, transport, possess or sell a conventional pet, provided it is not intended for release into the wild. Idaho answers by category rather than by species list, which is unusual and is why so few of its cells need a species search.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake
NH.note: A bearded dragon is an exotic, non-venomous reptile and is neither an alligator nor a crocodile, so it is non-controlled for both possession and importation. New Hampshire clears exotic reptiles as a class rather than by species, with three exceptions, and Fis 803.03(b)(4) repeats the clearance for importation, so neither possessing nor bringing one into the state needs a permit. The rule was readopted in full in April 2026 and this structure survived unchanged.

WY.quote: The animals listed in this section may be imported or possessed without securing an importation/possession permit and shall not require written authorization from the Chief of Fisheries. A certificate of veterinary inspection or a fish health and AIS inspection are not required. (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.
WY.note: A bearded dragon is a reptile and appears on neither restricted list. Section 8, the no-permit-will-issue list, is federal injurious and endangered listings, aquatic invasive species, Xenopus, three frogs and toads, grass carp and mosquitofish. Section 9 requires a permit for venomous reptiles, for herptiles listed in Commission Regulation Chapter 52 that need a scientific or educational take permit, for Wyoming-indigenous herptiles imported for commercial use, and for aquatic turtles in ornamental ponds. Neither reaches this animal, so Section 10 applies and nothing at all is required, not even a veterinary certificate.

KY.quote: Except as established in Section 5 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport into Kentucky, or possess the following exotic wildlife that are considered potentially injurious to native ecosystems
KY.note: A bearded dragon is exotic wildlife under § 1, having never naturally existed in the wild in Kentucky. Kentucky's only possession bars for an exotic are the two lists in § 4, the potentially injurious species at (1) and the inherently dangerous species at (2), and this animal is on neither. It is also not on the § 7 permit-exempt list, so a transportation permit under § 2(1) is needed to bring one into the state; possession itself is unrestricted once it is here.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state due to the potential risk of establishment in the wild and detrimental hazard to native wildlife and public health and safety
LA.note: A bearded dragon is a nonnative reptile and appears on neither list. Louisiana rewrote this rule in January 2025 and it is now one of the strictest reptile chapters in the country, but it works by two short named lists rather than by a general permit. § 101.K.2.a is the prohibited nonnative list, fourteen entries covering crocodilians, tegus, two monitors, the green iguana, the brown anole, the Burmese python, the brown tree snake, four groups of venomous snake and three amphibians. § 101.K.2.c is the restricted nonnative list, ten entries needing a permit. This animal is on neither, and § 101.K.1's restricted snake permit reaches only constrictors over eight feet and venomous snakes, so nothing attaches.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: A bearded dragon is a nonvenomous reptile, so it is on the clean list and needs no possession permit. Alaska's clean list is otherwise a roll call of individual species, so this one class-wide entry is the widest clearance in it, and it is what makes the strictest exotic pet state in the country an easy one for a lizard keeper. Subsection (e) is the only thing riding on it: a listed species that is endangered still needs a federal permit.

MT.quote: unless otherwise regulated pursuant to 87-5-116, all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous lizards not on the controlled or prohibited lists, including but not limited to the following families or subfamilies
MT.note: The bearded dragon is an agamid, and Agamidae is the first family named in the clause. Montana runs a white list and this clause is where nonvenomous lizards are let onto it. The two lists it defers to are short: ARM 12.6.2208 classifies no reptile as controlled at all, and ARM 12.6.2215(6) prohibits fifteen reptiles, all of them crocodilians, large constrictors, venomous snakes or the red-eared slider. The clause is also open, "including but not limited to", so a family it does not name is not thereby excluded.

WA.quote: "Wildlife" means all species of the animal kingdom whose members exist in Washington in a wild state. This includes but is not limited to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, and invertebrates.
WA.note: Pogona vitticeps does not exist in Washington in a wild state, so it is not Washington wildlife. Washington answers by a geographic qualifier rather than by a species list, which is why it is one of the shortest states to read. Three things then have to be checked and all three come back empty: the animal is not designated deleterious exotic wildlife at WAC 220-640-200(1), which is a mute swan, mongooses, wild boar, javelina, six bovid genera and a run of cervids; it is not a potentially dangerous wild animal under RCW 16.30.010(2), whose enumerated definition reaches only mammals and reptiles named in it; and WAC 220-450-030's importation and possession rules are written for "live wild animals, wild birds, or game fish", which are the same geographically limited terms.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department, if consistent with the department's fish and wildlife management program, to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table and in 4VAC15-20-210 that the board finds and declares to be predatory or undesirable
VA.note: A bearded dragon is a nonnative (exotic) animal under 4VAC15-20-50, not naturalized in Virginia, and absent from the permit table. Virginia permits by table and the reptile block of that table is four entries: all alligators and caimans, all crocodiles, all gavials, and the brown tree snake. Nothing here is on it, and 4VAC15-30-20 attaches the special permit only to animals the board has classed as predatory or undesirable, which is what the table is.

HI.note: Part A is headed FOR RESEARCH AND EXHIBITION, so a listed animal has no pet route: a university or a licensed exhibitor can hold one and a private keeper cannot. Named individually in the Gekkonidae block, so there is no argument to be had about genus or family coverage.

CA.note: California's restricted reptile list runs to crocodilians, snapping turtles, venomous snakes and the Gila monster, and nothing else. No gecko appears on the restricted list; the only lizard California restricts is the reticulate Gila monster.

PA.note: The leopard gecko is a Central and South Asian species and is absent from the Fish and Boat Commission's list of Pennsylvania native species. Pennsylvania's Chapter 79 regulates native reptiles and amphibians only, and the Game and Wildlife Code reaches wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so a non-native reptile falls outside both agencies.

MI.note: The leopard gecko is a Central and South Asian species and is not a Michigan species. Michigan's Fisheries Order 224.21 reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR captive game permit reaches a reptile, so nothing in Michigan restricts it. Bringing one in calls for a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules.

VT.quote: Squamata | Scleroglossa | Gekkonidae | all species | Geckos
VT.note: The whole family is unrestricted and the Restricted list claws back no gecko, so every pet gecko is clear here.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Lizard | Gekkonidae | Eublepharis macularius | Leopard Gecko | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The leopard gecko is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The leopard gecko is on none of it, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: The leopard gecko is covered by the entry for geckos is named on the exempt list at regulation 6.1, so it needs no permit at all. Delaware exempts lizards generously and exempts no snake, turtle or tortoise at all, which is the sharpest line in this state's rules.

CO.quote: Any species from the families Diplodactylidae (eyelash geckos), Eublepharidae (eyelid geckos), or Gekkonidae (geckos) except Mediterranean house geckos (Hemidactylus turcicus)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. Eublepharidae is cleared outright in the Other Species block rather than through the native-range test, which matters for this species: the leopard gecko's Afghanistan-to-northwest-India range would be a hard call under that test. CPW files Eublepharis macularius against this line. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The leopard gecko is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A leopard gecko is a lizard, so the breeder-source condition applies to it as much as to a Minnesota native. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Geckos -- Gekkonidae and Eublepharidae -- All species;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Eublepharidae is named in its own right, so the leopard gecko is squarely inside it. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No gecko appears in any category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. No gecko is native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The leopard gecko is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Eublepharis macularius is not indigenous to Texas, so 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O does not reach it, and the dangerous wild animal list at Health & Safety Code § 822.101(4) contains no reptile. Texas has no general exotic reptile permit: the only reptiles it regulates by name are the six controlled exotic snakes, the venomous species, and its own native herpetofauna through the nongame and threatened species subchapters. The native the list does name is the Texas banded gecko, Coleonyx brevis, capped at 25, which is a different genus.

MA.quote: All Geckos (Gekkonidae) may be kept without a permit except for those species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3) and the Big Bend Gecko (Coleonyx reticulatus) which require a permit.
MA.note: Geckos are cleared as a family with one named exception, the Big Bend gecko, plus the categorical bar. Eublepharis macularius is IUCN least concern and appears on no list, so it is exempt. The Big Bend gecko exception is a native-range conservation matter rather than a pet-trade one.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Eublepharis macularius is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Eublepharis macularius is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the leopard gecko is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the leopard gecko is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The reptile clause is a list of families and the leopard gecko belongs to none of them: not Helodermatidae, not a venomous snake family, not Boidae, Pythonidae, Varanidae, Iguanidae, teiidae, Chelydridae or Crocodylia. Gekkonidae and Eublepharidae appear nowhere in the article.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: ... xiv. Geckos - Family Gekkonidae other than Tokay Gecko;
NJ.note: The leopard gecko is answered by name on the 4.3 permit list rather than by the catch-all. The entry is "Geckos - Family Gekkonidae other than Tokay Gecko", which takes every gecko but one. The list is written by family as often as by species, and 4.3 is open-ended, "include, but are not limited to", so being on it settles the permit question but not being on it settles nothing. The permit is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, subject to the general possession criteria at 4.7. Eublepharis macularius has since been moved to Eublepharidae, but the list is using Gekkonidae in the older broad sense that covered all geckos, which is the only reading on which the tokay carve-out makes sense, since the tokay would otherwise not need excluding.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work.
