The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the leopard gecko is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. The one native gecko Utah does regulate is the western banded gecko, Coleonyx variegatus, at Limited, two a day and four in total, so a Utah-caught gecko and a captive-bred Eublepharis macularius get very different answers. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Alabama works from a prohibited list rather than a permitted one, so the question is only whether the leopard gecko is on it, and it is not. 220-2-.26(1) reaches non-native venomous reptiles, tegus, mongooses, wild rabbits and hares, a block of mammals when they come from outside the state, a run of fish, and everything the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act. The other half of Alabama is 220-2-.92, which protects native nongame species, and that one is about Alabama's own wildlife.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana splits its reptiles cleanly and The leopard gecko lands on the free side of the split. 312 IAC 9-5 governs reptiles and amphibians native to Indiana, and it is the rule that does the real work: 9-5-1(b) makes every native a protected wild animal, 9-5-6(f) caps possession at four per species, and 9-5-7 bars selling one regardless of where it came from, against a list of 99 taxa named by binomial. The leopard gecko is on none of them. The other rule, 312 IAC 9-11, requires a permit only for Class I animals, which is the cottontail and three squirrels, Class II, which is Indiana's furbearers and a named run of small wild cats, and Class III, which is purebred wolves, bears, wild cats, venomous reptiles and crocodilians at least five feet long. Nothing there reaches it either.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided, monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license; except those which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma and which may be potentially injurious or detrimental to Oklahoma's wildlife, agriculture or public safety in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations.
OK.note: Oklahoma exempts non-indigenous reptiles and amphibians as a class rather than species by species. 800:25-25-3(c) clears them from import and export requirements and from both wildlife breeder licences, and the leopard gecko is squarely inside it. The carve-out at the end of the same sentence has two limbs joined by "and", so it bites only on a species that is biologically capable of establishing a self-sustaining population in the wild of Oklahoma AND is injurious under federal rules; neither is true here. What remains is the statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A), which reaches closed-season wildlife, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats. Not one of the three touches the leopard gecko.

WI.quote: A person is exempt from holding a license or other approval as required under this chapter to possess live nonnative wild animals that are not endangered or threatened species, except for any of the following: 1. Pheasants ... 2. Nonnative wild birds of the family anatidae that are migratory birds. 3. Nonnative wild animals that are harmful wild animals.
WI.note: Wisconsin runs its captive wildlife chapter on an exemption rather than a list, and the leopard gecko is exempt by class. 169.04(1)(b) bars possessing any live wild animal without a licence, and then 169.04(4)(b) exempts every nonnative wild animal that is not endangered or threatened, with three carve-outs: hunting-preserve game birds, nonnative migratory waterfowl, and harmful wild animals. Harmful wild animals under 169.11(1)(a) are cougars, bears, wild swine and feral swine plus anything the department adds by rule, and no lizard has been added. The other rule to know about is NR 40, the invasive species chapter, which runs on a separate authority and lists no pet reptile.

NC.quote: Wild Animals. - Game animals; fur-bearing animals; feral swine; and all other wild mammals except marine mammals found in coastal fishing waters. In addition, this definition includes members of the following groups which are on the federal list of endangered or threatened species: wild amphibians, wild reptiles except sea turtles inhabiting and depending upon coastal fishing waters, and wild invertebrates except invertebrates declared to be pests under the Structural Pest Control Act of North Carolina of 1955 or the North Carolina Pesticide Law of 1971.
NC.note: North Carolina answers this in its definitions rather than its permit sections, and the answer is that the Wildlife Resources Commission has no jurisdiction. § 113-129(15) defines wild animals as game animals, fur-bearing animals, feral swine and other wild mammals, and then extends only to "wild amphibians, wild reptiles ... and wild invertebrates" that are "on the federal list of endangered or threatened species". The leopard gecko is not federally listed, so it is not a wild animal in North Carolina at all and the captivity licence at § 113-272.5 has nothing to attach to. § 14-417 reaches venomous reptiles and large constrictors, and § 153A-131 lets counties regulate dangerous animals, which is where any local restriction would come from.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: 1. tropical fishes 2. rats and mice 3. rabbits ... 15. reptiles 16. amphibians. The provisions of this section do not privilege the import or possession of a species otherwise protected or regulated by other provisions of this title.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts the leopard gecko from its one import permit and then has nothing else to say. § 50-16-20(A) requires a permit only for furbearers, cervids, non-domestic pigs and bovids, coyote, bear, turkey, and marine or freshwater species not already found here. § 50-16-60 separately exempts a list of pet-trade animals from the permit requirement, and reptiles and amphibians are on it as whole classes. The one Restricted Nonnative Wildlife designation the state has made, at Regulation 123-152, is the Argentine black and white tegu.

OH.quote: "Restricted snake" means any of the following: ... (c) Reticulated pythons; (d) Indian pythons; (e) Burmese pythons; (f) North African rock pythons; (g) South African rock pythons; (h) Amethystine pythons.
OH.note: Ohio's two restrictive schemes both miss the leopard gecko. § 935.01(C) lists the dangerous wild animals, which are big cats, bears, primates, hyenas, elephants and the like, and § 935.01(L) lists the restricted snakes, which are venomous species and six named giant pythons. Neither reaches a lizard. The other scheme is the propagating licence at § 1533.71, which covers game birds, game quadrupeds, reptiles, amphibians and fur-bearing animals and is about propagating rather than keeping.

RI.quote: All Gekkos (Gekkonidae) may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit except the Big Bend Gekko (Coleonyx reticulatus)
RI.note: The rule writes Gekkonidae, and on current taxonomy the leopard gecko is a eublepharid rather than a gekkonid. The single exception settles it: Coleonyx reticulatus is itself a eublepharid, in the same family as Eublepharis, so the family name is being used in the broad pre-split sense for all geckos. Reading it narrowly would leave the one named exception outside the clause it excepts.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Reptiles, Geckos and Lizards
AR.quote: Leopard Gecko (Eublepharis macularius)
AR.note: Named by species, and the genus is separately cleared under Eublepherine Geckos alongside Coleonyx, Goniurosaurus and Hemitheconyx. No possession, breeding or importation permit.

ME.quote: all species in infraorder Gekkota Except for: Nephrurus deleani
ME.note: Maine clears geckos at infraorder rank, which sidesteps the family-splitting problem that other states run into: Eublepharidae, Diplodactylidae and Gekkonidae are all inside Gekkota. Eublepharis macularius is IUCN Least Concern, not CITES Appendix I and on neither USFWS list, so the asterisk on the entry does not remove it. The one exception, the Pernatty knob-tail, is Category 2. The whole Reptilia section of the list sits under the heading "Captive Bred Origin Only", which is the condition on the clearance: a wild-caught animal of the same species is not unrestricted and falls back to § 7.06(4), under which an uncategorised animal may not be possessed at all.

MO.quote: Except for federally-designated endangered species and species listed in 3 CSR 10-4.117 and 3 CSR 10-9.240, the following may be bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit: Asian clams (Corbicula species) taken from impoundments that are not waters of the state; bison; amphibians, reptiles, and mammals not native to Missouri except those mammals located in a licensed big game hunting preserve; and those birds (except ring necked pheasants and gray partridge) not native to the continental United States.
MO.note: A non-native reptile, so no permit to buy, sell, possess, transport or exhibit. Nothing in the confined wildlife chapter attaches to it: Class I at 3 CSR 10-9.230 is birds native to the continental United States plus mammals and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri, and a leopard gecko is none of those.

ID.quote: Conventional Pets. Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders.
ID.note: A leopard gecko is a non-venomous, non-dangerous reptile and is not native Idaho wildlife, so it is a conventional pet. Section 200.06 then says no Department permit is needed to import, export, transport, possess or sell a conventional pet, provided it is not intended for release into the wild. Idaho answers by category rather than by species list, which is unusual and is why so few of its cells need a species search.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake
NH.note: A leopard gecko is an exotic, non-venomous reptile, so it is non-controlled for both possession and importation. New Hampshire clears exotic reptiles as a class rather than by species, with three exceptions, and Fis 803.03(b)(4) repeats the clearance for importation, so neither possessing nor bringing one into the state needs a permit. The rule was readopted in full in April 2026 and this structure survived unchanged.

WY.quote: The animals listed in this section may be imported or possessed without securing an importation/possession permit and shall not require written authorization from the Chief of Fisheries. A certificate of veterinary inspection or a fish health and AIS inspection are not required. (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.
WY.note: A leopard gecko is a reptile and appears on neither restricted list. Section 8, the no-permit-will-issue list, is federal injurious and endangered listings, aquatic invasive species, Xenopus, three frogs and toads, grass carp and mosquitofish. Section 9 requires a permit for venomous reptiles, for herptiles listed in Commission Regulation Chapter 52 that need a scientific or educational take permit, for Wyoming-indigenous herptiles imported for commercial use, and for aquatic turtles in ornamental ponds. Neither reaches this animal, so Section 10 applies and nothing at all is required, not even a veterinary certificate.

KY.quote: Except as established in Section 5 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport into Kentucky, or possess the following exotic wildlife that are considered potentially injurious to native ecosystems
KY.note: A leopard gecko is exotic wildlife under § 1 and appears on neither § 4 list. Kentucky restricts exactly two groups of lizard, the Helodermatidae at § 4(2)(i) and the Komodo dragon at § 4(2)(m). Kentucky's only possession bars for an exotic are the two lists in § 4, the potentially injurious species at (1) and the inherently dangerous species at (2), and this animal is on neither. It is also not on the § 7 permit-exempt list, so a transportation permit under § 2(1) is needed to bring one into the state; possession itself is unrestricted once it is here.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state due to the potential risk of establishment in the wild and detrimental hazard to native wildlife and public health and safety
LA.note: A leopard gecko is a nonnative reptile and appears on neither list. Louisiana rewrote this rule in January 2025 and it is now one of the strictest reptile chapters in the country, but it works by two short named lists rather than by a general permit. § 101.K.2.a is the prohibited nonnative list, fourteen entries covering crocodilians, tegus, two monitors, the green iguana, the brown anole, the Burmese python, the brown tree snake, four groups of venomous snake and three amphibians. § 101.K.2.c is the restricted nonnative list, ten entries needing a permit. This animal is on neither, and § 101.K.1's restricted snake permit reaches only constrictors over eight feet and venomous snakes, so nothing attaches.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: A leopard gecko is a nonvenomous reptile, so it is on the clean list and needs no possession permit. Alaska's clean list is otherwise a roll call of individual species, so this one class-wide entry is the widest clearance in it, and it is what makes the strictest exotic pet state in the country an easy one for a lizard keeper. Subsection (e) is the only thing riding on it: a listed species that is endangered still needs a federal permit.

MT.quote: unless otherwise regulated pursuant to 87-5-116, all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous lizards not on the controlled or prohibited lists, including but not limited to the following families or subfamilies
MT.note: Montana names Eublepharidae (eyelid geckos) separately from Gekkonidae, so the leopard gecko is inside the clause on current taxonomy rather than on a broad reading of a family name, which is how most states reach it. Montana runs a white list and this clause is where nonvenomous lizards are let onto it. The two lists it defers to are short: ARM 12.6.2208 classifies no reptile as controlled at all, and ARM 12.6.2215(6) prohibits fifteen reptiles, all of them crocodilians, large constrictors, venomous snakes or the red-eared slider. The clause is also open, "including but not limited to", so a family it does not name is not thereby excluded.

WA.quote: "Wildlife" means all species of the animal kingdom whose members exist in Washington in a wild state. This includes but is not limited to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, and invertebrates.
WA.note: Eublepharis macularius does not exist in Washington in a wild state, so it is not Washington wildlife. Washington answers by a geographic qualifier rather than by a species list, which is why it is one of the shortest states to read. Three things then have to be checked and all three come back empty: the animal is not designated deleterious exotic wildlife at WAC 220-640-200(1), which is a mute swan, mongooses, wild boar, javelina, six bovid genera and a run of cervids; it is not a potentially dangerous wild animal under RCW 16.30.010(2), whose enumerated definition reaches only mammals and reptiles named in it; and WAC 220-450-030's importation and possession rules are written for "live wild animals, wild birds, or game fish", which are the same geographically limited terms.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department, if consistent with the department's fish and wildlife management program, to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table and in 4VAC15-20-210 that the board finds and declares to be predatory or undesirable
VA.note: A leopard gecko is a nonnative (exotic) animal, not naturalized in Virginia, and absent from the permit table. Virginia permits by table and the reptile block of that table is four entries: all alligators and caimans, all crocodiles, all gavials, and the brown tree snake. Nothing here is on it, and 4VAC15-30-20 attaches the special permit only to animals the board has classed as predatory or undesirable, which is what the table is.

HI.quote: The introduction into Hawaii of live animals or live non-domestic animals as defined in this chapter is only allowed: (1) For those animals on the list designated as conditionally approved and dated November 28, 2006, or on the list designated as restricted entry, dated September 25, 2018
HI.note: Hawaii runs an inverted rule, and this is the clause that creates it. Introduction is allowed only for animals on the conditionally approved or restricted lists, so an animal on none of them is barred by default rather than left unregulated. The crested gecko appears on no Hawaii list under either name, Correlophus ciliatus or the older Rhacodactylus ciliatus. Its congener Rhacodactylus leachianus is on the restricted list, which shows the geckos were worked through one species at a time and this one was simply never reached, most likely because it was thought extinct until 1994 and had no pet trade when the lists were written. Absence from the lists here is a ban, not a gap.

CA.note: California's restricted reptile list runs to crocodilians, snapping turtles, venomous snakes and the Gila monster, and nothing else. No gecko appears on the restricted list.

PA.note: The crested gecko is a New Caledonian species and is absent from the Fish and Boat Commission's list of Pennsylvania native species. Pennsylvania's Chapter 79 regulates native reptiles and amphibians only, and the Game and Wildlife Code reaches wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so a non-native reptile falls outside both agencies.

MI.note: The crested gecko is a New Caledonian species and is not a Michigan species. Michigan's Fisheries Order 224.21 reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR captive game permit reaches a reptile, so nothing in Michigan restricts it. Bringing one in calls for a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules.

VT.quote: Squamata | Scleroglossa | Gekkonidae | all species | Geckos
VT.note: Covered by the family-wide entry, which is the opposite of Hawaii, where the crested gecko falls through the gaps of a species-by-species list and is barred by default.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Lizard | Gekkonidae | Rhacodactylus cillatus | Crested Gecko | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Listed under the older genus Rhacodactylus, now Correlophus, and with the species misspelled cillatus for ciliatus.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The crested gecko is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The crested gecko is on none of it, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: The crested gecko is covered by the entry for geckos is named on the exempt list at regulation 6.1, so it needs no permit at all. Delaware exempts lizards generously and exempts no snake, turtle or tortoise at all, which is the sharpest line in this state's rules.

CO.quote: Any species from the families Diplodactylidae (eyelash geckos), Eublepharidae (eyelid geckos), or Gekkonidae (geckos) except Mediterranean house geckos (Hemidactylus turcicus)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. Diplodactylidae is named in its own right, so the crested gecko does not depend on the older taxonomy that filed Correlophus and Rhacodactylus inside Gekkonidae. CPW files Correlophus ciliatus against this line, and the gargoyle and leachianus geckos with it. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The crested gecko is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A crested gecko is a lizard, so the breeder-source condition applies to it as much as to a Minnesota native. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Geckos -- Gekkonidae and Eublepharidae -- All species;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Worth a note on taxonomy: the crested gecko is placed in Diplodactylidae today, and Oregon names only Gekkonidae and Eublepharidae. The pairing of those two families is itself pre-2008 gecko taxonomy, under which Diplodactylinae was a subfamily of Gekkonidae, so the entry reads as covering it. Colorado writes the same clearance with Diplodactylidae named, which is the version that leaves nothing to argue about. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No gecko appears in any category, so the family reclassification that complicates this species in Colorado and Oregon does not arise here. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. No gecko is native to Maryland, so the family reclassification that complicates this species in Colorado and Oregon does not arise. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The crested gecko is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial. Tennessee names no gecko family, so the reclassification that complicates this species in Colorado and Oregon does not arise.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Correlophus ciliatus is not indigenous to Texas, so 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O does not reach it, and the dangerous wild animal list at Health & Safety Code § 822.101(4) contains no reptile. Texas has no general exotic reptile permit: the only reptiles it regulates by name are the six controlled exotic snakes, the venomous species, and its own native herpetofauna through the nongame and threatened species subchapters.

MA.quote: All Geckos (Gekkonidae) may be kept without a permit except for those species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3) and the Big Bend Gecko (Coleonyx reticulatus) which require a permit.
MA.note: The gecko family clearance is expressly subject to 9.01(3), and Correlophus ciliatus is assessed by the IUCN as vulnerable, so it is categorically non-exempt. MassWildlife's own summary phrases the clearance as "All geckos except rare species and the Big Bend gecko", which is the same reading. This is the most surprising entry in Massachusetts, because the crested gecko is an ordinary captive-bred pet-shop animal whose entire trade is captive stock, and the rule that catches it turns on the wild population in New Caledonia. The regulation offers no captive-bred exception of the kind it wrote for the chinchilla. MassWildlife's own guidance is blunt about what that means in practice: permits for non-exempt wildlife "are issued only for certain scientific, educational, commercial, or other specific reasons" and "You will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet." The statute is less absolute, since § 23 contemplates "an individual license for an animal that is not on the special exemption list" and even sets a preference for captive-bred animals where wild depletion is an issue, so the licence exists on paper and the agency says it will not grant one for a pet.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Correlophus ciliatus is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Correlophus ciliatus is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004. Florida attaches no conservation-status test to its clearance, so unlike Massachusetts the IUCN listing for this species does not reach it.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the crested gecko is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the crested gecko is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The reptile clause is a list of families and the crested gecko belongs to none of them: not Helodermatidae, not a venomous snake family, not Boidae, Pythonidae, Varanidae, Iguanidae, teiidae, Chelydridae or Crocodylia. No gecko family is named.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: ... xiv. Geckos - Family Gekkonidae other than Tokay Gecko;
NJ.note: The crested gecko is Correlophus ciliatus, placed in Diplodactylidae under current taxonomy, so whether 4.3(a)3.xiv reaches it depends on reading Gekkonidae in the older broad sense that covered all geckos. It does not change the answer. If the entry reaches it, the permit comes from 4.3; if it does not, 4.4 has no crested gecko on it and 4.5 requires a permit for any other exotic reptile. Both roads end at the individual hobby permit under 4.6(a)1.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the crested gecko is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Correlophus ciliatus is a New Caledonian animal and appears on none of the division's tables. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Alabama works from a prohibited list rather than a permitted one, so the question is only whether the crested gecko is on it, and it is not. 220-2-.26(1) reaches non-native venomous reptiles, tegus, mongooses, wild rabbits and hares, a block of mammals when they come from outside the state, a run of fish, and everything the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act. The other half of Alabama is 220-2-.92, which protects native nongame species, and that one is about Alabama's own wildlife.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana splits its reptiles cleanly and The crested gecko lands on the free side of the split. 312 IAC 9-5 governs reptiles and amphibians native to Indiana, and it is the rule that does the real work: 9-5-1(b) makes every native a protected wild animal, 9-5-6(f) caps possession at four per species, and 9-5-7 bars selling one regardless of where it came from, against a list of 99 taxa named by binomial. The crested gecko is on none of them. The other rule, 312 IAC 9-11, requires a permit only for Class I animals, which is the cottontail and three squirrels, Class II, which is Indiana's furbearers and a named run of small wild cats, and Class III, which is purebred wolves, bears, wild cats, venomous reptiles and crocodilians at least five feet long. Nothing there reaches it either.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided, monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license; except those which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma and which may be potentially injurious or detrimental to Oklahoma's wildlife, agriculture or public safety in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations.
OK.note: Oklahoma exempts non-indigenous reptiles and amphibians as a class rather than species by species. 800:25-25-3(c) clears them from import and export requirements and from both wildlife breeder licences, and the crested gecko is squarely inside it. The carve-out at the end of the same sentence has two limbs joined by "and", so it bites only on a species that is biologically capable of establishing a self-sustaining population in the wild of Oklahoma AND is injurious under federal rules; neither is true here. What remains is the statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A), which reaches closed-season wildlife, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats. Not one of the three touches the crested gecko.

WI.quote: A person is exempt from holding a license or other approval as required under this chapter to possess live nonnative wild animals that are not endangered or threatened species, except for any of the following: 1. Pheasants ... 2. Nonnative wild birds of the family anatidae that are migratory birds. 3. Nonnative wild animals that are harmful wild animals.
WI.note: Wisconsin runs its captive wildlife chapter on an exemption rather than a list, and the crested gecko is exempt by class. 169.04(1)(b) bars possessing any live wild animal without a licence, and then 169.04(4)(b) exempts every nonnative wild animal that is not endangered or threatened, with three carve-outs: hunting-preserve game birds, nonnative migratory waterfowl, and harmful wild animals. Harmful wild animals under 169.11(1)(a) are cougars, bears, wild swine and feral swine plus anything the department adds by rule, and no lizard has been added. The other rule to know about is NR 40, the invasive species chapter, which runs on a separate authority and lists no pet reptile.

NC.quote: Wild Animals. - Game animals; fur-bearing animals; feral swine; and all other wild mammals except marine mammals found in coastal fishing waters. In addition, this definition includes members of the following groups which are on the federal list of endangered or threatened species: wild amphibians, wild reptiles except sea turtles inhabiting and depending upon coastal fishing waters, and wild invertebrates except invertebrates declared to be pests under the Structural Pest Control Act of North Carolina of 1955 or the North Carolina Pesticide Law of 1971.
NC.note: North Carolina answers this in its definitions rather than its permit sections, and the answer is that the Wildlife Resources Commission has no jurisdiction. § 113-129(15) defines wild animals as game animals, fur-bearing animals, feral swine and other wild mammals, and then extends only to "wild amphibians, wild reptiles ... and wild invertebrates" that are "on the federal list of endangered or threatened species". The crested gecko is not federally listed, so it is not a wild animal in North Carolina at all and the captivity licence at § 113-272.5 has nothing to attach to. § 14-417 reaches venomous reptiles and large constrictors, and § 153A-131 lets counties regulate dangerous animals, which is where any local restriction would come from.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: 1. tropical fishes 2. rats and mice 3. rabbits ... 15. reptiles 16. amphibians. The provisions of this section do not privilege the import or possession of a species otherwise protected or regulated by other provisions of this title.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts the crested gecko from its one import permit and then has nothing else to say. § 50-16-20(A) requires a permit only for furbearers, cervids, non-domestic pigs and bovids, coyote, bear, turkey, and marine or freshwater species not already found here. § 50-16-60 separately exempts a list of pet-trade animals from the permit requirement, and reptiles and amphibians are on it as whole classes. The one Restricted Nonnative Wildlife designation the state has made, at Regulation 123-152, is the Argentine black and white tegu.

OH.quote: "Restricted snake" means any of the following: ... (c) Reticulated pythons; (d) Indian pythons; (e) Burmese pythons; (f) North African rock pythons; (g) South African rock pythons; (h) Amethystine pythons.
OH.note: Ohio's two restrictive schemes both miss the crested gecko. § 935.01(C) lists the dangerous wild animals, which are big cats, bears, primates, hyenas, elephants and the like, and § 935.01(L) lists the restricted snakes, which are venomous species and six named giant pythons. Neither reaches a lizard. The other scheme is the propagating licence at § 1533.71, which covers game birds, game quadrupeds, reptiles, amphibians and fur-bearing animals and is about propagating rather than keeping.

RI.quote: All Gekkos (Gekkonidae) may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit except the Big Bend Gekko (Coleonyx reticulatus)
RI.note: Correlophus ciliatus is a diplodactylid on current taxonomy, but the clause covers all geckos: its only exception, Coleonyx reticulatus, is a eublepharid, which shows Gekkonidae is being used here for the whole group rather than for one modern family. The crested gecko is IUCN Vulnerable and CITES Appendix II, and Rhode Island only excepts species that are endangered, so neither listing reaches it.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Reptiles, Geckos and Lizards
AR.quote: Crested Gecko (Correlophus ciliates)
AR.note: Named by species, with the binomial misspelled as ciliates for ciliatus, and cleared a second time under Diplodactylid Geckos, whose genus list opens with Correlophus. Its IUCN Vulnerable listing is irrelevant here: unlike Maine and Massachusetts, Arkansas attaches no conservation-status condition to its unrestricted list.

ME.quote: all species in infraorder Gekkota Except for: Nephrurus deleani
ME.note: Correlophus ciliatus is a diplodactylid and therefore inside Gekkota. The asterisk is the thing to check here rather than the taxonomy: it removes anything the IUCN rates Endangered, Critically Endangered or Extinct in the Wild, and the crested gecko is Vulnerable, one rung below the cut. Its CITES listing is Appendix II, and the filter names Appendix I. Both are close enough that a reassessment or an uplisting would move this cell without Maine changing anything, which is the same exposure Massachusetts carries for the ball python. The whole Reptilia section of the list sits under the heading "Captive Bred Origin Only", which is the condition on the clearance: a wild-caught animal of the same species is not unrestricted and falls back to § 7.06(4), under which an uncategorised animal may not be possessed at all.

MO.quote: Except for federally-designated endangered species and species listed in 3 CSR 10-4.117 and 3 CSR 10-9.240, the following may be bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit: Asian clams (Corbicula species) taken from impoundments that are not waters of the state; bison; amphibians, reptiles, and mammals not native to Missouri except those mammals located in a licensed big game hunting preserve; and those birds (except ring necked pheasants and gray partridge) not native to the continental United States.
MO.note: A non-native reptile and therefore outside the permit scheme entirely. Its IUCN Vulnerable listing does not matter here, because 3 CSR 10-9.110(2) excepts only federally designated endangered species, and Correlophus ciliatus has no federal listing.

ID.quote: Conventional Pets. Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders.
ID.note: A crested gecko is a non-venomous, non-dangerous reptile and is not native Idaho wildlife, so it is a conventional pet. Its IUCN Vulnerable listing plays no part: Idaho's pet exemption carries no conservation-status filter, unlike Maine's and Massachusetts's. Section 200.06 then says no Department permit is needed to import, export, transport, possess or sell a conventional pet, provided it is not intended for release into the wild. Idaho answers by category rather than by species list, which is unusual and is why so few of its cells need a species search.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake
NH.note: A crested gecko is an exotic, non-venomous reptile, so it is non-controlled. Its IUCN Vulnerable listing is irrelevant here: New Hampshire attaches no conservation-status filter to its non-controlled list, unlike Maine, whose asterisk removes anything the IUCN rates Endangered or worse. New Hampshire clears exotic reptiles as a class rather than by species, with three exceptions, and Fis 803.03(b)(4) repeats the clearance for importation, so neither possessing nor bringing one into the state needs a permit. The rule was readopted in full in April 2026 and this structure survived unchanged.

WY.quote: The animals listed in this section may be imported or possessed without securing an importation/possession permit and shall not require written authorization from the Chief of Fisheries. A certificate of veterinary inspection or a fish health and AIS inspection are not required. (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.
WY.note: A crested gecko is a reptile and appears on neither restricted list. Its IUCN Vulnerable status does not engage Section 8(d), which reaches only wildlife listed as endangered or threatened at 50 CFR § 17.11. Section 8, the no-permit-will-issue list, is federal injurious and endangered listings, aquatic invasive species, Xenopus, three frogs and toads, grass carp and mosquitofish. Section 9 requires a permit for venomous reptiles, for herptiles listed in Commission Regulation Chapter 52 that need a scientific or educational take permit, for Wyoming-indigenous herptiles imported for commercial use, and for aquatic turtles in ornamental ponds. Neither reaches this animal, so Section 10 applies and nothing at all is required, not even a veterinary certificate.

KY.quote: Except as established in Section 5 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport into Kentucky, or possess the following exotic wildlife that are considered potentially injurious to native ecosystems
KY.note: A crested gecko is exotic wildlife under § 1. Its IUCN Vulnerable listing plays no part: the only conservation bar in the regulation is § 3(8), which reaches federally endangered exotic species. Kentucky's only possession bars for an exotic are the two lists in § 4, the potentially injurious species at (1) and the inherently dangerous species at (2), and this animal is on neither. It is also not on the § 7 permit-exempt list, so a transportation permit under § 2(1) is needed to bring one into the state; possession itself is unrestricted once it is here.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state due to the potential risk of establishment in the wild and detrimental hazard to native wildlife and public health and safety
LA.note: A crested gecko is a nonnative reptile and appears on neither list. Its IUCN Vulnerable status does not engage § 101.J.5 or J.6, which reach federal injurious listings and the federal endangered and threatened list. Louisiana rewrote this rule in January 2025 and it is now one of the strictest reptile chapters in the country, but it works by two short named lists rather than by a general permit. § 101.K.2.a is the prohibited nonnative list, fourteen entries covering crocodilians, tegus, two monitors, the green iguana, the brown anole, the Burmese python, the brown tree snake, four groups of venomous snake and three amphibians. § 101.K.2.c is the restricted nonnative list, ten entries needing a permit. This animal is on neither, and § 101.K.1's restricted snake permit reaches only constrictors over eight feet and venomous snakes, so nothing attaches.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: A crested gecko is a nonvenomous reptile, so it is on the clean list. Its IUCN Vulnerable listing does not engage § 92.029(e), which reaches only species that are endangered and asks for a federal rather than a state permit. Alaska's clean list is otherwise a roll call of individual species, so this one class-wide entry is the widest clearance in it, and it is what makes the strictest exotic pet state in the country an easy one for a lizard keeper. Subsection (e) is the only thing riding on it: a listed species that is endangered still needs a federal permit.

MT.quote: unless otherwise regulated pursuant to 87-5-116, all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous lizards not on the controlled or prohibited lists, including but not limited to the following families or subfamilies
MT.note: The crested gecko is a diplodactylid on current taxonomy and Montana names Gekkonidae, but the clause is expressly open, "including but not limited to the following families or subfamilies", so a gecko family it does not list is still a nonvenomous lizard within the head phrase. Montana runs a white list and this clause is where nonvenomous lizards are let onto it. The two lists it defers to are short: ARM 12.6.2208 classifies no reptile as controlled at all, and ARM 12.6.2215(6) prohibits fifteen reptiles, all of them crocodilians, large constrictors, venomous snakes or the red-eared slider. The clause is also open, "including but not limited to", so a family it does not name is not thereby excluded.

WA.quote: "Wildlife" means all species of the animal kingdom whose members exist in Washington in a wild state. This includes but is not limited to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, and invertebrates.
WA.note: Correlophus ciliatus does not exist in Washington in a wild state, so it is not Washington wildlife. Its IUCN Vulnerable listing has nothing to attach to here. Washington answers by a geographic qualifier rather than by a species list, which is why it is one of the shortest states to read. Three things then have to be checked and all three come back empty: the animal is not designated deleterious exotic wildlife at WAC 220-640-200(1), which is a mute swan, mongooses, wild boar, javelina, six bovid genera and a run of cervids; it is not a potentially dangerous wild animal under RCW 16.30.010(2), whose enumerated definition reaches only mammals and reptiles named in it; and WAC 220-450-030's importation and possession rules are written for "live wild animals, wild birds, or game fish", which are the same geographically limited terms.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department, if consistent with the department's fish and wildlife management program, to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table and in 4VAC15-20-210 that the board finds and declares to be predatory or undesirable
VA.note: A crested gecko is a nonnative (exotic) animal, not naturalized in Virginia, and absent from the permit table. Virginia attaches no conservation-status condition to the table, so the IUCN Vulnerable listing does not engage. Virginia permits by table and the reptile block of that table is four entries: all alligators and caimans, all crocodiles, all gavials, and the brown tree snake. Nothing here is on it, and 4VAC15-30-20 attaches the special permit only to animals the board has classed as predatory or undesirable, which is what the table is.

HI.note: Part A is headed FOR RESEARCH AND EXHIBITION, so a listed animal has no pet route: a university or a licensed exhibitor can hold one and a private keeper cannot. Named individually. Several other Tiliqua are listed beside it, so the whole pet-trade group is covered rather than just this species.

CA.note: California's restricted reptile list runs to crocodilians, snapping turtles, venomous snakes and the Gila monster, and nothing else. No skink is restricted.

PA.note: The blue-tongue skink is Australian and is absent from the Fish and Boat Commission's list of Pennsylvania native species. Pennsylvania's Chapter 79 regulates native reptiles and amphibians only, and the Game and Wildlife Code reaches wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so a non-native reptile falls outside both agencies.

MI.note: The blue-tongue skink is Australian and is not a Michigan species. Michigan's Fisheries Order 224.21 reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR captive game permit reaches a reptile, so nothing in Michigan restricts it. Bringing one in calls for a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules.

VT.quote: Squamata | Autarchoglossa | Scincidae | All species of skinks, except those listed in Appendix that require an importation and possession permit
VT.note: Skinks are unrestricted as a family with an exception, and the exception is Eumeces, not Tiliqua. The blue-tongue skink is therefore clear.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Lizard | Scincidae | Tiliqua sp. | Blue Tongued Skink | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Named at genus level, so every blue-tongue in the trade is covered.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The blue-tongue skink is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The blue-tongue skink is on none of it, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Skinks are exempt with one carve-out, the five-lined skink, which is a Delaware native rather than a pet-trade animal. The blue-tongue skink is Australian and needs no permit. Delaware exempts lizards generously and exempts no snake, turtle or tortoise at all.

CO.quote: Any species of lizard native only to the tropical and subtropical region from the following families: Scincidae (skinks)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. CPW files Tiliqua at genus level as well as three named forms, the Indonesian, Halmahera and northern blue-tongues, all on Appendix A. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The blue-tongue skink is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. Illinois has native skinks, the five-lined, broad-headed and ground skinks, so the family is represented on the § 885.40 list; Tiliqua is not, and the list works to the species and subspecies level rather than by family. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A blue-tongue skink is a lizard, so the breeder-source condition applies to it as much as to a Minnesota native. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Skinks -- Scincidae -- All nonnative species except Eumeces spp.;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. Tiliqua is a nonnative skink and not Eumeces, the genus Oregon carves out for its own natives. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No skink appears in any category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. Maryland has three native skinks, the common five-lined, little brown and broad-headed, and a fourth on its prohibited tier, the northern coal skink. Tiliqua is none of them. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The blue-tongue skink is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Tiliqua scincoides is not indigenous to Texas, so 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O does not reach it, and the dangerous wild animal list at Health & Safety Code § 822.101(4) contains no reptile. Texas has no general exotic reptile permit: the only reptiles it regulates by name are the six controlled exotic snakes, the venomous species, and its own native herpetofauna through the nongame and threatened species subchapters. Texas does list five native Eumeces skinks across its two nongame lists, so the genus matters here rather than the common name.

MA.quote: All Skinks (Scincidae) except for the following which require a permit: Species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3). Florida Sand Skinks (Neoseps spp.) Solomon Island Ground Skink (Tribolonotus spp.)
MA.note: Skinks are cleared as a family with two named exceptions, neither of which is Tiliqua, and Tiliqua scincoides is IUCN least concern so the categorical bar does not apply. Worth noting that the exempted family includes the Solomon Island prehensile-tailed skink while excluding the Solomon Island ground skink, which is a pair of very similar names on opposite sides of the line.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Tiliqua scincoides is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list. Nebraska's own skinks go the other way: the five-lined and Great Plains skinks are nongame species in need of conservation with no take at all, and the prairie and many-lined skinks are capped at three.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Tiliqua scincoides is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the blue-tongue skink is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and the blue-tongue skink is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it. Georgia's own skinks, the broadhead, coal, five-lined, ground and mole skinks, are all on the prohibited natives list, so the genus matters here.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The reptile clause is a list of families and the blue-tongue skink belongs to none of them: not Helodermatidae, not a venomous snake family, not Boidae, Pythonidae, Varanidae, Iguanidae, teiidae, Chelydridae or Crocodylia. Scincidae appears nowhere in the article.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: ... x. Skinks - Family Scincidae;
NJ.note: The blue-tongue skink is answered by name on the 4.3 permit list rather than by the catch-all. The list takes the family whole, "Skinks - Family Scincidae", and Tiliqua scincoides is inside it. The list is written by family as often as by species, and 4.3 is open-ended, "include, but are not limited to", so being on it settles the permit question but not being on it settles nothing. The permit is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, subject to the general possession criteria at 4.7.
