UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the blue-tongue skink is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Utah has skinks of its own, the many-lined and the western, both Controlled at Standard, but Tiliqua scincoides is not one of them. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Alabama works from a prohibited list rather than a permitted one, so the question is only whether the blue-tongue skink is on it, and it is not. 220-2-.26(1) reaches non-native venomous reptiles, tegus, mongooses, wild rabbits and hares, a block of mammals when they come from outside the state, a run of fish, and everything the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act. The other half of Alabama is 220-2-.92, which protects native nongame species, and that one is about Alabama's own wildlife. Alabama protects two of its own skinks, the coal skink and the southeastern five-lined skink, both by binomial rather than by family, so Tiliqua scincoides is not swept in with them.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana splits its reptiles cleanly and The blue-tongue skink lands on the free side of the split. 312 IAC 9-5 governs reptiles and amphibians native to Indiana, and it is the rule that does the real work: 9-5-1(b) makes every native a protected wild animal, 9-5-6(f) caps possession at four per species, and 9-5-7 bars selling one regardless of where it came from, against a list of 99 taxa named by binomial. The blue-tongue skink is on none of them. The other rule, 312 IAC 9-11, requires a permit only for Class I animals, which is the cottontail and three squirrels, Class II, which is Indiana's furbearers and a named run of small wild cats, and Class III, which is purebred wolves, bears, wild cats, venomous reptiles and crocodilians at least five feet long. Nothing there reaches it either. Indiana has skinks of its own on the native list, the common five-lined and the broad-headed among them, but they are named by binomial rather than by family, so Tiliqua scincoides is not swept along.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided, monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license; except those which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma and which may be potentially injurious or detrimental to Oklahoma's wildlife, agriculture or public safety in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations.
OK.note: Oklahoma exempts non-indigenous reptiles and amphibians as a class rather than species by species. 800:25-25-3(c) clears them from import and export requirements and from both wildlife breeder licences, and the blue-tongue skink is squarely inside it. The carve-out at the end of the same sentence has two limbs joined by "and", so it bites only on a species that is biologically capable of establishing a self-sustaining population in the wild of Oklahoma AND is injurious under federal rules; neither is true here. What remains is the statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A), which reaches closed-season wildlife, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats. Not one of the three touches the blue-tongue skink.

WI.quote: A person is exempt from holding a license or other approval as required under this chapter to possess live nonnative wild animals that are not endangered or threatened species, except for any of the following: 1. Pheasants ... 2. Nonnative wild birds of the family anatidae that are migratory birds. 3. Nonnative wild animals that are harmful wild animals.
WI.note: Wisconsin runs its captive wildlife chapter on an exemption rather than a list, and the blue-tongue skink is exempt by class. 169.04(1)(b) bars possessing any live wild animal without a licence, and then 169.04(4)(b) exempts every nonnative wild animal that is not endangered or threatened, with three carve-outs: hunting-preserve game birds, nonnative migratory waterfowl, and harmful wild animals. Harmful wild animals under 169.11(1)(a) are cougars, bears, wild swine and feral swine plus anything the department adds by rule, and no lizard has been added. The other rule to know about is NR 40, the invasive species chapter, which runs on a separate authority and lists no pet reptile.

NC.quote: Wild Animals. - Game animals; fur-bearing animals; feral swine; and all other wild mammals except marine mammals found in coastal fishing waters. In addition, this definition includes members of the following groups which are on the federal list of endangered or threatened species: wild amphibians, wild reptiles except sea turtles inhabiting and depending upon coastal fishing waters, and wild invertebrates except invertebrates declared to be pests under the Structural Pest Control Act of North Carolina of 1955 or the North Carolina Pesticide Law of 1971.
NC.note: North Carolina answers this in its definitions rather than its permit sections, and the answer is that the Wildlife Resources Commission has no jurisdiction. § 113-129(15) defines wild animals as game animals, fur-bearing animals, feral swine and other wild mammals, and then extends only to "wild amphibians, wild reptiles ... and wild invertebrates" that are "on the federal list of endangered or threatened species". The blue-tongue skink is not federally listed, so it is not a wild animal in North Carolina at all and the captivity licence at § 113-272.5 has nothing to attach to. § 14-417 reaches venomous reptiles and large constrictors, and § 153A-131 lets counties regulate dangerous animals, which is where any local restriction would come from.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: 1. tropical fishes 2. rats and mice 3. rabbits ... 15. reptiles 16. amphibians. The provisions of this section do not privilege the import or possession of a species otherwise protected or regulated by other provisions of this title.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts the blue-tongue skink from its one import permit and then has nothing else to say. § 50-16-20(A) requires a permit only for furbearers, cervids, non-domestic pigs and bovids, coyote, bear, turkey, and marine or freshwater species not already found here. § 50-16-60 separately exempts a list of pet-trade animals from the permit requirement, and reptiles and amphibians are on it as whole classes. The one Restricted Nonnative Wildlife designation the state has made, at Regulation 123-152, is the Argentine black and white tegu.

OH.quote: "Restricted snake" means any of the following: ... (c) Reticulated pythons; (d) Indian pythons; (e) Burmese pythons; (f) North African rock pythons; (g) South African rock pythons; (h) Amethystine pythons.
OH.note: Ohio's two restrictive schemes both miss the blue-tongue skink. § 935.01(C) lists the dangerous wild animals, which are big cats, bears, primates, hyenas, elephants and the like, and § 935.01(L) lists the restricted snakes, which are venomous species and six named giant pythons. Neither reaches a lizard. The other scheme is the propagating licence at § 1533.71, which covers game birds, game quadrupeds, reptiles, amphibians and fur-bearing animals and is about propagating rather than keeping.

RI.quote: All Skinks (Scincidae) may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit except for the following: Florida Sand Skinks (Neoseps spp.), Solomon Island Ground Skink (Tribolonotus spp.)
RI.note: Tiliqua scincoides is a scincid and is neither exception, so no permit. Rhode Island has native skinks but names none of them in the native-reptile bar at § 3.17(A)(4), which lists only turtles and snakes, so nativity does not come into this one.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Reptiles, Geckos and Lizards
AR.quote: Blue-tongue skinks (Genus Tiliqua)
AR.note: The whole genus is cleared, and the neighbouring Cyclodomorphus entry, the blue-tongue skinks’ sister genus, is spelled out species by species, so this is a considered listing rather than a loose one. No possession, breeding or importation permit.

ME.quote: All Species in Family Scincidae (Skinks) Family Scincidae*
ME.note: A family-wide clearance with no species excepted. Tiliqua scincoides is IUCN Least Concern and on none of the four lists the asterisk points at. The whole Reptilia section of the list sits under the heading "Captive Bred Origin Only", which is the condition on the clearance: a wild-caught animal of the same species is not unrestricted and falls back to § 7.06(4), under which an uncategorised animal may not be possessed at all.

MO.quote: Except for federally-designated endangered species and species listed in 3 CSR 10-4.117 and 3 CSR 10-9.240, the following may be bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit: Asian clams (Corbicula species) taken from impoundments that are not waters of the state; bison; amphibians, reptiles, and mammals not native to Missouri except those mammals located in a licensed big game hunting preserve; and those birds (except ring necked pheasants and gray partridge) not native to the continental United States.
MO.note: A non-native reptile, cleared to be bought, sold, possessed, transported and exhibited without permit. Missouri's own skinks are Class I wildlife, but Tiliqua is Australian and the clearance turns on where the species lives rather than on what it resembles.

ID.quote: Conventional Pets. Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders.
ID.note: A blue-tongue skink is a non-venomous, non-dangerous reptile and is not native Idaho wildlife, so it is a conventional pet. Section 200.06 then says no Department permit is needed to import, export, transport, possess or sell a conventional pet, provided it is not intended for release into the wild. Idaho answers by category rather than by species list, which is unusual and is why so few of its cells need a species search.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake
NH.note: A blue-tongue skink is an exotic, non-venomous reptile, so it is non-controlled for both possession and importation. New Hampshire clears exotic reptiles as a class rather than by species, with three exceptions, and Fis 803.03(b)(4) repeats the clearance for importation, so neither possessing nor bringing one into the state needs a permit. The rule was readopted in full in April 2026 and this structure survived unchanged.

WY.quote: The animals listed in this section may be imported or possessed without securing an importation/possession permit and shall not require written authorization from the Chief of Fisheries. A certificate of veterinary inspection or a fish health and AIS inspection are not required. (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.
WY.note: A blue-tongue skink is a reptile and appears on neither restricted list. Section 8, the no-permit-will-issue list, is federal injurious and endangered listings, aquatic invasive species, Xenopus, three frogs and toads, grass carp and mosquitofish. Section 9 requires a permit for venomous reptiles, for herptiles listed in Commission Regulation Chapter 52 that need a scientific or educational take permit, for Wyoming-indigenous herptiles imported for commercial use, and for aquatic turtles in ornamental ponds. Neither reaches this animal, so Section 10 applies and nothing at all is required, not even a veterinary certificate.

KY.quote: Except as established in Section 5 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport into Kentucky, or possess the following exotic wildlife that are considered potentially injurious to native ecosystems
KY.note: A blue-tongue skink is exotic wildlife under § 1 and appears on neither § 4 list. Kentucky's only possession bars for an exotic are the two lists in § 4, the potentially injurious species at (1) and the inherently dangerous species at (2), and this animal is on neither. It is also not on the § 7 permit-exempt list, so a transportation permit under § 2(1) is needed to bring one into the state; possession itself is unrestricted once it is here.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state due to the potential risk of establishment in the wild and detrimental hazard to native wildlife and public health and safety
LA.note: A blue-tongue skink is a nonnative reptile and appears on neither list. Louisiana rewrote this rule in January 2025 and it is now one of the strictest reptile chapters in the country, but it works by two short named lists rather than by a general permit. § 101.K.2.a is the prohibited nonnative list, fourteen entries covering crocodilians, tegus, two monitors, the green iguana, the brown anole, the Burmese python, the brown tree snake, four groups of venomous snake and three amphibians. § 101.K.2.c is the restricted nonnative list, ten entries needing a permit. This animal is on neither, and § 101.K.1's restricted snake permit reaches only constrictors over eight feet and venomous snakes, so nothing attaches.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: A blue-tongue skink is a nonvenomous reptile, so it is on the clean list and needs no possession permit. Alaska's clean list is otherwise a roll call of individual species, so this one class-wide entry is the widest clearance in it, and it is what makes the strictest exotic pet state in the country an easy one for a lizard keeper. Subsection (e) is the only thing riding on it: a listed species that is endangered still needs a federal permit.

MT.quote: unless otherwise regulated pursuant to 87-5-116, all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous lizards not on the controlled or prohibited lists, including but not limited to the following families or subfamilies
MT.note: Tiliqua is a scincid and Scincidae is named. Montana runs a white list and this clause is where nonvenomous lizards are let onto it. The two lists it defers to are short: ARM 12.6.2208 classifies no reptile as controlled at all, and ARM 12.6.2215(6) prohibits fifteen reptiles, all of them crocodilians, large constrictors, venomous snakes or the red-eared slider. The clause is also open, "including but not limited to", so a family it does not name is not thereby excluded.

WA.quote: "Wildlife" means all species of the animal kingdom whose members exist in Washington in a wild state. This includes but is not limited to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, and invertebrates.
WA.note: Tiliqua scincoides does not exist in Washington in a wild state, so it is not Washington wildlife. Washington answers by a geographic qualifier rather than by a species list, which is why it is one of the shortest states to read. Three things then have to be checked and all three come back empty: the animal is not designated deleterious exotic wildlife at WAC 220-640-200(1), which is a mute swan, mongooses, wild boar, javelina, six bovid genera and a run of cervids; it is not a potentially dangerous wild animal under RCW 16.30.010(2), whose enumerated definition reaches only mammals and reptiles named in it; and WAC 220-450-030's importation and possession rules are written for "live wild animals, wild birds, or game fish", which are the same geographically limited terms.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department, if consistent with the department's fish and wildlife management program, to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table and in 4VAC15-20-210 that the board finds and declares to be predatory or undesirable
VA.note: A blue-tongue skink is a nonnative (exotic) animal, not naturalized in Virginia, and absent from the permit table. Virginia permits by table and the reptile block of that table is four entries: all alligators and caimans, all crocodiles, all gavials, and the brown tree snake. Nothing here is on it, and 4VAC15-30-20 attaches the special permit only to animals the board has classed as predatory or undesirable, which is what the table is.

HI.quote: The introduction into Hawaii of live animals or live non-domestic animals as defined in this chapter is only allowed: (1) For those animals on the list designated as conditionally approved and dated November 28, 2006, or on the list designated as restricted entry, dated September 25, 2018
HI.note: Hawaii runs an inverted rule, and this is the clause that creates it. Introduction is allowed only for animals on the conditionally approved or restricted lists, so an animal on none of them is barred by default rather than left unregulated. The Chamaeleonidae block on the restricted list names only Chamaeleo chamaeleon and Furcifer oustaleti, and Jackson's chameleon appears on no Hawaii list under either Trioceros jacksonii or the older Chamaeleo jacksonii. The result reads oddly, because this is the chameleon most associated with Hawaii, having established wild populations there after escaping the pet trade, and yet keeping one is not permitted. Absence from the lists here is a ban, not a gap.

CA.note: California's restricted reptile list runs to crocodilians, snapping turtles, venomous snakes and the Gila monster, and nothing else. The only chameleons named anywhere in section 671 are absent entirely, so no chameleon is restricted.

PA.note: Jackson's chameleon is an East African species and is absent from the Fish and Boat Commission's list of Pennsylvania native species. Pennsylvania's Chapter 79 regulates native reptiles and amphibians only, and the Game and Wildlife Code reaches wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so a non-native reptile falls outside both agencies.

MI.note: Jackson's chameleon is an East African species and is not a Michigan species. Michigan's Fisheries Order 224.21 reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR captive game permit reaches a reptile, so nothing in Michigan restricts it. Bringing one in calls for a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules.

VT.quote: Squamata | Iguania | Chamaelonidae | all species | Chameleons
VT.note: The whole family is unrestricted. A striking contrast with Hawaii, where this species is barred by default despite living wild on the islands.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Lizard | Chamaeleonidae | Chamaeleo jacksoni | Jackson's chameleon | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required. Listed under the older genus Chamaeleo, now Trioceros.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: Jackson's chameleon is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. Jackson's chameleon is on none of it, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Jackson's chameleon is covered by the entry for chameleons is named on the exempt list at regulation 6.1, so it needs no permit at all. Delaware exempts lizards generously and exempts no snake, turtle or tortoise at all, which is the sharpest line in this state's rules.

CO.quote: Any species of lizard native only to the tropical and subtropical region from the following families: Chamaeleonidae (chameleons)
CO.note: On Appendix A, which under § 703(A) may be possessed, propagated, sold, purchased or transported without a licence or documentation. CPW files Trioceros jacksonii against this line. Its native East African montane range straddles the equator. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. Jackson's chameleon is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A Jackson's chameleon is a lizard, so the breeder-source condition applies to it as much as to a Minnesota native. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Chameleons -- Chamaeleonidae -- All species;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. The whole family is cleared at once. Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. No chameleon appears in any category. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. No chameleon is native to Maryland. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. Jackson's chameleon is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Trioceros jacksonii is not indigenous to Texas, so 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O does not reach it, and the dangerous wild animal list at Health & Safety Code § 822.101(4) contains no reptile. Texas has no general exotic reptile permit: the only reptiles it regulates by name are the six controlled exotic snakes, the venomous species, and its own native herpetofauna through the nongame and threatened species subchapters. Hawaii is the state that regulates this animal heavily, because it is established in the wild there. Texas has no equivalent concern and no equivalent rule.

MA.quote: All true Chameleons (Chamaelenoidae) may be kept without a permit, except species categorically non-exempt pursuant to 321 CMR 9.01(3).
MA.note: Trioceros jacksonii clears the family listing and is IUCN least concern, so the categorical bar does not apply. Massachusetts has no ecological objection of the kind Hawaii has, where this species is established in the wild and regulated hard for that reason.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Trioceros jacksonii is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Trioceros jacksonii is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and Jackson's chameleon is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia's three tiers are closed lists, and Jackson's chameleon is on none of them: not prohibited under .03, not inherently dangerous under .04, and not within any order or species licensed under .05. It is not a Georgia native either, so the separate native wildlife restriction does not reach it.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: The reptile clause is a list of families and Jackson's chameleon belongs to none of them: not Helodermatidae, not a venomous snake family, not Boidae, Pythonidae, Varanidae, Iguanidae, teiidae, Chelydridae or Crocodylia. Chamaeleonidae appears nowhere in the article, and this species is not protected under any federal or state law that § 161.01(b)(ii) would import.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4.
NJ.note: New Jersey is a closed-list state in the strict sense. 7:25-4.2(a) bars possession of any exotic or nongame species without a permit, 4.4 then names the handful that may be kept without one, and 4.5 sweeps everything else back in. Jackson's chameleon appears on none of the Division's three lists, so it is not exempt under 4.4, not one of the families singled out in 4.3, and not potentially dangerous under 4.8. That leaves 4.5, and the permit it points to is the individual hobby permit at 4.6(a)1, which 4.7 conditions on diet, caging that prevents escape, lawful acquisition, veterinary care and freedom from disease. The Division's own handout tells readers to phone the permits office for anything the lists do not name, which is a fair signal that the catch-all is where these end up rather than an oversight. Chamaeleonidae is absent from 4.3 altogether, so the chameleons all arrive through the catch-all rather than through a named family.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and Jackson's chameleon is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Trioceros jacksonii is an east African animal, absent from every division table. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Alabama works from a prohibited list rather than a permitted one, so the question is only whether Jackson's chameleon is on it, and it is not. 220-2-.26(1) reaches non-native venomous reptiles, tegus, mongooses, wild rabbits and hares, a block of mammals when they come from outside the state, a run of fish, and everything the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act. The other half of Alabama is 220-2-.92, which protects native nongame species, and that one is about Alabama's own wildlife.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana splits its reptiles cleanly and Jackson's chameleon lands on the free side of the split. 312 IAC 9-5 governs reptiles and amphibians native to Indiana, and it is the rule that does the real work: 9-5-1(b) makes every native a protected wild animal, 9-5-6(f) caps possession at four per species, and 9-5-7 bars selling one regardless of where it came from, against a list of 99 taxa named by binomial. Jackson's chameleon is on none of them. The other rule, 312 IAC 9-11, requires a permit only for Class I animals, which is the cottontail and three squirrels, Class II, which is Indiana's furbearers and a named run of small wild cats, and Class III, which is purebred wolves, bears, wild cats, venomous reptiles and crocodilians at least five feet long. Nothing there reaches it either.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided, monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license; except those which are biologically capable of establishing self-sustaining populations in the wild of Oklahoma and which may be potentially injurious or detrimental to Oklahoma's wildlife, agriculture or public safety in accordance with existing USDI or APHIS regulations.
OK.note: Oklahoma exempts non-indigenous reptiles and amphibians as a class rather than species by species. 800:25-25-3(c) clears them from import and export requirements and from both wildlife breeder licences, and Jackson's chameleon is squarely inside it. The carve-out at the end of the same sentence has two limbs joined by "and", so it bites only on a species that is biologically capable of establishing a self-sustaining population in the wild of Oklahoma AND is injurious under federal rules; neither is true here. What remains is the statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A), which reaches closed-season wildlife, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats. Not one of the three touches Jackson's chameleon.

WI.quote: A person is exempt from holding a license or other approval as required under this chapter to possess live nonnative wild animals that are not endangered or threatened species, except for any of the following: 1. Pheasants ... 2. Nonnative wild birds of the family anatidae that are migratory birds. 3. Nonnative wild animals that are harmful wild animals.
WI.note: Wisconsin runs its captive wildlife chapter on an exemption rather than a list, and Jackson's chameleon is exempt by class. 169.04(1)(b) bars possessing any live wild animal without a licence, and then 169.04(4)(b) exempts every nonnative wild animal that is not endangered or threatened, with three carve-outs: hunting-preserve game birds, nonnative migratory waterfowl, and harmful wild animals. Harmful wild animals under 169.11(1)(a) are cougars, bears, wild swine and feral swine plus anything the department adds by rule, and no lizard has been added. The other rule to know about is NR 40, the invasive species chapter, which runs on a separate authority and lists no pet reptile.

NC.quote: Wild Animals. - Game animals; fur-bearing animals; feral swine; and all other wild mammals except marine mammals found in coastal fishing waters. In addition, this definition includes members of the following groups which are on the federal list of endangered or threatened species: wild amphibians, wild reptiles except sea turtles inhabiting and depending upon coastal fishing waters, and wild invertebrates except invertebrates declared to be pests under the Structural Pest Control Act of North Carolina of 1955 or the North Carolina Pesticide Law of 1971.
NC.note: North Carolina answers this in its definitions rather than its permit sections, and the answer is that the Wildlife Resources Commission has no jurisdiction. § 113-129(15) defines wild animals as game animals, fur-bearing animals, feral swine and other wild mammals, and then extends only to "wild amphibians, wild reptiles ... and wild invertebrates" that are "on the federal list of endangered or threatened species". Jackson's chameleon is not federally listed, so it is not a wild animal in North Carolina at all and the captivity licence at § 113-272.5 has nothing to attach to. § 14-417 reaches venomous reptiles and large constrictors, and § 153A-131 lets counties regulate dangerous animals, which is where any local restriction would come from.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: 1. tropical fishes 2. rats and mice 3. rabbits ... 15. reptiles 16. amphibians. The provisions of this section do not privilege the import or possession of a species otherwise protected or regulated by other provisions of this title.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts Jackson's chameleon from its one import permit and then has nothing else to say. § 50-16-20(A) requires a permit only for furbearers, cervids, non-domestic pigs and bovids, coyote, bear, turkey, and marine or freshwater species not already found here. § 50-16-60 separately exempts a list of pet-trade animals from the permit requirement, and reptiles and amphibians are on it as whole classes. The one Restricted Nonnative Wildlife designation the state has made, at Regulation 123-152, is the Argentine black and white tegu.

OH.quote: "Restricted snake" means any of the following: ... (c) Reticulated pythons; (d) Indian pythons; (e) Burmese pythons; (f) North African rock pythons; (g) South African rock pythons; (h) Amethystine pythons.
OH.note: Ohio's two restrictive schemes both miss Jackson's chameleon. § 935.01(C) lists the dangerous wild animals, which are big cats, bears, primates, hyenas, elephants and the like, and § 935.01(L) lists the restricted snakes, which are venomous species and six named giant pythons. Neither reaches a lizard. The other scheme is the propagating licence at § 1533.71, which covers game birds, game quadrupeds, reptiles, amphibians and fur-bearing animals and is about propagating rather than keeping.

RI.quote: Old World Chameleons (Chameleonidae) may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit.
RI.note: A family-wide clearance with no exception at all, which is unusual in this rule: every other lizard family entry names species that are carved back out. Trioceros jacksonii is a chamaeleonid and is IUCN Least Concern, so the § 3.17(A) proviso for endangered species does not engage either.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Reptiles, Geckos and Lizards
AR.quote: Cameleons (in part) (Family: Chamaeleonidae: Genera: Calumma, Chameleo, Fucifer, Trioceros)
AR.note: The listing is by genus and Trioceros jacksonii is a Trioceros, so it is inside the clearance. The words "in part" matter: Chamaeleonidae genera outside those four, Bradypodion, Kinyongia, Rhampholeon and Rieppeleon among them, are not on R1.01 and fall under the closing clause at R1.02, "Species not listed in Addenda R1.01, R1.02, or R1.03 are prohibited until evaluated". The veiled chameleon is listed separately by species.

ME.note: Named by species. Maine does not clear Chamaeleonidae as a family: it lists ten chameleons individually, two Trioceros, two Chamaeleo, three Furcifer, Calumma parsonii, Rhampholeon spectrum and Rieppeleon brevicaudatus, so the species entry is what answers this and a chameleon outside those ten is uncategorised. All chameleons are CITES Appendix II, and the asterisk filter names Appendix I. The whole Reptilia section of the list sits under the heading "Captive Bred Origin Only", which is the condition on the clearance: a wild-caught animal of the same species is not unrestricted and falls back to § 7.06(4), under which an uncategorised animal may not be possessed at all.

MO.quote: Except for federally-designated endangered species and species listed in 3 CSR 10-4.117 and 3 CSR 10-9.240, the following may be bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit: Asian clams (Corbicula species) taken from impoundments that are not waters of the state; bison; amphibians, reptiles, and mammals not native to Missouri except those mammals located in a licensed big game hunting preserve; and those birds (except ring necked pheasants and gray partridge) not native to the continental United States.
MO.note: A non-native reptile, so no permit of any kind. The CITES Appendix II listing that covers all chameleons plays no part: the only conservation carve-out in the clearance is for federally designated endangered species.

ID.quote: Conventional Pets. Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders.
ID.note: Jackson's chameleon is a non-venomous, non-dangerous reptile and is not native Idaho wildlife, so it is a conventional pet. Section 200.06 then says no Department permit is needed to import, export, transport, possess or sell a conventional pet, provided it is not intended for release into the wild. Idaho answers by category rather than by species list, which is unusual and is why so few of its cells need a species search.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake
NH.note: Jackson's chameleon is an exotic, non-venomous reptile, so it is non-controlled for both possession and importation. New Hampshire clears exotic reptiles as a class rather than by species, with three exceptions, and Fis 803.03(b)(4) repeats the clearance for importation, so neither possessing nor bringing one into the state needs a permit. The rule was readopted in full in April 2026 and this structure survived unchanged.

WY.quote: The animals listed in this section may be imported or possessed without securing an importation/possession permit and shall not require written authorization from the Chief of Fisheries. A certificate of veterinary inspection or a fish health and AIS inspection are not required. (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.
WY.note: Jackson's chameleon is a reptile and appears on neither restricted list. Section 8, the no-permit-will-issue list, is federal injurious and endangered listings, aquatic invasive species, Xenopus, three frogs and toads, grass carp and mosquitofish. Section 9 requires a permit for venomous reptiles, for herptiles listed in Commission Regulation Chapter 52 that need a scientific or educational take permit, for Wyoming-indigenous herptiles imported for commercial use, and for aquatic turtles in ornamental ponds. Neither reaches this animal, so Section 10 applies and nothing at all is required, not even a veterinary certificate.

KY.quote: Except as established in Section 5 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport into Kentucky, or possess the following exotic wildlife that are considered potentially injurious to native ecosystems
KY.note: Jackson's chameleon is exotic wildlife under § 1 and appears on neither § 4 list. Kentucky's only possession bars for an exotic are the two lists in § 4, the potentially injurious species at (1) and the inherently dangerous species at (2), and this animal is on neither. It is also not on the § 7 permit-exempt list, so a transportation permit under § 2(1) is needed to bring one into the state; possession itself is unrestricted once it is here.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state due to the potential risk of establishment in the wild and detrimental hazard to native wildlife and public health and safety
LA.note: Jackson's chameleon is a nonnative reptile and appears on neither list. Louisiana rewrote this rule in January 2025 and it is now one of the strictest reptile chapters in the country, but it works by two short named lists rather than by a general permit. § 101.K.2.a is the prohibited nonnative list, fourteen entries covering crocodilians, tegus, two monitors, the green iguana, the brown anole, the Burmese python, the brown tree snake, four groups of venomous snake and three amphibians. § 101.K.2.c is the restricted nonnative list, ten entries needing a permit. This animal is on neither, and § 101.K.1's restricted snake permit reaches only constrictors over eight feet and venomous snakes, so nothing attaches.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: Jackson's chameleon is a nonvenomous reptile, so it is on the clean list and needs no possession permit. Alaska's clean list is otherwise a roll call of individual species, so this one class-wide entry is the widest clearance in it, and it is what makes the strictest exotic pet state in the country an easy one for a lizard keeper. Subsection (e) is the only thing riding on it: a listed species that is endangered still needs a federal permit.

MT.quote: unless otherwise regulated pursuant to 87-5-116, all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous lizards not on the controlled or prohibited lists, including but not limited to the following families or subfamilies
MT.note: Chamaeleonidae is named, which is what already put the veiled chameleon on this map as legal in Montana; Jackson's chameleon sits in the same family. Montana runs a white list and this clause is where nonvenomous lizards are let onto it. The two lists it defers to are short: ARM 12.6.2208 classifies no reptile as controlled at all, and ARM 12.6.2215(6) prohibits fifteen reptiles, all of them crocodilians, large constrictors, venomous snakes or the red-eared slider. The clause is also open, "including but not limited to", so a family it does not name is not thereby excluded.

WA.quote: "Wildlife" means all species of the animal kingdom whose members exist in Washington in a wild state. This includes but is not limited to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, and invertebrates.
WA.note: Trioceros jacksonii does not exist in Washington in a wild state, so it is not Washington wildlife. Washington answers by a geographic qualifier rather than by a species list, which is why it is one of the shortest states to read. Three things then have to be checked and all three come back empty: the animal is not designated deleterious exotic wildlife at WAC 220-640-200(1), which is a mute swan, mongooses, wild boar, javelina, six bovid genera and a run of cervids; it is not a potentially dangerous wild animal under RCW 16.30.010(2), whose enumerated definition reaches only mammals and reptiles named in it; and WAC 220-450-030's importation and possession rules are written for "live wild animals, wild birds, or game fish", which are the same geographically limited terms.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department, if consistent with the department's fish and wildlife management program, to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table and in 4VAC15-20-210 that the board finds and declares to be predatory or undesirable
VA.note: Jackson's chameleon is a nonnative (exotic) animal, not naturalized in Virginia, and absent from the permit table. Virginia permits by table and the reptile block of that table is four entries: all alligators and caimans, all crocodiles, all gavials, and the brown tree snake. Nothing here is on it, and 4VAC15-30-20 attaches the special permit only to animals the board has classed as predatory or undesirable, which is what the table is.

HI.quote: The introduction into Hawaii of live animals or live non-domestic animals as defined in this chapter is only allowed: (1) For those animals on the list designated as conditionally approved and dated November 28, 2006, or on the list designated as restricted entry, dated September 25, 2018
HI.note: Hawaii runs an inverted rule, and this is the clause that creates it. Introduction is allowed only for animals on the conditionally approved or restricted lists, so an animal on none of them is barred by default rather than left unregulated. The Iguanidae block on the restricted list names Anolis equestris, the knight anole, and stops there. The green anole appears on no Hawaii list, so it is barred by default even though it has been established in the wild across the islands for decades. Absence from the lists here is a ban, not a gap.

CA.note: California's restricted reptile list runs to crocodilians, snapping turtles, venomous snakes and the Gila monster, and nothing else. No anole is restricted.

PA.note: The green anole is native to the southeastern United States but not to Pennsylvania, and it is absent from the Fish and Boat Commission's list of Pennsylvania native species. Pennsylvania's Chapter 79 regulates native reptiles and amphibians only, and the Game and Wildlife Code reaches wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so a non-native reptile falls outside both agencies.

MI.note: The green anole is a southeastern species and is not a Michigan species. Michigan's Fisheries Order 224.21 reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR captive game permit reaches a reptile, so nothing in Michigan restricts it. Bringing one in calls for a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules.

VT.quote: Squamata | Iguania | Polychrotidae | Anolis | all species | Anoles
VT.note: The genus is unrestricted in full.

NM.quote: Rep/Amph | Lizard | Polychrotidae | Anolis carolinensis | Green Anole | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (aa) Nonvenomous, nonindigenous reptile species and subspecies;
NV.note: The green anole is nonvenomous and not indigenous to Nevada, so it is cleared by a single line that covers the entire pet reptile trade in one sweep and needs no Department permit.  Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Crocodilia ... All species of the family Chelydridae. Common name: snapping turtles; and All species of the genus Gopherus. Common name: gopher tortoises, including the desert tortoise
AZ.note: Arizona's restricted reptile list is short and aimed at danger and at its own natives: crocodilians, the venomous families, four named colubrids, snapping turtles and the genus Gopherus. The green anole is on none of it, so no special licence is required.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: The green anole is covered by the entry for anoles is named on the exempt list at regulation 6.1, so it needs no permit at all. Delaware exempts lizards generously and exempts no snake, turtle or tortoise at all, which is the sharpest line in this state's rules.

CO.cite: CPW, Wildlife and Animal Possession in Colorado, Regulated Wildlife
CO.quote: Any species of wildlife that is not specifically listed in Chapter W-11 as Domestic or Unregulated or in Chapter W-07 as Appendix A or Appendix B, the species is regulated wildlife and a CPW license is required. CPW will not issue a license for private possession (eg pet) of regulated wildlife.
CO.note: The anoles are on Appendix A as a family, Dactyloidae, but the listing carries the same qualifier as the rest of the lizard block, native only to the tropical and subtropical region, and CPW has read Anolis carolinensis as failing it. Its herpetofauna list records the species against Appendix A, B, 8 with the finding "native range outside tropical/subtropical", which is a determination against, not for. The green anole breeds up the southeastern United States well north of the 26 degree line Chapter W-7 § 700(G) draws, so the family listing does not carry it. That leaves it regulated wildlife with no pet licence available. This is the clearest case on the map of a family appearing on an allow-list without the species being allowed.

IL.quote: The following list comprises Illinois' indigenous or native herptile taxa to the subspecies level, if applicable.
IL.note: Illinois regulates herptiles through one Act, and almost everything in it turns on whether the animal is an Illinois native taxon. The green anole is not on the § 885.40 native list, so the possession cap on indigenous herptiles, the sport fishing licence needed to collect one, and the Herpetoculture permit needed to breed or sell one all fall away. It is not a special use herptile either: those are the venomous reptiles, the crocodilians, the medically significant amphibians, and monitor lizards as § 25-5 narrowly defines them. Illinois' native lizards are six species, the six-lined racerunner, slender glass lizard, five-lined and broad-headed skinks, eastern fence lizard and ground skink. Anolis is not among them. One thing to know whatever the species: 510 ILCS 68/5-5(a) sets a possession limit of "no more than 4 total per species" for herptiles, and § 5-5(e) says a resident over that limit needs a Herptile Scientific Collection or Herpetoculture permit "regardless of the origin of the species". The administrative rule at § 885.20(d) writes the same cap as applying to native taxa only. Statute and rule are not saying the same thing, and the statute is the one with the broader words, so a keeper with five of one non-native species is in an unresolved spot. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: The commissioner must prescribe conditions and may issue permits to breed, propagate, and sell snakes, lizards, and salamanders. A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Minnesota gets here in three steps, and the surprise is that none of them turns on the species being native. Section 97A.015, subd. 55 defines wild animals as creatures wild by nature and includes reptiles, with no geographic limit. Subd. 39 makes snakes, lizards and salamanders protected wild animals as whole categories. Section 97A.501, subd. 1 then bars possessing a protected wild animal unless the game and fish laws allow it, and this subdivision is the allowance. A green anole is a lizard, so the breeder-source condition applies to it as much as to a Minnesota native. Two things to know about how firm this is. The statute says the commissioner "must" prescribe conditions, but there is no snake, lizard or salamander breeder permit on the DNR's permits page, Minnesota Rules chapter 6256 covers only frogs and turtles, and no rule chapter implements the subdivision. And the DNR's own pet-trade page describes the change as reaching "wild collected Minnesota snakes, lizards, and/or salamanders", which is narrower than the statute's words and does not mention the breeder permit at all. So the condition is real on paper and its machinery is not visibly in place.

OR.quote: Iguanid lizards -- Iguanaidae -- All nonnative species except: Crotaphytus spp., Gambelia spp., Sceloporus spp., Uta spp., Phrynosoma spp.;
OR.note: Oregon runs a closed list for nonnative wildlife: OAR 635-056-0130(1) bars possessing any species the rules do not list, so being on the Noncontrolled list is a permission rather than an absence of one. This one turns on which Iguanidae the rule means. Anolis sits in Dactyloidae today, but the five genera Oregon excepts are Crotaphytus, Gambelia, Sceloporus, Uta and Phrynosoma, which now belong to Crotaphytidae and Phrynosomatidae and were only ever grouped together inside the broad old Iguanidae. The exceptions are what date the entry, and under that taxonomy the anoles are in it. Recorded legal on that reading; the alternative would put the species outside every list and into the default bar at OAR 635-056-0130(1). Reptiles and amphibians are wildlife in Oregon by statute rather than by rule, so every pet reptile question runs through this division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. Anolis appears in no category, and neither does any broader grouping that would reach it. Connecticut regulates reptiles by naming them, and what it names is danger and its own natives: crocodilians, the elapids and viperids, four large pythons, three anacondas, nine rear-fanged colubrid genera, the helodermatids, five monitors and the Komodo dragon in Category Two, and eight native herptiles in Category Three.

MD.quote: The following species or subspecies are considered native to Maryland and may be lawfully possessed, bred, or commercially traded only as provided in Regulations .04 — .09 of this chapter
MD.note: Maryland regulates reptiles and amphibians by nativity rather than by danger. COMAR 08.03.11 lists the native species in three tiers and reaches nothing else, and the only reptiles in the Crim. Law § 10-621 list are the crocodilians and the four venomous snake families. Anolis is not among the six lizards Maryland lists as native. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Nonpoisonous reptiles and amphibians except caimans and gavials
TN.note: Tennessee sorts reptiles by venom rather than by species: Class I takes the crocodilians and all venomous snakes, and subdivision (3)(A) puts every other reptile and amphibian in the no-permit class, with caimans and gavials carved back out. The green anole is nonvenomous and is neither a caiman nor a gavial.

TX.quote: A person without a nongame or nongame dealer’s permit may: (A) possess six or fewer specimens of a species of nongame wildlife listed in §65.331(e) of this title, provided the person does not engage in commercial activity involving the nongame wildlife; and (B) possess 25 or fewer specimens of a species of nongame wildlife listed in §65.331(d) of this title, provided the person does not engage in commercial activity involving the nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Anolis carolinensis is on the § 65.331(d) list, and it is native across the eastern half of Texas, so a keeper may hold 25 without a permit but may not sell, offer for sale, exchange or barter one. The cap reaches captive-bred animals: § 65.325(a) says nongame wildlife "includes captive-bred nongame wildlife", so a pet shop receipt does not lift it. This is the animal on this map where the Texas cap is most likely to surprise someone, because green anoles are sold nationally as cheap starter lizards and the buyer is the one the cap follows.

MA.quote: The following Iguanid Lizards (Iguanidae) may be kept without a permit: ... New World Chameleons (Anolis spp. and Ctenotus spp.) ...
MA.note: Cleared as a genus under the common name the regulation uses for it, "New World Chameleons (Anolis spp.)", which is an old usage worth knowing because searching the rule for "anole" finds nothing. MassWildlife's summary spells it out as "New World chameleons (including green and brown anoles)". Anolis carolinensis is IUCN least concern.

NE.quote: 001.03 Regulated Taking of Reptiles and Amphibians - The provisions of 001.03 apply to all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska except those legally designated as Game species, Nongame Species in Need of Conservation, and Threatened or Endangered species. It shall be unlawful for any person to take, possess, transport, export, process, sell or offer for sale, or ship any reptile or amphibian species defined in this section except as provided in 001.03A. ... 001.03A2 For those individual specimens or parts thereof legally obtained by purchase or consignment from outside of Nebraska, sale, offer of sale and associated transport, possession or processing will be permitted without regard to limits or numbers for the species listed below in 001.03A3 and 001.03A4, provided that such authority shall be contingent upon a persons ability to provide proof of legal acquisition including bill of sale or consignment.
NE.note: Nebraska regulates reptiles and amphibians only where they are its own. 166 NAC 10 § 001.03 opens by limiting itself to "all species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians native to Nebraska", and Anolis carolinensis is not one. The captive wildlife chapter does not reach it either, because § 001.01B is written about wild birds and wild mammals and §§ 37-245 and 37-246 define both by Nebraska geography. So no permit, no cap and no list. No Anolis is native to Nebraska, so the whole genus sits outside the chapter.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Cleared by the first entry on the no-permit list, "Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected)", which is the broadest single clearance on this map: it is not a species list, and it takes in every nonvenomous reptile and amphibian that no other Florida rule reaches. Anolis carolinensis is nonvenomous, is on no imperiled species list at 68A-27.003, and is on neither the prohibited list at 68-5.006 nor the conditional list at 68-5.004. Answered twice over, since 68A-6.003(12) separately says no permit is required for the sale of "chameleons (Anolis)", using the old trade name for the genus.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the green anole is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. No Anolis is a New York species, so the small game definition does not reach it either. The reptile clause of the wild animal list is a named-species list, not a family one, so an unnamed reptile is simply outside it.

GA.cite: DNR Guide to Legal Pets; O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4(b)(1)
GA.quote: By Georgia Law, most native species of wildlife cannot be held without permits or licenses. These licenses are not issued for the purpose of holding native wildlife as pets. These restrictions apply to the various species of animal, regardless of the origin or morphology. ... The following list of species native to Georgia may not be held as a pet regardless of its origin or morphology.
GA.note: Georgia handles its own wildlife separately from the wild animal rule, and the sentence that matters is "These restrictions apply to the various species of animal, regardless of the origin or morphology." A captive-bred animal from an out-of-state breeder is in the same position as one caught in a Georgia yard, and a colour morph is too. The green anole is on DNR's list of native species that may not be held as a pet. Licences exist under O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4 and DNR says in terms that they "are not issued for the purpose of holding native wildlife as pets". Worth flagging because green anoles are sold nationally as cheap starter lizards, and in the state where they are native they cannot be kept.

NYC.quote: Reptiles (Reptilia). All Helodermatidae ...; all front-fanged venomous snakes, even if devenomized ...; all venomous, mid-or rear-fanged, Duvernoy-glanded members of the family Colubridae, even if devenomized; any member, or hybrid offspring of the family Boidae, including, but not limited to, the common or green anaconda and yellow anaconda; any member of the family Pythonidae, including, but not limited to, the African rock python, Indian or Burmese python, Amethystine or scrub python; any member of the family Varanidae, including the white throated monitor, Bosc's or African savannah monitor, Komodo monitor or dragon, Nile monitor, crocodile monitor, water monitor, Bornean earless monitor; any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana; any member of the family teiidae, including, but not limited to, the golden, common, or black and white tegu; all members of the family Chelydridae, including snapping turtle and alligator snapping turtle; all turtles and tortoises with a carapace length of less than four (4) inches; and all members of the order Crocodylia ...
NYC.note: This one turns entirely on which decade's taxonomy the Code is using, and the article gives no answer. The reptile clause prohibits "any member of the family Iguanidae, including the green or common iguana". Anolis carolinensis was placed in Iguanidae sensu lato for most of the twentieth century, was moved to Polychrotidae in the 1989 Frost and Etheridge revision, and now sits in Dactyloidae. On the taxonomy current when this list was drafted the green anole is an iguanid and prohibited; on current taxonomy it is not one and the clause does not touch it. Nothing in the article dates its family names or says whether they float with revisions, and the Code elsewhere uses family names loosely, printing "teiidae" in lower case and calling hedgehogs Insectivora. Recorded unclear rather than guessing, because a green anole is a five dollar pet-shop lizard whose legality in the five boroughs rests on a 1989 systematics paper.

NJ.quote: Reptiles: i. American Anole - Anolis carolinensis;
NJ.note: The green anole is on the closed exempt list at 4.4, which is the only route to keeping an animal in New Jersey with no permit at all. It heads the reptile section of the exempt list as the "American Anole - Anolis carolinensis". 4.4(b) attaches the one condition that survives exemption, that the animal "must be housed or caged in such a manner as to prevent liberation".
