It is one of only three lizards New Jersey lets anyone keep without a permit, with the green iguana and the tokay gecko, while the leopard gecko, the bearded dragon and the blue-tongue skink all need one.

UT.quote: Total possession limits apply to all amphibians and reptiles acquired in-state, imported into the state, or lawfully acquired by intrastate transfer, except the following do not count towards an individual's applicable limit: (a) animals and their parts that are captive bred, not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12, and accompanied by documentation described in R657-53-5 verifying lawful acquisition and possession; ... (c) animals and their parts that are legally obtained outside of Utah and not classified as Prohibited or subject to certificate of registration requirements in R657-53-12
UT.note: Utah's herp rule is written for people going out and catching things, and that shape is what decides the pet question. R657-53-4(1) opens with a flat bar on possessing any reptile or amphibian "except as provided in this rule", and the exceptions then do the work. The only certificate of registration that attaches to possession itself is R657-53-12, which covers venomous reptiles native to Utah, and the green anole is not one. It is not Prohibited either: R657-53-9 prohibits only non-native venomous squamates and the whole of Crocodilia, and the division's published prohibited list is six declining native species. R657-53-8(1) then says animals that are captive bred, or "legally obtained outside of Utah", do not count towards a possession limit at all. A lawfully acquired captive-bred one therefore needs no wildlife document and carries no cap. Anolis carolinensis is not a Utah animal and appears on none of the division's tables. The catch worth knowing is R657-53-7(8): any species the division has not classified defaults to Controlled, at three a day and nine in total. That default governs an animal taken from the wild in Utah, which for a species that does not live here is a hypothetical.

AL.quote: It shall be unlawful to take, capture, kill, or attempt to take, capture or kill; possess, sell, trade for anything of monetary value, or offer to sell or trade for anything of monetary value; or propagate the following nongame wildlife species, or any parts or reproductive products of such species, or any hybrids of such species without a scientific collection permit or written permit from the Commissioner, Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, which shall specifically state what the permittee may do with regard to said species:
AL.note: The green anole is an Alabama native, which in most of the South is the start of a problem, and here it is not. 220-2-.92(1)(c) protects reptiles species by species, and its lizards are the eastern slender glass lizard, the mimic glass lizard, the coal skink and the southeastern five-lined skink. Anolis carolinensis is on none of them, and it is on no other Alabama list either. So native status alone does not restrict a reptile in Alabama, which is worth stating plainly, because Georgia next door bans keeping any native species as a pet and readers carry that assumption across the state line.

IN.quote: This section governs the: (1) sale; (2) transport for sale; or (3) offer for sale; of any reptile or amphibian native to Indiana regardless of place of origin. (b) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in section 9 of this rule, an individual must not sell, transport for sale, or offer to sell a reptile or amphibian that is native to Indiana.
IN.note: Indiana splits its reptiles cleanly and The green anole lands on the free side of the split. 312 IAC 9-5 governs reptiles and amphibians native to Indiana, and it is the rule that does the real work: 9-5-1(b) makes every native a protected wild animal, 9-5-6(f) caps possession at four per species, and 9-5-7 bars selling one regardless of where it came from, against a list of 99 taxa named by binomial. The green anole is on none of them. The other rule, 312 IAC 9-11, requires a permit only for Class I animals, which is the cottontail and three squirrels, Class II, which is Indiana's furbearers and a named run of small wild cats, and Class III, which is purebred wolves, bears, wild cats, venomous reptiles and crocodilians at least five feet long. Nothing there reaches it either. Anolis carolinensis is a southeastern animal whose range stops well short of Indiana, so it is not on the native list. Alabama, which is inside its range, reaches the opposite conclusion by the same method and still ends at legal, because it protects native reptiles species by species and never listed the anole.

OK.quote: No closed season. All reptiles except those listed in (3) and (5) of this section shall have a year-round season. (2) Bag limit. The bag limit is 6 per day or in possession for each species allowed in section (1) of this section.
OK.note: The green anole is an Oklahoma animal, which moves it out of the exemption at 800:25-25-3(c), since that clause is written for species "not indigenous to Oklahoma". What applies instead is the reptile and amphibian part at 800:25-7. Two provisions matter to a keeper. 7-7(2)(A) requires a resident or nonresident hunting licence of anyone "taking or attempting to take reptiles and amphibians or possessing reptiles or amphibians" that are land dwelling, which is a possession hook and not merely a collecting one. And 7-8 gives every reptile a year-round season except a closed list of twelve, with a limit of "6 per day or in possession for each species". Recorded as conditional on those two rather than as a permit, because there is no application and no discretion: a hunting licence is sold over the counter. 29 O.S. § 7-502(B)(4) separately exempts anyone possessing legally obtained wildlife "from a source other than the wild, as pets" from the statutory possession bar, which is why a captive-bred animal is not caught by the closed-season rule. Anolis carolinensis reaches into southeastern Oklahoma, which is what takes it out of the non-indigenous exemption. Oklahoma's closed list at 7-8(5) does close the season on four lizards, the Texas horned lizard, the side-blotched lizard, the checkered whiptail and the lesser earless lizard among them, and the anole is not one of them, so it keeps the year-round season and the six-animal cap.

WI.quote: A person is exempt from holding a license or other approval as required under this chapter to possess live nonnative wild animals that are not endangered or threatened species, except for any of the following: 1. Pheasants ... 2. Nonnative wild birds of the family anatidae that are migratory birds. 3. Nonnative wild animals that are harmful wild animals.
WI.note: Wisconsin runs its captive wildlife chapter on an exemption rather than a list, and the green anole is exempt by class. 169.04(1)(b) bars possessing any live wild animal without a licence, and then 169.04(4)(b) exempts every nonnative wild animal that is not endangered or threatened, with three carve-outs: hunting-preserve game birds, nonnative migratory waterfowl, and harmful wild animals. Harmful wild animals under 169.11(1)(a) are cougars, bears, wild swine and feral swine plus anything the department adds by rule, and no lizard has been added. Nativity is the thing to check here, because Wisconsin treats native and nonnative animals under different subsections and its native herps carry the purchase restriction at NR 16.13 that catches the milk snake and the garter snake. Anolis carolinensis is a southeastern animal whose range stops far south of Wisconsin, so it is nonnative and 169.04(4)(b) applies. The other rule to know about is NR 40, the invasive species chapter, which runs on a separate authority and lists no pet reptile.

NC.quote: Wild Animals. - Game animals; fur-bearing animals; feral swine; and all other wild mammals except marine mammals found in coastal fishing waters. In addition, this definition includes members of the following groups which are on the federal list of endangered or threatened species: wild amphibians, wild reptiles except sea turtles inhabiting and depending upon coastal fishing waters, and wild invertebrates except invertebrates declared to be pests under the Structural Pest Control Act of North Carolina of 1955 or the North Carolina Pesticide Law of 1971.
NC.note: North Carolina answers this in its definitions rather than its permit sections, and the answer is that the Wildlife Resources Commission has no jurisdiction. § 113-129(15) defines wild animals as game animals, fur-bearing animals, feral swine and other wild mammals, and then extends only to "wild amphibians, wild reptiles ... and wild invertebrates" that are "on the federal list of endangered or threatened species". The green anole is not federally listed, so it is not a wild animal in North Carolina at all and the captivity licence at § 113-272.5 has nothing to attach to. § 14-417 reaches venomous reptiles and large constrictors, and § 153A-131 lets counties regulate dangerous animals, which is where any local restriction would come from. This is the entry that shows how far the definition reaches. The green anole is a North Carolina native, and in most southeastern states that alone starts a problem: Georgia bans keeping a native, Alabama and Oklahoma protect natives species by species, South Carolina bars selling one. North Carolina simply does not treat a non-listed reptile as wildlife, so its own native lizard is unregulated.

SC.quote: No native reptile or amphibian, including parts, products, eggs, and derivatives may be sold, purchased, traded, exchanged, bartered, exported or shipped, transferred and/or re-homed, except:
SC.note: The green anole is a South Carolina native, which is what takes it out of the pet-trade exemption. § 50-16-60 clears reptiles as a class from the import permit, and Regulation 123-151.4(I) then says that section "does not privilege" a native reptile: the 2021 rules control instead. 123-151.3(A) bars selling, purchasing, trading, exchanging, bartering, exporting, shipping, transferring and re-homing any native reptile, and its twelve exceptions do not reach a lizard. They are: transfers to the department, transfers authorised by other law, accredited zoos and research institutions, laboratory venom, non-native morphs of native snake species, three named snakes under 10 inches, three more under 20, the pine snake under 24, two named turtles from permitted sources, alligators, bullfrogs, and rehabilitators. So a green anole may be kept and may not change hands, and giving one away is expressly included in the bar.

OH.quote: "Restricted snake" means any of the following: ... (c) Reticulated pythons; (d) Indian pythons; (e) Burmese pythons; (f) North African rock pythons; (g) South African rock pythons; (h) Amethystine pythons.
OH.note: Ohio's two restrictive schemes both miss the green anole. § 935.01(C) lists the dangerous wild animals, which are big cats, bears, primates, hyenas, elephants and the like, and § 935.01(L) lists the restricted snakes, which are venomous species and six named giant pythons. Neither reaches a lizard. The other scheme is the propagating licence at § 1533.71, which covers game birds, game quadrupeds, reptiles, amphibians and fur-bearing animals and is about propagating rather than keeping. Nativity is worth checking because Ohio does treat it as a category, defining native wildlife at § 1531.01(RR) as "any species of the animal kingdom indigenous to this state". Anolis carolinensis is a southeastern animal and is not indigenous to Ohio, so the propagating licence, which is built around game and native species, is not the route either.

RI.quote: The following Iguanid Lizards (Iguanidae) may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit: Basilisks (Basiliscus spp.), Collared and Leopard Lizards (Crotaphytus spp.), Common or Green Iguanas (Iguana i. iguana), False or Spring-tailed Iguanas (Ctenosaurus spp.), (Liolaemus spp.), New World Chameleons (Anolis spp. and Ctenotus spp.), Spiny Lizards (Sceloporus spp.), Tree and Bush Lizards (Urosaurus spp.), (Uranoscodon spp.), Zebra-tailed Lizards (Callisaurus spp.)
RI.note: Anolis is cleared as a genus under the old Iguanidae heading. That the rule uses drafting-era taxonomy cuts the opposite way here from New York City, whose Health Code bans "any member of the family Iguanidae" and leaves the anole hanging on which revision you read: Rhode Island lists the genus by name inside the family, so the taxonomy question never arises. The green anole is not native to Rhode Island, so the § 3.7(C) bar on native wildlife does not reach it.

AR.cite: Addendum R1.01, Reptiles, Geckos and Lizards; Code 09.14(B)
AR.quote: Anoline Lizards (Genera: Anolis, Audantia, Chamaelinorops, Ctenonotus, Dactyloa, Deiroptyx, Norops, Xiphosurus) except Brown Anoles (Anolis sagrei) or species native to Arkansas
AR.note: Two exceptions, and the second is written for this animal: Anolis carolinensis is the only anole native to the United States, and the Arkansas Herpetological Atlas vouchers it in 29 of the state’s 75 counties across the Ouachita Mountains and South Central Plains. Off R1.01 it becomes a Code 09.14 native pet, six per household, either hand-captured in Arkansas or commercially obtained and captive born from a Commission-permitted Wildlife Breeder/Dealer or under a Wildlife Importation Permit. The first exception, the brown anole, is an invasive rather than a native, which is why the entry needed both.

ME.quote: All Species in Genus Anolis (Anoles) Anolis spp.*
ME.note: The genus is cleared outright. The green anole is not native to Maine, so the native-reptile provisions at 12 M.R.S. § 12152(1-B) and § 7.01 do not come into it, and Anolis carolinensis is IUCN Least Concern, so the asterisk does not remove it. The whole Reptilia section of the list sits under the heading "Captive Bred Origin Only", which is the condition on the clearance: a wild-caught animal of the same species is not unrestricted and falls back to § 7.06(4), under which an uncategorised animal may not be possessed at all.

MO.quote: Except for federally-designated endangered species and species listed in 3 CSR 10-4.117 and 3 CSR 10-9.240, the following may be bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit: Asian clams (Corbicula species) taken from impoundments that are not waters of the state; bison; amphibians, reptiles, and mammals not native to Missouri except those mammals located in a licensed big game hunting preserve; and those birds (except ring necked pheasants and gray partridge) not native to the continental United States.
MO.note: The whole answer is whether the green anole is a Missouri native, and the Department of Conservation's own A Guide to Missouri's Lizards settles it: the state has eleven native lizards, three collared and horned and prairie lizards, six skinks, the prairie racerunner and the western slender glass lizard, plus one introduced Italian wall lizard, and no anole. So Anolis carolinensis is a reptile not native to Missouri and needs no permit. Missouri is the northern edge of this question: the same animal is a native, and therefore a restricted one, in Arkansas next door.

ID.quote: Conventional Pets. Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders.
ID.note: The green anole is a non-venomous, non-dangerous reptile and is nowhere near native to Idaho, so it is a conventional pet. IDAPA 13.01.06.200.04 makes all native reptiles Protected Nongame, which is the provision the qualifier "not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho" points at; it has nothing to catch here. Section 200.06 then says no Department permit is needed to import, export, transport, possess or sell a conventional pet, provided it is not intended for release into the wild. Idaho answers by category rather than by species list, which is unusual and is why so few of its cells need a species search.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake
NH.note: The green anole is exotic to New Hampshire, whose indigenous reptiles are listed in Tables 800.1 and 800.2 and are seven turtles and ten snakes and no lizard at all, so it falls under the exotic clearance rather than the two-per-species indigenous allowance. New Hampshire clears exotic reptiles as a class rather than by species, with three exceptions, and Fis 803.03(b)(4) repeats the clearance for importation, so neither possessing nor bringing one into the state needs a permit. The rule was readopted in full in April 2026 and this structure survived unchanged.

WY.quote: The animals listed in this section may be imported or possessed without securing an importation/possession permit and shall not require written authorization from the Chief of Fisheries. A certificate of veterinary inspection or a fish health and AIS inspection are not required. (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.
WY.note: The green anole is a reptile, is not indigenous to Wyoming, and appears on neither restricted list. Section 9(c) is the clause nativity would engage, and it reaches indigenous reptiles only when they are imported for commercial use. Section 8, the no-permit-will-issue list, is federal injurious and endangered listings, aquatic invasive species, Xenopus, three frogs and toads, grass carp and mosquitofish. Section 9 requires a permit for venomous reptiles, for herptiles listed in Commission Regulation Chapter 52 that need a scientific or educational take permit, for Wyoming-indigenous herptiles imported for commercial use, and for aquatic turtles in ornamental ponds. Neither reaches this animal, so Section 10 applies and nothing at all is required, not even a veterinary certificate.

KY.quote: Except as established in Section 5 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport into Kentucky, or possess the following exotic wildlife that are considered potentially injurious to native ecosystems
KY.note: The green anole counts as exotic wildlife here, which is the part worth checking rather than assuming: the Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources gives Kentucky ten lizards, five skinks, the Mediterranean house gecko, the eastern slender glass lizard, the northern fence lizard, the six-lined racerunner and the common wall lizard, and no anole. So § 1 catches it, 301 KAR 2:081 does not, and neither § 4 list names it. Kentucky's only possession bars for an exotic are the two lists in § 4, the potentially injurious species at (1) and the inherently dangerous species at (2), and this animal is on neither. It is also not on the § 7 permit-exempt list, so a transportation permit under § 2(1) is needed to bring one into the state; possession itself is unrestricted once it is here.

LA.quote: Green Anole Rule. It shall be illegal to sell or purchase any Green Anole (Anolis carolinesis) with a snout-vent length of less than 1 3/4 inches or an overall length of less than 5 inches with the tail intact.
LA.note: Louisiana is the only jurisdiction on this map with a rule written for the green anole by name, and it is a size rule on the transaction rather than a bar on keeping: below 1 3/4 inches snout to vent, or five inches overall, the animal may not be sold or bought. The anole is also a Louisiana native, listed without qualifier in the § 101.I checklist while the brown anole beside it is marked "established nonnative", so the native provisions at § 101.J apply too: a basic recreational fishing licence for "collection and possession of native reptiles and amphibians for recreational purposes", and a Reptile and Amphibian Wholesale/Retail Dealer's Licence for whoever sells it, "regardless of the number of generations removed from the wild". It is not on the § 101.J.4 conservation-concern list, so it may be taken from the wild.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: The green anole is a nonvenomous reptile, so it is on the clean list. Nativity does not come into it: AS 16.05.940(19) defines game as species "found or introduced in the state", and either way the class-wide reptile entry covers it. Alaska's clean list is otherwise a roll call of individual species, so this one class-wide entry is the widest clearance in it, and it is what makes the strictest exotic pet state in the country an easy one for a lizard keeper. Subsection (e) is the only thing riding on it: a listed species that is endangered still needs a federal permit.

MT.quote: unless otherwise regulated pursuant to 87-5-116, all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous lizards not on the controlled or prohibited lists, including but not limited to the following families or subfamilies: ... (xix) Polychrotidae (anoles)
MT.note: Montana names the anoles by family, using the pre-split Polychrotidae rather than Dactyloidae. The clause carries a geographic qualifier, "tropical and subtropical", and the green anole is the entry on this list where that is worth stopping over: its range runs from subtropical Florida and the Gulf coast up into warm temperate North Carolina and Tennessee. It reads as satisfied, because the family Montana chose is overwhelmingly neotropical and the green anole is its only North American member, so the entry would have nothing else to do. Worth re-checking if Fish, Wildlife and Parks ever publishes a determination, because Colorado shows what a range qualifier on an allow-list can do: there Boidae is listed and the rosy boa is still banned, off the same line that clears the boa constrictor.

WA.quote: "Wildlife" means all species of the animal kingdom whose members exist in Washington in a wild state. This includes but is not limited to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, and invertebrates.
WA.note: Anolis carolinensis does not exist in Washington in a wild state, so it is not Washington wildlife. Washington is far outside its range and it is on no state list. Washington answers by a geographic qualifier rather than by a species list, which is why it is one of the shortest states to read. Three things then have to be checked and all three come back empty: the animal is not designated deleterious exotic wildlife at WAC 220-640-200(1), which is a mute swan, mongooses, wild boar, javelina, six bovid genera and a run of cervids; it is not a potentially dangerous wild animal under RCW 16.30.010(2), whose enumerated definition reaches only mammals and reptiles named in it; and WAC 220-450-030's importation and possession rules are written for "live wild animals, wild birds, or game fish", which are the same geographically limited terms.

VA.quote: it shall be lawful to capture and possess live for private use and not for sale or export no more than one individual of any native or naturalized, as defined in 4VAC15-20-50, species of amphibian or reptile per physical address
VA.note: The exotic permit table is the wrong rule for this animal. Virginia fixes native and naturalized status by an incorporated document, the department's List of Native and Naturalized Fauna of Virginia, and that list carries "Green Anole * Anolis carolinesis *", the asterisk denoting a naturalized species. A naturalized animal is expressly excluded from the definition of a nonnative (exotic) animal at 4VAC15-20-50, so 4VAC15-30-40 does not reach it and 4VAC15-360-10 does: one individual per physical address, live, for private use, and not for sale or export. That the cap binds a keeper rather than only a collector is confirmed from the other direction by the domestic animal list, which writes an express carve-out for "Domesticated morphs of red cornsnake ... visibly distinguishable from native red cornsnakes"; that exception would have nothing to do if ordinary keeping of a native herp were free.

HI.quote: domesticated races of European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)... and domestic hybrids (crosses between two domestic animals). As used in this chapter, the term or word, "animal," shall mean "non-domestic animal"
HI.note: The answer that most Hawaii summaries get wrong, and the reason is structural. The domestic rabbit is not on the conditionally approved list, and in Hawaii being unlisted normally means barred. But § 4-71-2 names domesticated races of the European rabbit as a domestic animal and then says that as used in the chapter the word animal means non-domestic animal, so the lists never reach a pet rabbit in the first place. Wild hares in the genus Lepus are separately prohibited. Bringing one to the islands still needs an import permit under HRS chapter 150A.

CA.quote: except domesticated races of rabbits and hares of the family Leporidae are not restricted
CA.note: California restricts the order Lagomorpha as a whole and then carves the pet rabbit straight back out by name. Wild rabbits and hares stay restricted, so the exemption turns on the animal being a domesticated race rather than on the family.

PA.note: The rabbit appears in none of the eleven categories the Game Commission prohibits. Pennsylvania's definitional chain technically makes every mammal but livestock a wild animal, and § 137.1(a)(11) reads on any wildlife captive bred out of state, but the Commission applies that to undomesticated species and the domestic rabbit is not one.

MI.note: The permit to hold game in captivity is a closed list of native game species and the rabbit is not on it; Michigan's native lagomorphs are the snowshoe hare and the eastern cottontail, not the European rabbit behind every pet breed. Nothing else in Michigan reaches it. Importing one calls for a certificate of veterinary inspection as a domestic rabbit.

NM.quote: Mammal | Rabbit | Leporidae | Oryctolagus cuniculus | Rabbit, European (common) | I
NM.note: Group I on the Director's list, which means semi-domesticated and no importation permit required.  One caveat on all of this: 19.35.7 NMAC is an importation rule, its stated scope being persons who desire to bring wildlife species into New Mexico, so it governs getting the animal here rather than keeping one already in the state.

NV.quote: (5) Wild European Rabbit....................... Oryctolagus cuniculus
NV.note: The two columns of this row disagree with each other. The scientific classification names Oryctolagus cuniculus, which is the species every domestic rabbit belongs to, while the common name column says Wild European Rabbit. Nothing in the section says whether domesticated races are carved out, and unlike the chinchilla, mink, rat, mouse, turkey and duck entries elsewhere in these rules, no domesticated races wording appears here. Pet rabbits are plainly sold in Nevada and the definition of wildlife at NRS 501.097 reaches animals found naturally in a wild state, which a domesticated breed arguably is not. Rendered grey rather than guessed, because the text arguably reaches the animal and clearly was aimed at the wild form. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: Order Erinaceomorpha, all species, except members of the genus Atelerix, which are not restricted. Common name: longeared and pygmy hedgehogs; Order Lagomorpha, all species, except members of the genus Oryctolagus containing domestic rabbits, which are not wildlife and are not restricted; Order Rodentia, the families Capromyidae, Castoridae, Dipodidae, Echimyidae, Erethizontidae, Geomyidae, Sciuridae
AZ.note: Arizona goes further than clearing the rabbit, it declines to call it wildlife at all. The order Lagomorpha is restricted with the genus Oryctolagus carved out in terms, and the carve-out says domestic rabbits are not wildlife and are not restricted. That phrasing puts the pet rabbit outside Title 17 rather than merely exempting it, which is the cleanest rabbit answer on this map.

DE.quote: 6.1.1 Mammals: Chinchillas, Degus, Ferrets, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Hedgehogs, Mice, Norway rats, Possums, Rabbits and Sugar gliders. 6.1.2 Reptiles: Anoles, Agamas, Asian Water Dragons, Basilisks, Bearded dragons, Chameleons, Geckos, Iguanas, Skinks (except the five-lined skink), Swift lizards, and Tegus.
DE.note: Rabbits appear by name on the exempt mammal list, so no permit is required.

CO.quote: Domesticated races of European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
CO.note: Colorado reaches the rabbit the way most states do that address it at all, by naming the domesticated race of the European rabbit rather than the wild species. CPW's own mammal list files Oryctolagus cuniculus domesticus against this line. CPW tells keepers to check their city or county as well, so a local ordinance can still be the binding rule.

IL.quote: No person shall release, hold, possess, or engage in raising San Juan (sometimes called European) rabbits or finnraccoons (sometimes called raccoon dogs) (Nyctereutes procyonoides) in this State and no permit shall be issued therefor.
IL.note: Illinois is the state where the rabbit needs the most care, because two provisions name the animal and neither writes an express carve-out for domestic stock. This one bars holding or possessing San Juan rabbits with no permit available at all, and the San Juan is a feral strain of Oryctolagus cuniculus kept for dog training rather than a pet breed. The injurious species list at 17 Ill. Adm. Code 805.20(a) then names "Any species of European rabbit of the genus Oryctolagus", carried over from the federal injurious wildlife listing at 50 CFR 16.11. Read at face value that pair would reach a house rabbit. Read in place they do not: the Part 805 heading is "Wild Mammals" and the federal section it copies is titled "Importation of live wild mammals", the Wildlife Code says in its own words that it applies only to wild birds and wild mammals, and the Animal Welfare Act licenses Illinois pet shops to sell animals customarily obtained as pets. Recorded legal on that reading, and flagged because the wording is the kind that gets quoted out of context in both directions. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.cite: Minn. R. 6216.0250, subp. 5(C); Minn. Stat. § 84D.05, subd. 1
MN.quote: A person may not possess, import, purchase, sell, propagate, transport, or introduce a prohibited invasive species, except: (1) under a permit issued by the commissioner under section 84D.11
MN.note: Minnesota designates the European rabbit, Oryctolagus cuniculus, a prohibited invasive species by rule, with no strain or domestication qualifier, and § 84D.05 then bars possessing one outright. The DNR restates that on its own invasive species page, listing the European rabbit among the prohibited mammals and saying it is a misdemeanour to possess, import, purchase, transport or introduce them except under a permit for disposal, control, research or education. None of those permit categories is pet-keeping, no carve-out for domesticated stock appears in the rule, the statute or the agency page, and the DNR has published no species profile or guidance for it at all. Against that sits the obvious: Minnesota licenses pet shops and runs county-fair rabbit shows, and the listing descends from the federal injurious wildlife entry aimed at wild-type animals. Recorded unclear because the text says one thing plainly and practice says another, and nothing published resolves it. Illinois names the same animal and lands differently, because there the possession bar is written for the San Juan strain and the injurious list is headed "Wild Mammals".

OR.quote: Pursuant to the definition of "wildlife," the following species are not subject to these rules because they are not "wild" ... (9) European Rabbit — Oryctolagus cuniculus.
OR.note: This is the strongest position an animal can hold in Oregon. ORS 496.004(19) leaves it to the commission to define which mammals count as wild, and this rule is that definition: the 32 species on it are declared not wild and fall outside the wildlife rules altogether, rather than being permitted by them. Oregon is the clean counter-example to the states that name this species and leave the pet unaddressed: here Oryctolagus cuniculus is declared not wild outright, with no strain qualifier needed, while nonnative hares and cottontails are prohibited by the same division. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Domestic animal" means any animal that humans have selectively bred in captivity to produce genetic changes affecting the temperament, color, conformation, or other attributes of the species to an extent that makes such animal unique and distinguishable from wild individuals of the species, and that has been raised in a life intimately associated with and advantageous to humans. "Domestic animal" does not include any wild animal raised in captivity, even over many generations, that has become accustomed to human interaction but that is still wild by nature.
CT.note: Connecticut is the state that shows how the rabbit question should be drafted. Category Two reaches "a species referenced as injurious wildlife in 50 CFR 16.11", and the European rabbit is on that federal list, so on the lists alone a pet rabbit would be barred outright. It is not, because the categories only ever apply to a "wild animal", which the regulation defines as excluding a domestic animal, and it defines a domestic animal by what selective breeding has done to it rather than by species name. A house rabbit is selectively bred to be distinguishable from wild individuals and raised in a life intimately associated with humans, so it is outside the scheme entirely. Minnesota and Illinois name the same species with no equivalent definition and end up much harder to answer.

MD.quote: A person may not import into the State, offer for sale, trade, barter, possess, breed, or exchange a live: (i) fox, skunk, raccoon, or bear; (ii) caiman, alligator, or crocodile; (iii) member of the cat family other than the domestic cat; (iv) hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds; (v) member of the dog family other than the domestic dog; (vi) hybrid of a member of the dog family and a domestic dog; (vii) nonhuman primate ...; or (viii) poisonous snake in the family groups of Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae, or Crotolidae.
MD.note: Maryland answers a pet question with three rules and this animal is outside all of them. Crim. Law § 10-621 is a closed list of eight clauses. Nat. Res. § 10-902 requires a permit only for wildlife native to Maryland. COMAR 08.03.11 covers native reptiles and amphibians. The pet rabbit is Oryctolagus cuniculus and is not native to Maryland, whose native lagomorph is the eastern cottontail, so the § 10-902 permit does not attach. Maryland does not adopt the federal injurious wildlife list, which is what makes this species awkward in Minnesota and Illinois. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: Class III--This class requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes and includes, but is not limited to, those listed in subdivisions (3)(A)-(Q). ... Rabbits, hares, moles and shrews
TN.note: Named in its own subdivision of the no-permit class. Tennessee reaches the rabbit by common name and by group rather than by the binomial that makes this species awkward in Minnesota and Illinois, and it does not adopt the federal injurious wildlife list anywhere in this part.

TX.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means: (A) a lion; (B) a tiger; (C) an ocelot; (D) a cougar; (E) a leopard; (F) a cheetah; (G) a jaguar; (H) a bobcat; (I) a lynx; (J) a serval; (K) a caracal; (L) a hyena; (M) a bear; (N) a coyote; (O) a jackal; (P) a baboon; (Q) a chimpanzee; (R) an orangutan; (S) a gorilla; or (T) any hybrid of an animal listed in this subdivision.
TX.note: Two Texas rules mention rabbits and neither reaches this one. The § 65.331(d) nongame list names the black-tailed jackrabbit, a Lepus, and 31 TAC § 65.325(b)(4) expressly excepts rabbits of the genus Sylvilagus from the whole subchapter. Oryctolagus cuniculus is neither, and it is not indigenous to Texas in any event, so the definition never reaches it. That is a cleaner answer than Minnesota or Illinois manage, where the same species is named outright on an injurious species list.

MA.quote: Domestic animals as listed in 321 CMR 9.02(3) shall be exempt from the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131, § 23, and may be possessed, propagated, maintained, imported, bought, sold, or otherwise disposed of ... Any vertebrate taxa not listed in 321 CMR 9.02 shall be presumed to be wild and shall be subject to the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131.
MA.note: The domestic animal list reads "Domestic rabbit, including breeds, varieties, and strains derived from the European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) but not including the European rabbit ferae naturae and not including the so-called 'San Juan' rabbit." Massachusetts is the cleanest answer on this map to a question three other states cannot settle: it names the same species Minnesota and Illinois struggle with, and disposes of it by separating the domestic strains from wild-type and San Juan stock in one sentence.

NE.quote: Wildlife means any member of any nondomesticated species of the animal kingdom, whether reared in captivity or not, including any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate and includes any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof or the dead body or parts thereof.
NE.note: The cottontail, Sylvilagus floridanus, is on the § 001.01B list of native species that need a Captive Wildlife Permit, and the domestic rabbit is not that animal. Oryctolagus cuniculus is not native to Nebraska and has no established free-ranging population here, so it is not a wild mammal, and as a domesticated species it is outside § 37-247 as well. Nebraska is another state where the rabbit question is answered by the animal simply not being the one the law is about.

FL.quote: No permit shall be required to possess the following wildlife for personal use, unless possession of a species is otherwise regulated by other rules of the Commission: (a) Reptiles or amphibians (nonvenomous, unprotected) (b) Gerbils, hedgehogs (c) Honey possums, sugar gliders (d) Rats and mice (e) Moles; shrews (f) Rabbits (g) Squirrels; chipmunks (h) Ferrets (domestic; European) (i) Guinea pigs (j) Hamsters (k) Prairie dogs (l) Chinchillas (m) Shell parakeets (n) Canaries (o) Lovebirds (p) Cockatiels (q) Parrots (r) Finches (s) Myna birds (t) Toucans (u) Doves; ringed, ruddy, and diamond (v) Button quail
FL.note: Named at (14)(f) with no qualifier, so the entry reaches the domestic rabbit without the wild-versus-domestic sorting that Minnesota, Illinois and Massachusetts each have to do for the same species.

NY.quote: "Wild animal" shall not include "companion animal" as defined in section three hundred fifty of the agriculture and markets law. Wild animal includes, and is limited to, any or all of the following orders and families: (1) Nonhuman primates and prosimians, (2) Felidae and all hybrids thereof, with the exception of the species Felis catus ... and hybrids of Felis catus that are registered by the American Cat Fanciers Association or the International Cat Association provided that such cats be without any wild felid parentage for a minimum of five generations, (3) Canidae (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda)), (4) Ursidae, (5) All reptiles that are venomous by nature, pursuant to department regulation, and the following species and orders: Burmese Python (Python m. bivittatus), Reticulated Python (Python reticulatus), African Rock Python (Python sabae), Green Anaconda (Eunectes maurinus), Yellow Anaconda (Eunectes notaeus), Australian Amethystine Python (Morelia amethistina and Morelia kinghorni), Indian Python (Python molurus), Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator), Nile Monitor (Varanus nilocitus), White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis), Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides) and Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori), Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodensis) and any hybrid thereof, (6) Crocodylia.
NY.note: New York regulates exotic animals through a closed list rather than an open standard, and the domestic rabbit is on neither version of it. The statutory wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses covering primates, Felidae, Canidae, Ursidae, a named set of constrictors and monitors plus venomous reptiles, and Crocodylia. The department's dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 adds the raccoon dog, wolverine, badgers, raccoons, skunks, bats, elephants and rhinoceroses. Neither reaches this animal, and the native wildlife route does not either, because that one runs through the small game definition and this is not a New York species. New York's native lagomorphs, the cottontail and the varying hare, are small game and therefore protected wildlife, and Oryctolagus cuniculus is neither of them.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are subject to licensing requirements pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4. (a) Mammals ... 3. Order Carnivora (weasels, ferrets, cats, bears, wolves, etc.) - All species, except that European ferret (Mustela putorius furo) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 7. Orders Diprotodontia and Peramelemorphia (Marsupials) - All species except that Petaurus breviceps (sugar glider) may be sold, purchased, exhibited, or held as a pet without a license or permit ... 8. Order Erinaceopmorpha (hedgehogs) - All species ... 10. Order Lagomorpha (Rabbits, hares, etc) - All species ... 16. Order Rodentia (rats, mice, etc.) - All species except Genera Cavia, Chinchilla, Gerbillus, Meriones, Mesocricetus, and species Mus musculus, Rattus rattus, and Rattus norvegicus
GA.note: Georgia licenses whole taxonomic orders and then writes short exception lists inside them, so being named in one of those lists is the whole answer here. Lagomorpha is licensed as a whole order with no exception written into the rule, and the answer comes from the definition instead: the rule reaches "wild animals" as defined at O.C.G.A. § 27-1-2, and DNR states the result as "Rabbits and hares; all species except those normally domesticated." Georgia's native rabbits, the cottontail, marsh and swamp rabbits, are on the prohibited natives list, so the distinction is doing real work here.

NYC.quote: In addition to domesticated dogs and cats, an animal may be kept, possessed, harbored or sold in the City of New York provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law, including federal, state and local laws regulating domestic animals and livestock or protecting wildlife and endangered species. Such animals include, but are not limited to, gerbil, hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and fowl or small birds such as parakeet, parrot, canary and finch.
NYC.note: Named in § 161.01(c) as "domesticated rabbit", and § 161.19 separately governs keeping rabbits alongside livestock and live poultry. § 161.01(c) is the article's short affirmative list, and it is written as examples rather than as a closed set: "an animal may be kept ... provided that possession of the animal is not otherwise prohibited by law", followed by gerbil, hamster, guinea pig, domesticated rabbit and small birds. So the question in New York City is always whether something else in § 161.01(b) reaches the animal.

NJ.quote: "Exotic animal" means any species of mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian, fish, mollusk, or crustacean that is not indigenous to New Jersey as determined by the Fish and Game Council in rules and regulations adopted pursuant to the "Administrative Procedure Act," and shall include the young or eggs of any such species, but shall not include (1) domesticated companion animals or farm livestock as defined by the Fish and Game Council, or (2) fish, shellfish, or game species not indigenous to New Jersey for which fishing, harvesting, hunting, or trapping is authorized and regulated pursuant to law, the State Fish and Game Code, or rules and regulations of the Fish and Game Council;
NJ.note: The domestic rabbit is not on any of the Division's three lists, and in a closed-list state that would normally mean a permit under 4.5. It does not here, because the possession bar the subchapter implements is N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3, whose definition of "exotic animal" excludes domesticated companion animals, and Oryctolagus cuniculus is a domesticated species rather than a wild one. Subchapter 4 is adopted under the Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act, which reaches wildlife, defined at N.J.S.A. 23:2A-3 as wild animals. Two loose threads are worth naming rather than hiding. The statute says domesticated companion animals are those "defined by the Fish and Game Council", and the Council has not defined the term anywhere in N.J.A.C. 7:25. And 4.4 goes to the trouble of exempting the hamster, the gerbil and the guinea pig, which are domesticated pets on the same footing, so the exempt list is belt and braces rather than a sign that unlisted domestic pets are caught. The native cottontail is a different animal and a game species under 7:25-5.3.

UT.cite: Utah Admin. Code R657-3b-1(3); Table 3b-1, domestic mammals
UT.quote: Domestic mammals and mammalian livestock not covered under this rule ... Rabbit, European Oryctolagus cuniculus
UT.note: Utah puts the domestic rabbit in the cleanest category it has. R657-3b-1(3) says "domestic animals not governed by this rule are listed in Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1", and the table's first section is headed "Domestic mammals and mammalian livestock not covered under this rule". Oryctolagus cuniculus is on it by name. That is stronger than an exemption, because the animal is outside the rule rather than excused from it, and it matters in Utah more than it would elsewhere: the same table's header says every species not listed is "presumed prohibited". Utah is also the state where the domestic and the wild answers do not collide, since the native lagomorphs it excludes from protected wildlife at 23A-1-101(46)(b) are the jack rabbits, a different genus.

AL.quote: San Juan Rabbits, Jack Rabbits or any other species of wild rabbit or hare;
AL.note: Alabama bans "San Juan Rabbits, Jack Rabbits or any other species of wild rabbit or hare", and the San Juan rabbit is a feral population of Oryctolagus cuniculus, the same species as the pet. Read on the binomial alone that clause would ban a house rabbit. It does not, because the category the clause names is wild rabbits and hares and the two examples are given as members of it: the San Juan is on the list as a feral animal used for stocking and dog training, not as a domestic pet. The domestic rabbit is on no other Alabama list and 220-2-.92 protects native nongame, which the eastern cottontail is not, since it is a game species with a season. Illinois and Minnesota raise the same question and this map answers them differently, so the reasoning is set out rather than assumed.

IN.quote: A permit is required under this rule for the following Class I wild animals: (1) Rabbit (Sylvilagus floridanus). (2) Squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis, Sciurus niger, and Glaucomys volans).
IN.note: Indiana names a rabbit in its permit rule and it is not this one. 312 IAC 9-11-6(a)(1) reads "Rabbit (Sylvilagus floridanus)", the eastern cottontail, and puts it in Class I, defined as a wild animal that "because of its nature, habits, or status, is not a threat to personal or public safety". A permit is still required for one, applied for within five days of taking possession. The domestic rabbit is Oryctolagus cuniculus, a different genus and not a wild animal at all, so none of this touches it. That precision is worth noting because Illinois and Minnesota name Oryctolagus itself and this map answers them very differently as a result.

OK.quote: (24) Rabbits (except cottontails, jackrabbits and swamp rabbits, and other such species normally found in the wild).
OK.note: Oklahoma writes the rabbit exemption the way a careful drafter should, naming the category and then the exceptions: rabbits are exempt "except cottontails, jackrabbits and swamp rabbits, and other such species normally found in the wild". The domestic rabbit is Oryctolagus cuniculus and is not a species normally found in the wild here, so it is exempt from import and export permits and from both wildlife breeder licences. It is worth reading against Alabama, which bans "San Juan Rabbits, Jack Rabbits or any other species of wild rabbit or hare" and gets the same result by naming a feral population of the pet's own species, and against Illinois and Minnesota, which name Oryctolagus itself and reach much harder answers.

VT.quote: Mammals Lagomorpha Leporidae Oryctolagus cuniculus Domestic rabbit  Including breeds, varieties, and strains derived from the European rabbit but not including the Eurpoean rabbit ferae naturae and not including the so-called "San Juan" rabbit.
VT.note: Vermont is the state that answers the rabbit question most carefully, and it is worth reading because three other states on this map get tangled in exactly what Vermont pins down. The Domestic Species List names Oryctolagus cuniculus and then draws the line inside the species: breeds, varieties and strains derived from the European rabbit are domestic, the European rabbit ferae naturae is not, and the San Juan rabbit is expressly not. Being on the Domestic list means the animal is outside the wild animal permit scheme entirely. Compare Alabama, which bans "San Juan Rabbits, Jack Rabbits or any other species of wild rabbit or hare" and leaves a reader to work out that the pet is the same species as the San Juan; and Illinois and Minnesota, which name Oryctolagus with no strain qualifier at all and produce much harder answers.

WI.quote: "Wild animal" means any animal of a wild nature that is normally found in the wild and that is not a domestic animal.
WI.note: The domestic rabbit never enters Wisconsin's captive wildlife chapter, because 169.01(37) defines a wild animal as one "of a wild nature that is normally found in the wild and that is not a domestic animal", and Oryctolagus cuniculus in its domestic form is neither of a wild nature nor normally found in the wild here. 169.01(7) then defines domestic animal to include anything the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection lists as one. That is a cleaner route than most states manage: Illinois and Minnesota both name Oryctolagus in an invasive or injurious rule with no domestic carve-out, and this map answers them much less comfortably.

NC.quote: Wild Animals. - Game animals; fur-bearing animals; feral swine; and all other wild mammals except marine mammals found in coastal fishing waters. In addition, this definition includes members of the following groups which are on the federal list of endangered or threatened species: wild amphibians, wild reptiles except sea turtles inhabiting and depending upon coastal fishing waters, and wild invertebrates except invertebrates declared to be pests under the Structural Pest Control Act of North Carolina of 1955 or the North Carolina Pesticide Law of 1971.
NC.note: The mammal limb of § 113-129(15) reaches "game animals; fur-bearing animals; feral swine; and all other wild mammals", and a domestic rabbit is none of those. The definition adds that wildlife includes "species normally wild, or indistinguishable from wild species, which are raised or kept in captivity", which is the clause that would catch a captive cottontail, and Oryctolagus cuniculus in its domestic breeds is neither normally wild nor indistinguishable from one. The captivity licence at § 113-272.5 is therefore not engaged, which matters because that section says the Executive Director must find the animal was not acquired "merely as a pet" before issuing one.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: 1. tropical fishes 2. rats and mice 3. rabbits ... 15. reptiles 16. amphibians. The provisions of this section do not privilege the import or possession of a species otherwise protected or regulated by other provisions of this title.
SC.note: Rabbits are the third entry on the pet-trade list at § 50-16-60, which exempts them from the import permit. The section's closing line reserves anything "otherwise protected or regulated by other provisions of this title", and what that reserves for reptiles is the 2021 native rules; for a domestic rabbit there is no corresponding provision, since the native lagomorph South Carolina regulates is the cottontail as a game animal.

OH.quote: "Wild animals" includes mollusks, crustaceans, aquatic insects, fish, reptiles, amphibians, wild birds, wild quadrupeds, and all other wild mammals, but does not include domestic deer.
OH.note: The mammal limb of § 1531.01(X) reaches "wild quadrupeds, and all other wild mammals", and a domestic rabbit is not a wild mammal. Ohio's wild rabbit, the eastern cottontail, is a game animal with a season and is what the chapter is written about. Nothing in the dangerous wild animal list at § 935.01(C) reaches a lagomorph either, and the propagating licence at § 1533.71 covers game birds, game quadrupeds, reptiles, amphibians and fur-bearing animals, all of which are categories a pet rabbit sits outside.

RI.quote: Domestic Rabbit, including breeds, varieties, and strains derived from the European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) but not including the European rabbit (Ferae naturae) and not including the so-called "San Juan" rabbit
RI.note: Rhode Island answers the rabbit the way Connecticut does, by defining domestication rather than by naming the species on an allow-list. A domestic rabbit is a "domestic animal" under § 3.6(A)(5), and § 3.9(C) says an exotic animal possession permit "is not required for importation or possession of domestic animals". The carve-out from the carve-out, wild-type Oryctolagus and the San Juan rabbit, is the same animal Illinois names in 520 ILCS 5/3.23 and Minnesota lists as a prohibited invasive species, and Rhode Island is the state that separates the two cleanly.

AR.cite: Code 01.00 definitions, WILD and WILDLIFE
AR.quote: WILD – To be living in a state of nature and not domesticated.
AR.note: Arkansas defines WILDLIFE as "All wild birds, mammals, fish, reptiles, amphibians, other wild aquatic forms, and all other wild animals", and then defines WILD by domestication, so a domestic rabbit is outside Chapter 09.00 altogether rather than exempted within it. Nothing else in the code contradicts that: Oryctolagus is absent from all three R1 addenda, and the "rabbit" Code 09.14 allows to be hand-captured six per household is the wild cottontail. This is the Connecticut device, one definition doing the work that Illinois and Minnesota cannot do with lists.

ME.note: Named by species, and unconditionally: the "Captive Bred Origin Only" heading that qualifies the reptile, turtle and lungfish sections does not appear over Mammalia, and the entry carries no asterisk. Maine answers by naming the species rather than by defining domestication, which is why it does not have to distinguish wild-type Oryctolagus the way Rhode Island and Connecticut do.

MO.quote: Except for federally-designated endangered species and species listed in 3 CSR 10-4.117 and 3 CSR 10-9.240, the following may be bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit: Asian clams (Corbicula species) taken from impoundments that are not waters of the state; bison; amphibians, reptiles, and mammals not native to Missouri except those mammals located in a licensed big game hunting preserve; and those birds (except ring necked pheasants and gray partridge) not native to the continental United States.
MO.note: A domestic rabbit is a mammal not native to Missouri, so the clearance reaches it on its own terms and Missouri never has to decide what domestication does, which is the question that leaves the same animal unresolved in Minnesota and thin in Illinois. Missouri's own lagomorphs, the cottontail, swamp rabbit and jackrabbit, are game mammals under 3 CSR 10-20.805(33) and a different animal. The one qualifier in the clause, "except those mammals located in a licensed big game hunting preserve", is about where the animal is rather than what it is.

ID.quote: Conventional Pets. Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale that are not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho: dogs, cats ferrets, rabbits, rodents, non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders.
ID.note: Rabbits are named outright in the conventional pets definition, so no Department permit is needed to import, possess, transport or sell one. Idaho does not have to distinguish domestic Oryctolagus from wild-type stock the way Rhode Island and Connecticut do, because the qualifier that runs across the whole definition, "not native wildlife captured from the wild in Idaho", does the same job: Idaho's wild lagomorphs are cottontails, jackrabbits and the pygmy rabbit, and none of them is Oryctolagus. The Department of Agriculture's deleterious exotic animal list at IDAPA 02.04.27 contains no lagomorph.

NH.quote: Rabbits, domesticated
NH.note: Named on both non-controlled lists, so no possession permit and no importation permit. New Hampshire answers by the word "domesticated" attached to the common name rather than by binomial, so a wild-type Oryctolagus is not cleared by it; the same device covers the chinchillas, gerbils, guinea pigs, hamsters, mice, rats, ferrets and pot-bellied pigs on the same list.

WY.quote: domesticated European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
WY.note: Wyoming runs two closed enumerations, Domestic Animals at Ch. 10 § 2(i) and Domesticated Animals at § 2(j), each introduced by "For the purpose of this regulation, only the following animals are considered" its category. The domesticated European rabbit is named in the second, so § 16(a) lets it be imported, possessed or transported with no permit and no certificate of veterinary inspection from the Department. The word "domesticated" is doing the same work it does in New Hampshire: a wild-type Oryctolagus is not what the list names.

KY.quote: Domesticated races of the European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) morphologically distinguishable from wild European rabbits
KY.note: Kentucky splits the species in two and writes both halves. § 4(1)(dd) prohibits importing, transporting or possessing a "European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) that morphologically resembles wild European rabbits", and § 7(9) puts the domesticated races on the permit-exempt list, so a pet rabbit needs no transportation permit either. The test is what the animal looks like rather than where it came from, which is the same device Kentucky uses for mink, turkeys, ducks and geese on the same list.

LA.quote: Game quadrupeds: wild deer, bears, squirrels, and wild rabbits.
LA.note: Louisiana never mentions Oryctolagus. Its game quadrupeds are defined as a closed list ending in "wild rabbits", and the game breeder pen specifications at LAC 76:V.107(B)(7) spell the category out as "Rabbits (cottontail, swamp and wild hares endemic to North America)", which is the state's own Sylvilagus and Lepus rather than a domestic European rabbit. Nothing else reaches it: LAC 76:V.115 is three bears, two wolves, wolf-dog hybrids, all primates and six big cats.

AK.quote: European rabbit   Oryctolagus cuniculus Var.
AK.note: Named on the clean list, and named as "Var.", the abbreviation Alaska uses through the list for a domesticated variety: the white rat, the white mouse, the pigeon, the chicken and the canary all carry it. So the entry is written for domestic stock rather than for wild-type Oryctolagus. Being on the list means the animal may be possessed, imported, exported, bought, sold or traded without a permit, but § 92.029(b) still bars releasing it into the wild.

MT.quote: "Domestic animal" means an animal that, through long association with humans, has been bred to a degree that has resulted in genetic changes affecting color, temperament, conformation, or other attributes of the species to an extent that makes the animal unique and distinguishable from wild individuals of the species and that is readily controllable if accidentally released into the wild.
MT.note: Montana answers by definition rather than by list, and it has to, because the domestic rabbit appears on none of the three species lists and § 87-5-705(1) would otherwise bar an unlisted exotic outright, which is what bans the tarantula and the giant millipede here. § 87-5-702(12)(b) says wildlife "does not include domestic animals", and the general definition at (2) fits a domestic rabbit on its first limb. Its second limb, "readily controllable if accidentally released into the wild", is the soft spot, since the European rabbit is the textbook animal that is not, though the pet breeds are a poor bet in a Montana winter. The enumeration that follows, "livestock, as defined in 81-2-702, dogs, cats, rodents, Eurasian ferrets, and poultry", is inclusive rather than closed and does not name the rabbit, and 81-2-702(5) livestock does not either. What settles it in practice is the other agency: the Department of Livestock lists rabbits with the small rodents on its import requirements, asking for a health certificate and no import permit and no Fish, Wildlife and Parks permit at all.

WA.quote: The term "wildlife" does not include feral domestic mammals, old world rats and mice of the family Muridae of the order Rodentia, or those fish, shellfish, and marine invertebrates classified as food fish or shellfish by the director.
WA.note: Washington is the one state where the geographic test would otherwise catch the rabbit, because feral European rabbits do live wild here, on San Juan Island among other places. The exclusion for feral domestic mammals is what takes the species back out, and it does the same work in the parallel definition of "wild animals" at subsection (72). So a domestic rabbit is neither wildlife nor a wild animal, and nothing in RCW 16.30 or WAC 220-640-200 reaches it either.

VA.quote: Domesticated breeds of European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) recognized by the American Rabbit Breeders Association, Inc. and any lineage resulting from crossbreeding recognized breeds.
VA.note: Virginia is the only jurisdiction on this map to settle the rabbit by naming a breed registry. Oryctolagus cuniculus is on the permit table at 4VAC15-30-40 as a predatory or undesirable nonnative, so a wild European rabbit needs a special permit and, under 4VAC15-20-50(B), any kept without one had to be declared to the department by 1 January 2018 and may not be bred or sold. The domestic animal definition lifts the ARBA-recognised breeds and their crosses out of that, and 4VAC15-30-30 then says the chapter "does not prohibit the possession, importation, and sale of ... those domestic animals as defined in 4VAC15-20-50". The department publishes the recognised breed list on its website, so the line moves when ARBA's does.

HI.quote: The introduction into Hawaii of live animals or live non-domestic animals as defined in this chapter is only allowed: (1) For those animals on the list designated as conditionally approved and dated November 28, 2006, or on the list designated as restricted entry, dated September 25, 2018
HI.note: Hawaii runs an inverted rule, and this is the clause that creates it. Introduction is allowed only for animals on the conditionally approved or restricted lists, so an animal on none of them is barred by default rather than left unregulated. Hawaii's insect entries across all three lists are a short list of named species, the mealworm, the pomace fly, the honey bee, a green bottle blow fly, a parasitic wasp and a few butterflies. The Madagascar hissing cockroach is on none of them, and on an island chain that quarantines insects harder than anywhere else in the country that absence is decisive. Absence from the lists here is a ban, not a gap.

PA.note: Pennsylvania's two animal agencies divide the field and a terrestrial invertebrate falls in the gap. The Game Commission holds wildlife, defined as wild birds and wild mammals, and the Fish and Boat Commission holds reptiles and amphibians. No state possession rule applies.

MI.note: Not a reptile or amphibian, so the herp order does not reach it, and not a cat, a bear or native game, so the Large Carnivore Act and the captive game permit do not either. Michigan handles invertebrates through its invasive species list rather than any pet law.

VT.quote: All species of Invertebrates, except those listed in Appendix that require an importation and possession permit. Note: Importation of any invertebrate species also requires compliance with USDA regulations.
VT.note: The Madagascar hissing cockroach is covered by the blanket invertebrate entry, and the Restricted list claws back no terrestrial invertebrate at all. The USDA condition attaches to importing rather than to keeping.

NM.cite: Director's Species Importation List, 2023, and 19.35.7 NMAC
NM.quote: Any species of live non-domesticated animal not currently on the species importation list will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.
NM.note: The Madagascar hissing cockroach is not on the Director's list, and neither is any other terrestrial invertebrate: the roughly 1,300 rows are mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish. Read literally the default clause would designate it group IV and bar it, since it is a live non-domesticated animal. Read in context that looks wrong, because the rule is titled importation of live non-domesticated animals, birds and fish, its scope speaks of wildlife species, and its machinery is veterinary inspection certificates and disease testing built for vertebrates. The regulation never uses the word invertebrate. Recorded unclear rather than banned, because the definition arguably reaches the animal and plainly was not written with it in mind.

NV.quote: "Wildlife" means any wild mammal, wild bird, fish, reptile, amphibian, mollusk or crustacean found naturally in a wild state
NV.note: The Madagascar hissing cockroach is an arthropod, and Nevada's definition of wildlife lists mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks and crustaceans and stops there. Insects and arachnids are outside the Department of Wildlife's authority altogether, so neither the prohibited list nor the importation rule reaches one. A cleaner answer than New Mexico gives, where the same animals fall into a default clause written for vertebrates. Nevada leaves county and city ordinances untouched, and Clark County, Las Vegas and Henderson are all stricter than the state, so check the municipality before the state.

AZ.quote: "Wildlife" means all wild mammals, wild birds and the nests or eggs thereof, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans and fish, including their eggs or spawn.
AZ.note: The Madagascar hissing cockroach is an arthropod, and Arizona's definition of wildlife runs to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, mollusks, crustaceans and fish. Insects and arachnids are not in it, so Title 17 and the restricted live wildlife rule made under it do not reach one at all. Arizona and Nevada answer this the same clean way; New Mexico does not, which is why the same animals sit unclear there.

DE.quote: No person shall bring into this State, possess, sell or exhibit any live wild mammal or hybrid of a wild mammal or live reptile not native to or generally found in Delaware without first securing a permit under this chapter.
DE.note: The permit requirement reaches live wild mammals, hybrids of wild mammals and non-native reptiles only. The Madagascar hissing cockroach is an arthropod and falls outside the chapter entirely, as it does outside the exotic animal regulations made under it.

CO.quote: "Wildlife" means wild vertebrates, mollusks, and crustaceans, whether alive or dead, including any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof, that exist as a species in a natural wild state in their place of origin, presently or historically
CO.note: The Madagascar hissing cockroach is an insect, and Colorado's statutory definition of wildlife runs to wild vertebrates, mollusks and crustaceans and stops there. Everything CPW does about private possession, the licensing scheme in Chapter W-11, the prohibited list in Chapter W-0 and the new herpetofauna chapter, is built on that definition, so none of it reaches this animal. CPW's own species lists are divided into birds, mammals, herpetofauna and fish and marine animals, with no terrestrial invertebrate category at all, which is the same gap seen from the other side. Arizona and Nevada answer this the same clean way; New Mexico does not, which is why the same animals sit unclear there.

IL.quote: This Act shall apply only to the wild birds and parts of wild birds (including, but not limited to, their nests and eggs), and wild mammals and parts of wild mammals, which shall include their green hides, in the State of Illinois, or which may be brought into the State.
IL.note: The Madagascar hissing cockroach is an insect, and Illinois divides its animal law up in a way that leaves it out of every piece. The Wildlife Code says in its own words that it applies only to wild birds and wild mammals. The Herptiles-Herps Act covers reptiles and amphibians. The Fish and Aquatic Life Code covers aquatic life. The injurious species list at 17 Ill. Adm. Code 805 has a category for invertebrates, and it is headed "Fish, Mollusks and Aquatic Invertebrates". A terrestrial arthropod falls in the gap, the same way it does in Pennsylvania, so no state possession rule applies. Illinois is a home rule state, so a municipal ordinance can be stricter than anything above and is often the rule that actually decides this.

MN.quote: "Wild animals" means all creatures, whether dead or alive, not human, wild by nature, endowed with sensation and power of voluntary motion, and includes mammals, birds, fish, amphibians, reptiles, crustaceans, and mollusks.
MN.note: The Madagascar hissing cockroach is an insect, and Minnesota's definition of wild animals lists seven groups, of which the only invertebrates are crustaceans and mollusks. That places it outside chapter 97A altogether, including the protected wild animal list and the possession bar built on it. The invasive species rules stop in the same place: the invertebrates designated under Minn. R. 6216.0250 are aquatic snails, rusty crayfish and the spiny waterflea. Minnesota is unusual in that its wild animal definition is broad enough to catch a ball python and still narrow enough to miss a tarantula.

OR.quote: Invertebrate species listed as approved may be imported, possessed, sold, purchased, exchanged, transported, or released in Oregon without a permit from the Department. This applies only to stock collected within the continental United States. ... Madagascar hissing cockroach, Gromphadorhina portentosa (education, pet). ... Live invertebrates not on the list of approved invertebrates in any life stage may not be imported, possessed, sold, purchased, exchanged, transported, or released in the state unless a permit is first obtained from the Department.
OR.note: Oregon runs two closed lists, and this animal is on the second one. ORS 496.004(19) defines wildlife as fish, shellfish, amphibians, reptiles, feral swine, wild birds and wild mammals, so a terrestrial arthropod is outside the Fish and Wildlife rules entirely; the Department of Agriculture picks it up instead under its plant pest authority. Named to the species and marked for pet use, in a roach section of nearly twenty entries that separates the hissing cockroaches from the pest species listed for education and research only. The condition is a real one and easy to miss: the clearance applies only to stock collected within the continental United States, so an animal imported from abroad needs a Department permit even though the species is approved. Nothing on this list is unregulated; an invertebrate absent from it may not be possessed at all without a permit. Oregon cities and counties may prohibit exotic animals by ordinance on top of state law, so check the municipality as well.

CT.quote: "Wild animal" means any bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian, or invertebrate that is, or historically has been found, in the wild or in the wild state, and that is not otherwise a domestic animal
CT.note: Connecticut restricts only what its four categories name. Category One is four mammal families, Category Two is a long specific list running from elephants and primates through the whole order Rodentia to five monitors and the venomous snake families, Category Three is Connecticut's own native species and bars import and export rather than possession, and Category Four is the state endangered, threatened and special concern list. The Madagascar hissing cockroach appears in none of them. This one is worth stating carefully, because Connecticut is unusual in that its definition of wild animal does reach invertebrates, and the section is titled importation, possession or liberation of wild birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates. So the answer here is not the jurisdictional gap that clears the same animal in Arizona, Nevada and Pennsylvania; Connecticut has the authority and has simply not used it against any terrestrial arthropod. The only invertebrates that could be caught are ones on the state endangered, threatened and special concern list, which is Connecticut's own beetles, dragonflies and mussels.

MD.quote: "Wildlife" means, except as provided in § 10-2A-01 of this title, every living creature, not human, wild by nature, endowed with sensation and power of voluntary motion. (2) "Wildlife" includes mammals, birds, amphibians, and reptiles which spend a majority of their life cycle on land
MD.note: The Madagascar hissing cockroach is worth reading carefully in Maryland, because the definition is broad rather than narrow. Unlike Arizona, Nevada and Oregon, whose wildlife definitions list vertebrate groups and stop, Maryland's opening words are "every living creature, not human, wild by nature", with the vertebrate list following as an inclusion rather than a limit. What saves the answer is the operative section rather than the definition: § 10-902 attaches its permit only to wildlife native to Maryland, and this species is not. Section 10-903 gives the Secretary a separate power to restrict non-native wildlife by regulation, and Maryland has used it for nonnative aquatic organisms at COMAR 08.02.19, a list of fish, crustaceans, molluscs and two plants, and for nothing terrestrial. Crim. Law § 10-621 reaches no invertebrate either. Subsection (e) of § 10-621 preserves stricter county and municipal rules, and Maryland counties use that power, so the local ordinance is worth checking before the state list.

TN.quote: "Wildlife" means wild vertebrates, mollusks, crustaceans, and fish
TN.note: The Madagascar hissing cockroach is an insect, and Tennessee's definition of wildlife runs to wild vertebrates, mollusks, crustaceans and fish. Section 70-4-403 classifies "live wildlife", so the five classes never reach a terrestrial arthropod at all, and neither does the possession prohibition in § 70-4-401(a), which is written about wildlife. Arizona, Nevada and Colorado draw the line in almost the same words. It matters less here than in a closed-list state, since Tennessee's catch-all would have put the animal in the no-permit class in any event.

TX.quote: In this subchapter, nongame wildlife means those species of vertebrate wildlife, living or dead, that are indigenous to this state and are not classified as game animals, birds, fish, furbearing animals, endangered species, alligators, marine penaeid shrimp, or oysters. Nongame wildlife includes captive-bred nongame wildlife, parts of nongame wildlife, and the eggs of nongame wildlife.
TX.note: Texas regulates nongame wildlife through 31 TAC Chapter 65 Subchapter O, and the rule defines its own subject as "species of vertebrate wildlife". That is narrower than the statute it was written under: Parks & Wild. Code § 67.001 defines nongame as "those species of vertebrate and invertebrate wildlife indigenous to Texas". The department had the power to reach invertebrates and did not use it, so Gromphadorhina portentosa sits outside the scheme entirely. The dangerous wild animal list is mammals only, and 31 TAC Chapter 57 Subchapter A, the harmful exotic species rule, covers fish, shellfish and aquatic plants and no terrestrial arthropod. As with the millipede, the constraint that actually exists is a federal USDA permit for interstate movement, not a Texas one.

MA.quote: Species means an individual or individuals of any distinct non-domestic vertebrate animal population whose members interbreed when mature or are self-perpetuating through the production of viable offspring and can include any subspecies or variety of vertebrate animal.
MA.note: Massachusetts is a closed-list state, so the question worth asking first is whether the list applies at all, and for the Madagascar hissing cockroach it does not. M.G.L. c. 131, § 23 reaches "fish, birds, mammals, reptiles, or amphibians", and 321 CMR 9.01(2) defines the species the exemption list is made of as vertebrate populations. A terrestrial arthropod is outside the licensing scheme entirely rather than unlisted within it, which is a different answer from the one the closed list gives a mammal nobody put on it.

NE.quote: Wildlife means any member of any nondomesticated species of the animal kingdom, whether reared in captivity or not, including any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate and includes any part, product, egg, or offspring thereof or the dead body or parts thereof.
NE.note: Nebraska defines wildlife broadly enough to include the Madagascar hissing cockroach, since § 37-247 reaches "any mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate". What it does not do is regulate one. The captivity prohibition at § 37-477(1) and at 166 NAC 8 § 001.01B is written about wild birds, wild mammals, nongame species in need of conservation and listed species, none of which is an arthropod; 166 NAC 10 covers only reptiles and amphibians; and the importation list at § 001.08A contains nothing but mammals and birds.
