The one loose end is that the list is headed "the following wildlife may be imported" and wildlife on the statutory definition includes arthropods, so a very literal reading of that heading would bar importing a tarantula. Nothing in the chapter turns that heading into a prohibition, and every operative sentence in it is about birds and mammals. As with the millipede, the real constraint is the USDA permit for interstate movement rather than anything in Nebraska law.

FL.quote: It is unlawful to introduce, multiply, possess, move, or release any arthropod, plant pest, biological control agent, noxious weed, or invasive plant regulated by the Department or the USDA except under permit issued by the Department unless a federal permit, PPQ 526, has been issued by the USDA with concurrence by the Department. No permit shall be issued nor concurrence with a federal permit, PPQ 526 made unless the Department has determined that the arthropod, plant pest, biological control agent, noxious weed, or invasive plant can be contained to prevent escape into the environment or that it will not pose a threat to agriculture, beneficial organisms, or the environment or become a public nuisance.
FL.note: Florida answers this animal through its agriculture department, not FWC, and the wildlife chapters give no hint of it. 5B-57.004(1) makes it unlawful to possess any arthropod "regulated by the Department or the USDA" without a permit from the Division of Plant Industry, unless a federal PPQ 526 has already issued with the Department's concurrence. Gromphadorhina portentosa moves interstate under exactly that federal permit, which is what brings it inside the sentence. The permit standard is containment: the Department must find the animal can be contained to prevent escape into the environment, which in practice means secure enclosure rather than a fee. Nothing in Chapter 68-5 or Chapter 68A-6 names it, so an entry resting on those chapters alone would read this as unrestricted. The same reasoning reaches it as reaches the millipede, and for the same reason: it is the federal plant-pest status that does the work, not anything Florida wrote about the species.

NY.quote: Prohibited invasive species cannot be knowingly possessed with the intent to sell, import, purchase, transport or introduce. In addition, no person shall sell, import, purchase, transport, introduce or propagate prohibited invasive species. Regulated invasive species, on the other hand, are species which cannot be knowingly introduced into a free-living state, or introduced by a means that one should have known would lead to such an introduction, although such species shall be legal to possess, sell, buy, propagate and transport.
NY.note: New York has two ways to reach an invertebrate and neither takes in the Madagascar hissing cockroach. ECL § 11-0103(6)(a) defines wildlife as "wild game and all other animal life existing in a wild state, except fish, shellfish and crustacea", which is wide enough to include arthropods, but the closed wild animal list at § 11-0103(6)(e) is six clauses of vertebrates and Crocodylia and the dangerous animals regulation at 6 NYCRR § 180.1 names none. The other route is Part 575, whose own definition of animal expressly includes "arthropods, insects, and their eggs, larvae or young", and whose invertebrate entries are the zebra mussel, the Asian longhorned beetle and their kind. Nothing on either list is a pet arthropod. As with the millipede, the USDA permit for interstate movement is the rule that actually applies.

GA.quote: The following wild animals are considered inherently dangerous to human beings and pursuant to O.C.G.A. Sec. 27-5-4 are subject to licensing and liability insurance requirements. (a) Mammals: ... 2. Order Carnivora: (i) Family Canidae: Genera Canis, Chrysocyon, Cuon, and Lycaon (wolves, jackals, dingos, etc.) - All species ...; (ii) Family Felidae (cats) - All species; (iii) Family Hyaenidae (hyenas) - All species; ...
GA.note: Georgia regulates invertebrates in three places and none of them reaches the Madagascar hissing cockroach. The prohibited list at .03(1)(d) covers dreissenid mussels, giant African land snails and the marbled crayfish. The inherently dangerous list at .04(1)(d) is scorpions only, and it is species-specific: the fattail, bark and burrowing thicktail genera, the deathstalker, and one Scorpionidae species, Opistophthalmus glabrifons. The licence list at .05(1)(f) is molluscs, crayfishes and shrimps. Every entry across all three is either aquatic or venomous. As with the millipede, the USDA permit for interstate movement is the operative rule.

NYC.quote: No person shall sell or give to another person, possess, harbor, keep, or yard wild or other animals identified in this section ... other than in: (i) a zoological park or aquarium ...; or (ii) a laboratory ...; or (iii) a veterinary hospital ...; or (iv) a temporary exhibit, performance or display that has been issued a permit by the Commissioner. ... For the purposes of this Code, a wild animal is deemed to be any animal which is naturally inclined to do harm and capable of inflicting harm upon human beings and all such animals are hereby prohibited ... Such animals shall also include: (i) any animals specified by the Commissioner in regulations ...; (ii) any native or exotic wildlife whose possession or sale is prohibited because they are designated as protected or endangered pursuant to any federal, state or local law, regulation, or rule; and (iii) any of the following animals:
NYC.note: The article reaches invertebrates in two clauses and both turn on venom. Clause (12) is "All venomous insects", with bees other than non-aggressive honey bees, hornets and wasps as its examples. Clause (13) is "Arachnida and Chilopoda: All venomous spiders ...; scorpion; all venomous arthropods including, but not limited to, centipede". The Madagascar hissing cockroach is neither venomous nor a chilopod, so neither clause applies. It is an insect and not a venomous one, so clause (12) does not reach it. As with the millipede, the operative rule is the federal USDA permit for interstate movement. § 161.01(d) is worth knowing alongside the prohibition: a prohibited animal may be seized by any authorized city employee, the owner has three business days to request a hearing, and with the Department's written consent the animal may be removed to a jurisdiction where it is not prohibited. That last provision is the closest thing to relief in the article.

NJ.quote: "Nongame species" means any wildlife for which a legal hunting or trapping season has not been established in New Jersey or which has not been classified as an endangered species by statute or regulation of this State.
NJ.note: The same invertebrate gap as the tarantula and the millipede, with the same two readings and no Division list naming an insect. Gromphadorhina portentosa has an extra layer that New Jersey's wildlife rules do not speak to at all: it is a USDA-regulated organism, so moving one interstate needs a PPQ 526 permit, and several states reach it through their agriculture department rather than their wildlife agency. New Jersey's plant pest rules sit at N.J.A.C. 2:20 under the Department of Agriculture, a separate agency from the one that writes subchapter 4, which is where the answer would be if there is one.

UT.quote: "Wildlife" means: (a) crustaceans, including brine shrimp and crayfish; (b) mollusks; and (c) vertebrate animals living in nature, except feral animals.
UT.note: Utah answers the invertebrates at the level of the statute rather than the rule, and it answers them cleanly. Utah Code 23A-1-101(65) defines wildlife as crustaceans, molluscs, and "vertebrate animals living in nature, except feral animals". A cockroach is an insect, and a terrestrial insect is none of the three, so the Division of Wildlife Resources has no authority over it, and its rules divide the same way: R657-53 reaches Amphibia and Reptilia, R657-3b birds and mammals, R657-3c aquatic animals. There is a trap in R657-3a worth naming, because reading it alone gives the wrong answer. Its own definition of "Animal" carries no class limit, and 3a-2(20)(b) says a prohibited species "also means a species or subspecies that has not gone through the division's species classification process", which on its face would make every unclassified arthropod prohibited. It does not, because 3a-1(1) makes the rule under Title 23A and the rule cannot reach further than the code's definition of wildlife does. Utah does mention insects once, at 23A-1-101(4), where aquatic insects are aquatic wildlife, and then removes them again at (45)(b), which says protected aquatic wildlife does not include aquatic insects. A Madagascar hissing cockroach is not aquatic and never reaches even that. The federal PPQ 526 permit for interstate movement applies to this species regardless.

AL.quote: It shall be unlawful to take, capture, kill, or attempt to take, capture or kill; possess, sell, trade for anything of monetary value, or offer to sell or trade for anything of monetary value the following invertebrate species (or any parts or reproductive products of such species) without a scientific collection permit or written permit from the Commissioner, Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, which shall specifically state what the permittee may do with regard to said species:
AL.note: On neither list, so unrestricted under Alabama's wildlife rules. As with the millipede the live question is federal rather than state, since Gromphadorhina portentosa is a USDA-regulated organism and interstate movement needs a PPQ 526 permit. Note that 220-2-.26 shows Alabama will name an invertebrate when it wants to, since it bans the giant African land snail by both of its binomials, so the absence of arthropods from these rules reads as a choice rather than an oversight.

IN.quote: Any invertebrate not identified in this rule is an exempted wild animal.
IN.note: Indiana answers this in one sentence, which no other state on this map does. 312 IAC 9-9 governs invertebrates in five short sections, covering crayfish, mussels and a list of endangered mussels and beetles, and 9-9-5 then says "any invertebrate not identified in this rule is an exempted wild animal". 312 IAC 9-1-6 defines an exempted wild animal as one "which is unprotected and may be taken or possessed at any time". A cockroach is not identified in the rule, so it is expressly unprotected rather than merely unmentioned. As with the millipede, Gromphadorhina portentosa is a USDA-regulated organism and interstate movement needs a PPQ 526 permit, which is a separate question from what Indiana asks.

OK.quote: Except as otherwise provided by law, no person may possess: 1. Any wildlife or parts thereof during the closed season for that particular wildlife species; 2. Any endangered or threatened species or parts thereof at any time; or 3. Any native bear or native cat that will grow to reach the weight of fifty (50) pounds or more. B. Persons exempt from provisions of paragraphs 1 and 2 of subsection A of this section are: ... 4. Persons possessing legally obtained wildlife, from a source other than the wild, as pets or for the purpose of training hunting dogs, except as provided for by law or under rules promulgated by the Wildlife Conservation Commission;
OK.note: Oklahoma reaches invertebrates and then lets the Madagascar hissing cockroach through. 800:25-25-3(a)(19) exempts "native invertebrates" from the licence requirements, carving out only crayfish and freshwater mussels, which shows the Department treats invertebrates as wildlife it could regulate. the Madagascar hissing cockroach is not native, so that clause is not the answer; the answer is that nothing else applies. The statutory possession bar at 29 O.S. § 7-502(A) reaches wildlife in a closed season, endangered and threatened species, and native bears and big cats, and a captive-bred pet is separately exempted by § 7-502(B)(4). The reptile and amphibian licence at 800:25-7-7(2) is written about reptiles and amphibians. As with the millipede the live question is federal, since Gromphadorhina portentosa is a USDA-regulated organism and interstate movement needs a PPQ 526 permit.

CA.cite: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 14, § 671(a), (c); Fish & Game Code § 2116
CA.quote: It shall be unlawful to import, transport, or possess live animals restricted in subsection (c) below except under permit issued by the department.
CA.note: California has the longest restricted species list of any state on this map and it never reaches an insect. Both the statute and the rule are built on a closed set of taxonomic classes: Fish and Game Code § 2116 defines a wild animal by class, running through Aves, Mammalia, Amphibia, Osteichthyes, Monorhina, Reptilia, Crustacea and Gastropoda, and § 671(c)'s restricted list is organised the same way, in eleven groups from Class Aves through Class Bivalvia and transgenic aquatic animals. Insects and arachnids appear in neither. So the answer here has the same shape as Utah's: the regulated group is defined by a list of classes that leaves the animal out, rather than by an omission from a species list. One route is named but unused. Fish and Game Code § 2118(k) says classes, families, genera and species may be added to the restricted lists by commission regulation "in cooperation with the Department of Food and Agriculture", which is where a California restriction on a pet arthropod would have to come from, and no such addition has been made for this species.

WI.quote: A person is exempt from holding a license or other approval as required under this chapter to possess live native wild animals if the wild animals are not endangered or threatened species and are any of the following: 1. Arthropods.
WI.note: Wisconsin answers the invertebrates from both directions and gets to the same place. Native arthropods are the first entry on the 169.04(4)(a) exemption list, ahead of chipmunks and pocket gophers, and nonnative wild animals are exempt as a class under 169.04(4)(b) unless endangered or designated harmful. A Madagascar hissing cockroach is nonnative and is neither. The rule that could reach it is NR 40, the invasive species chapter, which is a separate authority from the captive wildlife chapter and lists no pet arthropod.

NC.quote: Wild Animals. - Game animals; fur-bearing animals; feral swine; and all other wild mammals except marine mammals found in coastal fishing waters. In addition, this definition includes members of the following groups which are on the federal list of endangered or threatened species: wild amphibians, wild reptiles except sea turtles inhabiting and depending upon coastal fishing waters, and wild invertebrates except invertebrates declared to be pests under the Structural Pest Control Act of North Carolina of 1955 or the North Carolina Pesticide Law of 1971.
NC.note: North Carolina answers this in its definitions rather than its permit sections, and the answer is that the Wildlife Resources Commission has no jurisdiction. § 113-129(15) defines wild animals as game animals, fur-bearing animals, feral swine and other wild mammals, and then extends only to "wild amphibians, wild reptiles ... and wild invertebrates" that are "on the federal list of endangered or threatened species". The Madagascar hissing cockroach is not federally listed, so it is not a wild animal in North Carolina at all and the captivity licence at § 113-272.5 has nothing to attach to. § 14-417 reaches venomous reptiles and large constrictors, and § 153A-131 lets counties regulate dangerous animals, which is where any local restriction would come from. The invertebrate limb of the definition carries its own exception, for "invertebrates declared to be pests under the Structural Pest Control Act of North Carolina of 1955 or the North Carolina Pesticide Law of 1971", which is a reminder that the pest agencies are the ones with authority over arthropods here. The federal PPQ 526 permit still governs moving this species across a state line.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: 1. tropical fishes 2. rats and mice 3. rabbits ... 15. reptiles 16. amphibians. The provisions of this section do not privilege the import or possession of a species otherwise protected or regulated by other provisions of this title.
SC.note: South Carolina's definition of wildlife at § 50-16-10 is one of the broadest on this map, reaching "a mammal, fish, bird, amphibian, reptile, mollusk, crustacean, arthropod, or other invertebrate", so an arthropod is unambiguously wildlife here. It does not follow that it is restricted. The only permit requirement, at § 50-16-20(A), lists furbearers and other mammals in its first paragraph and then marine and freshwater invertebrates in its second and third, and a terrestrial arthropod is in none of them. The 2021 native reptile rules reach reptiles and amphibians only. The federal PPQ 526 permit governs moving this species across a state line.

OH.quote: "Wild animals" includes mollusks, crustaceans, aquatic insects, fish, reptiles, amphibians, wild birds, wild quadrupeds, and all other wild mammals, but does not include domestic deer.
OH.note: Ohio settles the invertebrates with one adjective. § 1531.01(X) defines wild animals as "mollusks, crustaceans, aquatic insects, fish, reptiles, amphibians, wild birds, wild quadrupeds, and all other wild mammals", and the word aquatic in front of insects does the work: a terrestrial insect is not a wild animal, so the Division of Wildlife has no authority over one. An arachnid or a myriapod is not in the list at all. That is the same shape as Utah, which limits wildlife to crustaceans, molluscs and vertebrates, and California, whose restricted list is organised by a closed set of classes with no insect among them. The federal PPQ 526 permit still governs interstate movement of this species.

RI.quote: Nothing in this Part shall prohibit any person from possession of exotic animals or native animals of the class Insecta unless the animals of that class appear on the list of prohibited insects as is published by the USDA at the following URL: https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/terrestrial/invertebrates under the heading of "Invasive Species."
RI.note: The exemption is doing real work rather than papering over a gap. § 3.6(A)(1) defines "animal" to include insects and § 3.6(A)(9) defines an exotic animal as "any vertebrate or invertebrate", so invertebrates are inside the scheme and had to be exempted out of it. The cross-referenced USDA page is a list of forest, crop and stored-product pests and names no cockroach, and § 3.17(A)(1)(c), which is where Rhode Island writes its own invertebrate prohibitions, reaches only zebra and quagga mussels, two waterfleas, non-indigenous crayfish, the Asiatic clam and the giant African land snail. A federal listing would flip this cell without Rhode Island changing anything.

AR.cite: Code 09.01, Exceptions (E)
AR.quote: Persons possessing terrestrial invertebrate species not otherwise prohibited by this Code or by federal or state regulations.
AR.note: Arkansas is one of the states whose wildlife definition reaches an arthropod, "all other wild animals, regardless of classification", and whose captive wildlife chapter then bars holding any live wildlife unless otherwise specified. The express terrestrial-invertebrate exception is what settles it, and the identical exception is repeated in Code 09.07 and Code 09.10, so breeding one and bringing one into the state are free as well. Without it the Madagascar hissing cockroach would be caught by the closing clause of the species addenda, "Species not listed in Addenda R1.01, R1.02, or R1.03 are prohibited until evaluated", because those three lists between them contain amphibians, birds, mammals and reptiles and not one invertebrate.

ME.note: Maine settles the invertebrate question by naming the animal. Invertebrates are inside the scheme rather than outside it: 09-137 CMR ch. 7 § 7.06(1) says the Unrestricted List covers "species of fish and wildlife, including tropical fish and invertebrates", and the list has sections for insects, worms and millipedes. Only one cockroach shares the entry, the dubia roach, so this is a considered listing. No asterisk, so no conservation-status filter, and no captive-bred condition, which the list applies only to reptiles, turtles and lungfishes.

MO.quote: No bird, fish, crayfish, mussel, amphibian, reptile, mammal, or other form of wildlife, including wildlife raised or held in captivity, or their homes, dens, nests, eggs, and larvae in Missouri shall be molested, pursued, taken, hunted, trapped, tagged, marked, enticed, poisoned, killed, transported, stored, served, bought, sold, given away, accepted, possessed, propagated, imported, exported, or liberated to the wild in any manner ... except as specifically permitted by these rules ...; however, this Code shall not apply to other invertebrates except as specifically provided.
MO.note: Missouri answers the invertebrate question inside its own general prohibition, which is the cleanest version of it on this map. The statute is broad enough to catch an insect: RSMo § 252.020(3) defines wildlife as "all wild birds, mammals, fish and other aquatic and amphibious forms, and all other wild animals, regardless of classification". The Code then disclaims it, applying to invertebrates other than crayfish and mussels only where it says so. The one place it says so is 3 CSR 10-9.110(1)(B), which reaches native invertebrates on the Missouri Species and Communities of Conservation Concern Checklist. A Madagascar hissing cockroach is neither native nor on that checklist, so no rule touches it and the non-native clearance at 10-9.110(2), which lists only amphibians, reptiles, mammals and birds, is not needed.

ID.quote: "Wildlife" means any form of animal life, native or exotic, generally living in a state of nature provided that domestic cervidae as defined in section 25-3701, Idaho Code, shall not be classified as wildlife.
ID.note: Two readings, both textual, and Idaho has published nothing that chooses between them. Read one way an insect is a form of animal life and therefore wildlife, IDAPA 13.01.10.200.01 bars possessing live wildlife without a Department licence, and the conventional pets definition at 010.06 is a closed enumeration naming mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians and no invertebrate, so an imported cockroach would need a captive possession licence. Read the other way the commission's scheme never reaches a terrestrial invertebrate at all: the eight classes at Idaho Code § 36-201 are vertebrate groups, IDAPA 13.01.06 classifies no invertebrate anywhere, and chapter 13.01.10 opens by excluding crustaceans from its own use of the word. The agriculture side is clean either way, because the invasive insect list at IDAPA 02.06.09.146 is a closed list of three forest pests and names no cockroach. Recorded unclear rather than guessed, on the same footing as New Jersey and New Mexico.

NH.quote: All species not specifically listed under the categories of non-controlled, prohibited, or controlled shall be designated as prohibited.
NH.note: This is the strictest invertebrate answer on the map and it comes out of four provisions rather than one. RSA 207:1, XXXV defines wildlife to include invertebrates by name, so an insect is inside Fis 800. Fis 804.02, the non-controlled possession list, contains no invertebrate. Table 800.2, the controlled table, runs amphibians, reptiles, fish, birds and mammals and stops. Fis 804.03(b)(1) does have an invertebrates heading, and it names five aquatic nuisance species, which shows the Department writes invertebrate entries when it means to. Fis 804.04(b) then makes everything unlisted prohibited, and Fis 804.03(a) says no permit shall be issued for anything prohibited under it. The waiver at Fis 802.05 that would otherwise cover an unlisted species is closed to private keepers by subsection (c), which withholds it from permittee categories 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 and leaves only exhibitors. So a Madagascar hissing cockroach, a tarantula and a pet millipede are all barred in New Hampshire with no route for an individual. Recorded banned rather than unclear because the closing clause is express and the waiver exclusion is express.

WY.quote: "Wildlife" means all wild mammals, birds, fish, amphibians, reptiles, crustaceans and mollusks, and wild bison designated by the Wyoming game and fish commission and the Wyoming livestock board within Wyoming.
WY.note: Wyoming answers the invertebrate question at the level of the statute, the way Utah and Alaska do, and it answers it twice. The statutory definition is a closed list of taxa with no insect or arachnid in it, and Commission Regulation Chapter 69 then repeats the closure in its own words at § 2(c): "Cold-Blooded Wildlife means all fish, amphibians, reptiles, mollusks, crustaceans, their viable gametes ... and any transgenic product or hybrid thereof". Chapter 10 covers only warm-blooded wildlife. A Madagascar hissing cockroach is therefore outside the Game and Fish Department entirely rather than unlisted within it, which is the distinction that decides this cell in the opposite direction from New Hampshire, where the statute names invertebrates and the closed list then swallows them.

KY.quote: Except as established in Section 5 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport into Kentucky, or possess the following exotic wildlife that are considered potentially injurious to native ecosystems
KY.note: KRS 150.010 defines wildlife as "any normally undomesticated animal ... or other terrestrial or aquatic life", which reaches an insect, so a Madagascar hissing cockroach is exotic wildlife rather than outside the scheme. It is then answered by absence: § 4(1) is birds, rodents, foxes, a toad, a frog and three families, and § 4(2) is drawn entirely around vertebrates. Kentucky's only possession bars for an exotic are the two lists in § 4, the potentially injurious species at (1) and the inherently dangerous species at (2), and this animal is on neither. It is also not on the § 7 permit-exempt list, so a transportation permit under § 2(1) is needed to bring one into the state; possession itself is unrestricted once it is here.

LA.quote: "Wildlife" means all species of wild vertebrates.
LA.note: Six words settle it. Louisiana defines wildlife as vertebrates only, so a terrestrial arthropod is outside the Department of Wildlife and Fisheries entirely rather than unlisted within it, which is the Utah and Wyoming shape. The rest of Title 76 confirms it by structure: Part V is wild quadrupeds and wild birds, Part VII is fish and other aquatic life, and Part XV is reptiles and amphibians. Nothing in the code covers a terrestrial invertebrate.

AK.quote: "game" means any species of bird, reptile, and mammal, including a feral domestic animal, found or introduced in the state, except domestic birds and mammals
AK.note: The strictest live-animal rule in the country reaches three classes and stops. An insect is not a bird, a reptile or a mammal, so it is not game, and 5 AAC 92.029 is a permit rule for live game, which means it never engages. Alaska is the state where the definition rather than the list does the work, and it works in the keeper's favour here in the same way it does for the axolotl and the tarantula.

MT.quote: A person may not import into the state, possess, or sell any exotic wildlife unless: (a) the importation, possession, or sale of the exotic wildlife is allowed by law or commission rule
MT.note: Montana is a white list and an insect is inside it. § 87-5-702(12)(a) defines wildlife as "any wild mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian, fish, mollusk, crustacean, or other wild animal", and the catch-all reaches an arthropod; § 87-5-702(3) makes anything not native to Montana exotic wildlife; and § 87-5-705(1) then bars possessing it unless a law or commission rule allows it. Nothing does. The statutory noncontrolled list at § 87-5-706 runs birds, gallinaceous birds, fish, snakes, lizards, turtles, frogs, caecilians and salamanders and contains no invertebrate. ARM 12.6.2205 clears two scorpions and a hermit crab and no insect, ARM 12.6.2208 classifies one shrimp as controlled, and ARM 12.6.2215 prohibits a crayfish and three molluscs. So the cockroach falls where the tarantula and the giant millipede already sit on this map, banned by absence. Montana is the state where clearing the emperor scorpion by name and stopping there decides every other arthropod.

WA.quote: "Wildlife" means all species of the animal kingdom whose members exist in Washington in a wild state. This includes but is not limited to mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, and invertebrates.
WA.note: Invertebrates are inside the taxonomic reach of the definition, which names them, and outside its geographic reach, because Gromphadorhina portentosa does not live wild in Washington. That is the reverse of New Hampshire, where naming invertebrates in the statute is what pulls them into a closed list and bans them. Washington answers by a geographic qualifier rather than by a species list, which is why it is one of the shortest states to read. Three things then have to be checked and all three come back empty: the animal is not designated deleterious exotic wildlife at WAC 220-640-200(1), which is a mute swan, mongooses, wild boar, javelina, six bovid genera and a run of cervids; it is not a potentially dangerous wild animal under RCW 16.30.010(2), whose enumerated definition reaches only mammals and reptiles named in it; and WAC 220-450-030's importation and possession rules are written for "live wild animals, wild birds, or game fish", which are the same geographically limited terms.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department, if consistent with the department's fish and wildlife management program, to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table and in 4VAC15-20-210 that the board finds and declares to be predatory or undesirable
VA.note: Virginia is one of the few states whose definition of a wild animal names arthropods outright, so the cockroach is inside the scheme rather than outside it, and then it is answered by absence: the only invertebrates on the permit table are eight crayfish and a mitten crab under CRUSTACEANS and a run of freshwater molluscs. No insect appears anywhere in it. Virginia permits by table and the reptile block of that table is four entries: all alligators and caimans, all crocodiles, all gavials, and the brown tree snake. Nothing here is on it, and 4VAC15-30-20 attaches the special permit only to animals the board has classed as predatory or undesirable, which is what the table is.
